chapters.title: Chapter 501
paragraphs: “When is it?”
On the way back after parting with Zhuge Feng, I asked the question out of the blue. Jin Wikyung answered quietly.
“In a month. Mount Song, Henan Province.”
“Mount Song...”
The very place where Shaolin Temple—the Mount Tai and Northern Dipper of the Murim—stood.

Only three months ago, the Star-Array Grand Banquet, a grand gathering of the Murim under Heaven, had begun there. Dark Heaven had unleashed a storm of blood on that same ground. Now the New Murim Alliance would be born there.
Given the symbolism of Mount Song and Shaolin Temple, it was a fitting place for the Murim Alliance to begin again after more than fifty years.
But if there was only a month left...
“It had already been decided when you came to Sichuan, hadn’t it?”
Contrary to my expectations, Jin Wikyung gave a small shake of his head.
“It hadn’t?”
“Why do you think Wipeng happened to be in Henan at just the right time?”
“Then Great Hero Wipeng came because...”

“The Jin Dragon Squad is our family’s finest fighting force. As the Lesser Family Head, I would never summon half its members merely to serve as porters, even if they were carrying the Son of Heaven’s jade seal.”
“So the date was moved up.”
“Dark Heaven moved more aggressively, and faster, than we expected. The Sichuan Blood Tragedy was decisive.”
To catch an enemy who was ahead of you, you had to run.
The storm of blood that had swept through Shaolin Temple had spread to Sichuan and now reached Hubei. The leaders in Henan had to make a choice.
“Bringing the Murim under Heaven together is no easy task. But it seems they have finally made up their minds.”
Muttering quietly, Jin Wikyung pulled a sealed dispatch from inside his robes and held it out to me.
“What’s this?”
“A letter Wipeng brought from Henan.”
“From Henan? Did the Murim Alliance send it?”
“You guessed.”
“I thought so. I saw you give one to Sir Zhuge earlier.”
Even at a glance, it looked nothing like an ordinary letter.
But what made it special were the three characters written across its face in a bold, soaring hand:
Murim Alliance.
“Read it yourself, youngest.”
“I’m already reading it, so stop talking. I can’t concentrate.”
“...Oh. Right.”
Leaving Jin Wikyung looking dejected, I unfolded the letter and skimmed it.
It began, To the Murim under Heaven, and was short and forceful. That made it easy to sum up in three lines.
1. Hey, let me tell you about Dark Heaven. These guys are seriously fucking crazy, so listen up.
2. You remember the Great Faction War PTSD? Let’s stop this by any means necessary.
3. Any dumbasses who don’t know where Mount Song is? Be there by the stated date. Anyone who doesn’t show up is Dark Heaven.
Put that way, it sounded pretty pathetic.
Of course, that was not what the letter actually said.
Some unknown calligrapher’s bold strokes flowed like clouds. Every sentence was solemn, charged with feeling, and deeply moving.
Personally, I almost wanted to show it to that bastard, the Lord of Heaven.
If he saw this, even the Lord of Heaven might join the Murim Alliance.

Everyone could have enjoyed a happy ending if the Lord of Heaven joined the Murim Alliance. It was simply unfortunate that the possibility of that happening was less than the amount of earwax in Hyuk Mujin’s ear.
“In any case, the Murim Alliance will be born soon.”
“In a month, the Murim under Heaven will gather beneath the Murim Alliance’s banner.”
After a moment’s thought, Jin Wikyung added, “Not the Murim under Heaven. I should say the orthodox Murim of the Central Plains.”
I knew what he meant.
Right... It’s a stretch to call the orthodox faction the whole Murim under Heaven.
The orthodox faction, led by the Nine Sects and One Gang and the Five Great Families, was unquestionably the dominant force in the Murim today.
But it had not been the only side to survive the Great Faction War and emerge victorious.
“The unorthodox faction.”
Jin Wikyung nodded at my mutter.
“Yes. We cannot leave them out.”
The fishbowl called the world held more than one color of fish.
The unorthodox faction was weak compared to the orthodox faction, but it had carved out territories of its own. It also included the dark-path figures who ruled the streets at night.
At first, I wondered why they had left those people alive while shouting about eliminating every demonic and heterodox element.
There was a reason for everything.
The unorthodox forces still around today had survived because they sided with the orthodox faction during the Great Faction War.
The trouble was, they had not done it out of goodwill.
“Do you know why the unorthodox forces now active in the Central Plains sided with the orthodox Murim?”
“You haven’t forgotten who I’ve spent the past year with, have you?”
“Great Hero Jeok told you.”
“I picked up quite a bit.”
As the old saying went, green went with green, and crayfish took the crab’s side.
When the Demonic Cult crossed Qinghai and surged toward the Central Plains during the Great Faction War, the unorthodox faction quickly joined them while shouting, “Long live the Cult Leader!”
The Demonic Cult’s momentum was overwhelming, but the unorthodox faction also wanted people they saw as their own kind to rule the Murim under Heaven.
For unorthodox martial artists already living in the Central Plains, though, things were different.
If they don’t side with the orthodox faction, they’ll be hunted down before they can even leave the Central Plains. Those bastards wouldn’t dare refuse to join this side.
Jeok Cheongang had once said that with a snort. For the unorthodox martial artists of the Central Plains, it had been the plain truth.
“I heard they were practically eating dumplings through their tears.”
“I did not live through that era either, but what I found confirms it.”
“What you found?”
“After you left for Sichuan, I stayed in Henan and searched the old archives. There were countless records, including ones about the unorthodox faction.”
The Murim Alliance had disbanded when peace returned, but the memories of those who had lived through the Great Faction War—and records of what had happened—remained.
That made sense. In the long history of the Murim, fifty years was only half a century.
“What did the records say?”
“What do you think?”
“I can guess. I’ve heard a few stories.”
“I do not know exactly what Great Hero Jeok told you, but most of it was probably true.”
“...If that’s true, it’s pretty damn ridiculous.”
From the start of the Great Faction War well into its middle and later stages, the unorthodox martial artists who joined the orthodox faction betrayed them again and again.

Considering what Jeok Cheongang had said about the Murim Alliance’s leadership even discussing root-and-branch eradication to remove every unorthodox member from within the orthodox faction, the situation must have been serious.
“But I heard they fought hard later on.”

“Unlike at the beginning, neither side’s victory was certain. The Hidden Shadow Pavilion, led by Sir Song, the Thousand-Faced Fox, also kept them under close watch. And according to the records, the unorthodox martial artists sensed the leadership’s mood changing and began cutting off their own tails.”
Not everyone in the orthodox faction was righteous, and not everyone in the unorthodox faction was a monster.
But unlike the orthodox faction, the unorthodox faction possessed the decisiveness and cruelty to cut off its own tail without hesitation.
The instant someone was suspected of being a spy for the Demonic Cult, they slit his throat first and asked questions later.
“In the end, the body survived without its tail. By cooperating with the orthodox faction, it shared in the victory.”
The surviving unorthodox forces carried on in the shade of the great tree that was the orthodox faction. Naturally, they could no longer wield the influence they once had.
Their reputation had been bad enough to begin with, and there had been countless instances of them siding with the Demonic Cult.

Most people agreed that if the Murim Alliance’s leaders had not acknowledged at least some of their contributions and rights, hardline heroes calling for the extermination of demonic and heterodox elements would have dragged them out and torn them limb from limb.
The contempt directed at the unorthodox faction after the war had endured like an ancient tradition.
That alone was not a serious problem. What came next was.
“We need them to fight alongside us.”
“Yes. If they do not join the Murim Alliance, they will side with Dark Heaven.”
“I don’t like the thought of bringing them into the fold.”
“They are not people I would want to trust with my back on a battlefield. There is the precedent, and they must have spent decades resenting how honors and rewards were divided after the war.”
“What if we tell them to stay neutral?”
“Suppose the Murim Alliance looks certain to lose. What would you do if you were an unorthodox martial artist, youngest?”
Put that bluntly, I had no answer. I smacked my lips before speaking.
“I hate to say it, but I’d side with Dark Heaven.”
“Why?”
“If the Murim Alliance wins, they break even. But as you said, the scales are already tilted, and Dark Heaven is on the verge of becoming the master of the Central Plains Murim.”
“Exactly.”

“And what kind of people are Dark Heaven? They wouldn’t leave the unorthodox faction alone. They wouldn’t praise them for staying neutral—they’d be furious they hadn’t helped when it mattered and kill every last one of them.”
“Precisely. That is why the unorthodox faction is a chicken rib.”
A chicken rib. That was a good way to put it.
It offered little benefit, but it was too wasteful to throw away. Fighting alongside them felt unpleasant, but if we discarded them, Dark Heaven would pick them up and throw them back at us.
No matter how soft a chicken bone was, it was still a bone. Getting hit by one would hurt quite a bit.
Which meant...
“Henan has already sent them a letter too, hasn’t it?”
Jin Wikyung gave a small nod.
“Without a doubt. If we must choose between the two, we need to draw the unorthodox Murim to our side.”
For a chicken rib, the unorthodox faction had plenty of meat on it.
Even the dark-path knife-men who wandered the back alleys after sunset belonged to the unorthodox faction. Weren’t we at a point where we would be grateful for a single Third Rate knife-man?
More importantly, it was better to keep them close and hold their leash than let them side with Dark Heaven. That would be far too great a loss...
Wait. Dark-path figures?
Something came back to me, and I frowned.
“What is it?”
“No, I just remembered something I heard recently. Regarding the Water God Dragon incident, didn’t we accuse the dark-path figures of Hubei Province of being the culprits and wipe them all out?”
“We did.”
“...Then the unorthodox faction might be upset. In the end, we accepted the government’s proposal and wiped out their own people.”
It was a bad look. They might even reject the Murim Alliance’s offer of membership over it.
Jin Wikyung, however, looked perfectly calm.
“Two things are wrong with that.”
“What?”

“First, the unorthodox Murim has been fractured since the war ended. Those people were rivals, not family. We used this opportunity to uproot the unusually numerous dark-path figures in Hubei. Other unorthodox forces will move into the space they left. For them, it is a new opportunity.”
“We have given them enough to feed on. They will be satisfied. And when they hear what happened in Hubei, they will understand that it was also a warning.”
We had thrown them food and fastened a leash of fear around their necks.
That was how the Murim Alliance tamed the hunting dog known as the unorthodox Murim.
“And second. The government did not make the proposal and receive our acceptance.”
Jin Wikyung’s voice went dry.
“We did. No—I made the proposal first.”
“Oh.”
“The government merely accepted it. That distinction matters a great deal.”
“...The government agreed that easily?”

“The Provincial Administration Commissioner of Hubei holds a post that can sway an entire province. But people know only that the new commissioner formerly served as an Assistant Provincial Administrator in Shanxi Province. They do not know he is a secret loyal retainer of Prince Shangshan.”
A memory of when we had first arrived in Hubei suddenly flashed through my mind.
The hostile looks from the people. And Jin Wikyung questioning the official who had surrounded the ferry landing with government soldiers.
“By the way, do you know a man surnamed Yi whose given name is Hongcheon?”
“H-he was recently appointed Provincial Administration Commissioner. May I ask what your relationship with him is...?”
“I have met him a few times and shared a drink or two. I helped him when he needed it.”
Jin Wikyung looked straight at me. His gaze was gentle, but a cold blade lay behind it.
For an instant, I saw the strategist and politician in him. Then that look melted away.
“Do not worry. Everything will work out.”
Tap, tap.
I could feel the strength in the hand patting my shoulder. I gazed silently at Jin Wikyung, then suddenly spoke.
“What was the Family Head... No, what was Father like?”
The faint smile on Jin Wikyung’s lips vanished.
“No, the mood was so nice. Why bring up that bastard?”
“As you know, I hurt my head back then. I don’t remember him very well.”
“You don’t need to remember him! Just erase him from your mind! I’m your father!”
I knew he had grievances, but apparently there were more than I had realized.
Jin Wikyung’s fist trembled, as if he were remembering the paperwork hell of those days.
“But why do you ask?”
“No reason. I was just thinking how lucky it is that you took charge of the family after Father disappeared.”
“...Youngest. Please don’t cross the line.”
I shrugged and turned away.
Jin Wikyung asked where I thought I was going when hyung was talking to me, and whether my affection for him had cooled. Without turning around, I answered,
“You said it’s in a month. I’m going to get ready to leave.”
It was time to leave Hubei behind.
With the people who were by my side, and whom I wanted beside me in the days to come.
“I think I’ve given you enough time by now... Don’t you?”
The mutter that slipped between my lips vanished without a trace beneath the noise around us.
I scratched my chin and looked up at the dizzyingly high cliff.

chapters.title: Chapter 502
paragraphs: “Here you are.”
At the sudden voice behind him, the old man sitting cross-legged with his eyes closed twitched his brow.
“I don’t recall inviting anyone.”
“Not my problem. Still, it’s narrower than I expected. Absurdly so.”
“It has to be narrow. I didn’t set aside any room for uninvited guests.”
“Was it around seven days and nights ago? I’m sure I said something similar to someone...”
For some reason, the old man’s small back shuddered at those words.
Before his uninvited guest could wonder why, a sharp voice cut through the cave.
“Leave. You’re disturbing my meditation.”
“Continue your meditation. I’ll personally stand guard for you.”
The old man—Jeok Cheongang, the Fire King—opened his eyes.
The darkness gave way to damp cave walls mottled with moss. A testy voice escaped between his tightly pressed lips.
“You expect this old man to let the Slaughter Saint stand guard over him? What a ridiculous joke.”
“I thought you could trust me with an old man’s life, if not your precious Disciple’s. Was I mistaken?”
Jeok Cheongang’s eyelids trembled. Then—
Shuuk.
Still sitting cross-legged, his small figure rose into the air, turned slowly, and landed facing the cave entrance.
Jeok Cheongang silently stared at the man blocking the narrow cave entrance before asking, “How did you know I was here?”
Mungyeong answered dryly. “When I came up, a great tiger walked over and rubbed its head against me. It had clearly done that before.”
“I left no tracks.”
“Finding people used to be my work.”
“So you can pretend to be a medical apprentice all you like, but you’re still an assassin?”
“There are things you can’t forget, however hard you try. That’s all. There are eyes everywhere, and nothing but river around us. You didn’t have many places to go.”
A fine sword kept its edge no matter how many years passed.
More than forty years had passed, and the blade called the Slaughter Saint was as sharp as ever. No—his instincts as an assassin might have dulled, but his realm as a martial artist had risen higher.
“...Perhaps I should have found somewhere harder to reach.”
“It would have taken me a little longer.”
Assassins were masters of both killing and pursuit.
Reading the confidence in Mungyeong’s calm expression, Jeok Cheongang muttered, “Damn it. What an irritating assassin.”
“I can hear you.”
“I meant you to.”
“Cursing me out of nowhere. What a foul-tempered host.”
“Are you any better, barging in on someone’s secluded meditation without warning?”
“The Fire King, in secluded meditation.”
Mungyeong’s flat voice echoed through the cave.
He looked around. The place was so cramped and damp that calling it a cave seemed generous. Apart from the old man sitting cross-legged, it held nothing at all.
Which made the signs on that one man impossible to miss.
Jeok Cheongang. He’s...
Cracked lips. Knobby bones standing out beneath his skin. Mungyeong’s gaze darkened as he took in Jeok Cheongang’s condition.
From his gaunt appearance, he clearly hadn’t eaten a thing in seven days and nights—not even taken a drop of water. Even for a Supreme Peak master, that would take a toll.
“You’re doing something foolish.”
Jeok Cheongang understood what Mungyeong meant. A fierce light shone from his sunken eyes.
“I’ll give you your own words back. Not your problem.”
“What about the fasting pills?”
“I’m not eating them. They taste like shit.”
“...Did you take after him in that, too?”
“What?”
“Nothing.”
He’d said something pointless. Almost as pointless as Jeok Cheongang’s flimsy claim that he refused the fasting pills because they tasted bad.
Mungyeong shook his head. “As a medical apprentice, I’m telling you this is a poor choice.”
“And as this old man, I’m telling you to mind your own business.”
“You’re even more stubborn than I expected.”
“And you’re more meddlesome than I expected. Since when did you care so much about other people’s business?”
“That...”
Mungyeong fell silent. He wanted to argue, but nothing came to mind. That was as good as admitting Jeok Cheongang had a point.
Maybe he isn’t entirely wrong.
He hadn’t been like this when he left Sichuan. Somewhere along the way, though, he had begun to change, little by little.

To fool the people watching him, he had played an innocent young medical apprentice who smiled and talked freely. But when he was alone with Jeok Cheongang or Jin Taekyung, he had no reason to keep up an act that didn’t suit him.

No. Perhaps it wasn’t only today.
Why?

Mungyeong opened his mouth.

“Ask what?”
“About Jin Taekyung.”
Now it was Jeok Cheongang’s turn to fall silent.
He had tried so hard to avoid that name. He had hoped Mungyeong would let it pass unspoken. Hearing it was enough to stir the feelings he had forced down.

“He’s keeping up, more or less. Not bad.”
Jeok Cheongang couldn’t hold back a hollow laugh.
“Why are you laughing?”
“Because I know that’s nonsense. ‘More or less’? That’s the funniest thing I’ve heard in a while.”
“Never mind me. Tell me what you really think.”
Mungyeong studied him. “His progress is astonishingly fast. Enough to surprise even me.”
“I said to tell me what you really think.”
“That is what I think.”
“Half of it. You left out the part where you want him for yourself.”
“Yes. It was always like that.”
A faint smile touched Jeok Cheongang’s lips.

From the day he first met Jin Taekyung, every day had brought a new surprise. With a Heaven-given physique and extraordinary martial talent, Taekyung was someone any Supreme Peak master who had established martial arts of his own would want as a Disciple.
Jeok Cheongang was no exception.
“When I first got to know Taekyung, a thought struck me. If I passed the Fire Gate Clan’s martial arts on to this boy, perhaps he might see the very limits of martial arts.”
The Fire Gate Clan needed someone to carry on a lineage hundreds of years old, and Jin Taekyung fit that need better than anyone else.
That was how it had started.
“At first, I was simply amazed. Then I felt regret. I didn’t have much time left.”

Alone, he had defeated a thousand Demonic Cult martial artists and brought countless fiends to their knees. By the strength of his own martial arts, he had turned the tide of battle and led the charge toward victory in the Great Faction War.
Yet the Supreme Peak master revered throughout Murim as the Fire King had another, truer enemy.
“It was long ago that the Heart Demon came for me.”
The wound left by his first Disciple ran deep. It ate away at the body and mind of the Master left alone. Little by little, slowly, without ever stopping.
“It was strange. Everything else kept moving forward, while I alone was walking backward.”
The years flew like an arrow. By the time it struck its target, more than thirty had passed.
Jeok Cheongang had let them flow downriver without gaining the slightest enlightenment. Then, one day, he came face-to-face with something he could scarcely believe.
“It was a clear blue day. I was enjoying the cool breeze, and then I came to my senses among a crowd of people. Half a day had passed, and I knew nothing of it. Heh.”
He had laughed like that on the day the infirmities of old age first came upon him.
He had laughed neither from happiness nor from resignation. He simply had not known what else to do.
It was only when that first lost half-day became two full days that Jeok Cheongang knew what he had to do.
“I left Mount Jiuhua to kill one person.”
And returned with one person.
“He was my first Disciple. I had to deal with him myself before it was too late.”
After meeting Jin Taekyung, though, Jeok Cheongang had realized that wasn’t the only thing he had left too late.
“Slaughter Saint. May I ask you for another favor?”
His gaze and tone had changed. Both were gentler than Mungyeong had ever known them.
“If I am not here, become that boy’s dependable shelter. Become his new Master.”
A deep furrow formed on Mungyeong’s smooth forehead. He stared at Jeok Cheongang through narrowed eyes.
“Do you mean that?”
“More than anything I have ever said.”
“Why?”
“Just as I said. I have no time left.”
“What is this...”
A new Master, out of nowhere? No time left?

Mungyeong knew Jeok Cheongang’s condition, but he couldn’t make sense of this. His innate qi, the source of everything, had been disrupted. He would gradually lose his strength, but that should have taken years.
This was too soon.
“I ask this of you.”
Jeok Cheongang bowed his head. The Fire King himself.
Mungyeong was bewildered by a sight no one else in Murim had ever witnessed.
“Why? Seven days and nights ago, you were clearly...”
Mungyeong’s voice cut off abruptly. He swallowed the rest of his words and silently stared at the ripples stirring in Jeok Cheongang’s eyes.
A thought struck him in the suffocating silence.
So that’s it. That’s what happened.
If he was right, it explained everything: Jeok Cheongang’s excessive worry, his disappearance from Jin Taekyung and the others, and his strange reactions throughout their conversation.
“It wasn’t seven days and nights ago, was it?”
“No. It was definitely seven days and nights ago.”
Jeok Cheongang smiled bitterly.
“But to me, those seven days and nights were only five days.”
Time flowed equally for everyone. Not everyone experienced it equally.
The first uninvited guest, arriving a step ahead of Mungyeong, had been the infirmities of old age. They had stolen two days from Jeok Cheongang and fled.
“...When did it start?”
“Sichuan.”
“Sichuan? But when I took your pulse, you were clearly...”
“The symptoms appeared immediately after I left Sichuan. After that, I did my best to avoid you.”
Why had he hidden it? Why?
The question died on Mungyeong’s tongue. He already knew.
How small a person felt when they first realized they had grown old. How frightening it was to realize their mind had begun to come and go with the infirmities of old age.
Seeing Mungyeong fall silent, Jeok Cheongang gave a rueful smile.

“Even if I’d come to tell you, nothing would have changed. I know my own body. You may be the Divine Physician, with medical skill that reaches Heaven, but even you can’t stop innate qi once it starts leaking away.”
“At first, my memory grew hazy. Then one day, moments were missing from my day. I knew what it meant because I’d been through it before.”
Those moments became the time it took to drink a cup of tea. That became fifteen minutes. Now it was two days.
Jeok Cheongang had searched desperately for a way to stop it, to no avail.
“Acquired qi from elixirs can’t restore a balance that’s already been broken. That left me one choice.”
“...Enlightenment.”
“Yes. Enlightenment.”
“So that’s why you began this secluded meditation.”

“I wanted to live as the Fire King Jeok Cheongang. Not as an old man with infirmities who cannot even remember his own name, but as the current Sect Leader of the Fire Gate Clan and someone’s Master.”
His desolate voice echoed through the cave. Drops gathered on the damp ceiling and fell, like an old man’s tears.

chapters.title: Chapter 503
paragraphs: A curse laid upon him by time.
The infirmities of old age.
Mungyeong silently rolled the words over his tongue. They left a dry, bitter taste, though he never spoke them aloud. Jeok Cheongang’s voice was just as bitter.
“I intend to leave. I’ll rest my body and mind at Mount Jiuhua.”
“If anyone understands why, it’s you. Please don’t try to stop me.”
Just as Jeok Cheongang said, Mungyeong knew exactly why he wanted to leave.
He’s afraid of becoming a burden.
The infirmities of old age would come for Jeok Cheongang again and again. If his mind went hazy at a crucial moment, everyone beside him would be in danger.
His enemies feared the Fire King Jeok Cheongang, not an old man who couldn’t remember his own name or where he lived.
More precisely, he’s afraid his Disciple will be in danger.
Everyone had something precious they could not afford to lose.

To a beggar begging in the marketplace, a half-crushed dumpling was his life. To an emperor who commanded all the civil and military officials, the jade seal symbolizing his authority and power was more precious than a thousand or ten thousand subjects.
Jin Taekyung was that precious to Jeok Cheongang.
Someone he would trade his life for. Someone he could not lose, no matter what.
“You’re awfully fond of your Disciple.”
“My Disciple. Yes, my Disciple.”
“If you’re going to spout the same nonsense you did last time, spare me.”
Jeok Cheongang gave a bitter smile at Mungyeong’s hard tone.
“No, you’re right. He’s this old man’s one and only Disciple.”
“So you think you’re a burden to him? You’re so afraid of that you’d leave him of your own accord?”
“It’s the only choice. I’m doing it for the boy.”
“There are other choices. The imugi’s inner core you obtained, for one.”
“You know as well as I do that acquired qi from elixirs can’t cure this. Besides...”
Jeok Cheongang looked down at his wrinkled hands and muttered,
“This old man has grown too old. Even if the imugi’s inner core could help, I can’t use it on an old man like me on the slim chance that it might work.”
“Patch the bottom of an old boat, and water will still leak through somewhere else in the hull. But the boy—my Disciple—is different.”
Light entered his downcast eyes. Joy and hope. Mungyeong could see everything Jeok Cheongang felt for his Disciple in them.
“I have no choice. Please grant this old man’s request, so I can leave with peace of mind.”
“...You have no choice. Is that what you’re saying?”
“Will you look after the boy for me again?”
Mungyeong stared at him for a moment, then said, “Take a boat east from Zhejiang and you’ll come to a small island country.”
“An island country?”
“You must have heard the name. The Wa Kingdom.”
“You haven’t?”
Jeok Cheongang blinked at the sudden question.
“Of course I have. Wa pirates have been coming here to raid us for ages.”
“Have you ever seen one?”
“No, but I hear they’re strange-looking fellows. They carry swords as long as their own bodies, shave half their foreheads back, and walk around wearing rags like undergarments.”
“Whoever told you got it right.”
“But why bring this up all of a—”
“A long time ago,” Mungyeong cut in, “I fought the finest ninja in the Wa Kingdom.”

Jeok Cheongang had heard of ninjas. They were much like the assassins of the Central Plains: not especially skilled in martial arts, but excellent at concealment techniques and at using hidden weapons such as throwing blades.
“There’s no need to ask how it turned out. So are you boasting that you killed the finest ninja in the Wa Kingdom?”
“I didn’t kill him. My objective was to capture him alive.”
A captured target had two choices: speak after a little pain, or speak after terrible pain.
No matter which one he chose, death waited at the end. In the end, the difference was only how painfully he died.
“He chose the latter.”

As befitted the Wa Kingdom’s finest ninja, he held out for quite some time. Unfortunately for him, Salcheonmun—the sect Mungyeong belonged to then—was unquestionably the finest assassin sect in the Central Plains.

They used every torture method they knew. Amid pain worse than death, the ninja was forced to spit out every piece of information he possessed. Not just information, but every memory buried in his mind.
“That was when I heard about a custom in the Wa Kingdom.”
“A custom?”
“Did you know some people there abandon their elderly parents in the mountains?”
“...I can’t say I’m surprised, but those bastards ought to make heaven and earth furious.”
“I was told it was to have fewer mouths to feed. They leave their parents there without caring whether they starve or get torn apart by wild animals. They’re too old to work anymore.”
Abandoning the parents who had raised them simply because they had grown old—if it was true, those people were vicious beyond belief.
Commoners sometimes broke even the bonds between parent and child during terrible disasters. But for it to be a custom was another matter entirely.
Mungyeong continued flatly. “The ninja I captured said he’d abandoned his mother the same way. What do you think she said to her son as he left her deep in the mountains?”
“You fucking bastard.”
“You motherless bastard.”
Seeing Mungyeong’s face harden until it was stiffer than Ten-Thousand-Year Cold Iron, Jeok Cheongang continued with a laugh in his voice.
“That boy Taekyung would answer like that. But she was different. A mother doesn’t stop caring for her child so easily, even when he abandons her. So what did she say?”
“She told him to go slowly. It might get dark and he could fall, so he shouldn’t hurry. He should watch his step on the mountain path.”
Jeok Cheongang could understand what that mother had felt. His decision to leave was rooted in something similar.
He wasn’t being abandoned like the mother in Mungyeong’s story, but he, too, wanted to go before he became a burden to someone precious.
And if the Slaughter Saint is telling this old man such a story...
Relief and bitterness mingled in his eyes as he looked at Mungyeong.
“May I take that to mean you’ll grant my request?”

Mungyeong always called himself a medical apprentice. Jeok Cheongang thought he had brought up a past he hated remembering to compare him to the ninja’s mother—and, in doing so, tacitly accept his proposal.
Then Mungyeong shook his head.
“What does that mean?”
“I thought shaking one’s head meant the same thing everywhere, in every age. Is it different in the Fire Gate Clan?”
“Then why tell me that story...?”

“I forgot to tell you the ending. The ninja’s mother lived out her natural lifespan and was buried in a sunny spot. Her last words brought her unfilial son to his senses, and he went back and brought her home.”
At that moment, Jeok Cheongang’s body abruptly froze.
At last he understood what Mungyeong had been telling him. How foolish the thought that had consumed him was.
Even as she was being abandoned, the ninja’s mother worried about her son. And I was going to leave that boy of my own accord.
Jeok Cheongang hadn’t wanted to burden Jin Taekyung, his one and only Disciple. That was all.
But this wasn’t a selfless act for his Disciple’s sake. It was the stubborn delusion of a proud old man thinking only of himself.
When had it been? He remembered a conversation he had shared with Jin Taekyung one ordinary day at Mount Jiuhua, when they had lain side by side on a broad rock.
You’re holding up better than I expected. Is your body made of iron?
I’m Iron Man.
For spouting nonsense, I’m adding two hundred geun of iron balls.
Ha! I’m joking. Strange. I’ve grown so used to your nonsense that it doesn’t even annoy me anymore.
It’s fine. Put the iron balls on me later.
Must you make me say it twice? I said I was joking.
I’m serious.
Hmm?

There’ll be plenty of people stronger than me once we leave. I don’t want to be treated like a burden later on for no reason. They say the iron balls weigh less if you put them on early, so just add them.
Look at you. Add two hundred geun, and you think you’ll never be a burden?
No, but I should at least try as hard as I can. That way, if I collapse someday, you’ll pick me up, won’t you, Old Master?
Now you’re proudly calling yourself a burden. Fine. If this old man does that, what will you do for me?
If you ever collapse, Old Master, I’ll carry you on my back.
Hah. You think this old man will collapse?
If you get tired, I could at least support you, couldn’t I? So tell me when it gets hard.
...I hear you’re an arrogant, impertinent brat. Five hundred geun of iron balls added.
Are you insane, human?
It had been an ordinary conversation on an unremarkable day.

Yet Jeok Cheongang had often thought back to it. How he’d barked at the boy, turned away, and let out a quiet laugh. How he’d added more iron balls, then hidden nearby to watch, worried the boy might hurt himself.
Even now, at this very moment, Jin Taekyung’s voice from that day echoed in Jeok Cheongang’s ears like a distant refrain.
If you ever collapse, Old Master, I’ll carry you on my back.
He had always pictured himself in front, Taekyung behind him. All the more reason he could never collapse.
If you get tired, I could at least support you, couldn’t I?
He hadn’t wanted Taekyung to see him stagger, either. Like every father, he wanted to be invincible, at least to him.
It had been the same on the day he charged forward ready to die.
Dance of the Fire God and Demon... That’s a pretty cool name.
Y-you bastard, how did you—
You should’ve crushed his head. Made sure of it.
Cough!
Old Master!
But Jeok Cheongang wasn’t invincible.

Only after waking from his long sleep did he learn what his Disciple had endured with his fallen, pitiful Master on his back. How many times Taekyung had risked his precious life and fought through desperate odds.
So Jeok Cheongang had resolved never to collapse again. Never to become a burden that put his Disciple in danger.
But he had been wrong.
We were walking side by side. Following the same path, from the beginning until now. Always together.
One thought filled his mind.
Then dark, damp memories surged from the depths of his past and clouded his vision.
Fwoosh!
Countless memories and emotions stretched back to a beggar boy struggling to pick up a single dumpling.
Rage and despair. Sorrow and guilt. They crashed over Jeok Cheongang like waves and gripped his entire body.
But why did he feel no pain?
The tightness in his chest that always came when he recalled the past was gone. So was the headache that felt as if it would split his skull.
What is this?
For the first time in a very long while, he felt at peace. A cool breeze brushed against him from somewhere, carrying voices with it.
Oh, that feels good.
Ahem. This is the finest auspicious site on Mount Jiuhua, personally selected by this old man.
“This rock is practically a Jangsu stone bed. Five stars.”
Ahem!
Warmth. Brilliant light seeped in.
The darkness that had crouched deep in Jeok Cheongang’s heart for decades was slowly scattering.
The Heart Demon.
That was the name of the darkness he carried within himself, the chain that had bound him. And all it took to drive it away was a cool breeze on a clear day at Mount Jiuhua, and someone’s voice.
Fwoosh!
Old Master.
Light swallowed the darkness. Swallowed the Heart Demon. Though his eyes were closed, everything around him shone so brightly it dazzled him.
A faint smile touched Jeok Cheongang’s wrinkled lips.
Yes.
His snow-white hair stirred in a breeze that had blown from somewhere. It was neither an illusion nor a mistake.
Fwoooosh!

sentences.text: A curse laid upon him by time.
The infirmities of old age.
Mungyeong silently rolled the words over his tongue.
They left a dry, bitter taste, though he never spoke them aloud.
Jeok Cheongang’s voice was just as bitter.
“I intend to leave.
I’ll rest my body and mind at Mount Jiuhua.”
“If anyone understands why, it’s you.
Please don’t try to stop me.”
Just as Jeok Cheongang said, Mungyeong knew exactly why he wanted to leave.
He’s afraid of becoming a burden.
The infirmities of old age would come for Jeok Cheongang again and again.
If his mind went hazy at a crucial moment, everyone beside him would be in danger.
His enemies feared the Fire King Jeok Cheongang, not an old man who couldn’t remember his own name or where he lived.
More precisely, he’s afraid his Disciple will be in danger.
Everyone had something precious they could not afford to lose.
To a beggar begging in the marketplace, a half-crushed dumpling was his life.
To an emperor who commanded all the civil and military officials, the jade seal symbolizing his authority and power was more precious than a thousand or ten thousand subjects.
Jin Taekyung was that precious to Jeok Cheongang.
Someone he would trade his life for.
Someone he could not lose, no matter what.
“You’re awfully fond of your Disciple.”
“My Disciple.
Yes, my Disciple.”
“If you’re going to spout the same nonsense you did last time, spare me.”
Jeok Cheongang gave a bitter smile at Mungyeong’s hard tone.
“No, you’re right.
He’s this old man’s one and only Disciple.”
“So you think you’re a burden to him?
You’re so afraid of that you’d leave him of your own accord?”
“It’s the only choice.
I’m doing it for the boy.”
“There are other choices.
The imugi’s inner core you obtained, for one.”
“You know as well as I do that acquired qi from elixirs can’t cure this.
Besides...”
Jeok Cheongang looked down at his wrinkled hands and muttered,
“This old man has grown too old.
Even if the imugi’s inner core could help, I can’t use it on an old man like me on the slim chance that it might work.”
“Patch the bottom of an old boat, and water will still leak through somewhere else in the hull.
But the boy—my Disciple—is different.”
Light entered his downcast eyes.
Joy and hope.
Mungyeong could see everything Jeok Cheongang felt for his Disciple in them.
“I have no choice.
Please grant this old man’s request, so I can leave with peace of mind.”
“...You have no choice.
Is that what you’re saying?”
“Will you look after the boy for me again?”
Mungyeong stared at him for a moment, then said, “Take a boat east from Zhejiang and you’ll come to a small island country.”
“An island country?”
“You must have heard the name.
The Wa Kingdom.”
“You haven’t?”
Jeok Cheongang blinked at the sudden question.
“Of course I have.
Wa pirates have been coming here to raid us for ages.”
“Have you ever seen one?”
“No, but I hear they’re strange-looking fellows.
They carry swords as long as their own bodies, shave half their foreheads back, and walk around wearing rags like undergarments.”
“Whoever told you got it right.”
“But why bring this up all of a—”
“A long time ago,” Mungyeong cut in, “I fought the finest ninja in the Wa Kingdom.”
Jeok Cheongang had heard of ninjas.
They were much like the assassins of the Central Plains: not especially skilled in martial arts, but excellent at concealment techniques and at using hidden weapons such as throwing blades.
“There’s no need to ask how it turned out.
So are you boasting that you killed the finest ninja in the Wa Kingdom?”
“I didn’t kill him.
My objective was to capture him alive.”
A captured target had two choices: speak after a little pain, or speak after terrible pain.
No matter which one he chose, death waited at the end.
In the end, the difference was only how painfully he died.
“He chose the latter.”
As befitted the Wa Kingdom’s finest ninja, he held out for quite some time.
Unfortunately for him, Salcheonmun—the sect Mungyeong belonged to then—was unquestionably the finest assassin sect in the Central Plains.
They used every torture method they knew.
Amid pain worse than death, the ninja was forced to spit out every piece of information he possessed.
Not just information, but every memory buried in his mind.
“That was when I heard about a custom in the Wa Kingdom.”
“A custom?”
“Did you know some people there abandon their elderly parents in the mountains?”
“...I can’t say I’m surprised, but those bastards ought to make heaven and earth furious.”
“I was told it was to have fewer mouths to feed.
They leave their parents there without caring whether they starve or get torn apart by wild animals.
They’re too old to work anymore.”
Abandoning the parents who had raised them simply because they had grown old—if it was true, those people were vicious beyond belief.
Commoners sometimes broke even the bonds between parent and child during terrible disasters.
But for it to be a custom was another matter entirely.
Mungyeong continued flatly.
“The ninja I captured said he’d abandoned his mother the same way.
What do you think she said to her son as he left her deep in the mountains?”
“You fucking bastard.”
“You motherless bastard.”
Seeing Mungyeong’s face harden until it was stiffer than Ten-Thousand-Year Cold Iron, Jeok Cheongang continued with a laugh in his voice.
“That boy Taekyung would answer like that.
But she was different.
A mother doesn’t stop caring for her child so easily, even when he abandons her.
So what did she say?”
“She told him to go slowly.
It might get dark and he could fall, so he shouldn’t hurry.
He should watch his step on the mountain path.”
Jeok Cheongang could understand what that mother had felt.
His decision to leave was rooted in something similar.
He wasn’t being abandoned like the mother in Mungyeong’s story, but he, too, wanted to go before he became a burden to someone precious.
And if the Slaughter Saint is telling this old man such a story...
Relief and bitterness mingled in his eyes as he looked at Mungyeong.
“May I take that to mean you’ll grant my request?”
Mungyeong always called himself a medical apprentice.
Jeok Cheongang thought he had brought up a past he hated remembering to compare him to the ninja’s mother—and, in doing so, tacitly accept his proposal.
Then Mungyeong shook his head.
“What does that mean?”
“I thought shaking one’s head meant the same thing everywhere, in every age.
Is it different in the Fire Gate Clan?”
“Then why tell me that story...?”
“I forgot to tell you the ending.
The ninja’s mother lived out her natural lifespan and was buried in a sunny spot.
Her last words brought her unfilial son to his senses, and he went back and brought her home.”
At that moment, Jeok Cheongang’s body abruptly froze.
At last he understood what Mungyeong had been telling him.
How foolish the thought that had consumed him was.
Even as she was being abandoned, the ninja’s mother worried about her son.
And I was going to leave that boy of my own accord.
Jeok Cheongang hadn’t wanted to burden Jin Taekyung, his one and only Disciple.
That was all.
But this wasn’t a selfless act for his Disciple’s sake.
It was the stubborn delusion of a proud old man thinking only of himself.
When had it been?
He remembered a conversation he had shared with Jin Taekyung one ordinary day at Mount Jiuhua, when they had lain side by side on a broad rock.
You’re holding up better than I expected.
Is your body made of iron?
I’m Iron Man.
For spouting nonsense, I’m adding two hundred geun of iron balls.
Ha!
I’m joking.
Strange.
I’ve grown so used to your nonsense that it doesn’t even annoy me anymore.
It’s fine.
Put the iron balls on me later.
Must you make me say it twice?
I said I was joking.
I’m serious.
Hmm?

I don’t want to be treated like a burden later on for no reason.

Look at you.

No, but I should at least try as hard as I can.

Now you’re proudly calling yourself a burden.
Fine.

Hah.
You think this old man will collapse?

chapters.title: Chapter 504
paragraphs: Enlightenment comes when you least expect it.
When you have forgotten everything around you in a state of selflessness. When death is right before your eyes. Or when you finally cast off the chains that have bound your body and mind for decades.
That was how enlightenment came.
Fwoooooosh!
A wind of qi surged from one man and swept in every direction.
The cave interior was dark, deprived of even a ray of light, but it was now brightly illuminated by a halo of light.
Mungyeong watched the strange sight in silence. Then the boy spoke softly.
“Have you finally escaped your Heart Demon?”
He hadn’t set out to bring this about. He had only wanted Jeok Cheongang to know that he wasn’t alone. That he didn’t have to isolate himself and carry every worry and burden on his own.
The result had gone beyond anything Mungyeong expected.
The Supreme Peak master known as the Fire King had broken the chains that had bound him for so many years and was stepping into a new realm.
“Seems I wasn’t meddling for nothing after all.”
Complex emotions mingled in Mungyeong’s eyes as he murmured to himself.
He didn’t know why he had sought out Jeok Cheongang or helped a man he barely knew.
No—even if he did know, he would have pretended otherwise. That was the kind of person he was. It was how he had lived his entire life.
But...
It doesn’t feel so bad.
Mungyeong didn’t realize that a faint smile had crossed his lips.
Nor did he know that the same thing had happened once before, a few days ago.
The smile had come and gone too quickly for him to notice. He slowly turned and stepped out of the cramped cave into the world beyond.
Whoosh.
As if on cue, a breeze from outside blew past, stirring his hair and tickling his nose.
Mungyeong gazed silently at the thick grass and flowers around the cave, then at the wild animals that had gathered there. At last, he spoke.
“Someone will have to stand guard. If those animals wander into the cave without knowing any better, all the enlightenment he worked so hard to attain will go to waste.”
Squeak?
A fawn grazing beside its sleeping mother pricked up its ears.
Under the animals’ wary, curious gazes, Mungyeong looked up at the blue sky.
“It’s a beautiful day. I can’t stay cooped up in a cave in weather like this.”
Step.
Muttering as if to himself, Mungyeong began to walk, neither quickly nor slowly.
The wind blew once more, as though seeing him off while he left the cave behind and disappeared.
Whoosh.
A clear sky without a single cloud. A cool breeze. Wild animals lying together among the grass and flowers, enjoying the sunlight.
And...
Someone lingering outside, unable to bring himself to go in.
Master and Disciple alike.
No matter how he looked at it, those two were alike.
Two butterflies fluttered down and landed on Mungyeong’s shoulder as he smiled without a sound.
It was truly a beautiful day.
The fawn had only recently been born, and it was curious about everything.
It bounded after butterflies and stuck its black nose into the thick grass and flowers to sniff them.
As always, it soon lost interest and wandered off in search of something else to do.
Squeak?
This time was different.
The cave’s pitch-black entrance drew it in, while its mother slept, worn out from caring for it.
Most importantly, the strange two-legged animal it had never seen before had disappeared into the distance.
Squeak.
What’s in there? I want to go inside.
Squeak!
All right. Let’s go!
But the fawn’s firm resolve lasted only as long as it took to nibble a few mouthfuls of grass.
Step.
Someone approached, and a shadow fell over its round head.
The fawn startled and backed away. A large figure appeared in its black eyes.
“Not right now. We’ll go in later.”
The stranger stroked the frightened fawn’s head, then stared at the pitch-black cave.
The stranger’s gaze was so profoundly somber that the fawn, which had instinctively been about to wake its mother, swallowed its cry.
Squeeeeak.
“That’s right. Good. Now go back to your mother.”
The figure watched the fawn tilt its head and approach its sleeping mother, then straightened from his bent posture.
His steps toward the cave were steady. The wind blurred his voice.
“Now... I should go, too.”
The path to the cave was long.
A year and several months had passed since the old man and the young man first met. After taking the long way around, they could finally meet again.
Not one in front and the other behind, but side by side, shoulder to shoulder.
“When the hell is Jin Taekyung coming?”
At Gung Gibang’s irritated complaint, Hyuk Mujin clicked his tongue.
“Tsk, tsk. With a temper that impatient, how are you ever going to beg? Try waiting patiently for once.”
“Listen to the way that Hyuk bastard talks. Beggars aren’t allowed to be impatient?”
“You need patience if you want someone to give you even one iron coin.”
“Was it the Hyuk Family Textile Shop? Want me to send a hundred thousand Beggars’ Sect disciples over to take a shit there, one by one?”
“...Let’s leave family out of this.”
“Then watch your mouth. My boys might not have money, but you think they don’t have shit?”
Hyuk Mujin looked at him in disgust.
“You’re driving me crazy. I just ate, so why the hell are you talking about shit? We have to board the ship soon, too.”
“So before the Hyuk Family Textile Shop gets covered in shit—”
“Ah, I said stop! Hearing about food after talking about eating shit is making my stomach turn!”
As the two men tilted their heads, sensing something was wrong, Jin Wikyung addressed someone nearby.
“Tell me, are you certain he’ll be here soon?”
Mungyeong, the young medical apprentice known as the Divine Physician’s Disciple, bowed politely.
“Yes. Young Master Jin said so himself.”
“We need to leave before sunset...”
Jin Wikyung murmured as he gazed at the sky slowly turning red.

The ceremony declaring the new Murim Alliance in Henan was only about a month away. They had to set out now and keep up a good pace if they were to arrive on time, allowing for anything that might happen along the way.
No. I should be grateful Great Hero Jeok is coming with us at all.
Rumors had been swirling about Jeok Cheongang, who had shut himself away for seven days and nights.

Some said, hopefully, that he had finally found a clue to enlightenment. Others made the impious suggestion that something might be wrong with his health. Still others insisted he simply had no particular reason to show himself.
Jin Wikyung didn’t know which of the three was true, but he had certainly worried in private.
I was afraid he might refuse to join the Murim Alliance... It seems my youngest managed to persuade him.

Most martial artists of the orthodox faction had forgotten it, but the Fire King Jeok Cheongang had never belonged to the orthodox, unorthodox, or Demonic factions. He stood between the orthodox and unorthodox factions.

That independence was the foundation of the Fire Gate Clan, which had preserved its lineage through one-person succession for hundreds of years. Each Sect Leader had defended its position outside every faction with overwhelming martial might.
Especially since it was Great Hero Jeok.
Even a child with a runny nose knew that the Fire King Jeok Cheongang had helped the orthodox faction and led it to victory in the Great Faction War.
But few people knew that this Supreme Peak master from two generations ago had been deeply disappointed by the orthodox faction both during and after the war.
“Come to think of it, I’m reminded of something my grandfather once said about Senior Jeok.”
Zhuge Feng had come out to see them off. At his words, Jin Wikyung’s ear twitched.
“About Great Hero Jeok?”
“Yes.”
“I’ve heard the previous Family Head was wise and had remarkable insight. May I ask what he said?”
“Well, I heard it in the Family Head’s hall when I was thirteen.”
“I see. And what did he say...?”
“I remember it clearly. My grandfather was talking about the Great Faction War. Ah, have you heard how the members of our family played a major role in the great battle in Sichuan?”
Crack.
Zhuge Feng, who had been leisurely fanning himself, suddenly stopped.
He glanced back and forth between Jin Wikyung’s tightly clenched fist and his flushed face, then slowly lowered the fan.
Jin Wikyung’s martial arts were in no way inferior, but even his appearance alone made him little different from a human weapon.
Besides, with the priceless Water God Dragon’s corpse in his hands, was he not the one holding all the cards?
Zhuge Feng discreetly gauged the mood, cleared his throat, and continued.
“Ahem. In any case, I asked him first. I asked when he thought the tide had first begun to turn in favor of the orthodox faction.”
Jin Wikyung’s voice was low and level.
“Was it because the Zhuge Clan played such an important role in the great battle in Sichuan?”
“No! That wasn’t it! It really wasn’t!”
“That’s a relief. Please continue.”
Zhuge Feng began speaking while glancing sideways at the clenched fist.
“It was the first and last time I ever saw my grandfather think so long over a question. Can you guess what he finally said, Lesser Family Head?”

“You said it was connected to Great Hero Jeok... Perhaps it was the great battle in Shaanxi. I’ve heard the other Seniors distinguished themselves there, but Great Hero Jeok’s achievements were truly astounding.”
The battle in Shaanxi that Jin Wikyung had mentioned was one of the particularly brilliant victories among the countless battles of the blood-soaked Great Faction War.
Jin Wikyung had given his answer some thought, but Zhuge Feng let out a quiet laugh and shook his head.
“Wrong.”
“Then what was it?”
“Anhui.”
“Anhui... You mean that?”
“That’s right. No one expected the Demonic Cult’s elite Black Wind Corps—a thousand men marching across Anhui—to be wiped out by one man. Not even my grandfather.”
Jin Wikyung nodded.

On the day Mount Jiuhua was engulfed in flames, an unknown old man living in obscurity became known as the Fire King, while the Demonic Cult lost an elite strike force that had accumulated countless achievements since the beginning of the Great Faction War.
“That makes sense. It was when Great Hero Jeok first emerged into the world.”
“But if not for my wise and perceptive grandfather’s judgment, not only would the Black Wind Corps not have been annihilated, Senior Jeok would never have gained the title of Fire King.”
“What do you mean...?”
Zhuge Feng looked around, then lowered his voice as much as possible.
“At the time, every road through Anhui was open to the Black Wind Corps. They had no reason to pass through Mount Jiuhua.”
“Wait. Then do you mean...?”

“My grandfather never forgot anything he had seen once. This was no different. He remembered a record about a one-person sect in our family’s archives, one describing events from more than a hundred years ago.”
“Heh heh. It was a bold gamble, but it worked. A stratagem to put even Zhuge Wuhou to shame, wouldn’t you say?”
As Zhuge Feng casually put his own clan’s ancestor to shame, a deep voice reached his ear.
“So that’s what happened.”
Zhuge Feng turned in bewilderment and saw him.
“Zhuge Clan, assemble.”
A middle-aged man was approaching from far beyond the distance his voice should have carried.
And walking beside him, shoulder to shoulder, was a young man.

The stranger’s gaze was so profoundly somber that the fawn, which had instinctively been about to wake its mother, swallowed its cry.
Squeeeeak.
“That’s right.
Good.
Now go back to your mother.”
The figure watched the fawn tilt its head and approach its sleeping mother, then straightened from his bent posture.
His steps toward the cave were steady.
The wind blurred his voice.
“Now...
I should go, too.”
The path to the cave was long.
A year and several months had passed since the old man and the young man first met.
After taking the long way around, they could finally meet again.
Not one in front and the other behind, but side by side, shoulder to shoulder.
“When the hell is Jin Taekyung coming?”
At Gung Gibang’s irritated complaint, Hyuk Mujin clicked his tongue.
“Tsk, tsk.
With a temper that impatient, how are you ever going to beg?
Try waiting patiently for once.”
“Listen to the way that Hyuk bastard talks.
Beggars aren’t allowed to be impatient?”
“You need patience if you want someone to give you even one iron coin.”
“Was it the Hyuk Family Textile Shop?
Want me to send a hundred thousand Beggars’ Sect disciples over to take a shit there, one by one?”
“...Let’s leave family out of this.”
“Then watch your mouth.
My boys might not have money, but you think they don’t have shit?”
Hyuk Mujin looked at him in disgust.
“You’re driving me crazy.
I just ate, so why the hell are you talking about shit?
We have to board the ship soon, too.”
“So before the Hyuk Family Textile Shop gets covered in shit—”
“Ah, I said stop!
Hearing about food after talking about eating shit is making my stomach turn!”
As the two men tilted their heads, sensing something was wrong, Jin Wikyung addressed someone nearby.
“Tell me, are you certain he’ll be here soon?”
Mungyeong, the young medical apprentice known as the Divine Physician’s Disciple, bowed politely.
“Yes.
Young Master Jin said so himself.”
“We need to leave before sunset...”
Jin Wikyung murmured as he gazed at the sky slowly turning red.
The ceremony declaring the new Murim Alliance in Henan was only about a month away.
They had to set out now and keep up a good pace if they were to arrive on time, allowing for anything that might happen along the way.
No.
I should be grateful Great Hero Jeok is coming with us at all.
Rumors had been swirling about Jeok Cheongang, who had shut himself away for seven days and nights.
Some said, hopefully, that he had finally found a clue to enlightenment.
Others made the impious suggestion that something might be wrong with his health.
Still others insisted he simply had no particular reason to show himself.
Jin Wikyung didn’t know which of the three was true, but he had certainly worried in private.
I was afraid he might refuse to join the Murim Alliance...
It seems my youngest managed to persuade him.
Most martial artists of the orthodox faction had forgotten it, but the Fire King Jeok Cheongang had never belonged to the orthodox, unorthodox, or Demonic factions.
He stood between the orthodox and unorthodox factions.
That independence was the foundation of the Fire Gate Clan, which had preserved its lineage through one-person succession for hundreds of years.
Each Sect Leader had defended its position outside every faction with overwhelming martial might.
Especially since it was Great Hero Jeok.
Even a child with a runny nose knew that the Fire King Jeok Cheongang had helped the orthodox faction and led it to victory in the Great Faction War.
But few people knew that this Supreme Peak master from two generations ago had been deeply disappointed by the orthodox faction both during and after the war.
“Come to think of it, I’m reminded of something my grandfather once said about Senior Jeok.”
Zhuge Feng had come out to see them off.
At his words, Jin Wikyung’s ear twitched.
“About Great Hero Jeok?”
“Yes.”
“I’ve heard the previous Family Head was wise and had remarkable insight.
May I ask what he said?”
“Well, I heard it in the Family Head’s hall when I was thirteen.”
“I see.
And what did he say...?”
“I remember it clearly.
My grandfather was talking about the Great Faction War.
Ah, have you heard how the members of our family played a major role in the great battle in Sichuan?”
Crack.
Zhuge Feng, who had been leisurely fanning himself, suddenly stopped.
He glanced back and forth between Jin Wikyung’s tightly clenched fist and his flushed face, then slowly lowered the fan.
Jin Wikyung’s martial arts were in no way inferior, but even his appearance alone made him little different from a human weapon.
Besides, with the priceless Water God Dragon’s corpse in his hands, was he not the one holding all the cards?
Zhuge Feng discreetly gauged the mood, cleared his throat, and continued.
“Ahem.
In any case, I asked him first.
I asked when he thought the tide had first begun to turn in favor of the orthodox faction.”
Jin Wikyung’s voice was low and level.
“Was it because the Zhuge Clan played such an important role in the great battle in Sichuan?”
“No!
That wasn’t it!
It really wasn’t!”
“That’s a relief.
Please continue.”
Zhuge Feng began speaking while glancing sideways at the clenched fist.
“It was the first and last time I ever saw my grandfather think so long over a question.
Can you guess what he finally said, Lesser Family Head?”
“You said it was connected to Great Hero Jeok...
Perhaps it was the great battle in Shaanxi.
I’ve heard the other Seniors distinguished themselves there, but Great Hero Jeok’s achievements were truly astounding.”
The battle in Shaanxi that Jin Wikyung had mentioned was one of the particularly brilliant victories among the countless battles of the blood-soaked Great Faction War.
Jin Wikyung had given his answer some thought, but Zhuge Feng let out a quiet laugh and shook his head.
“Wrong.”
“Then what was it?”
“Anhui.”
“Anhui...
You mean that?”
“That’s right.
No one expected the Demonic Cult’s elite Black Wind Corps—a thousand men marching across Anhui—to be wiped out by one man.
Not even my grandfather.”
Jin Wikyung nodded.

On the day Mount Jiuhua was engulfed in flames, an unknown old man living in obscurity became known as the Fire King, while the Demonic Cult lost an elite strike force that had accumulated countless achievements since the beginning of the Great Faction War.
“That makes sense.
It was when Great Hero Jeok first emerged into the world.”
“But if not for my wise and perceptive grandfather’s judgment, not only would the Black Wind Corps not have been annihilated, Senior Jeok would never have gained the title of Fire King.”
“What do you mean...?”
Zhuge Feng looked around, then lowered his voice as much as possible.
“At the time, every road through Anhui was open to the Black Wind Corps.
They had no reason to pass through Mount Jiuhua.”
“Wait.
Then do you mean...?”
“My grandfather never forgot anything he had seen once.
This was no different.
He remembered a record about a one-person sect in our family’s archives, one describing events from more than a hundred years ago.”
“Heh heh.
It was a bold gamble, but it worked.
A stratagem to put even Zhuge Wuhou to shame, wouldn’t you say?”
As Zhuge Feng casually put his own clan’s ancestor to shame, a deep voice reached his ear.
“So that’s what happened.”
Zhuge Feng turned in bewilderment and saw him.
“Zhuge Clan, assemble.”
A middle-aged man was approaching from far beyond the distance his voice should have carried.
And walking beside him, shoulder to shoulder, was a young man.

chapters.title: Chapter 505
paragraphs: Returned to Youth was the realm every martial artist in Murim dreamed of reaching.
When immense internal energy combined with enlightenment, the body was remade, restoring the youth it had once possessed.

But if Returned to Youth were easy, countless martial artists wouldn’t have died dreaming of it. It was impossible without Heaven’s help. And walking beside me now was a man who, after long years of painstaking effort, had finally received that stroke of heavenly luck.
“Zhuge Clan, assemble.”
Blazing red hair streamed in the wind. A solid frame of taut muscle stood nearly seven feet tall, and his voice had the weight of an iron club.
...I really can’t get used to this.
Could a person change that much? The longer I looked, the stranger I felt.

The Fire King Jeok Cheongang I knew had been a short, impossibly old man who stood barely five feet tall. He had looked like he could hardly grow any older—not like a fit middle-aged man who appeared to be in his mid-to-late forties.
Jeok Cheongang noticed me staring. He stopped walking and muttered under his breath.
“Why? Why are you looking at me again?”
“I mean, come on. How did this happen? How old were you when you looked like this?”
“I was probably not yet sixty. My hair was never red, though. Not once.”
“How did you get so much shorter as you aged? I know people shrink, but... did someone cut off your legs when you were around eighty?”
“No one cut off mine. I could cut off the legs of a certain bastard who’s been running his mouth since earlier, though.”
Jeok Cheongang glared at me, then smacked his lips.
“Anyway, stop looking at me like that. Even this old man isn’t used to it yet.”
“If you’re not used to it yourself—wait. It feels weird calling you Old Master now.”
“Then what will you call me?”
“Mister?”
“Hey, Mr. Jeok?”
“...Do you want to fucking die?”
What a relief. That murderous tone was definitely Jeok Cheongang’s.
As I felt oddly reassured, familiar faces drew near and looked between us in confusion.
“Huh?”
“Captain, who’s that beside you?”
A perfectly normal reaction. Mungyeong and the few others who knew what had happened reacted differently.
“M-my youngest.”
“B-Benefactor. Is that...?”

Jin Wikyung and Cheongpung caught on quickly. Jin Wikyung always kept his composure and read the situation, while Cheongpung was the strongest Supreme Peak master here after Mungyeong. It wasn’t surprising that they’d guessed.
Then there was Zhuge Feng. He fixed me with a grave look.

“Red hair and a red beard. According to the reports I received, no martial artist with such distinctive features has come through here. More importantly, he’s walking right beside you, which suggests you’re quite close. But you don’t have any friends, do you?”
“...That pisses me off, but you’re not wrong. So?”
“Thus, my brilliant mind leads me to suspect that the martial artist beside you might be Senior Jeok, Returned to Youth... Ha ha. What do you think? Fairly plausible nonsense, isn’t it?”
“That’s right.”
“No, it isn’t. It’s nonsense.”
“What do you mean, no? I’m telling you it’s true.”
“Please tell me it’s nonsense. I beg you.”
“It’s true.”
That answer didn’t come from me. Jeok Cheongang stepped forward with that short, weighty declaration, and the air around us stirred.
“Gasp!”
“R-Returned to Youth?”
“Then that man really is...!”

There was a truckload of Wudang and Zhuge Clan martial artists stationed around the makeshift wharf to guard and investigate the area. Ship-Fire Boy Mu Song and the river bandits of Water Dragon Stronghold were there too, ready to take us out.
As everyone stared wide-eyed, Zhuge Feng’s gaze wavered.
Why is the Fire King here...?
It was written all over his face. Amid the uproar, he looked silently at Jeok Cheongang, then respectfully cupped his hands.
“Senior, it is good to see you. I was terribly worried something might have happened to you...”
“I’d wondered why those Demonic Cult bastards came to Mount Jiuhua when they had so many other roads to take. Now I know.”
Zhuge Feng gave an awkward laugh at the razor edge in Jeok Cheongang’s voice.
“I’m afraid I don’t know what you mean.”
“Pretend you don’t know one more time, and you won’t like what happens.”
“...May I ask how much you heard?”
“From ‘if not for my wise and perceptive grandfather’s judgment.’”
“Ah. You heard all of it.”
“I did.”
“If I said everything I told them was a misunderstanding...”
“I’d burn the Zhuge Clan to the ground.”
“No wonder those goddamn Demonic Cult bastards came this way with all those other roads available.”

Jeok Cheongang clenched his fist, his eyes cold. Even when he’d looked like he might drop dead any day, that look had made everyone back down. Now that he’d Returned to Youth, the force of his aura was enough to make knees buckle.
“I woke from a nap to find Mount Jiuhua on fire. What do you think of that?”
“I don’t think it was good.”
“And?”
Zhuge Feng swallowed hard.
“I imagine you were displeased.”
“It was fucking awful. If this old man hadn’t hurried over, even my home would’ve burned to ash.”
“Your home survived, then. Thank goodness.”
“Everything but my home burned. My heart, too.”
“Now, I’ll give you two choices.”
Jeok Cheongang raised a finger.
“First, I round up every bastard named Zhuge, line them up five abreast, and slap them all across the face.”
That would be quite a sight.
Before I’d finished the thought, Zhuge Feng answered without taking a breath.
“I accept the second proposal.”
“Do you even know what it is?”
“Whatever it is, I choose the second.”
I would’ve picked number two myself.

To a martial artist, pride was nearly as important as life itself. If word spread that the entire Zhuge Clan had been slapped in a line by the Fire King Jeok Cheongang, the clan would have to take down its sign from that very day onward. Even a member of the Five Great Families like the Zhuge Clan would be no exception.
Zhuge Feng had chosen wisely. Still, he couldn’t quite hide his unease.
“What is the second proposal?”
Jeok Cheongang stroked his short red beard. He slowly looked over everyone present, me included, then spoke.
“Do better from now on.”
“Senior, forgive me, but what exactly—”
“The war has already begun. Do as well as the Zhuge Clan did in the Great Faction War—no, better. Like your grandfather.”

“Well, your grandfather didn’t conspire with the Demonic Cult and tell them to burn Mount Jiuhua. And it’s absurd to stay angry at a man who’s dead and buried. I can’t exactly go to his grave and turn it over again.”
Jeok Cheongang looked at me.
“Besides, if those Demonic Cult bastards hadn’t set Mount Jiuhua on fire that day, another bond would never have formed... Why are you making that face?”
I hurriedly composed my expression before answering.
“This is my normal face.”
“...I have an idea what you’re thinking, but I’ll let it pass.”
If I admitted I’d expected him to visit the former Family Head’s grave and piss on it, Jeok Cheongang would try to kill me. Judging by everyone else’s faces, I wasn’t the only one who’d thought it.
Still, he’s giving it this much thought. I’m a little touched.

As Jeok Cheongang had said, if he had remained a reclusive master in Mount Jiuhua, we would never have ended up working together. We would have lived in our separate worlds, never knowing the other existed.
But the pendulum of fate had led me to the Murim and connected me with Jeok Cheongang.
And whether this was fate as well or not, we had to move toward our next destination once more.
Henan.
The moment that word filled my mind, Mungyeong spoke up. He’d been standing apart all this time, his expression unreadable.
“The sun is about to set.”
The western mountains were already red. Jeok Cheongang, whose hair was redder still, grinned at me.
“Come. Let’s go.”
“Yes.”
Right. Let’s go.
To Henan. To the New Murim Alliance.
“So they’ve all left?”
The first to speak was an old Daoist with a refined face. His skin was as taut as a young man’s, without a single age spot, and the long hem of his robe was dazzling white.
The Daoist who had brought him the news was old too, but his many-times-patched clothes spoke to his unassuming nature.
Clack.
Perfected Being Hyeongong set down his teacup.
“Yes, Sect Leader Senior Brother.”
The two boys who had studied under the same master since childhood were now respected Perfected Beings and pillars of Wudang.

Hyeongong, who had cared for little besides martial arts, had reached Supreme Peak and made a name for himself. His Senior Brother, seven years his elder, had succeeded their master as Sect Leader of Wudang. He was the refined-looking old Daoist, Perfected Being Hyeoncheon.
“I’d hoped to meet them at least once before they left.”
Hyeongong answered his Senior Brother’s regretful murmur.
“It couldn’t be helped. You didn’t send me in your place because you didn’t want to meet them.”

“No, but I still regret missing them. There are the Two Dragons the Jin Family of Taiyuan and Huashan are so proud of, and I hear Senior Jeok has gained enlightenment as well. I should have seen him.”
“Ha ha. Don’t be too disappointed. We’ll see him again soon.”
“Yes, I suppose we will. If what this letter says is true.”
Hyeoncheon gazed down at the letter on the table. Across its envelope, written in a bold, soaring hand, were three characters:
Murim Alliance.
Only three characters, yet their weight was unmistakable.
The Murim Alliance represented orthodox Murim itself. It was also proof that a war rivaling the Great Faction War was approaching.
Is it truly... beginning like this?

Hyeoncheon’s expression grew heavy. He could almost hear the screams of the countless Senior and Junior Brothers who had fallen bleeding in the Great Faction War. The horrors of his youth were about to repeat themselves.
This unworthy Disciple finally understands your heart, Master.
Hyeoncheon was thinking of the master who had died after failing to overcome the injuries he had suffered during the Great Faction War when—
“S-Sect Leader!”
An urgent shout came from outside the pavilion.
Hyeoncheon sensed something strange and flicked his sleeve. A soft stream of internal force shot out and flung open the pavilion door.
Hyeongong recognized the face beyond it and frowned.
The man who had shouted was a second-generation Wudang Disciple, one of the pursuit party sent after the Killing Ghost. As Hyeongong watched him struggle for breath, his eyes widened.
“Could it be?”
“Yes. We caught him.”
“Good! At last, the Killing Ghost who committed those heinous atrocities—”
Hyeongong broke off. His Senior Brother’s expression was grim.
And Hyeongong’s suspicion was exactly right.
Hyeoncheon silently stared at the second-generation Disciple, who seemed not to know what to do, then spoke in a low voice.
“We ought to be glad you caught the Killing Ghost, yet you look troubled. What happened?”
“Th-that is...”
“Has someone else been killed or injured?”
“No. It isn’t that...”
Unable to go on, the Disciple lowered his head.
“We’re bringing the Killing Ghost’s body here now. I think it would be best if you saw it and judged for yourself, Sect Leader.”
“What is this supposed to—”
Hyeoncheon did not have to wait long for an answer.
Half an hour later, Wudang Disciples brought the body before him. He saw what the Killing Ghost truly was and remained silent for a long time before speaking.
“It seems... I have one more reason to go to Henan.”
Reflected in the old Daoist’s clear eyes was something neither beast nor human.
