The man who had shouted was a second-generation Wudang Disciple, one of the pursuit party sent after the Killing Ghost.
As Hyeongong watched him struggle for breath, his eyes widened.
“Could it be?”
“Yes.
We caught him.”
“Good!
At last, the Killing Ghost who committed those heinous atrocities—”
Hyeongong broke off.
His Senior Brother’s expression was grim.
And Hyeongong’s suspicion was exactly right.
Hyeoncheon silently stared at the second-generation Disciple, who seemed not to know what to do, then spoke in a low voice.
“We ought to be glad you caught the Killing Ghost, yet you look troubled.
What happened?”
“Th-that is...”
“Has someone else been killed or injured?”
“No.
It isn’t that...”
Unable to go on, the Disciple lowered his head.
“We’re bringing the Killing Ghost’s body here now.
I think it would be best if you saw it and judged for yourself, Sect Leader.”
“What is this supposed to—”
Hyeoncheon did not have to wait long for an answer.
Half an hour later, Wudang Disciples brought the body before him.
He saw what the Killing Ghost truly was and remained silent for a long time before speaking.
“It seems...
I have one more reason to go to Henan.”
Reflected in the old Daoist’s clear eyes was something neither beast nor human.

chapters.title: Chapter 506
paragraphs: Fwoosh.

A northwest wind blew in from the distance, filling the sail. The burly, rough-faced river bandits rowed hard in rhythm, while the bow split the water into white foam that formed and vanished on either side.
Peaceful, as if nothing had happened.
Maybe it was because of all the tragedies we’d seen lately, but the Yangtze, stretching endlessly before us like a sea, looked beautiful today.
As if he’d read my mind, Jeok Cheongang spoke from beside me.
“Same shitty scenery as ever.”
“If I had to pick two things that ought to disappear from this world right now, they’d be Dark Heaven and the Yangtze.”
So much for reading my mind.
What could I say? In more ways than one, it was nice that he hadn’t changed. I watched his red hair whip in the wind and sighed.
“Don’t sigh so loudly. The ground—”
“The ground won’t sink just because I sigh.”
“No. You’ll die by this old man’s hand before you set foot on land.”
“Wow. You keep exceeding my expectations.”
“You seem to have forgotten how to use your eyes while we were apart. One says ‘dis,’ and the other says ‘respect.’ What am I to do with them?”
“They say ‘re’ and ‘spect,’ actually.”
“Want me to beat some ‘feet-spect’ into you?”
Whoosh—whack!
“Ugh!”
Lightning flashed before my eyes. At my cry, and the sight of me clutching the back of my head, Jeok Cheongang flinched.
“I-I barely hit you. What a fuss.”
“Does this look like I’m making a fuss? My skull’s ringing.”
“Your skull is... ringing?”
“I’m tough, but I’m still human. Of course it is.”
“...Did it hurt that much? I didn’t mean to hit you so hard. Let me see.”
He was fidgeting like a puppy that needed to poop. I let out a quiet laugh.
“Why—why are you laughing?”
“No reason.”
“Ah, I’m all better. Anyway, how long will it take us to reach Henan at this rate?”
At my casual change of subject, Jeok Cheongang’s face turned bright red.
“H-how dare you toy with this old man!”
Whack!
“Ah, that really hurt!”
“Just take it!”
It hurt. It really did.
So why did I keep laughing even as he hit me?
Maybe I missed this.
Yes. That was probably it.

Sometimes you miss the little things that never seemed important at the time. For me, it was my father’s scratchy beard, which had stung so much when I was young. And it was Jeok Cheongang’s palm, gradually growing slower and weaker.
But things were all right now. My father had died long ago, and I could only see him in photographs. Jeok Cheongang, though, had regained his strength.
Whack!
Feeling the speed and power he’d recovered along with his youth made me laugh again.
This is nice, too.
Whack! Whack! Whaaack!
“...Uh, wait a second.”
“How dare you make a fool of this old man!”
“Ugh!”
On second thought, it wasn’t that nice.
There was a limit to how much something ought to hurt. This was crossing it.
My lunatic grin had vanished without a trace. I was twisting desperately to dodge Jeok Cheongang’s thick palms when a voice cut in.
“Um... should I come back later?”
Jeok Cheongang stopped dead. I seized the chance to slip away and hide behind the speaker.
My precious meat shield—no, Ship-Fire Boy Mu Song—cried out in alarm.
“H-hey, Junior!”
“Junior. That sounds especially nice today, Senior.”
“What are you doing?”
“Inheriting your position as Stronghold Lord.”
“If you’re going to get beaten, get beaten alone!”
“A Senior’s supposed to help his Junior at times like this. Don’t you want to be that kind of Senior?”
“Why the hell should I—gasp, Great Hero Jeok!”
Unfortunately, Mu Song and I didn’t get beaten together.
With the moment broken, Jeok Cheongang lowered his clenched fist instead of bringing it down. He smacked his lips and looked Mu Song up and down.
“Never mind. What is it?”
Mu Song, who had squeezed his eyes shut in expectation of a merciless beating, hurriedly pried me off him.
“I came because I heard you’d called for me. One of my subordinates said you were looking for me...”
“This old man called for you? When?”
“I-I was told you’d asked when we would arrive in Henan.”
I’d been quietly watching the exchange. Now I raised my hand.
“Uh, I think that was me.”
One of the river bandits must have overheard me mutter it while I was changing the subject and passed it on to Mu Song.
“...It was you, Junior?”
“Yes. I was just thinking aloud.”
“I see. I see.”
Judging by Mu Song’s grim voice, the river bandit who had passed along the wrong information probably would not escape a taste of the Yangtze today.
I turned toward Mu Song, who was glaring somewhere with a dangerous look in his eyes.
“I did want to know, though. When do you think we’ll arrive?”
Although Mu Song was startlingly young compared with the other old martial-world veterans, he was still an experienced river bandit who had spent his entire life on the Yangtze.
He took a moment to work it out, then said, “We should be able to cut the travel time considerably. If weather like today’s continues, we’ll reach Xixia within ten days at the latest.”
“Xixia?”

I’d traveled plenty, but not enough to know every place name in the world. In Murim, I’d been too busy to learn them. I’d tried looking them up online in the modern world, but the names and locations didn’t always match.
Just look at Dongting Lake.
Here in Murim, Dongting Lake lay in Hubei Province. On a modern Chinese map, it was in Hunan Province.
Discrepancies like that were decisive proof that the two worlds, however similar, were not the same.
“Is Xixia in Henan?”
Jeok Cheongang nodded.
“It’s on the southwestern edge of Henan. If this old man remembers correctly, a tributary of the Yangtze ends around there. From then on, we’ll have to travel by land. Is that correct?”
“Exactly right, Great Hero Jeok.”
“I passed near Xixia during the Great Faction War. Good. Very good.”
Was he pleased that Returned to Youth had cured his infirmities of old age and sharpened his memory? Or that we’d be off the Yangtze in ten days at most?
Maybe both.
Smiling with satisfaction, Jeok Cheongang turned to Mu Song.
“Come to think of it, you’ve had a hard time too. From Sichuan to Hubei, and now all the way to Henan.”
Mu Song shook his head, his expression bitter.
“How could I call this hardship? Thanks to it, I can finally lay Uncle Hwang and all the brothers who died before their time to rest. It’s what I ought to do, whether anyone asks me or not.”
After the Water God Dragon fell, Mu Song and the other river bandits of Water Dragon Stronghold had gathered the dead men’s bones and scattered them across the Yangtze.
They had lived on the Yangtze and died on the Yangtze. It was an end befitting river bandits of the Yangtze River Channel League.
“They must be grateful to you from the Nine Springs.”
“Was your name Mu Saeng? For a Disciple of the Seafaring King, you have decent manners. Yangtze One Saber raised you well.”
“He was like family to me. And it’s Mu Song, not Mu Saeng, Great Hero Jeok.”
“Right, Mu Saeng.”
Had his infirmities of old age not been completely cured after all?

For a moment, I wondered. Then I saw Jeok Cheongang glare and realized he was just being stubborn. Whatever Mu Song’s name really was, that look said he’d better change it if Jeok Cheongang called him Mu Saeng.
Mu Song swallowed under the aura of a man steeped in the Three Bonds and Five Relationships.
“What? Why?”
“N-no reason.”
“Good, Mu Saeng.”
Could anyone else hear dentures clacking?
I took pity on the man who’d lost his name and offered him a hand. Though, really, I was more interested in asking him something.
“By the way, Senior, are you planning to return to Sichuan?”
“Hm?”
“You know why we’re heading to Henan, don’t you?”
Mu Song understood what I meant. His gaze grew somber.
“You’re wondering whether I’ll join the Murim Alliance.”
“To be honest, yes.”
“Dark Heaven’s scheme killed someone I looked up to like a parent, along with countless brothers. What would you do in my place?”
“Whatever it took to avenge them.”
“So would I. I want to rush there and lend the Murim Alliance a hand right now. But...”
Mu Song bit his lip, then spoke on a sigh.

“I’m only one Stronghold Lord within the Yangtze River Channel League. I have no say in its decisions. Only one person can decide matters of importance for the League: my Master and its Alliance Leader, the Seafaring King.”

That was common enough in Murim, where strength commanded respect. A Sect Leader’s or Family Head’s authority was greater even than that of a conglomerate owner with an iron grip on the family business.
The problem was—
“Typical of a rootless band of river thieves. Then again, it’s ridiculous to expect anything from men who weighed the costs and benefits even during the Great Faction War.”
Yes. Exactly what Jeok Cheongang had said.

The Yangtze River Channel League had never belonged to the orthodox faction. River bandits scattered across the land like grass roots had gathered beneath its banner because the Seafaring King was strong enough to lead them and promised to protect their individual interests.
I’ve heard the Green Forest Alliance is much the same.

Both groups had begun as thieves banding together to take what belonged to others. They had survived and grown because they sided with orthodox Murim in the Great Faction War, backed the winners, and were rewarded with recognition of their activities.
They were treated much better than the other unorthodox factions that had survived the war. But grass roots didn’t become tree roots just because of that.
Jeok Cheongang gazed at the waves of the Yangtze with displeasure and muttered,
“Before this old man dies, I hope this goddamn Yangtze dries up and withers away. Then that bastard Seafaring King’s face will be a complete mess. Tsk, tsk.”
“Think carefully yourself, Mu Saeng. Your Master may make the wrong choice.”
“...I don’t believe he will.”

Despite hearing his Master insulted to his face, Mu Song merely gave a bitter smile. His reaction left me with the vague impression that his relationship with the Seafaring King wasn’t especially warm.
But what happens if the Yangtze River Channel League and the Green Forest Alliance side with Dark Heaven now?
The answer came quickly.
A real headache, that’s what.
If Dark Heaven was a blade approaching from the front, those two factions were daggers stabbing in from behind.
If they decided to harbor ulterior motives, even the mighty orthodox Murim would inevitably suffer a blow.
“The Sword Saint will have quite a headache. I wonder what those two will choose...”
Jeok Cheongang seemed to have reached the same thought. He was muttering to himself when someone spoke.
“Not two. Four.”
I turned. Mungyeong stood there, his expression composed.

chapters.title: Chapter 507
paragraphs: I knew Mungyeong was approaching. Seven days and nights of grueling—no, blood-shitting—training had sharpened my usual Qi Sense considerably.
The realm stage shown by the System hadn’t risen yet, but I could vaguely sense that I’d have to break through the wall in front of me before it would.
But what does he mean, not two, but four?
The question didn’t trouble me for long.

The Yangtze River Channel League and the Green Forest Alliance were powerful enough that even orthodox Murim couldn’t afford to dismiss them. And I could think of only one place with factions that belonged in the same set.
Vaguely recalling something Jeok Cheongang had once told me, I murmured, “The Outer Murim.”
The Murim beyond the Central Plains. The Murim outside the Murim.
Some people called the barbarians beyond the Great Wall built by an ancient emperor the Outer Lands, but Jeok Cheongang had always dismissed such talk with a snort.
Does the Great Wall surround the whole world? The world beneath the heavens is exactly that—the world beneath the heavens. The lands beneath the sky are boundlessly vast, and each has its own Murim.
Maybe it was just his nature, but Jeok Cheongang’s outlook was nothing like the stale Zhonghua chauvinism you’d expect from an old man of his era.

The records left by earlier Sect Leaders had probably helped. Unlike Jeok Cheongang, who’d been a Lü Bu stuck at the foot of a mountain whenever he wasn’t fighting in the Great Faction War, his predecessors had gone out and indulged their social-butterfly tendencies to the fullest.
Though their records read less like documents written for future generations and more like diaries written for their own satisfaction.
What a shock those had been.
I recalled a few I’d read in Fire Gate Cavern.
Year xx, Month x, Day x. Cheonbong, Third Sect Leader of the Fire Gate Clan.
I had grown sick of the Central Plains. War raged on all sides, and Murim was a complete mess. So I went to India to broaden my horizons.
After a long journey, I arrived at a river called the Gan... something.

It is not as large as the Yangtze, but it is wide... Anyway, to the younger Disciples of the Fire Gate Clan: if you ever go to India, wash yourselves in that Gan-whatever river first. Do not ask questions. Do not argue.
I was looking around when a mob of bald monks rushed over, shouted things I could not understand, and thrust swords at me. So I beat them senseless.
A Central Plains interpreter who happened to be passing by was horrified. He said they were from India’s Small Thunderclap Temple.
From the name, I had assumed they would be like the monks of Shaolin Temple. But these bald monks were violent beyond belief.
When more monks came with an even larger mob, I crippled every last one and burned down their strange-looking temples.
It was a fine sight.
Year xx, Month x, Day x. Songhak, Fifth Sect Leader of the Fire Gate Clan.
I have always held my Grandmaster, the Third Sect Leader, in the deepest respect. Following in his footsteps, I traveled the world and explored the Outer Murim.
I fought the Mad Wind Society of the great desert beyond the scorching sands, then visited the Potala Palace in Tibet and pulled out its pillars.
As a result, every man and beast in Tibet flew into a rage and chased after me.
But who am I? Songhak, the Ghost Flame Fist and Fifth Sect Leader of the great Fire Gate Clan.
Without suffering so much as a scratch, I... avoided them and returned safely to the Central Plains.
To whoever inherits the Fire Gate Clan’s true legacy in the distant future, remember this well.
If you face one hundred First Rate masters, fight them. If you face a thousand, unleash the Dance of the Fire God and Demon. If there are more than that, live to fight another day.
Of course, if you are stronger than I am, just fight them.
Ah, and if you go to that Gan-whatever river in India, jump in and wash yourself immediately. Wash yourself twice.
Year xx, Month x, Day x. Gu Jincheon, Ninth Sect Leader of the Fire Gate Clan.
I went to Nanman. I destroyed the Five Poisons Sect.
I went to Persia. I met people who wore things called turbans instead of hero headbands.
They were called Muslims, and they said they believed in a messenger and a prophet.
I said I wanted to meet the prophet, but they told me he was already dead. I could not understand this, so I asked several times. They drew their swords.
I had no choice but to send them to the prophet’s side.
Next was the Ice Palace in the North Sea. There was ice and water everywhere, so I turned back.
To the future Disciple reading this: you go.
Ah, and I learned the name of that Gan-whatever river. The Ganges River. If you go to India, make sure you wash yourself there first. Be sure to wash.
Year xx, Month x, Day x. Han Xin, Twelfth Sect Leader of the Fire Gate Clan.
This unworthy Disciple followed the records of his ancestors to India and went straight into the Ganges River.
As I washed my hair, I saw a corpse floating down from upstream.
I moved to another spot to wash my body and saw a turd float past.
When I went upstream, I found several hundred people throwing corpses into the river and taking shits.
For fuck’s sake, how could you pull this kind of bullshit on me?
They were unbelievable stories, even now.
I only had to skim through the records to see that whenever something displeased them, they smashed their way through anything and everything, whether in the Central Plains or the Outer Murim.
And telling their successors to bathe in the Ganges was like a sergeant about to be discharged writing “more field training” on a barracks survey out of pure spite.
The old you get fucked too mentality.

There were not many more records about the Outer Murim after his shit-water bath in the Ganges left the Twelfth Sect Leader royally pissed off. But once trade routes connecting the Central Plains to the outside world opened, information about the Murim beyond the Central Plains began to flow in.
The two factions Jeok Cheongang was now naming were the closest to the Central Plains, both geographically and in their dealings with it.
“The North Sea Ice Palace and the Nanman Beast Palace.”
Their names certainly made their respective locations and characters clear.
At Jeok Cheongang’s words, Mungyeong nodded with an infuriatingly bright smile.
“Yes, that’s right. My Master told me about them. He visited them long ago, and he said that, from what he saw, neither was inferior to the renowned great sects of the Central Plains.”
I’d bet everything Hyuk Mujin owned that he’d gone there to kill people.
The instant Jeok Cheongang and I exchanged similar looks, Mungyeong’s eyes slowly narrowed.
“Why are you looking at me like that?”
“...Huh? Oh, nothing.”
“Ahem. Nothing at all. Just what I’d expect of the Divine Physician, rushing wherever there are patients.”
I had to play along, of course. Jeok Cheongang had received considerable help from him too, so he was in the same position.
As if he had never done anything suspicious, Mungyeong returned to his medical-apprentice persona and continued.
“My Master said the Demonic Cult tried to recruit those two factions first during the Great Faction War. Is that true, Great Hero Jeok?”
“Hmm? Ah.”
Jeok Cheongang answered with a reluctant look.

“It is true. To the Demonic Cult, the wicked and unorthodox factions of the Central Plains were branches grown from the same root, so they naturally brought them into the fold. If the North Sea Ice Palace had accepted the Demonic Cult’s offer and moved south while the Nanman Beast Palace moved north, the Great Faction War would have taken a very difficult turn.”
But neither faction had taken the Demonic Cult’s hand.

The North Sea Ice Palace had declared itself cut off from the outside world, as it always had. The Nanman Beast Palace, geographically closer to the Central Plains, had weighed its options and sided with orthodox Murim.

“The Beast Palace bastards only meant to make a show of fighting at first, but later they were a great help. Each of the ferocious beasts they brought could do the work of several First Rate masters. And the Heavenly Eagles they’d trained with their secret methods caught the messenger eagles the Demonic Cult sent all over the land.”
The Nanman Beast Palace was practically the public enemy of modern-day animal lovers.
For ages, its people had captured and trained all sorts of creatures from Nanman’s jungles. They’d also developed and practiced martial arts modeled on the movements of ferocious beasts.
“Oh, wait. Didn’t you say you were close to someone over there?”
Jeok Cheongang frowned at my sudden question.
“Who?”
“The Palace Lord. The Palace Lord.”
“The Palace Lord? Ah, you mean the Beast Miao King?”
“Yes, him.”
The Beast Miao King was both the lowest-ranking and the most unusual of the Ten Kings.
He was the leader of the Miao people, who were native to Nanman, as well as the master of the Nanman Beast Palace, the region’s dominant power.

His achievements in the Great Faction War and his outstanding martial arts had earned him a place among the Ten Kings. But from the outside, the title looked almost like an honorary medal awarded to a foreigner. Perhaps that was why even people within Central Plains Murim were reluctant to mention him.
Why raise up some southern barbarian when we could just add another member of orthodox Murim?
That was supposedly where the claim that the Beast Miao King was overhyped had begun.
“I’ve met him a few times, that’s all,” Jeok Cheongang said.
“But I heard the Beast Miao King even came to pay his respects to you in person.”
“He did. In broad daylight, some dark-skinned fellow with his upper body bare showed up at my residence. I nearly hit him with a Flame Divine Palm.”
Mu Song had been standing awkwardly nearby for a while, looking anxious. Now his eyes widened.
“Is that really true?”
“Would this old man start making up lies at my age?”

“N-no, that’s not what I meant. I’m just surprised. My Master has mentioned the Beast Miao King too, but I heard he was short-tempered and arrogant, and that the Martial God was the only person he showed any courtesy to...”
“The Seafaring King? Has that young whelp gone senile already? The Beast Miao King didn’t show him courtesy because he’s a damn fool. Tsk, tsk.”
Jeok Cheongang clicked his tongue with an expression of utter disdain and continued.
“The Beast Miao King may look like that, but he knows when to show respect. If he were nothing but a brute with strength to spare, do you think the Miao people would have gathered under one banner?”
I had to nod at that.

Small and midsized sects with only a few dozen members disappeared for lack of Disciples all the time, only for others to spring up in their place. The Beast Miao King, meanwhile, was a chief who ruled at least several thousand Miao people.
“So?”
Jeok Cheongang stroked his glossy red beard.
“What do you mean, ‘so’? There was nothing special about it. He came to visit and spoke in a soft, ingratiating tone while bringing up a connection with the previous generation.”
“A connection between our predecessors?”
“Good grief, you ignorant little fool. You of all people should know!”
“Whoa. What’s wrong?”
Our Old Master had suddenly floored the accelerator and rocketed off.
After giving me a thorough scolding, Jeok Cheongang continued in an irritated voice.
“More than two hundred years ago, the Fifth Sect Leader of our sect destroyed Nanman’s Five Poisons Sect.”
“What does that have to... Ah, wait.”
“Back then, Nanman was like a cauldron standing on three legs. The Five Poisons Sect was the strongest, followed by the Nanman Beast Palace, then Poison Valley.”
“So when the Five Poisons Sect was destroyed, the Nanman Beast Palace rose to the top?”
“That’s right. It absorbed Poison Valley as well and took control of Nanman.”
“Wow, that’s insane. So that’s how it happened.”
“That’s why the Beast Miao King held goodwill toward our sect. It was also one reason he joined the Great Faction War. But did you just dare speak to me informally?”
“...I’ll correct myself. It just slipped out.”
I couldn’t help marveling at how the thuggish behavior of a Sect Leader from generations ago had paid off like this.
More importantly, the Beast Miao King was well disposed toward the Fire Gate Clan, and that was part of why he’d sided with orthodox Murim in the Great Faction War...
“Then there’s a good chance the Nanman Beast Palace will join this Murim Alliance.”
“I can’t say for sure. Even this old man cannot make an easy judgment about that. But if the Beast Miao King I remember is still the same, he will help orthodox Murim.”
“What about the North Sea Ice Palace?”
“If the envoy sent from Henan hasn’t frozen to death on the way, they’ll probably read the letter, at least. I wouldn’t get your hopes up.”
Jeok Cheongang’s seasoned gaze turned toward Mu Song.
“But our more urgent concern is right here. What will the Seafaring King do?”
Mu Song flinched. Then Mungyeong spoke quietly.
“There’s something I’ve been wanting to ask you for a while, Great Hero Mu Song.”
“Uh, yes?”
Mungyeong watched Mu Song’s trembling eyes in silence, then clicked his tongue.
“You know who I am, don’t you?”

The question didn’t trouble me for long.

The Murim outside the Murim.
Some people called the barbarians beyond the Great Wall built by an ancient emperor the Outer Lands, but Jeok Cheongang had always dismissed such talk with a snort.
Does the Great Wall surround the whole world?

The lands beneath the sky are boundlessly vast, and each has its own Murim.

Though their records read less like documents written for future generations and more like diaries written for their own satisfaction.
What a shock those had been.
I recalled a few I’d read in Fire Gate Cavern.
Year xx, Month x, Day x.
Cheonbong, Third Sect Leader of the Fire Gate Clan.
I had grown sick of the Central Plains.
War raged on all sides, and Murim was a complete mess.
So I went to India to broaden my horizons.
After a long journey, I arrived at a river called the Gan... something.
It is not as large as the Yangtze, but it is wide...
Anyway, to the younger Disciples of the Fire Gate Clan: if you ever go to India, wash yourselves in that Gan-whatever river first.
Do not ask questions.
Do not argue.
I was looking around when a mob of bald monks rushed over, shouted things I could not understand, and thrust swords at me.
So I beat them senseless.
A Central Plains interpreter who happened to be passing by was horrified.
He said they were from India’s Small Thunderclap Temple.
From the name, I had assumed they would be like the monks of Shaolin Temple.
But these bald monks were violent beyond belief.
When more monks came with an even larger mob, I crippled every last one and burned down their strange-looking temples.
It was a fine sight.
Year xx, Month x, Day x.
Songhak, Fifth Sect Leader of the Fire Gate Clan.
I have always held my Grandmaster, the Third Sect Leader, in the deepest respect.

I fought the Mad Wind Society of the great desert beyond the scorching sands, then visited the Potala Palace in Tibet and pulled out its pillars.
As a result, every man and beast in Tibet flew into a rage and chased after me.
But who am I?
Songhak, the Ghost Flame Fist and Fifth Sect Leader of the great Fire Gate Clan.
Without suffering so much as a scratch, I... avoided them and returned safely to the Central Plains.
To whoever inherits the Fire Gate Clan’s true legacy in the distant future, remember this well.
If you face one hundred First Rate masters, fight them.
If you face a thousand, unleash the Dance of the Fire God and Demon.
If there are more than that, live to fight another day.
Of course, if you are stronger than I am, just fight them.
Ah, and if you go to that Gan-whatever river in India, jump in and wash yourself immediately.
Wash yourself twice.
Year xx, Month x, Day x.
Gu Jincheon, Ninth Sect Leader of the Fire Gate Clan.
I went to Nanman.
I destroyed the Five Poisons Sect.
I went to Persia.
I met people who wore things called turbans instead of hero headbands.
They were called Muslims, and they said they believed in a messenger and a prophet.
I said I wanted to meet the prophet, but they told me he was already dead.
I could not understand this, so I asked several times.
They drew their swords.
I had no choice but to send them to the prophet’s side.
Next was the Ice Palace in the North Sea.
There was ice and water everywhere, so I turned back.
To the future Disciple reading this: you go.
Ah, and I learned the name of that Gan-whatever river.
The Ganges River.
If you go to India, make sure you wash yourself there first.
Be sure to wash.
Year xx, Month x, Day x.
Han Xin, Twelfth Sect Leader of the Fire Gate Clan.
This unworthy Disciple followed the records of his ancestors to India and went straight into the Ganges River.
As I washed my hair, I saw a corpse floating down from upstream.
I moved to another spot to wash my body and saw a turd float past.
When I went upstream, I found several hundred people throwing corpses into the river and taking shits.
For fuck’s sake, how could you pull this kind of bullshit on me?
They were unbelievable stories, even now.
I only had to skim through the records to see that whenever something displeased them, they smashed their way through anything and everything, whether in the Central Plains or the Outer Murim.
And telling their successors to bathe in the Ganges was like a sergeant about to be discharged writing “more field training” on a barracks survey out of pure spite.
The old you get fucked too mentality.
There were not many more records about the Outer Murim after his shit-water bath in the Ganges left the Twelfth Sect Leader royally pissed off.
But once trade routes connecting the Central Plains to the outside world opened, information about the Murim beyond the Central Plains began to flow in.

Their names certainly made their respective locations and characters clear.

“Yes, that’s right.
My Master told me about them.
He visited them long ago, and he said that, from what he saw, neither was inferior to the renowned great sects of the Central Plains.”
I’d bet everything Hyuk Mujin owned that he’d gone there to kill people.

chapters.title: Chapter 508
paragraphs: “You know who I am, don’t you?”
The air around us froze. I could hardly believe my ears, and Mu Song’s pupils trembled.
He stared at Mungyeong like he was about to wet himself, then squeezed out a hoarse reply.
“I-I don’t know anything.”
“Is that so?”
Mungyeong regarded him coolly.
“Then why are you speaking formally to me, Great Hero Mu Song?”
“You’re a fearless bastard, lying to my face.”
“Gasp!”
He’d walked right into that one. But how had Mu Song figured out who Mungyeong was?
No wonder he kept flinching like a dog that needed to shit.
From the way he’d been acting, Mu Song had known for some time. But given the level of martial arts I’d seen from him, that should have been nearly impossible.

Mungyeong had reached the realm of Returning to Simplicity and achieved Returned to Youth. To see through him, you’d need to be a master in a similar realm. At the very least, you’d have to be past the early stages of Supreme Peak to sense even the slightest thing amiss.
And Mu Song noticed?
No way. I’d sooner believe Hyuk Mujin had knocked Cheongpung down with one punch and sent three teeth flying.
While I was puzzling over it, Jeok Cheongang spoke in a bored tone.
“That’s enough. The fool kept his mouth shut, so he must have meant to pretend he didn’t know and let it pass. An old man threatening a child isn’t a pretty sight.”
“Old man? Threatening?”
Mungyeong snorted.
“Until yesterday, you were moping around like you could die any day. You get a little younger, and suddenly you’ve found your tongue. Stay out of this.”
“...What did you say?”
A deep furrow appeared on the forehead Returned to Youth had left smooth and wrinkle-free.
I hurried between them.
“Wait. Both of you, calm down. Calm down.”
“You, get out of the way.”
“Move.”
“Yes, sir.”
I slipped away without a moment’s hesitation. Mu Song, wedged between the two monsters like lettuce in a sandwich, shot me a pleading look.
Save me, or something like that.
But why should I get my guts burst in a fight between two whales?
I need to save myself first. Besides, they’re not about to have a life-and-death duel.
I was right. After glaring at each other in silence, Jeok Cheongang and Mungyeong lowered their auras at the same instant, as if they’d agreed to it.
“Hmph. I’ll let it go since you helped me.”
“What an ungrateful old man.”
They traded remarks like a pair of prim old men in a nursing home, then turned toward Mu Song. He had gone stiff as a statue.
“Come to think of it, you’re a remarkable fellow. How on earth did you know?”
I wanted to know that most of all. I watched Mu Song’s mouth, waiting for his answer, but it came from Mungyeong instead.
“It was them. The boatmen who came along when we went after the imugi. Or should I say the river bandits of Water Dragon Stronghold? Am I right?”
Mu Song swallowed.

“Y-yes, sir. They said the young medical apprentice named Mungyeong was actually a Supreme Peak master with formidable martial arts, and that his standing seemed high enough to treat even the Zhuge Family Head however he pleased...”
That happened without me knowing?
Well, it made sense. Mungyeong couldn’t have found me by running all over the vast Dongting Lake using Rising on Duckweed, Crossing Water.
So that’s how his identity got exposed.

Mungyeong had kept his true identity hidden for decades. Even after the Sichuan Blood Tragedy, apart from his Disciple, the Divine Physician, you could count the people who knew on one hand—including Jeok Cheongang and me.
Mu Song didn’t seem to have guessed he was the Slaughter Saint. Still, Mungyeong couldn’t be pleased that more people knew his secret.
Jeok Cheongang, of course, didn’t care. He looked ready to break out the popcorn.
“You stupid old man. You should’ve disguised yourself. Ha ha ha.”
“There was no time. Every moment counted while I was going to save your Disciple.”
“...Ahem. I do appreciate that.”
Jeok Cheongang stopped laughing dead. Mungyeong clicked his tongue softly and fixed his gaze on Mu Song.
“I clearly warned you through Sound Transmission, but it seems you have more loyal subordinates than I expected.”
“Gasp!”
Mu Song’s eyes widened at Mungyeong’s cold voice. The next moment, he shouted loudly enough to turn every head nearby—if a screen of internal energy hadn’t enclosed us.
“N-no, you can’t!”
“What can’t I do?”
“My subordinates have done nothing wrong! Take my head instead!”
“...Why would I kill you?”
Mu Song, Jeok Cheongang, and I all stared at him wide-eyed.
“What? Y-you won’t?”
“You’re not going to kill him?”
“That old man’s gone mad—wait. Can infirmities of old age spread to other people?”
Jeok Cheongang considered that for a moment, then cried out triumphantly.
“I’ve got it! Instead of killing him, you’re going to cripple his dantian or cut off a limb!”
Mungyeong looked at us, his eyes trembling, and muttered with regret, “You’re making me want to kill someone.”
Mu Song spoke, fear and resolve mingling on his face.
“My subordinates are innocent. Please, let me be enough—”
“Shut your damn mouth before I tear it apart.”
“Yes, sir.”
Mungyeong stared down at him in disbelief and sighed.
“Six, including you. Correct?”
“Y-yes, Senior. We’ve been together for many years, and they know how to keep their mouths shut.”
“I have never had a junior like you, and I am no longer a martial artist. But if you fail to keep them quiet, I can make all six of you disappear without leaving a trace.”
“If you want to live out your days in peace, keep your mouth shut forever. Don’t tell the Seafaring King. Don’t tell anyone. Understood?”
Mu Song pressed his lips together and gave a small nod. Mungyeong jerked his chin behind him.
“Go. Tell your subordinates to stay away from the stern until we reach Henan.”
“What?”
“Do you have another question?”
“N-no, sir. If you need anything, please call for me.”
Mu Song bowed and hurried away.
That left the three of us: Jeok Cheongang, Mungyeong, and me.
Jeok Cheongang smacked his lips in disappointment and poked me in the side.
“It would be more fun if that fool told everyone. Don’t you think?”
“In—cough.”
I hurriedly buried the rest of I agree in a cough.
Mungyeong was glaring our way, plainly not amused. He looked ready to grab the nearest easy target and beat him senseless for finding it funny.
“I didn’t say anything.”
“Neither did I. Feeling guilty about something?”
“No, I just thought I’d tell you that in advance.”
“And I was thinking of giving you a beating in advance.”
“I really didn’t mean anything.”
“I heard ‘in.’ What came after it?”
Panicking would only make this worse. I answered calmly.
“I meant, ‘Admittedly, I have a conscience. How could I do such a thing?’”
“That didn’t sound like it.”
“It’s true.”
“No, it isn’t.”
“It is. Why are you playing Gung Ye?”
Mungyeong didn’t know who Gung Ye was, but he could tell it wasn’t a compliment. I did my best to ignore his chilling gaze and changed the subject.
“Why did you tell them to stay away from the stern?”
“Don’t change the subject.”
That shut me up.
Mungyeong clicked his tongue at my awkward silence.
“You’ve done well raising this one as your Disciple.”
Jeok Cheongang had been watching with his arms folded, as though none of this concerned him. He let out a quiet laugh.
“It’s because he’s like this that I raised him.”
“This ill-mannered brat?”
“Is that what you think? I thought we were close enough to dispense with formalities. Perhaps we see things differently. Or perhaps someone’s trying hard to ignore that thought.”
Mungyeong looked silently from Jeok Cheongang to me and back.
“...You’re quite the smooth talker. Returned to Youth, and it’s your mouth that’s gained the most vigor.”
I had no idea what they were talking about.
As I stood there trying to follow the conversation, Jeok Cheongang pushed himself away from the swift ship’s wooden railing.
“I’m going into the cabin. I’m sick of looking at this goddamn river.”
“Wow, what a wonderful idea. Are you sure your surname isn’t Zhuge instead of Jeok?”
That was the best thing I’d heard all day. But when I took a step after him, Jeok Cheongang put out a hand to stop me.
Tap.
“Huh?”
“What do you mean, ‘huh’? Why are you following me?”
“You said you were going to the cabin.”
“So?”
“I was just about to go there myself.”
“Two men in that cramped cabin?”
“It’s a five-person cabin. Where’s your conscience—”
“I’m going to circulate my qi and sort through the enlightenment I’ve gained recently. You don’t need to come.”
“Oh, you’re going to circulate your qi. Then I’ll stand guard—”
“No need. Stay here.”
“What?”
Jeok Cheongang snapped.
“I said stay here!”
“Whoa, you startled me. Why are you shouting?”
“Quiet. Follow me and you’ll be sorry!”
I stared after him, bewildered. Then I felt someone’s gaze prickling at me and turned.
Mungyeong’s stare was drier than the sand by the Sphinx’s forepaws.
Fuck. I should’ve followed him.
What did I care if Jeok Cheongang gave me hell or rang a bell? I’d rather jump into the vast Yangtze than be left alone with a man who might cut off my head—
“The river looks unusually clear today. Don’t you want to go in?”
“What?”
What the hell? Could he read minds? Was he really Gung Ye?
A suspicion flashed through my head, and I found myself looking around for a palace guard with a mace.
That was when—
Whoom!
A mace swung at me.
No. It was a single, swift, stealthy wave of palm force.

I hastily crossed both arms to block it when the sound of splitting air pierced my ears, but the palm force fired by a once-in-an-age master known as the Slaughter Saint was not something I could block so easily.
Boom!
Fuck, that really does feel like a mace.
Pain throbbed in my chest as I flew off the swift ship. Just before I hit the river, I twisted my body, sent the internal energy in my lower dantian into my legs, and stepped onto the water.
Splash!
The calm surface splashed violently, as though I’d stepped into a puddle.
Standing on the water with Rising on Duckweed, Crossing Water, I glared at Mungyeong in disbelief.
“What are you doing all of a sudden?”
“The calm river’s been disturbed.”
“What are you—huh?”
“Your movements are so rough, you might stir up a storm.”

sentences.text: “You know who I am, don’t you?”
The air around us froze.
I could hardly believe my ears, and Mu Song’s pupils trembled.
He stared at Mungyeong like he was about to wet himself, then squeezed out a hoarse reply.
“I-I don’t know anything.”
“Is that so?”
Mungyeong regarded him coolly.
“Then why are you speaking formally to me, Great Hero Mu Song?”
“You’re a fearless bastard, lying to my face.”
“Gasp!”
He’d walked right into that one.
But how had Mu Song figured out who Mungyeong was?
No wonder he kept flinching like a dog that needed to shit.
From the way he’d been acting, Mu Song had known for some time.
But given the level of martial arts I’d seen from him, that should have been nearly impossible.
Mungyeong had reached the realm of Returning to Simplicity and achieved Returned to Youth.
To see through him, you’d need to be a master in a similar realm.
At the very least, you’d have to be past the early stages of Supreme Peak to sense even the slightest thing amiss.
And Mu Song noticed?
No way.
I’d sooner believe Hyuk Mujin had knocked Cheongpung down with one punch and sent three teeth flying.
While I was puzzling over it, Jeok Cheongang spoke in a bored tone.
“That’s enough.
The fool kept his mouth shut, so he must have meant to pretend he didn’t know and let it pass.
An old man threatening a child isn’t a pretty sight.”
“Old man?
Threatening?”
Mungyeong snorted.
“Until yesterday, you were moping around like you could die any day.
You get a little younger, and suddenly you’ve found your tongue.
Stay out of this.”
“...What did you say?”
A deep furrow appeared on the forehead Returned to Youth had left smooth and wrinkle-free.
I hurried between them.
“Wait.
Both of you, calm down.
Calm down.”
“You, get out of the way.”
“Move.”
“Yes, sir.”
I slipped away without a moment’s hesitation.
Mu Song, wedged between the two monsters like lettuce in a sandwich, shot me a pleading look.
Save me, or something like that.
But why should I get my guts burst in a fight between two whales?
I need to save myself first.
Besides, they’re not about to have a life-and-death duel.
I was right.
After glaring at each other in silence, Jeok Cheongang and Mungyeong lowered their auras at the same instant, as if they’d agreed to it.
“Hmph.
I’ll let it go since you helped me.”
“What an ungrateful old man.”
They traded remarks like a pair of prim old men in a nursing home, then turned toward Mu Song.
He had gone stiff as a statue.
“Come to think of it, you’re a remarkable fellow.
How on earth did you know?”
I wanted to know that most of all.
I watched Mu Song’s mouth, waiting for his answer, but it came from Mungyeong instead.
“It was them.
The boatmen who came along when we went after the imugi.
Or should I say the river bandits of Water Dragon Stronghold?
Am I right?”
Mu Song swallowed.
“Y-yes, sir.

They said the young medical apprentice named Mungyeong was actually a Supreme Peak master with formidable martial arts, and that his standing seemed high enough to treat even the Zhuge Family Head however he pleased...”
That happened without me knowing?
Well, it made sense.
Mungyeong couldn’t have found me by running all over the vast Dongting Lake using Rising on Duckweed, Crossing Water.
So that’s how his identity got exposed.
Mungyeong had kept his true identity hidden for decades.
Even after the Sichuan Blood Tragedy, apart from his Disciple, the Divine Physician, you could count the people who knew on one hand—including Jeok Cheongang and me.
Mu Song didn’t seem to have guessed he was the Slaughter Saint.
Still, Mungyeong couldn’t be pleased that more people knew his secret.
Jeok Cheongang, of course, didn’t care.
He looked ready to break out the popcorn.
“You stupid old man.
You should’ve disguised yourself.
Ha ha ha.”
“There was no time.
Every moment counted while I was going to save your Disciple.”
“...Ahem.
I do appreciate that.”
Jeok Cheongang stopped laughing dead.
Mungyeong clicked his tongue softly and fixed his gaze on Mu Song.
“I clearly warned you through Sound Transmission, but it seems you have more loyal subordinates than I expected.”
“Gasp!”
Mu Song’s eyes widened at Mungyeong’s cold voice.
The next moment, he shouted loudly enough to turn every head nearby—if a screen of internal energy hadn’t enclosed us.
“N-no, you can’t!”
“What can’t I do?”
“My subordinates have done nothing wrong!
Take my head instead!”
“...Why would I kill you?”
Mu Song, Jeok Cheongang, and I all stared at him wide-eyed.
“What?
Y-you won’t?”
“You’re not going to kill him?”
“That old man’s gone mad—wait.
Can infirmities of old age spread to other people?”
Jeok Cheongang considered that for a moment, then cried out triumphantly.
“I’ve got it!
Instead of killing him, you’re going to cripple his dantian or cut off a limb!”
Mungyeong looked at us, his eyes trembling, and muttered with regret, “You’re making me want to kill someone.”
Mu Song spoke, fear and resolve mingling on his face.
“My subordinates are innocent.
Please, let me be enough—”
“Shut your damn mouth before I tear it apart.”
“Yes, sir.”
Mungyeong stared down at him in disbelief and sighed.
“Six, including you.
Correct?”
“Y-yes, Senior.
We’ve been together for many years, and they know how to keep their mouths shut.”
“I have never had a junior like you, and I am no longer a martial artist.
But if you fail to keep them quiet, I can make all six of you disappear without leaving a trace.”
“If you want to live out your days in peace, keep your mouth shut forever.
Don’t tell the Seafaring King.
Don’t tell anyone.
Understood?”
Mu Song pressed his lips together and gave a small nod.
Mungyeong jerked his chin behind him.
“Go.
Tell your subordinates to stay away from the stern until we reach Henan.”
“What?”
“Do you have another question?”
“N-no, sir.
If you need anything, please call for me.”
Mu Song bowed and hurried away.
That left the three of us: Jeok Cheongang, Mungyeong, and me.
Jeok Cheongang smacked his lips in disappointment and poked me in the side.
“It would be more fun if that fool told everyone.
Don’t you think?”
“In—cough.”
I hurriedly buried the rest of I agree in a cough.
Mungyeong was glaring our way, plainly not amused.
He looked ready to grab the nearest easy target and beat him senseless for finding it funny.
“I didn’t say anything.”
“Neither did I.
Feeling guilty about something?”
“No, I just thought I’d tell you that in advance.”
“And I was thinking of giving you a beating in advance.”
“I really didn’t mean anything.”
“I heard ‘in.’ What came after it?”
Panicking would only make this worse.
I answered calmly.
“I meant, ‘Admittedly, I have a conscience.
How could I do such a thing?’”
“That didn’t sound like it.”
“It’s true.”
“No, it isn’t.”
“It is.
Why are you playing Gung Ye?”
Mungyeong didn’t know who Gung Ye was, but he could tell it wasn’t a compliment.
I did my best to ignore his chilling gaze and changed the subject.
“Why did you tell them to stay away from the stern?”
“Don’t change the subject.”
That shut me up.
Mungyeong clicked his tongue at my awkward silence.
“You’ve done well raising this one as your Disciple.”
Jeok Cheongang had been watching with his arms folded, as though none of this concerned him.
He let out a quiet laugh.
“It’s because he’s like this that I raised him.”
“This ill-mannered brat?”
“Is that what you think?
I thought we were close enough to dispense with formalities.
Perhaps we see things differently.
Or perhaps someone’s trying hard to ignore that thought.”
Mungyeong looked silently from Jeok Cheongang to me and back.
“...You’re quite the smooth talker.
Returned to Youth, and it’s your mouth that’s gained the most vigor.”
I had no idea what they were talking about.
As I stood there trying to follow the conversation, Jeok Cheongang pushed himself away from the swift ship’s wooden railing.
“I’m going into the cabin.
I’m sick of looking at this goddamn river.”
“Wow, what a wonderful idea.
Are you sure your surname isn’t Zhuge instead of Jeok?”
That was the best thing I’d heard all day.
But when I took a step after him, Jeok Cheongang put out a hand to stop me.
Tap.
“Huh?”
“What do you mean, ‘huh’?
Why are you following me?”
“You said you were going to the cabin.”
“So?”
“I was just about to go there myself.”
“Two men in that cramped cabin?”
“It’s a five-person cabin.
Where’s your conscience—”
“I’m going to circulate my qi and sort through the enlightenment I’ve gained recently.
You don’t need to come.”
“Oh, you’re going to circulate your qi.
Then I’ll stand guard—”
“No need.
Stay here.”
“What?”
Jeok Cheongang snapped.
“I said stay here!”
“Whoa, you startled me.
Why are you shouting?”
“Quiet.
Follow me and you’ll be sorry!”
I stared after him, bewildered.
Then I felt someone’s gaze prickling at me and turned.
Mungyeong’s stare was drier than the sand by the Sphinx’s forepaws.
Fuck.
I should’ve followed him.
What did I care if Jeok Cheongang gave me hell or rang a bell?
I’d rather jump into the vast Yangtze than be left alone with a man who might cut off my head—
“The river looks unusually clear today.
Don’t you want to go in?”
“What?”
What the hell?
Could he read minds?
Was he really Gung Ye?
A suspicion flashed through my head, and I found myself looking around for a palace guard with a mace.
That was when—
Whoom!
A mace swung at me.
No.
It was a single, swift, stealthy wave of palm force.

I hastily crossed both arms to block it when the sound of splitting air pierced my ears, but the palm force fired by a once-in-an-age master known as the Slaughter Saint was not something I could block so easily.
Boom!
Fuck, that really does feel like a mace.
Pain throbbed in my chest as I flew off the swift ship.
Just before I hit the river, I twisted my body, sent the internal energy in my lower dantian into my legs, and stepped onto the water.
Splash!
The calm surface splashed violently, as though I’d stepped into a puddle.
Standing on the water with Rising on Duckweed, Crossing Water, I glared at Mungyeong in disbelief.
“What are you doing all of a sudden?”
“The calm river’s been disturbed.”
“What are you—huh?”
“Your movements are so rough, you might stir up a storm.”
Before I could say another word, Mungyeong clicked his tongue and went on.
“Then... it’s time to begin.”
Ding!
System Linked Quest Fake Murim Martial Artist—Stage 2 has begun!

chapters.title: Chapter 509
paragraphs: Ding.
System Linked Quest Fake Murim Martial Artist—Stage 2 has begun! - This Quest will proceed regardless of whether you accept it! - Quest forcibly accepted!
What the fuck?
My thoughts must have shown on my face. Mungyeong’s eyebrows twitched as he looked at me.
“I clearly told you there would be another training session. Don’t tell me you forgot?”
“Excuse me?”
Forgot? Is he messing with me right now?
Dumbfounded, I looked back at Mungyeong.
“How could I forget after shitting blood so many times? Even thinking about it makes my asshole twitch.”
“...I understand. Stop there. That’s disgusting.”
“Ha. Seriously.”
The head might forget, but the asshole—no, the body—remembered.
Even now, whenever I closed my eyes, memories of shitting blood day and night came flooding back.
To exaggerate a little, if all the bloody liquid I’d passed over the past seven days and nights were collected in a tub, every mosquito in Hubei Province could gather for a feast.
It was horrible.
Some memories wouldn’t go away no matter how hard I tried to forget them. The Linked Quest the System had announced on the day of my last duel with Mungyeong was no different.
It hadn’t been long ago, and it was far too important to forget. I’d have to be out of my mind.
“Anyway, I haven’t forgotten. I remember every single thing you said back then.”
“Is that so?”
Mungyeong studied me.
“Then your reaction makes even less sense. I even warned you in advance. Why do you look as though someone just hit you in the back of the head?”
Because that’s exactly how it feels.
I knew another training session was coming, but I’d been certain it wouldn’t happen right now.
There was only so much he could teach me aboard this swift ship, which was even narrower than an ordinary vessel.
At most, a cultivation technique?
But a cultivation technique, the foundation of martial arts and internal energy, was not something that could be swapped out as easily as a machine part.
Especially not in my case.

The Fire Gate Divine Technique was the very root of the Fire Gate Clan. It transformed the nature of our internal energy into fire qi and amplified its power, so the cultivation technique played a far greater role in our martial arts than it did in those of other sects.
Mungyeong of all people had to know that, but I asked just in case.
“Um, you’re not planning to teach me a cultivation technique, are you?”
Whoosh! Slash!
I turned my head at the sound of the wind. A throwing blade shot past like a streak of light, missing my neck by a hair before slicing through the river behind me.
“...I heard your answer loud and clear.”
“Don’t waste my time with that kind of nonsense.”
“Of course. I was just asking on the off chance.”
Then what is it? Another poison-tasting session?
Foreboding and curiosity struck at once, but I put both aside for the moment. Not for any particular reason—Mungyeong had simply grown much farther away while we talked.
Whoosh!
The favorable wind and the waterway men’s sailing experience certainly helped, but the swift ship was several notches faster than an ordinary vessel.
We’d barely exchanged a few words, yet he was already that far away. I almost wondered whether the bastards from the Yangtze River Channel League had installed a motor.
Damn, it’s fast.
Even a model student who routinely came first in the entire school was bound to have one weak subject. Mine was movement techniques.

As befitted a Supreme Peak master, I could keep up using Rising on Duckweed, Crossing Water, but I wasn’t used to it, and it consumed a considerable amount of internal energy. Unlike on Dongting Lake last time, there was nothing here for me to step on, either.
“I’ll climb aboard first and listen. I can’t stay out here like this.”
Mungyeong nodded readily.
“Do that.”
“You’re not going to throw a hidden weapon at me as a surprise, are you?”
“I said I understand. Stop talking nonsense and come up.”
“Yes, sir.”
I concentrated the internal energy I’d drawn up in my toes.
The greatest advantage of the Fire Gate Divine Technique was the explosive force it could produce. One leap would be more than enough to get me back onto the swift ship.
One, two.
Now.
Bang!
The internal energy released from my toes slammed into the water. The river surged upward like a massive wall from the shockwave, and a fierce wind swept across my entire body.
In a moment so brief it could not even be called an instant, I covered over a hundred feet and landed on the stern of the swift ship—
Thwack!
What the fuck?
I went flying back even faster than I’d approached. I hurriedly sent internal energy into the soles of my feet and flipped myself around.
I’d been plunging headfirst toward the river, but I regained my balance just in time to stand on its surface.
What is this, déjà vu?
I looked at Mungyeong, who stood tall on the stern, with a thoroughly displeased expression.
“What was that just now?”
“What was what?”
“That thing in your hand. You hit me with it.”
“Oh, this.”
Mungyeong waved the large object he was holding.
“This is an oar. It’s mainly used to row a boat.”
“I wasn’t asking because I didn’t know that.”
“I thought you were.”
“Didn’t you promise not to do anything strange?”
“To be precise, I said I wouldn’t throw a hidden weapon. This isn’t a hidden weapon.”
“Oh, I see. You used a lethal weapon instead of a hidden weapon.”
“Something like that.”
Is he insane? Seriously.
Mungyeong stared at me with a profound gaze. No—with a profound gaze at the water rippling around me.
“The Yangtze River is still calm, yet chaos breaks out wherever your feet touch.”
“If you keep pulling stunts like this, I’ll be the one making a scene. Seriously.”
“Do you know why it happens to you in particular?”
“I don’t, but why are you doing this?”
Mungyeong ignored my question.
“It isn’t because your movements are clumsy and rough.”
“You’re making my personality rough.”

“Every movement a master of a certain realm makes has its own reason and purpose. In your case, the cause is your internal energy itself. It’s too violent. This is one of the longstanding problems with the Fire Gate Clan’s martial arts.”
“Ah, now I’m pissed. I’ll climb aboard again, so put down that oar first and—”
I stopped mid-sentence.
This wasn’t just Mungyeong being spiteful or playing a prank.
“Wait. What did you just say?”
“So your ears do work. I said the reason your movements are rough on the water is a longstanding problem with the Fire Gate Clan’s martial arts.”
A longstanding problem...
I couldn’t brush that off.
After a moment’s thought, I asked, “What does that have to do with Rising on Duckweed, Crossing Water? I’m just clumsy because I’m not used to it. Aren’t you judging too quickly?”
“You fool. It isn’t that simple.”
“You mean...”
“The stability and precision of your internal energy.”
“Stability and precision...”

“Rising on Duckweed, Crossing Water is one measure of those qualities. The more stable and precise your internal energy, the more freely you can perform it. It’s an advanced movement technique, but a Peak master with deep enough attainment can use it without much difficulty.”
Mungyeong continued without pause, then suddenly leaped down from the stern.
He was far enough away that an ordinary person wouldn’t have been able to make out his face. But my senses were keen enough to see and hear him clearly.
Softly, he landed on the water, as light as air. Not a ripple rose around him. It was as though nothing had happened.
Mungyeong turned his dry gaze on me.
“And you?”
I instinctively lowered my head and looked at the water beneath my feet. But I already knew what I would see.
The path I’d taken chasing the swift ship was covered in white foam, as though another boat had passed through it.
Splash.
I took a cautious step. Dozens of ripples spread out from it, overlapping one another.
Even compared with Mungyeong, the difference was too great.
“You seem to know the answer yourself.”
I might have felt less embarrassed if he’d sounded scornful. Instead, his flat voice seemed to say, Yes, that’s about your level. My face burned.
“Do you understand what I meant now?”
“...I think I understand it to some extent.”
As Mungyeong had said, Rising on Duckweed, Crossing Water was an important measure of the stability and precision of one’s internal energy.
Depending on how well you distributed and controlled your power, the water beneath your feet could churn as though caught in a storm or remain as calm as a deserted lakeshore.
“Then tell me what you should gain from this. In your own words.”
“Hmm. I’ll be able to use my internal energy more efficiently.”
“I don’t like that answer.”
“I’ll gain stability and precision, and I’ll be able to produce the same amount of force while using less internal energy.”
“A little better. Still not enough.”
Each second seemed to stretch into a minute as I thought it over. Then the answer came to me.
“Amplification.”
“Explain further.”
“What I’ve said so far would let me apply the right amount of force where and when I need it. If I can control my internal energy that precisely... I can amplify it more than I do now, too.”
“So?”
“This isn’t just about stability and precision. The martial arts I’ve learned will become more powerful. Am I right?”
Mungyeong stared at me in silence before tossing out a single remark.
“...You’re not a complete idiot.”
That’s it. I got it right.
But the strange thrill I felt wasn’t from winning a little praise from Mungyeong.
If I can complete this training successfully, I can become stronger than I am now.
I’d hit a kind of stagnation. Maybe I’d grown too quickly. After advancing by leaps and bounds, my martial arts had stopped progressing, and I could feel a high wall blocking my path.
But with this training, I could improve my technique even without gaining some new enlightenment.
So I still had plenty of room to grow without enlightenment.
When had I started thinking about it all wrong? I hadn’t tried to fill the space I already had. I’d just kept wanting something newer and greater.
What a stupid thing to do.
It was like owning a one-terabyte external hard drive, filling only five hundred gigabytes of it with porn, then whining that I was out of space.
Mungyeong had shown me that I still had another five hundred gigabytes for porn—no, that I still had room to fill. No need to buy another external hard drive when the first one wasn’t full.
Ah, Great Lord Mun.
A halo seemed to shine behind Mungyeong’s shoulder.
At the sight of my eyes brimming with those feelings, Mungyeong opened his mouth.
“Keep your eyes straight ahead before I gouge them out.”
“...Ah, yes.”
“Anyway, you seem to have finally grasped the general idea.”
“Yes. I think I get it.”
“Then you must know what training you need to do now.”
Of course I did. I gave the answer I’d been expecting.
“Rising on Duckweed, Crossing Water. Am I right?”
“Yes. Better to experience it yourself than hear and think about it a hundred times. The Yangtze is the perfect place, so start now.”
So that was why he’d knocked me into the water without warning. He must have planned this from the beginning.
But I wasn’t annoyed or resentful. You couldn’t gain anything without paying a price.
It’s a little daunting with nothing but river around me, but I’ll get used to it if I keep practicing.
I answered without hesitation.
“Understood.”
“You’re more obedient than I expected. Keep that attitude.”
“Yes.”
If it meant becoming stronger than I was now, what wouldn’t I do?
I bowed to Mungyeong. Then I realized I’d forgotten the most important question.
“Um, by the way.”
“Hmm?”
“How long do I have to do this?”
“What a foolish question.”
Mungyeong spread both hands as though the answer were obvious.
Ten stars... no, ten shichen?
“W-wait. Even for me, ten shichen is impossible. I have to keep up with the swift ship using Rising on Duckweed, Crossing Water. You know how much internal energy that’ll take—”
“What are you talking about? Ten days.”
“Excuse me?”
“Not ten shichen. Ten days. Follow me the entire way until we reach Henan.”
“...Excuse me?”
As I froze in place, a familiar notification rang in my ears.
Ding.

System The training method for Fake Murim Martial Artist—Stage 2 has been newly established! - The Instructor has set the training period to 10 days! This period may become shorter or longer depending on how long it takes to reach the destination! - The countdown begins now! Hang in there—argh! Time limit: 9 days 23 hours 59 minutes 59 seconds.
Fuck. I have no words.
