“If you keep pulling stunts like this, I’ll be the one making a scene.
Seriously.”
“Do you know why it happens to you in particular?”
“I don’t, but why are you doing this?”
Mungyeong ignored my question.
“It isn’t because your movements are clumsy and rough.”
“You’re making my personality rough.”
“Every movement a master of a certain realm makes has its own reason and purpose.
In your case, the cause is your internal energy itself.
It’s too violent.
This is one of the longstanding problems with the Fire Gate Clan’s martial arts.”
“Ah, now I’m pissed.
I’ll climb aboard again, so put down that oar first and—”
I stopped mid-sentence.
This wasn’t just Mungyeong being spiteful or playing a prank.
“Wait.
What did you just say?”
“So your ears do work.
I said the reason your movements are rough on the water is a longstanding problem with the Fire Gate Clan’s martial arts.”
A longstanding problem...
I couldn’t brush that off.
After a moment’s thought, I asked, “What does that have to do with Rising on Duckweed, Crossing Water?
I’m just clumsy because I’m not used to it.
Aren’t you judging too quickly?”
“You fool.
It isn’t that simple.”
“You mean...”
“The stability and precision of your internal energy.”
“Stability and precision...”
“Rising on Duckweed, Crossing Water is one measure of those qualities.
The more stable and precise your internal energy, the more freely you can perform it.
It’s an advanced movement technique, but a Peak master with deep enough attainment can use it without much difficulty.”
Mungyeong continued without pause, then suddenly leaped down from the stern.
He was far enough away that an ordinary person wouldn’t have been able to make out his face.
But my senses were keen enough to see and hear him clearly.
Softly, he landed on the water, as light as air.
Not a ripple rose around him.
It was as though nothing had happened.
Mungyeong turned his dry gaze on me.
“And you?”
I instinctively lowered my head and looked at the water beneath my feet.
But I already knew what I would see.
The path I’d taken chasing the swift ship was covered in white foam, as though another boat had passed through it.
Splash.
I took a cautious step.
Dozens of ripples spread out from it, overlapping one another.
Even compared with Mungyeong, the difference was too great.
“You seem to know the answer yourself.”
I might have felt less embarrassed if he’d sounded scornful.
Instead, his flat voice seemed to say, Yes, that’s about your level.
My face burned.
“Do you understand what I meant now?”
“...I think I understand it to some extent.”
As Mungyeong had said, Rising on Duckweed, Crossing Water was an important measure of the stability and precision of one’s internal energy.
Depending on how well you distributed and controlled your power, the water beneath your feet could churn as though caught in a storm or remain as calm as a deserted lakeshore.
“Then tell me what you should gain from this.
In your own words.”
“Hmm.
I’ll be able to use my internal energy more efficiently.”
“I don’t like that answer.”
“I’ll gain stability and precision, and I’ll be able to produce the same amount of force while using less internal energy.”
“A little better.
Still not enough.”
Each second seemed to stretch into a minute as I thought it over.
Then the answer came to me.
“Amplification.”
“Explain further.”
“What I’ve said so far would let me apply the right amount of force where and when I need it.
If I can control my internal energy that precisely...
I can amplify it more than I do now, too.”
“So?”
“This isn’t just about stability and precision.
The martial arts I’ve learned will become more powerful.
Am I right?”
Mungyeong stared at me in silence before tossing out a single remark.
“...You’re not a complete idiot.”
That’s it.
I got it right.
But the strange thrill I felt wasn’t from winning a little praise from Mungyeong.
If I can complete this training successfully, I can become stronger than I am now.
I’d hit a kind of stagnation.
Maybe I’d grown too quickly.
After advancing by leaps and bounds, my martial arts had stopped progressing, and I could feel a high wall blocking my path.
But with this training, I could improve my technique even without gaining some new enlightenment.
So I still had plenty of room to grow without enlightenment.
When had I started thinking about it all wrong?
I hadn’t tried to fill the space I already had.
I’d just kept wanting something newer and greater.
What a stupid thing to do.
It was like owning a one-terabyte external hard drive, filling only five hundred gigabytes of it with porn, then whining that I was out of space.
Mungyeong had shown me that I still had another five hundred gigabytes for porn—no, that I still had room to fill.
No need to buy another external hard drive when the first one wasn’t full.
Ah, Great Lord Mun.
A halo seemed to shine behind Mungyeong’s shoulder.
At the sight of my eyes brimming with those feelings, Mungyeong opened his mouth.
“Keep your eyes straight ahead before I gouge them out.”
“...Ah, yes.”
“Anyway, you seem to have finally grasped the general idea.”
“Yes.
I think I get it.”
“Then you must know what training you need to do now.”
Of course I did.
I gave the answer I’d been expecting.
“Rising on Duckweed, Crossing Water.
Am I right?”
“Yes.
Better to experience it yourself than hear and think about it a hundred times.
The Yangtze is the perfect place, so start now.”
So that was why he’d knocked me into the water without warning.
He must have planned this from the beginning.
But I wasn’t annoyed or resentful.
You couldn’t gain anything without paying a price.
It’s a little daunting with nothing but river around me, but I’ll get used to it if I keep practicing.
I answered without hesitation.
“Understood.”
“You’re more obedient than I expected.
Keep that attitude.”
“Yes.”
If it meant becoming stronger than I was now, what wouldn’t I do?
I bowed to Mungyeong.
Then I realized I’d forgotten the most important question.
“Um, by the way.”
“Hmm?”
“How long do I have to do this?”
“What a foolish question.”
Mungyeong spread both hands as though the answer were obvious.
Ten stars... no, ten shichen?
“W-wait.
Even for me, ten shichen is impossible.
I have to keep up with the swift ship using Rising on Duckweed, Crossing Water.
You know how much internal energy that’ll take—”
“What are you talking about?
Ten days.”
“Excuse me?”
“Not ten shichen.
Ten days.
Follow me the entire way until we reach Henan.”
“...Excuse me?”
As I froze in place, a familiar notification rang in my ears.
Ding.
System The training method for Fake Murim Martial Artist—Stage 2 has been newly established! - The Instructor has set the training period to 10 days!
This period may become shorter or longer depending on how long it takes to reach the destination! - The countdown begins now!
Hang in there—argh!
Time limit: 9 days 23 hours 59 minutes 59 seconds.
Fuck.
I have no words.

chapters.title: Chapter 510
paragraphs: Ship-Fire Boy Mu Song had been a sailor from birth.

His parents, whose faces he could no longer remember, had been a pair of river bandits famous in the area for being inseparable. Both sides of his family were full of river bandits and fishermen, too.
River banditry ran deep in his blood.
Maybe that was why Mu Song much preferred being aboard a boat to being on land.

Dense forests and open fields made his hands and feet tingle and left him short of breath, as though he had swallowed deadly poison. But the sight of a wide-open river or sea brought him back to life.

And that wasn’t all. While other stronghold lords who had made fortunes as river bandits bought grand estates and indulged in wine, women, and gambling at pleasure houses, Mu Song decorated his boat, lay on a bed woven from nets, and watched the Yangtze.
Whenever he did, he had the same thought.
I wish the whole world were made of water. Then I could spend my entire life on a boat.
But now, Mu Song was staring blankly at the Yangtze and muttering to himself.
“Ah, fuck. This boat is fucking slow. I want to get off already...”
The mood turned icy.
The nearby Water Dragon Stronghold river bandits doubted their ears. They rolled their eyes toward one another, exchanged glances, and soon reached an obvious conclusion.
We must have heard wrong!
That’s it. All our ears must have gone bad at once.
The Stronghold Lord would never say that.
Everyone in the Yangtze River Channel League knew what kind of man Mu Song was, from the most senior Water Dragon Stronghold river bandit to the youngest recruit.
The very embodiment of a passionate sailor! A man who loved the Yangtze even more than his Master, the Seafaring King!
There was no way a man like that would curse the swift ship he treasured as much as his own life for being slow and say he wanted to go ashore—
“I should quit this whole damn business. Fuck this.”
An invisible shock swept across the deck. Mu Song’s sudden talk of retirement left everyone silent, faced with the prospect of Water Dragon Stronghold itself disbanding.
The silence might have gone on forever if a liquor barrel hadn’t slipped from a dazed river bandit’s shoulder.
Thud! Crack!
Full of liquor, it was heavy enough to shatter when it struck the deck. Alcohol splashed everywhere.
Only then did Mu Song snap out of his thoughts. He glared.
“What the hell are you doing?”
Mu Song already had a fearsome face. The river bandit who had dropped the barrel went pale and bent sharply at the waist.
“I-I’m sorry!”

“You bastard. You don’t know the value of liquor? I ought to hang you upside down and... What was it? The Yangtze, the Yangtze... Right. I might just sentence you to the Yangtze’s dip-and-taste punishment.”
“I deserve to die. Please, anything but that...”
“Watch yourself. I’m in a shitty enough mood without you making it worse.”
“Yes, sir!”
“Enough. Clean this up and put everything back the way it was. Bring another barrel of liquor, too.”
“Pardon? But...”
“Are you insane? How dare you talk back? Get moving!”
“A-at once, sir!”
As the subordinate hurried away, shouting frantic acknowledgments, Mu Song let out a deep sigh.
Nothing is going right.
It wasn’t just a complaint. Nothing was going right.
Even good fortune would not have been enough to make up for it, yet one bad thing after another kept happening.
He had reluctantly left his home base in Sichuan for Hubei. Not long ago, he had also had to part with Hwang Chung, the Yangtze One Saber, who had been like family to him.
Thinking he had to repay the gratitude and grudges he owed Hwang Chung, Mu Song had agreed to take Jin Taekyung’s group as far as Henan. And sure enough, the worst had happened.
I was going to keep pretending I didn’t know.
An unidentified old master who had clearly achieved Returned to Youth.
That beast wearing the guise of a young medical apprentice had realized that his identity had been exposed.
That monstrous old man. Who the hell is he?
From what Mu Song had observed, very few people in the traveling party knew the truth. The Fire King, Jeok Cheongang, and Jin Taekyung, at most?
Cheongpung was impossible to predict, but even he quieted down in front of Mungyeong. Chances were he knew, too.
Damn it. If I’d known this would happen, I should’ve taken the other ship.

Water Dragon Stronghold had two swift ships heading toward Henan. Jeok Cheongang had insisted on splitting the passengers between them because there were so many, and Mu Song hadn’t dared defy the Fire King.
Thinking of the Deputy Stronghold Lord traveling comfortably aboard the other swift ship, more than a hundred jang ahead, was enough to make his stomach hurt.
Compared to this, that ship’s a flower garden. A goddamn flower garden.
At least the people aboard the other ship could be reasoned with.
Gung Gibang’s smell was a problem you could solve by holding your breath for a moment, and the strange snake Cheongpung called Mimi was surprisingly entertaining to watch when it performed tricks.
But this ship?
Blazing Flame Divine Dragon Jin Taekyung. Fire King Jeok Cheongang. And another old monster hiding his identity.
It was a gathering of monsters.
At least Jin Taekyung, his junior in name only, still spoke politely to him. And after seeing Mu Song so often, Jeok Cheongang treated him more or less like a person.
The last one was the problem.
Those eyes...
Mu Song shuddered involuntarily at the memory of Mungyeong’s cold gaze.
One of the senior river bandits, who had been watching his Stronghold Lord’s strange behavior for some time, came over and asked cautiously, “Stronghold Lord, are you all right?”
“Do I look all right?”
“Not at all, sir.”
“Then why ask? You know what’s going on.”
“I worry about you, and that’s the thanks I get? Anyway, what did that old monster threaten you with to make you look so—mmph!”
Mu Song’s hand shot out at the speed of light and clamped over his subordinate’s mouth. His eyes darted around the deck.
Only after checking twice, then a third time, that no one had heard did his anger surge.
“Have you lost your mind? Do you have a death wish?”
“Mmph, phew!”
The senior river bandit finally pulled free and stammered, “I-I’m sorry, sir. It just slipped out.”
“I’ve told you again and again. Neither you nor the others are to say a word about him. Understood?”
“Yes, sir.”
The senior river bandit was one of the few who had seen Mungyeong’s true identity for himself.
Mu Song sighed deeply at the man’s anxious, darting eyes before speaking.
“More importantly, did you make sure everyone understood the orders I gave earlier?”
The senior river bandit nodded.
“Yes, sir. Just as you said, I made it clear they’re not to go anywhere near the stern.”
“Anyone get suspicious?”
There were dozens of river bandits aboard. With that many people, there was bound to be an idiot or two who couldn’t take a hint.
“One did. Chunsam. Even after I said it was your order, he asked me about it three times. Nearly gave me a heart attack.”
Mu Song ground his teeth.
“I knew it’d be that bastard. Where’s Chunsam now?”
“We dunked him in the Yangtze and hauled him back out. He’s been tossed down below. He won’t be saying anything like that again.”
“Whew. Good work. Keep the others in line even when I’m away. One slip, and every last one of us could end up drowned at the bottom of the Yangtze along with the swift ship.”
Mu Song’s expression darkened.

As if the monster known as the Fire King, Jeok Cheongang, weren’t enough, now an unidentified old monster who had achieved Returned to Youth was aboard as well. Mu Song almost missed the days when he hadn’t known.

Seeing his mighty Stronghold Lord look so vulnerable, the senior river bandit asked anxiously, “At this rate, are we ever going to make it back to Sichuan? We’ve already been away from the Water Dragon Stronghold for nearly two months. I’m worried it might stay vacant forever.”
“Don’t say such unlucky things. They say you can survive even in a tiger’s den if you keep your head.”
“That’s a tiger. Against a Returned to Youth Supreme Peak master, I don’t think keeping your head a hundred times over would help...”
Come to think of it, he was right.
Mu Song had no answer. He shut his mouth.
That was when a voice came from behind him.
“I brought the liquor barrel. Where should I put it?”
There was only one person who would be talking about a liquor barrel right now.
Irritation flared. Without even turning around, Mu Song snapped, “I’ve been letting it slide, but that useless bastard has been getting on my nerves since—”
“Did you just call me a useless bastard?”
A moment passed that felt like an eternity.
The senior river bandit was staring over Mu Song’s shoulder, mouth hanging open. Mu Song knew at once that he was thoroughly fucked.
Something else he’d forgotten flashed through his mind.
Ah. I left a spare liquor barrel at the stern.
No wonder his subordinate had started to say something when Mu Song told him to bring another one, then stopped.
Mu Song felt faint. He hadn’t been afraid even when he was caught in the whirlpool at Tianling Falls, but now he was sweating enough to bathe his neck in it.
“Great Hero Mu Song.”
Mu Song squeezed his eyes shut. Then he slowly turned around, forcing a smile.
The one person he never wanted to meet, even in his dreams, was standing there.
“O-oh, Mungyeong. W-what brings you here?”
“Nothing in particular.”
Mungyeong smiled like any other boy his age.
“I was watching the Yangtze from the stern when your subordinate came by. He said Great Hero Mu Song had ordered him to bring a liquor barrel...”
“I-I did?”
“Didn’t you?”
“Well, I... I don’t remember giving an order like that...”
A river bandit appeared behind Mungyeong with a barrel on his shoulder and called out briskly, “Stronghold Lord! I brought the liquor barrel you ordered!”
Mu Song fought down the urge to tear the man’s mouth apart.
“I... I do remember giving that order. Yes. I did. It was a clear mistake.”
“A mistake. I see.”
Mu Song felt Mungyeong’s gaze travel from one part of his body to another.
It had to be his imagination that made him feel as though Mungyeong was looking at his lethal acupoints.
Fortunately, perhaps his desperate wish had reached the heavens. Mungyeong soon withdrew his gaze and spoke.
“Great Hero Jeok was beside himself with rage. He said that if it happened again, you’d better be prepared.”
Of course, Jeok Cheongang hadn’t flown into a rage or said anything of the sort.
But Mu Song wasn’t stupid enough to miss what Mungyeong meant.
“Y-yes, I understand. Tell Great Hero Jeok I’ll bear it in mind. But...”
“Go ahead.”
“What if someone absolutely has to go to the stern? For ship’s business, say. Or to bring meals.”

Mungyeong thought for a moment before answering. “Great Hero Jeok told me to pass along instructions for that, too. If it’s ship’s business, you’re to come alone and take care of it. And you’re to deliver the meals yourself.”
“...You mean I have to do all that alone?”
“Would you rather not?”
Mu Song’s face went rigid.
“It’s been my lifelong wish. I couldn’t be happier.”
“I see. Then I’ll be going. See you at dinner.”
Mungyeong headed back toward the stern, leaving Mu Song behind. Then he stopped and turned around.
“Oh, and one more thing.”
“What else? Is there still something you need to tell me?”
“Two portions will be enough for each meal until we reach Henan.”
“Huh?”
“Young Master Jin is going to have no appetite for the time being, so keep that in mind.”
They had at least ten days left before they reached Henan. No matter how poor someone’s appetite was, going ten whole days without eating was absurd.
Curiosity got the better of Mu Song. He mustered his courage and asked, “Um... did something happen to Junior Jin?”
“Oh.”
A dimple appeared beside Mungyeong’s mouth.
His smile was so natural that even Mu Song, who thought of him as a monster, mistook him for an innocent boy for an instant.
“He must be busy right now. Very busy.”
Sometimes I feel like I’ve become a human smartphone.
A System window had appeared before my eyes, much like the warning you get when your battery falls below fifteen percent.
Beep.
System Most of your internal energy has been depleted. Circulate your qi to replenish your internal energy. If it runs out completely, you may suffer a Status abnormality!
But why was I more puzzled than alarmed?
If I ran out of internal energy right now, I’d sink in the middle of this vast stretch of the Yangtze. Yet the danger bothered me less than the questions.
And one reason for that was surely the presence of something approaching from far away.
Ssssh.
A large body drew closer with remarkable stealth. The fin poking above the water looked oddly familiar.
No, fuck.
Why the hell was there a shark in the Yangtze?

I do remember giving that order.
Yes.
I did.
It was a clear mistake.”
“A mistake.
I see.”
Mu Song felt Mungyeong’s gaze travel from one part of his body to another.
It had to be his imagination that made him feel as though Mungyeong was looking at his lethal acupoints.
Fortunately, perhaps his desperate wish had reached the heavens.
Mungyeong soon withdrew his gaze and spoke.
“Great Hero Jeok was beside himself with rage.
He said that if it happened again, you’d better be prepared.”
Of course, Jeok Cheongang hadn’t flown into a rage or said anything of the sort.
But Mu Song wasn’t stupid enough to miss what Mungyeong meant.
“Y-yes, I understand.
Tell Great Hero Jeok I’ll bear it in mind.
But...”
“Go ahead.”
“What if someone absolutely has to go to the stern?
For ship’s business, say.
Or to bring meals.”
Mungyeong thought for a moment before answering.
“Great Hero Jeok told me to pass along instructions for that, too.
If it’s ship’s business, you’re to come alone and take care of it.
And you’re to deliver the meals yourself.”
“...You mean I have to do all that alone?”
“Would you rather not?”
Mu Song’s face went rigid.
“It’s been my lifelong wish.
I couldn’t be happier.”
“I see.
Then I’ll be going.
See you at dinner.”
Mungyeong headed back toward the stern, leaving Mu Song behind.
Then he stopped and turned around.
“Oh, and one more thing.”
“What else?
Is there still something you need to tell me?”
“Two portions will be enough for each meal until we reach Henan.”
“Huh?”
“Young Master Jin is going to have no appetite for the time being, so keep that in mind.”
They had at least ten days left before they reached Henan.
No matter how poor someone’s appetite was, going ten whole days without eating was absurd.
Curiosity got the better of Mu Song.
He mustered his courage and asked, “Um... did something happen to Junior Jin?”
“Oh.”
A dimple appeared beside Mungyeong’s mouth.
His smile was so natural that even Mu Song, who thought of him as a monster, mistook him for an innocent boy for an instant.
“He must be busy right now.
Very busy.”
Sometimes I feel like I’ve become a human smartphone.
A System window had appeared before my eyes, much like the warning you get when your battery falls below fifteen percent.
Beep.
System Most of your internal energy has been depleted.
Circulate your qi to replenish your internal energy.
If it runs out completely, you may suffer a Status abnormality!
But why was I more puzzled than alarmed?
If I ran out of internal energy right now, I’d sink in the middle of this vast stretch of the Yangtze.
Yet the danger bothered me less than the questions.
And one reason for that was surely the presence of something approaching from far away.
Ssssh.
A large body drew closer with remarkable stealth.
The fin poking above the water looked oddly familiar.
No, fuck.
Why the hell was there a shark in the Yangtze?

chapters.title: Chapter 511
paragraphs: Deep in the night, with darkness on every side, two ships raced along the Yangtze under full sail.
Whoosh!
Any sailor with good night vision would have been startled once by the vessels’ extraordinary speed, then twice by the flag visible beyond their faint torchlight.
The Yangtze River Channel League.
Those five characters, written in blue dye, were a sure pass for traveling safely and freely across the vast Yangtze.
But the flag was both a pass and a symbol of raiders.
“What the...”
“Th-the Yangtze River Channel League! They’re river bandits!”
“Eek!”
The passengers aboard a pleasure boat, who had been holding a feast on the water, fell into a panic. The fishermen hauling in their nets some distance away reacted differently.
“What the hell are they screaming for? They ought to get back to guzzling their booze.”
“Pay them no mind. It’s not like this is the first time. But is that the swift ship the Yangtze River Channel League’s so proud of?”
“I’ve seen one before. It’s damn fast, so that must be it.”
“If I had a ship like that, I wouldn’t want for anything.”
“How many more fish are you planning to catch?”
“What are you talking about? If I had a swift ship, why would I keep fishing to make my fortune? I’d become a river bandit on the spot.”

There was only a hair’s breadth between a fisherman and a river bandit. When making a living got hard, a man could take the net and harpoon he’d used to catch fish just days before and turn to raiding.
Perhaps that was why the fishermen showed no particular fear of the river bandits.
“Oh, they’re coming this way.”
“Let them. They won’t rob us.”
“Damn it. We’re so poor even river bandits won’t rob us.”
The fishermen chatted as they watched with keen interest.
Fishermen were as tough as any sailors on the river. Even a green river bandit who knew nothing of the world left them alone. He might come looking for a few coins and end up skewered on a harpoon.
The Yangtze River Channel League saw it much the same way. Robbing fishermen for a few coins wasn’t worth the trouble.
So the fishermen watched as though it were someone else’s house on fire.
But a little while later, when the swift ships picked up speed and disappeared, they tilted their heads.
“Huh? They’re just leaving?”
“So they are. Think there’s a young master from some powerful family aboard that pleasure boat? Someone they’d regret crossing?”
“They didn’t even stop to check who was aboard.”
“Forget it. What does it matter? Let’s finish hauling in the nets and get home before it gets any later.”
“Yeah, all right.”
Once the two swift ships had vanished without incident, lively music rose from the pleasure boat again. The fishermen smacked their lips, then turned back to their work.
Half a shichen later, a strange cry rang out from somewhere.
“Kkyat-meu!”
At first, the fishermen thought little of it.
“Good grief. They ought to show some restraint. They’re making an awful racket.”
“Someone over there knows how to party.”
“I’m already half dead from exhaustion, and now I’ve got to listen to ‘Kkyat-meu’? I ought to punch a hole in the bottom of their boat.”
The graying fisherman who had muttered irritably pulled on his net again.
That was when another cry rang out.
“I’m going! I’m going! I’m going! Zoom, here I go!”
“Yeah, yeah. I’m coming right now, you bastards.”
The fisherman snatched up his harpoon, eyes rolling back in fury.
“Fuck this. I’ll hurry over, punch a hole in their hull, and come right back, so nobody try to stop me.”
“Wait. Just wait a moment.”
The other fishermen had finally noticed something odd. They pricked up their ears.
“That... doesn’t sound like it’s coming from the pleasure boat.”
“You’re right. Then what is it?”
“The sound came from over...”
As if on cue, they all raised their heads and looked around for its source.
The music stopped abruptly aboard the pleasure boat as well. Apparently wondering what was going on, men and women dressed in dazzling silk stood at the bow and stared out at the pitch-black Yangtze.
“Did we hear wrong?”
“I definitely heard something strange.”
“Huh. It’s not like a ghost’s bewitched us.”
Just as everyone began to doubt their ears—
Whoooosh!
Water roared as it was violently split apart, and a person appeared.
No, strictly speaking, he wasn’t alone.
“W-what the hell is that?”
Everyone stared wide-eyed at the uninvited guest.

It was astonishing enough to see a young man crossing the Yangtze in the middle of the night, bare from the waist up. But when they recognized the enormous creature swimming ahead of him, bound by some strange rope, they could hardly believe their eyes.
“A s-sa-eo! It’s a sa-eo! A man’s riding a sa-eo!”
The shout shattered the silence that had settled over the river.
And everyone realized that the bizarre noise they had heard was part of the reality unfolding before their eyes.
Whoosh, whoosh, whoosh!
A sa-eo. A monstrous fish with a huge, hideous body and a vicious nature, said to devour even humans.
And now one was swimming with a man riding behind it.
What was more—
“T-there’s more than one!”
“One fin, two... five! There are five sa-eo!”
It was a shocking sight. Sa-eo mostly lived in the open sea; seeing even one in the Yangtze was rare. Seeing five together was almost unthinkable.
But if that had been all, the fishermen wouldn’t have stood there speechless.
The reason they had been rendered speechless was simple.
“Tell me... am I dreaming?”
“I think I’m having the same dream.”
“It looks to me like that young man has put some sort of bridle on the sa-eo and is, well... driving it.”
“I don’t know what that is. It’s frightening...”
Just as the fishermen said, each of the five sa-eo wore something like a bridle. A faintly glowing rope was wound around their snouts, its ends held tight in the young man’s hand.
“Turn left!”
The young man shouted and pulled his wrist.
Whoooosh!
The sa-eo all moved left at once.
“Turn right!”
He twisted his wrist the other way.
Whoosh!
The sa-eo changed course with it.
With their great stamina and speed, the five sa-eo cut through the water ahead while the young man followed, keeping himself atop the river on his two feet.
They were every bit as fast as the swift ships that had passed earlier—faster, if anything.
“What in the world am I looking at?”
As someone muttered in a daze, the young man closed the distance in the blink of an eye and waved to the fishermen.
“Welcome, fishermen.”
“Sorry to ask when we’ve only just met, but could you give me directions? Did two ships pass through here earlier? Maybe half a shichen to one shichen ago?”
The fisherman who had been planning to attack the pleasure boat lowered his harpoon and answered awkwardly.
“W-we saw ’em. You mean the swift ships?”
“That’s right. Yangtze River Channel League. There’s a kid standing at the stern who looks like he has one hell of a nasty temper.”
“I-I don’t know about the kid. But the swift ships went that way. About half a shichen ago.”
“Half a shichen? I’ve almost caught up. Whew, fuck. I damn near shit blood getting here.”
The fisherman paused at language as colorful as anything he’d heard from a sailor. Just then, the young man loosened the strange rope in his hand.
The fishermen belatedly realized that one of the sa-eo had been released and panicked.
“Urgh!”
“Th-the sa-eo’s loose!”
“Back! Back! Row!”
But what they feared didn’t happen.
The sa-eo merely blinked at the young man as meekly as a crucian carp. The young man looked unconcerned.
“Sa-eo? Oh, you mean a shark.”
“W-what do you think you’re doing?”
“I know what you’re worried about, but my boy doesn’t bite.”
“Your boy?”
“I’ll show you. Here, fin.”
The fishermen’s eyes bulged.
No sooner had the young man held out his hand than the sa-eo, its eyes darting about, offered him its fin.
“See? He listens. I told you he’s a good boy.”
Not good. More like he’d been made good.
The fishermen swallowed the words before they could reach their lips.
The sa-eo’s ragged fin and trembling body were just their imagination. They had to be.
Whether he noticed the fishermen staring at his muscles or not, the young man went on calmly.
“He’s got anger-management issues, but he’s been controlling them fine since I beat the shit out of him. You’ll be all right. You won’t get another chance like this, so take one off my hands.”
“P-pardon?”
“As thanks for the directions. I need to let them go soon anyway. Got anything to eat? I’ve had raw fish three meals a day, and my stomach feels like an aquarium.”
The fisherman had no idea what was happening, but instinct told him what would be best for his safety. Trembling like a leaf, he handed over the food tucked inside his clothes.
“H-h-here.”
“Ah, yes. Th-thank you.”
The young man took the lightly seasoned rice ball and flashed a playful grin.
“Then catch lots of fish.”
Whoosh, whoosh, whoosh!
That was the last they saw of him.
The fishermen stared blankly as the sight of one man and four fish vanished into the distant darkness in an instant. Then they looked at the only trace he had left behind.
Shudder!
The sa-eo had foolishly picked a fight with the wrong person, been thoroughly beaten, and now feared human beings themselves. The shark—or rather, the white sturgeon—trembled violently.
And the fisherman who had become its new owner realized that his fate had just changed dramatically.
“...I guess I don’t need a swift ship anymore.”
That was the moment a new Morning Star was born among the river bandits.
I guarantee no one in either the modern world or Murim has ever experienced water skiing as eco-friendly as mine.
Whoosh!
“Shark number four. Your posture’s slipping.”
Flinch!
“Yeah, you. The one who just flinched. What, are you an individualist?”
Swish!
“Just keep going like that. You’re not going alone. Match fins with your friends and go together.”
Of course, I’d used a little violence.
A few punches hadn’t been enough to satisfy them, apparently, because they kept coming at me. So I worked over their fins and pulled out a few teeth.
If an environmental group had seen me, they’d have called me a destroyer of nature whose crimes outraged heaven and humanity, and a fish abuser doomed to suffer even after death.
I hadn’t cared from the start.
It’s not like I’m Shanks.
A bighearted guy who gives up an arm because a shark looks hungry only exists in old comic books.
I caught one, taught it a lesson, then called over more of its kind and founded the Shark Water-Ski Team. I called it the Catch-’Em Fish Farm.
Still, I wouldn’t have made it this far without them.
I looked fondly at the team members who had carried out their mission so well.

Over half a day of alternating between rest and travel, I’d replenished some of the internal energy that had bottomed out and closed much of the distance to the swift ships. Their reward for all that hard work was freedom.
“All right, everyone. Off you go.”
I was untying the ropes around their snouts—or rather, the Water God Dragon’s sinew I’d stashed away last time—when a voice reached my ear.
“...Would you look at this lunatic.”
I turned my head.
Beyond the deep darkness, someone was walking toward me across the surface of the water.

chapters.title: Chapter 512
paragraphs: “...Would you look at this lunatic.”
The voice was thick with disbelief, and the red hair stood out even in the deep darkness.
I widened my eyes at the last person I expected to see.
“Oh? What brings you here?”
“That...”
Jeok Cheongang hesitated, his voice trailing off.
“I got seasick, so I got off the ship for a bit.”
“Ah, seasick. The Old Master got seasick.”
This wasn’t just any Supreme Peak master. This was the Fire King himself.
Spider-Man retiring because he was afraid of heights would have been more believable than Jeok Cheongang suffering from seasickness.
“What’s with that smile?”
I forced down the corners of my mouth and answered.
“I just have one of those faces that looks like it’s smiling.”
“Want me to make it look ready to die?”
“No, thank you.”
“If you have a complaint, say it to my face. Don’t grin at me like a creep.”
“I never said I had a complaint. But what are you hiding behind your back?”
“H-hiding? What would this old man be hiding?”
“The thing you’re holding in your clasped hands. Whatever could it be that you’re so embarrassed you have to hide it? Are you some kind of Murim high-school girl boss?”
“I said I’m not hiding anything!”
Jeok Cheongang shouted at my sharp observation and awkwardly brought his hands out from behind his back.
He was fiddling with something wrapped in a large leaf, and the conflict in his movements was obvious.
Looks like food. And damn, does it smell good.
The meaty aroma carried on the wind was incredible. My stomach had spent more than half a day digesting nothing but raw fish and grilled fish, so of course it began to churn.
Grrrrowl.
“Is it pork?”
“Beef.”
“You didn’t catch it fishing, did you?”
“Of course not. It was loaded onto the ship beforehand. Those river bandits rubbed it with spices and grilled it. It’s quite good.”
“That sounds delicious.”
“Two people could be eating it while five dropped dead, and neither would notice.”
“That sounds like deadly poison.”
“It’s that delicious.”
“Then give me some. Let me taste it.”
“Hah. You’re not even funny. Did you think I brought it for you?”
“Ah, so you packed it for yourself?”
“Of course.”
“So you got seasick and abandoned the swift ship. It sailed off and left you in the middle of a river you hate, but you still made sure to bring food...”
I looked at Jeok Cheongang and slowly nodded.
“That makes perfect sense.”
“Give it here.”
Jeok Cheongang answered gruffly.
“Here. Stuff your face.”
“Why, thank you.”
“I brought it for myself, but I’ve lost my appetite. That’s why I’m giving it to you.”
“I know. I know everything. Why do you keep explaining something the whole world already knows?”
“...Damn it.”
I let his grumbling go in one ear and out the other as I devoured the meat.

By the time my short but fiercely fought meal was coming to an end, the four sharks that had been circling nearby while watching me warily had disappeared from sight. So had the swift ship that had been faintly visible in the distance.
“Ah, I missed it.”
“The sa-eo?”
“No. I was going to let them go soon anyway.”
“Then the swift ship?”
I sucked the seasoning off my fingers.
“Yes.”
“You don’t seem particularly disappointed for someone who missed it.”
“I’ve got no reason to be.”
“What a strange fellow. Didn’t you use the sa-eo to chase the swift ship all the way here so you could catch up?”
He was right. I couldn’t deny it.
But...
“I was starting to regret it.”

I wouldn’t have done this before.
To obtain something, you had to pay a price equal to its value.

Neither would the version who’d endured a year of brutal training on Mount Jiuhua without ever fleeing back to reality.

“It took me a whole half day. I’m sorry.”
“At first, I waited because I was worried about you. After that, I meant to give you a thorough scolding.”
From Jeok Cheongang’s perspective, it must have been utterly absurd. He had even outsourced my training, only for me to put together a Shark Water-Ski Team and use a cheap trick.
But his voice was gentle now.
“I did mean to scold you... but this will do. Try to catch up on your own strength from here.”
Jeok Cheongang stepped forward. The ripples spreading from his toes were far gentler than mine.
He noticed me watching and tossed out a remark.
“Our sect’s martial arts have an especially violent flow. It took me years to calm that storm on my own.”
“Years...”
“You already know this isn’t something you can learn overnight.”
“I know. I also know that it isn’t overnight. There are still ten days left.”
I shrugged and added,
“And I have two excellent advisors beside me to show me the way. That should make it a lot easier for me than it was for you, Old Master.”
The Fire King and the Slaughter Saint. Both were far stronger than I was, and both had traveled the path I was on long before me.
Those were much better circumstances than Jeok Cheongang had faced when he’d had to figure it all out for himself.
Jeok Cheongang let out a quiet laugh.
“Look at this sly bastard. Proudly announcing you’ll take another shortcut.”
“I’m hurt that you’d call it a shortcut. Most people call this a fortuitous encounter.”
“Hah. You certainly have a way with words.”
“But you’re not denying it.”
“Because, now that I think about it, you’re right. But that isn’t the only difference between us.”
“Martial talent. With that outrageously excellent body and talent of yours, you should be able to sprout at least one bud before reaching Henan.”
A towering tree and a gorgeous flower both began with a single small bud.

What a mischievous old man. He’d already guessed, but he was testing me anyway. I let out a quiet laugh.

“A little while? It’ll take you half a day.”
“It still doesn’t sit right with me. So yes, that’s the plan.”

The goal was the swift ship—no, Henan.
The entire Murim world seethed like water in a cauldron.

What had begun as a simple rumor spread in every direction on the lips of gossipmongers. Then one day, dozens—hundreds—of messenger pigeons rose from Mount Song in Henan, each carrying a letter that would turn the rumor into fact.

“So it’s finally come to this.”

Hadn’t even the mighty Demonic Cult failed to take the Central Plains and been driven back decades ago?
A bloody storm had swept through Shaolin and Sichuan, but to most martial artists, that was a reason to be angry and fight—not to retreat in fear.
“Anyone with the spirit to fight, any martial artist who bears a weapon—stand beneath the Murim Alliance’s banner!”
The call rang out across the land.
And some answered it.
“Shaolin of Mount Song requests to join the alliance.”
“Huashan will join the Murim Alliance as well.”
The Nine Sects and One Gang. The Five Great Families.
The fifteen pillars that supported Murim began to move.
Shaolin Temple and Huashan were the first to raise the Murim Alliance’s banner. The other renowned sects and great factions soon rushed to request membership too.

“It’s only been a day since the news broke. Already?”
“You’re behind. Of course they have. The question is what the other sects will do.”
“I heard the Shandong Yue Family plans to join too.”
“That’s a surprise. Aren’t they in an awkward position between Murim and the authorities?”
“Any news from the Hahou Sword Family?”

“I understand the former Family Head died in the Great Faction War. The current Family Head will probably join the war to avenge his father, if nothing else. Everyone knows Dark Heaven is the Demonic Cult’s successor by now.”
“The Murim Alliance is the symbol of orthodox Murim. The problem is those who practice demonic and heterodox arts—and the Outer Lands.”
Even as the gossips talked, people throughout Murim were making their own moves.
And as the fervor spread like wildfire, ten days passed.

“The thing you’re holding in your clasped hands.

Are you some kind of Murim high-school girl boss?”
“I said I’m not hiding anything!”

chapters.title: Chapter 513
paragraphs: Xixia in Henan Province, situated along a tributary of the Yangtze, was packed with people again today.
Boats of every size crowded the ferry landing. Merchants stood beside piles of goods, haggling with fire in their eyes.
“Come on, cheap, cheap! Musk that’s good for your virility! Just one silver nyang!”
“I don’t need that crap.”
“You there, lovely Young Lady! Wouldn’t you like a hand mirror?”
“I’m not buying that crap.”
“...What a pair of fucking assholes.”
Every kind of noise rang through the marketplace.
But in the end, the atmosphere of a place depended on the kind of people gathered there. The merchant who stopped a passing young martial artist out of habit had picked the wrong man.
“Sir, you look like a martial hero on your way to Mount Song. Could I interest you in a well-honed wea—ah!”
The merchant broke off with a gasp. The handsome face that had first caught his eye no longer registered.

The moment he saw the three characters embroidered in black thread across the young martial artist’s dark blue silk uniform, along with the dragon pattern, the merchant let out a cry that sounded almost like a moan.
“B-Black Dragon Demon Gate!”
Though the cry had not been particularly loud, the four-character name Black Dragon Demon Gate was enough to plunge the bustling thoroughfare into a pit of silence.
“B-Black Dragon Demon Gate?”
“It’s them. The unorthodox bastards making a name for themselves in Gansu.”
“I heard they arrived in Henan late yesterday... Could they be here to join the alliance?”
Silence spread in an instant. Merchants stopped calling out, commoners stopped wandering, and even the armed martial artists traveling in groups halted to look toward the cry.
Under all those eyes, the young man from the Black Dragon Demon Gate smiled at the merchant.
“You have a good eye for a merchant, recognizing our sect’s insignia.”
“Th-that’s...”
“You don’t seem to have much to do with Murim. Are you from Gansu? Or did you pick up a little knowledge from the Third Rate swordsmen who come here as customers?”
He glanced over the merchant’s shoulder at the weapons neatly arranged on the stall and clicked his tongue.
“Nothing but cheap junk. I wouldn’t take any of it for free. Show me your best.”
“Pardon?”
“Ah, I forgot you’re a merchant. Not your best, then. Your most expensive.”
“Y-yes, sir.”

With trembling hands, the merchant pulled out an iron chest he had tucked deep inside the stall and opened it. The young martial artist whistled at the lone sword inside, lying there without even a proper scabbard.
“Hm. This doesn’t belong in a place like this.”
The onlookers, especially the martial artists, found themselves nodding. The sword looked quite old, but its blade gleamed in five brilliant colors, and its edge had lost none of its sharpness.
It could easily be called a famed sword.
The merchant sensed greed in the eyes of several martial artists and drew his shoulders in.
“M-my late father left it to me.”
“Was your late father a martial artist?”
“Th-that’s impossible. Somehow, he came to own the sword, but he only told me to keep it secret from others and preserve it as a family heirloom for generations...”
“No wonder. There must have been plenty of people who wanted a sword like this.”

Too much greed led to bloodshed. Most martial artists would rather take a famed sword by force than pay several hundred silver nyang for it. Threatening someone with a cheap iron sword was far easier than coming up with the silver.
“Your late father must have been quite wise.”
“Y-yes. He was.”
“But it seems you didn’t inherit his wisdom, bringing it out like this.”
“Th-that’s...!”
The merchant could not finish. The young martial artist let out a quiet laugh. He knew exactly what the merchant had swallowed back.

The man facing him belonged to the Black Dragon Demon Gate, an unorthodox faction. With a knife at his throat, the merchant had no time to think things through. Fear that he might lose his head if he tried to pass off another weapon had paralyzed him.
This was a first for the merchant. For the young martial artist, it was familiar.
“I understand. Most people who meet me think and act just as you did.”
The young martial artist looked the merchant up and down. The merchant sat with his mouth shut, like someone who had swallowed his tongue.
“So I’ll save you.”
Suspicion flickered across the merchant’s eyes.
“Wh-what do you mean?”
“I’ll pay for the sword and take it.”
“Ah!”

The merchant’s face lit up. His heart had already been burning with anxiety. He had brought out the sword because staying alive came first, but now more than a few people had seen it. Once this young man left, wandering martial artists and petty thieves would surely catch the scent and come after him.

If the young man bought it, though, that problem was solved. He would still have to leave the area soon—there would be people after the silver he received—but he could keep his life and take enough money with him to live comfortably elsewhere.
The merchant finished calculating and bowed at once.
“G-Great Hero, if you would do that, I couldn’t ask for anything more!”
“You’re not completely clueless.”
With a quiet laugh, the young martial artist tossed a money pouch from his robes onto the stall.
Clink.
It landed with a weighty rattle. The merchant opened it and blinked.
“G-Great Hero. This...”
The young man had taken the sword from the chest and was examining it from every angle. He glanced over.
“What is it?”
“I’m afraid you may have the amount wrong.”
“The amount?”

The merchant swallowed hard at the young man’s puzzled look. The sword was a family heirloom, and by its value alone, he ought to receive at least several hundred silver nyang. The sum in the pouch was absurdly small.
“Twenty silver nyang is a little...”
“I disagree.”
“Pardon?”
“That’s plenty. I deducted the price of your life.”
The young man’s voice turned cold. So did the air around him.
The commoners watching with mingled curiosity and fear shuddered. The neighboring merchants who had shared the man’s hardships deliberately looked away.
But not everyone there stayed silent.
“The Black Dragon Demon Gate must have quite a reputation if even some wet-behind-the-ears brat is throwing his weight around like this.”
A rough voice rang out, and the crowd parted. A middle-aged man walked through the gap, baring yellow teeth in a grin at the young martial artist.
“I won’t waste words. Put down that sword and get the hell out of here.”
The young man blinked.
“Were you speaking to me?”
“Ha! Look at this brat. Who else would I be talking to?”
“Don’t misunderstand. I heard you perfectly well...”
He looked the middle-aged man up and down before continuing.
“I just never imagined someone like you would dare say it to my face.”
“...Someone like me? Say something like that?”
The middle-aged man stared at him for a moment, then burst into laughter.
“Someone like me! Ha! Hahaha! You’re funnier than you look.”
“How strange. No one in Gansu ever told me I had a talent for comedy.”
“Boy, what’s your name?”
“I have no reason to tell you, and no intention of doing so. Be on your way.”
“You don’t look so good. Scared?”
“Not really... I just find talking to someone like you unpleasant.”
“Heh.”
The middle-aged man laughed, but his eyes gleamed ominously. His scarred, heavily muscled arm was about to move when the young martial artist spoke.
“That’s enough, Blood Cudgel.”
The middle-aged man jerked at the sound of his sobriquet. The martial artists watching were startled too.
Enough was known about Blood Cudgel Do Sangho that his appearance and the red cudgel at his waist made him fairly easy to recognize. What surprised them was the young man’s attitude.
Here was a brat in the Black Dragon Demon Gate’s uniform, speaking to an accomplished Peak master as though he stood far above him.
Blood Cudgel sensed something was wrong as well.
“You... knew who I was?”
“I’d heard of you. Heard there was a man who’d lick a beggar’s ass for silver.”
His polite speech had vanished, replaced by open insult. Blood Cudgel’s eyes widened with rage as the young man went on.
“Now that we’ve met, it seems what I heard was true. How about an offer?”
“An... offer?”
“I’ll give you silver. Lick the top of my foot, and I’ll let you live.”
“H-how dare you!”
Blood Cudgel trembled. He was a Peak master whose martial prowess no one could dismiss. He wanted to rush forward and smash the brat’s head open.
But the name Black Dragon Demon Gate held him back. The young man was so young, yet so calm. Blood Cudgel had a gut feeling that a life-and-death duel with him would not end well.
“...Damn it.”
He lowered the weapon he had half-raised. The young martial artist smiled.
“You must really like silver. Ready to lick the top of my foot?”
“You bastard! Shut your mouth!”
His shout, laden with profound internal energy, struck in every direction. Third Rate martial artists whose skills were still meager groaned and stumbled backward. Terrified commoners screamed.
Through the chaos, Blood Cudgel glared at the young man with bloodshot eyes.
“I don’t know how important you are, but one day you’ll regret what happened here.”
The young martial artist clicked his tongue softly.
“You’re angry. But I think you’d better stop there.”
“I, Blood Cudgel Do Sangho, may forget a favor, but I never forget a grudge! I’ll retreat today, but the next time we meet will be the day of your funeral—”
Thud!
Blood sprayed in every direction.
The young martial artist looked at Blood Cudgel’s corpse, its head crushed, and sighed.
“I was trying to avoid bloodshed if I could. You could have held back a little longer.”
When had he appeared?
An eight-foot-tall man who had crushed Blood Cudgel’s head with a swing of his massive two-section staff answered in a halting voice.
“Dare... insult Young Sect Leader. This subordinate... will not tolerate it.”
“Well, Blood Cudgel should be all right. You could hardly call him orthodox.”
The young martial artist clicked his tongue. Only then did the people grasp what had happened and scatter in every direction, screaming.
“S-someone’s been killed!”
“Aaaah!”
“What the hell...!”
Even the martial artists had frozen at the sudden violence. Just then, the young man spotted something beyond the fleeing crowd.
“See? I knew there’d be trouble.”
A group of monks in yellow kasayas was approaching.
“Shaolin Temple...”

The handsome face that had first caught his eye no longer registered.

The moment he saw the three characters embroidered in black thread across the young martial artist’s dark blue silk uniform, along with the dragon pattern, the merchant let out a cry that sounded almost like a moan.
“B-Black Dragon Demon Gate!”
Though the cry had not been particularly loud, the four-character name Black Dragon Demon Gate was enough to plunge the bustling thoroughfare into a pit of silence.
“B-Black Dragon Demon Gate?”
“It’s them.
The unorthodox bastards making a name for themselves in Gansu.”
“I heard they arrived in Henan late yesterday...
Could they be here to join the alliance?”
Silence spread in an instant.
Merchants stopped calling out, commoners stopped wandering, and even the armed martial artists traveling in groups halted to look toward the cry.
Under all those eyes, the young man from the Black Dragon Demon Gate smiled at the merchant.
“You have a good eye for a merchant, recognizing our sect’s insignia.”
“Th-that’s...”
“You don’t seem to have much to do with Murim.
Are you from Gansu?
Or did you pick up a little knowledge from the Third Rate swordsmen who come here as customers?”
He glanced over the merchant’s shoulder at the weapons neatly arranged on the stall and clicked his tongue.
“Nothing but cheap junk.
I wouldn’t take any of it for free.
Show me your best.”
“Pardon?”
“Ah, I forgot you’re a merchant.
Not your best, then.
Your most expensive.”
“Y-yes, sir.”
With trembling hands, the merchant pulled out an iron chest he had tucked deep inside the stall and opened it.
The young martial artist whistled at the lone sword inside, lying there without even a proper scabbard.
“Hm.
This doesn’t belong in a place like this.”
The onlookers, especially the martial artists, found themselves nodding.
The sword looked quite old, but its blade gleamed in five brilliant colors, and its edge had lost none of its sharpness.
It could easily be called a famed sword.
The merchant sensed greed in the eyes of several martial artists and drew his shoulders in.
“M-my late father left it to me.”
“Was your late father a martial artist?”
“Th-that’s impossible.
Somehow, he came to own the sword, but he only told me to keep it secret from others and preserve it as a family heirloom for generations...”
“No wonder.
There must have been plenty of people who wanted a sword like this.”
Too much greed led to bloodshed.
Most martial artists would rather take a famed sword by force than pay several hundred silver nyang for it.
Threatening someone with a cheap iron sword was far easier than coming up with the silver.
“Your late father must have been quite wise.”
“Y-yes.
He was.”
“But it seems you didn’t inherit his wisdom, bringing it out like this.”
“Th-that’s...!”
The merchant could not finish.
The young martial artist let out a quiet laugh.
He knew exactly what the merchant had swallowed back.
The man facing him belonged to the Black Dragon Demon Gate, an unorthodox faction.
With a knife at his throat, the merchant had no time to think things through.
Fear that he might lose his head if he tried to pass off another weapon had paralyzed him.
This was a first for the merchant.
For the young martial artist, it was familiar.
“I understand.
Most people who meet me think and act just as you did.”
The young martial artist looked the merchant up and down.
The merchant sat with his mouth shut, like someone who had swallowed his tongue.
“So I’ll save you.”
Suspicion flickered across the merchant’s eyes.
“Wh-what do you mean?”
“I’ll pay for the sword and take it.”
“Ah!”
The merchant’s face lit up.
His heart had already been burning with anxiety.
He had brought out the sword because staying alive came first, but now more than a few people had seen it.
Once this young man left, wandering martial artists and petty thieves would surely catch the scent and come after him.
If the young man bought it, though, that problem was solved.
He would still have to leave the area soon—there would be people after the silver he received—but he could keep his life and take enough money with him to live comfortably elsewhere.
The merchant finished calculating and bowed at once.
“G-Great Hero, if you would do that, I couldn’t ask for anything more!”
“You’re not completely clueless.”
With a quiet laugh, the young martial artist tossed a money pouch from his robes onto the stall.
Clink.
It landed with a weighty rattle.
The merchant opened it and blinked.
“G-Great Hero.
This...”
The young man had taken the sword from the chest and was examining it from every angle.
He glanced over.
“What is it?”
“I’m afraid you may have the amount wrong.”
“The amount?”
The merchant swallowed hard at the young man’s puzzled look.
The sword was a family heirloom, and by its value alone, he ought to receive at least several hundred silver nyang.
The sum in the pouch was absurdly small.
“Twenty silver nyang is a little...”
“I disagree.”
“Pardon?”
“That’s plenty.
I deducted the price of your life.”
The young man’s voice turned cold.
So did the air around him.
The commoners watching with mingled curiosity and fear shuddered.
The neighboring merchants who had shared the man’s hardships deliberately looked away.
But not everyone there stayed silent.
“The Black Dragon Demon Gate must have quite a reputation if even some wet-behind-the-ears brat is throwing his weight around like this.”
A rough voice rang out, and the crowd parted.
A middle-aged man walked through the gap, baring yellow teeth in a grin at the young martial artist.
“I won’t waste words.
Put down that sword and get the hell out of here.”
The young man blinked.
“Were you speaking to me?”
“Ha!
Look at this brat.
Who else would I be talking to?”
“Don’t misunderstand.
I heard you perfectly well...”
He looked the middle-aged man up and down before continuing.
“I just never imagined someone like you would dare say it to my face.”
“...Someone like me?
Say something like that?”
The middle-aged man stared at him for a moment, then burst into laughter.
“Someone like me!
Ha!
Hahaha!
You’re funnier than you look.”
“How strange.
No one in Gansu ever told me I had a talent for comedy.”
“Boy, what’s your name?”
“I have no reason to tell you, and no intention of doing so.
Be on your way.”
“You don’t look so good.
Scared?”
“Not really...
I just find talking to someone like you unpleasant.”
“Heh.”
The middle-aged man laughed, but his eyes gleamed ominously.
His scarred, heavily muscled arm was about to move when the young martial artist spoke.
“That’s enough, Blood Cudgel.”
The middle-aged man jerked at the sound of his sobriquet.
The martial artists watching were startled too.
Enough was known about Blood Cudgel Do Sangho that his appearance and the red cudgel at his waist made him fairly easy to recognize.
What surprised them was the young man’s attitude.
Here was a brat in the Black Dragon Demon Gate’s uniform, speaking to an accomplished Peak master as though he stood far above him.
Blood Cudgel sensed something was wrong as well.
“You... knew who I was?”
“I’d heard of you.
Heard there was a man who’d lick a beggar’s ass for silver.”
His polite speech had vanished, replaced by open insult.
Blood Cudgel’s eyes widened with rage as the young man went on.
“Now that we’ve met, it seems what I heard was true.
How about an offer?”
“An... offer?”
“I’ll give you silver.
Lick the top of my foot, and I’ll let you live.”
“H-how dare you!”
Blood Cudgel trembled.
He was a Peak master whose martial prowess no one could dismiss.
He wanted to rush forward and smash the brat’s head open.
But the name Black Dragon Demon Gate held him back.
The young man was so young, yet so calm.
Blood Cudgel had a gut feeling that a life-and-death duel with him would not end well.
“...Damn it.”
He lowered the weapon he had half-raised.
The young martial artist smiled.
“You must really like silver.
Ready to lick the top of my foot?”
“You bastard!
Shut your mouth!”
His shout, laden with profound internal energy, struck in every direction.
Third Rate martial artists whose skills were still meager groaned and stumbled backward.
Terrified commoners screamed.
Through the chaos, Blood Cudgel glared at the young man with bloodshot eyes.
“I don’t know how important you are, but one day you’ll regret what happened here.”
The young martial artist clicked his tongue softly.
“You’re angry.
But I think you’d better stop there.”
“I, Blood Cudgel Do Sangho, may forget a favor, but I never forget a grudge!
I’ll retreat today, but the next time we meet will be the day of your funeral—”
Thud!
Blood sprayed in every direction.
The young martial artist looked at Blood Cudgel’s corpse, its head crushed, and sighed.
“I was trying to avoid bloodshed if I could.
You could have held back a little longer.”
When had he appeared?
An eight-foot-tall man who had crushed Blood Cudgel’s head with a swing of his massive two-section staff answered in a halting voice.
“Dare... insult Young Sect Leader.
This subordinate... will not tolerate it.”
“Well, Blood Cudgel should be all right.
You could hardly call him orthodox.”
The young martial artist clicked his tongue.
Only then did the people grasp what had happened and scatter in every direction, screaming.
“S-someone’s been killed!”
“Aaaah!”
“What the hell...!”
Even the martial artists had frozen at the sudden violence.
Just then, the young man spotted something beyond the fleeing crowd.
“See?
I knew there’d be trouble.”
A group of monks in yellow kasayas was approaching.
“Shaolin Temple...”

chapters.title: Chapter 514
paragraphs: Shaolin Temple, the Mount Tai and Northern Dipper of the Murim.

Whenever turmoil descended on the Central Plains, Shaolin had been at the forefront of the fighting. It had been so a thousand years ago, a hundred years ago, and during the Great Faction War several decades earlier.
They had shed more blood than any other sect in the Murim for it, but no one at Shaolin Temple regretted a drop.
It was what they ought to have done. They had fought for a brighter future, for a greater cause.
The monks making their way along a well-paved road held that same conviction in their hearts.
Whoosh!
Their yellow kasayas whipped in the wind.
Not a breath of wind stirred on that clear spring day, but the monks’ swift movement techniques raised a wind of their own.
“Xixia is in sight.”
There were twenty Shaolin monks. At the words of the martial monk leading them, a middle-aged monk nodded.
“Good. We won’t be late.”
“Yes. The appointed time is around shenshi. We still have nearly one shichen.”
Xixia covered a broad area, but these martial monks had reached a considerable realm. Even at an ordinary walking pace, one shichen was more than enough time to reach its ferry landing.
Having made the calculation, the middle-aged monk shook the Zen staff in his hand.
Clatter.
The martial monks understood the signal and stopped short.
Halting a movement technique at such speed in an instant spoke to the depth of their martial-arts mastery.
The middle-aged monk regarded them with satisfaction, then slowly turned.
Behind them stood someone with a conical hat pulled low over their face.
“We’re about to enter the main road. The commoners may be alarmed. May we slow down from here?”
The middle-aged monk spoke with utmost respect. Beneath the hat, tightly pressed lips parted.
“Please do.”
The voice was so hoarse that there was no guessing the speaker’s age. Grief and pity flickered across every face, including the middle-aged monk’s.
“Thank you for granting permission, Martial... Uncle.”
That form of address still felt unfamiliar. The middle-aged monk turned, and the others resumed walking toward Xixia.
Then—
“Aaaaaah!”
“M-murder! Someone’s been killed!”
Faint screams and shouts carried from far away.
Before the middle-aged monk, with his profound internal energy, could alert the other disciples, the person in the conical hat spoke.
“It seems we should hurry.”
Whoosh!
Twenty figures came hurtling through the wind.
At the sight of their fluttering yellow kasayas and the grim faces drawing rapidly closer, the young martial artist of the Black Dragon Demon Gate frowned.
“Shaolin...”
They were the last people he wanted to meet, especially now, when his simple-minded subordinate had killed someone in the middle of a main road.
“You idiot.”
Thwack!
The eight-foot-tall giant groaned as the blow struck his shin.
“Young Sect Leader. This subordinate hurts.”
“That’s why I hit you. I told you to be careful. Why must you act without thinking?”
“He deserved to die.”
“Whew. There’s no getting through to you. Fine. The water’s already spilled. What can we do?”
“We should find a way to put it back.”
At the curt voice, the giant blinked his calf-like eyes.
“Young Sect Leader. Not this subordinate.”
“You don’t have to tell me. I already know.”
The young martial artist turned with a faint smile. Facing the stern middle-aged monk five steps away, he offered a fist-palm salute.
“An honor to meet Shaolin’s esteemed monks. I didn’t expect to meet Master Jung Ho quite so soon.”
The middle-aged monk, Jung Ho, twitched his thick eyebrows.
“You know me? I don’t believe we’ve met.”
“We haven’t, but I’ve heard plenty about you.”
“This humble monk has no reputation worth speaking of. Nor am I worthy of being called Master.”
“Just as my father said. You really are modest.”
“Your father?”
“He once told me about an exceptionally fiery-tempered monk at Shaolin—ah, a monk of deep Buddhist faith who follows his principles to the letter.”
The young martial artist glanced at the Zen staff in Jung Ho’s hand.
“He also said you wield a Zen staff like a demon. One hung all over with prayer beads.”
“...Amitabha. You have a sharp eye.”
“I’m glad you’re the man I thought you were. This would have been rather embarrassing otherwise.”
Jung Ho regarded the young martial artist with a grave gaze, then spoke abruptly.
“That is fortunate. As I listen to you, a few things occur to me as well.”
“I’m listening.”
“Your clothing belongs to the Black Dragon Demon Gate of Gansu. Your aura and bearing are far from ordinary. You must be its Young Sect Leader, whom I’ve heard of only by reputation. Am I right?”
The young martial artist smiled and bowed his head.
“Allow me to introduce myself properly. I am Sama Pyo, Young Sect Leader of the Black Dragon Demon Gate.”
“I’ve heard much of the Black Dragon Saber. They say you’re a Morning Star in no way inferior to the Ten Dragons and Phoenixes.”
A murmur passed through the monks behind Jung Ho.

The sobriquet Black Dragon Saber was that widely known. And as the Young Sect Leader of the Black Dragon Demon Gate, a force counted among the three strongest unorthodox factions, Sama Pyo possessed an impressive background as well.
But none of them saw the sneer that brushed across Sama Pyo’s lips as he lowered his head.
When Sama Pyo looked up, he was smiling broadly.
“You praise me too highly. For Master Jung Ho to think so well of an unknown nobody like me—I hardly know what to say.”
“I will say it again: I am not worthy of being called Master. Nor do I mean to overestimate you. I speak only of what has been proven. However...”
Jung Ho looked at the corpse lying facedown in a pool of blood.
“I do not yet know the facts surrounding this unfortunate man’s death.”
Sama Pyo rubbed his stubbled chin.
“Well, that’s a long story.”
“There is no need to worry. There is a faster way.”
Clatter.
At Jung Ho’s signal, a lean martial monk stepped forward and examined the body.
Before joining Shaolin, he had traveled as a wandering martial artist and accumulated a wealth of experience. It did not take him long to identify the corpse.
“It’s Blood Cudgel.”
“Blood Cudgel Do Sangho? Are you certain?”
“Yes. His head was crushed, but I am certain.”
“Blood Cudgel. Blood Cudgel...”
Jung Ho ran his fingers over the prayer beads tied to his Zen staff, then turned to Sama Pyo.
“Did you know?”
“Know what?”
“That Blood Cudgel killed five innocent merchants in Shaanxi two days ago and has been on the run since?”
“Did he?”
“He must have thought himself safe because he did it in a remote mountain area. Bold enough to come all the way to Henan, at any rate.”
“...Good heavens. What a monstrous man.”
Sama Pyo made a show of frowning.
Blood Cudgel’s crime wasn’t what troubled him. What troubled him was the intelligence network that had uncovered and relayed the deed of an experienced wandering martial artist in just two days.
Is this the Murim Alliance’s reach, or Shaolin’s strength?
Blood Cudgel Do Sangho was a fairly well-known wandering martial artist, but that was because his methods were cruel and he went around boasting about himself.
The Murim was full of masters far above his level. To know this much about a man like Blood Cudgel suggested an intelligence network woven as tightly as a spiderweb.
Not welcome news... Then again, after everything that’s happened, I suppose it makes sense.
Sama Pyo gave nothing away.
“How fortunate.”
“What is?”
“The water I spilled turns out to have been rotten. You might say I dealt with it before anyone could drink it.”
Jung Ho’s gaze darkened.
“You were not unaware of that fact.”
“The outcome was good. Doesn’t that settle it?”
“How you reach an outcome matters just as much. Whatever you say, killing a man on a busy main road was unwise.”
“It was a dangerous situation. He had to be killed before he killed me. Ah, of course, that was not my intention either.”
Sama Pyo pointed to the eight-foot-tall giant beside him.
“This fellow did it.”
The giant blinked his bulging eyes.
“Young Sect Leader. A person?”
“We must make the facts clear. Wipe the blood off that vicious two-section staff before you make excuses.”
“That. True. Blood Cudgel killed. Me.”
“Please be generous with him, Master. He’s skilled in martial arts, but his head is a little...”
Sama Pyo put a finger to his temple and twirled it. Jung Ho watched him in silence before speaking.
“You—or rather, the Black Dragon Demon Gate—will have to explain this properly.”
“Of course. This happened because I failed to control my subordinate. I’ll cooperate in any way I can.”
“As you know, tensions have been high of late. The commoners in particular are afraid.”
The Murim was a powder keg about to explode.

Even an illiterate old villager who had never finished the Thousand Character Classic knew the Murim Alliance was no social club for martial artists. During the Great Faction War, the fighting had engulfed more than the martial artists of the Central Plains.
“If someone is openly killed on a main road in broad daylight at a time like this, people will inevitably look on us unfavorably.”
“I’ll bear that in mind.”
“Blood Cudgel may have been a criminal on the run, but those above us may still hold you accountable for his death.”
“I’ll gladly explain myself.”
“You must apologize to the commoners nearby as well.”
“Don’t worry. I’ll even compensate them if they wish.”
Jung Ho’s eyebrow twitched.
Though he was a martial monk, he had spent many years at Shaolin following the Buddhist path.
He was displeased that this had happened, and he was not particularly impressed by the attitude of the Black Dragon Demon Gate’s Young Sect Leader, whose reputation he had already heard.
But what could he do? Sama Pyo was nodding along obediently, at least on the surface. Jung Ho could only turn away.
“Then... that will be all.”
“We have met by fate. Why don’t we move somewhere else for a while?”
“Amitabha. I’m afraid I must decline. There is a guest I must receive.”
Jung Ho looked anything but regretful. He was about to turn when—
“The sword.”
“Hm?”
“You don’t appear to use a sword.”
The voice was hoarse, like metal scraping against metal. Someone wearing a conical hat pulled low over their face continued.
“That sword doesn’t seem to belong with you. Return it to its owner.”
“Ah, this?”
Sama Pyo smiled faintly as he looked at the sword in his hand.
“It’s mine.”
“Not to my eyes.”
“If you don’t mind my asking, who are you, Monk?”
“That has nothing to do with this.”
The smile at the corner of Sama Pyo’s mouth faded.
Then someone shouted from far away.
“The Jin Family of Taiyuan! It’s the Jin Family of Taiyuan!”
