Jung Ho’s eyebrow twitched.
Though he was a martial monk, he had spent many years at Shaolin following the Buddhist path.
He was displeased that this had happened, and he was not particularly impressed by the attitude of the Black Dragon Demon Gate’s Young Sect Leader, whose reputation he had already heard.
But what could he do?
Sama Pyo was nodding along obediently, at least on the surface.
Jung Ho could only turn away.
“Then... that will be all.”
“We have met by fate.
Why don’t we move somewhere else for a while?”
“Amitabha.
I’m afraid I must decline.
There is a guest I must receive.”
Jung Ho looked anything but regretful.
He was about to turn when—
“The sword.”
“Hm?”
“You don’t appear to use a sword.”
The voice was hoarse, like metal scraping against metal.
Someone wearing a conical hat pulled low over their face continued.
“That sword doesn’t seem to belong with you.
Return it to its owner.”
“Ah, this?”
Sama Pyo smiled faintly as he looked at the sword in his hand.
“It’s mine.”
“Not to my eyes.”
“If you don’t mind my asking, who are you, Monk?”
“That has nothing to do with this.”
The smile at the corner of Sama Pyo’s mouth faded.
Then someone shouted from far away.
“The Jin Family of Taiyuan!
It’s the Jin Family of Taiyuan!”

chapters.title: Chapter 515
paragraphs: The chaos in the marketplace clearly hadn’t reached the ferry landing yet.
If it had, no one would be shouting like that.
“The Jin Family of Taiyuan! The Jin Family of Taiyuan is here!”
“Waaaah!”
The main road was some distance from the landing, but everyone still gathered there could hear the cheers carrying from afar.
Black Dragon Saber Sama Pyo was among them.
The Jin Family of Taiyuan...
His gaze darkened.

In less than two years, the Jin Family of Taiyuan had grown into a formidable power. Though perhaps “newly risen” wasn’t quite right for a family with three hundred years of history and standing behind it.
And one man had brought that fading great family back to prominence.
Blazing Flame Divine Dragon Jin Taekyung.
The young man had once seemed like a sprout with no hope of growing. Now he had put down deep roots in the soil of the Murim and was growing into a mighty tree.
Every branch connected to him was thick and flourishing.

Fire King Jeok Cheongang. Huashan Divine Dragon Cheongpung. Cheongpung’s master, Sword Saint Mae Jonghak, and Huashan, one of the strongest powers among the Nine Sects and One Gang. Then there were the prestigious sects Taekyung had forged close ties with during his travels through the martial world.
And among them was Shaolin Temple, the Mount Tai and Northern Dipper of the Murim.
“I wondered what sort of guest would bring Shaolin’s Discipline Hall Master all the way here to greet him. Now I know.”
“Amitabha. This humble monk is not a man with time to spare.”
Jung Ho fixed Sama Pyo with a stony look.
“Nor am I so easygoing that I’ll stand by while someone starts a pointless quarrel.”
“Ah.”
Sama Pyo took his hand off the hilt of his saber. He hadn’t noticed it settling there.
“My apologies.” He smiled. “Force of habit.”
“I hope that is true.”
“I know how to conduct myself. Surely you don’t think I’d show disrespect to Shaolin.”
“Amitabha. It would be best to refrain from actions that could invite misunderstanding, Benefactor Sama Pyo.”
“I will. But...”
The smile at the corner of Sama Pyo’s mouth grew more pronounced. He looked from Jung Ho to the unidentified monk whose conical hat hid his face.
“For a devout Master like you to speak so firmly, he must be someone you care for a great deal.”
Jung Ho’s title alone made it clear that he held no minor position in Shaolin. His master had been one of the three disciples of Hong Dao, the late Abbot of Shaolin and Dharma King.
By both office and seniority, Jung Ho was a leading figure within the temple. Sama Pyo suspected his open hostility had less to do with temperament than with the identity of the monk beside him.
“I’ve heard you haven’t taken a Disciple yet, Master.”
“...You have sharp ears.”
“And a keen eye, as you know.”
Jung Ho frowned.
“Amitabha. Enough wordplay. Let us leave this for another time. We must greet a guest who has arrived earlier than expected.”
“Ah, I see. Have you taken on a new Disciple?”
“Benefactor.”
Woom.
The Zen staff in Jung Ho’s hand gave a low, resonant hum.
Then the person who had been watching in silence spoke.
“It’s all right, Martial Nephew.”
A voice as rough as metal scraping against metal came from beneath the low brim of the conical hat. The air seemed to grow heavy around it.
Jung Ho and the other Shaolin monks trembled at the immense internal energy in that voice. Beside Sama Pyo, the eight-foot-tall giant opened his bulging eyes wide.
But it wasn’t only the monk’s aura that startled Sama Pyo.
Martial Nephew? Did he call Jung Ho his Martial Nephew?
As Sama Pyo stood momentarily frozen, the monk in the conical hat spoke quietly.
“Return the sword to its owner. Here in Henan, we will tolerate no disturbances.”
“If fate brings us together, we shall meet again.”
That was all. Having let the words fall as lightly as if he were giving them to the wind, the monk turned and disappeared. The Shaolin monks followed him.
Sama Pyo watched them go without a word.
The giant turned toward Sama Pyo and spoke in his halting voice.
“Young Sect Leader. That monk. Who is he? I cannot beat him.”
“No hair. But skill. Very strong.”
He recalled the faint righteous gleam he had glimpsed in the monk’s eyes beneath the conical hat at the final moment, then muttered.
“The Discipline Hall Master’s young Martial Uncle.”
The glimpse had been brief, but enough to judge his age. The face beneath the hat had been astonishingly young. And yet...
“Young Sect Leader?”
“Yes, I heard you, you idiot.”
Sama Pyo returned from his thoughts and clicked his tongue softly. He tossed the sword back to the merchant cowering and trembling in a corner, then looked up at the sky and stretched.
“Come on. I could use a drink.”
“Pleasure house! Pleasure house!”
“Yes, yes.”
The sky was blue, and heroes who had roamed the Murim were gathering in Henan.
Far off, the crowd at the ferry landing kept calling the Jin Family of Taiyuan’s name.
“I apologize for troubling you, Martial Uncle.”
On the way to the ferry landing, Jung Ho quickened his steps to draw alongside the monk in the conical hat. The monk shook his head.
“It wasn’t your fault, Martial Nephew Jung Ho.”
“No. I should have settled the matter myself. I never imagined that young Benefactor would behave that way...”
Jung Ho’s displeasure showed plainly on his face. Sama Pyo’s conduct still rankled.
At a time like this, on a main road under countless eyes, the young man had not only beaten Blood Cudgel to death but had also tried to provoke one of Shaolin’s senior figures.
“I’d heard the Black Dragon Demon Gate held considerable power in Gansu, but its Young Sect Leader is more insolent than I expected.”
“Is that so?”
The voice beneath the hat was rough, but the monk’s manner was perfectly calm. He kept walking as he spoke.
“My experience is limited, and there is still much I don’t know. But I’ve heard that those who follow demonic, heterodox arts are not especially powerful.”
“That is true of most. Not every unorthodox sect is the same.”
“The Black Dragon Demon Gate is an exception, then.”
“Yes. Among the unorthodox sects of the Central Plains, it could easily be counted among the top three. It may even be their greatest rallying point.”
“What do you mean by ‘rallying point,’ Martial Nephew?”
“What it represents, Martial Uncle.”
“What it represents...”
“The Black Dragon Demon Gate has the longest history of any unorthodox faction in the Murim. It was once one of the Twelve Branches of the Demonic Cult.”
“Did they betray the Demonic Cult?”
“Amitabha. I think ‘compromise’ would be more accurate.”

The Black Dragon Demon Gate’s compromise had succeeded. Victory in the long, brutal war had ultimately gone to the orthodox faction, but the Black Dragon Demon Gate had drawn together the unorthodox martial artists scattered like grass roots across the Central Plains, recovered from its losses, and grown stronger.
“But for its Young Sect Leader to behave with such arrogance... Shaolin suffered enormous losses in that bloody conflict. To look down on us now is—”
Jung Ho broke off.
As though he could read his thoughts, the monk beside him spoke softly.
“It’s all right. Don’t let it trouble you, Martial Nephew Jung Ho.”
“...Martial Uncle.”
“Everyone in Shaolin was deeply wounded. Some lost the Senior Brothers and Junior Brothers who had shared their hardships. Others lost Disciples. I’m no different.”
Step. Step.
Step by step, their pace quickened. The rough voice continued from beneath the hat.
“I was... more grief-stricken than I thought I could bear. But just because that person has gone somewhere he can never return from doesn’t mean his will has vanished too.”
Jung Ho and the other Shaolin monks bit their lips.
How could they forget that day? How could they fail to understand his grief?
They all remembered. They all knew.
“I will carry on his will—my Master’s will. That one thought carried me through my time in Repentance Cave.”
The skin glimpsed beneath the conical hat was as rough as the monk’s voice, covered with countless scars.
For the unnamed monk, the past three months had been like hell.
Every day, he had repeated treatment and training while writhing in terrible pain. Those who heard the screams echoing from Repentance Cave could not keep themselves from shedding tears.
Three months of anguish and suffering.
But he had endured. Bearing the grief of his master’s death and his anger at the killers, he had kept going.
And at the end, enlightenment had come to him like a single ray of light.
“Martial Nephew Jung Ho.”
“Yes, Martial Uncle?”

“My Master would sometimes say this. Everything begins with one person. If one is not enough, then two. If even that is difficult, then three should step forward. That is how we raise up what has fallen and move onward.”
His master, who had gone where he could not return, had loved wine and meat.

He would lie on a rock and sleep all day, waking only when the world had grown dim. Then he would shake the shoulder of the Disciple who had come to wake him and fallen asleep beside him, and point high into the night sky.
Look. You’re up there too.
The Disciple, rousing himself with disheveled hair, would rub his eyes and ask in return.
Why do you call that star your Disciple?
Because I followed that star when I first went to bring you back.
But... it’s so small and faint.
That’s why it’s a good star.
What?
The star that shines brightest and clearest will soon disappear. Yours will stay there and light the sky for a very long time.
The Disciple still remembered what his Master had told him that day.
Even after a long time had passed, the heavenly patterns had become distorted, and a new star had risen somewhere in the north.
Even on the day his Master departed on a distant road and the grounds of Shaolin were stained with blood.
He remembered. Part of him still lingered in that place, on that day.
Master. Where is my star now? Have you become a star somewhere in the sky? Are you watching over me?
He stopped on a hill overlooking the ferry landing and raised his eyes to the clear blue sky.
There were no stars to be seen. Even after nightfall, he would not know which was his. He would not find his master’s star, either.

However hard he looked, all he could see were two ships moored at the landing and people filing down from them. However closely he listened, all he could hear were the cheers of the crowd gathered thick as clouds.
Master. Where are you?
He gently closed his eyes. But there were no stars in the darkness behind his eyelids, and no matter how intently he listened, his master’s voice did not come.
Today was no different.
He was about to open his eyes and face that truth once more when—
Splash!
“A person! Someone was running across the river and fell in!”
“Gasp! That’s... our youngest!”
Screams. Someone’s startled cry. Then a voice he knew, desperate and unmistakable.
“Fuck, don’t just stand there screaming! A rope! Throw me a rope!”
Light flickered before his eyes, where a moment ago there had been nothing but darkness.
It was the Morning Star that had risen in the north. A trace of his master.
Have you come?
A smile formed on the stiff lips of the monk in the conical hat, Unnamed.

chapters.title: Chapter 516
paragraphs: The closer you get to your destination, the harder the last stretch feels. That’s human nature. After ten days and nights of pushing my body to its limits, I had nothing left to squeeze out.
Dad, I’m coming.
Was this really how a father and son were going to reunite after so long? That was the moment the strength drained from my flailing limbs.
Grab!
My fading vision snapped back into focus.
Someone had caught my wrist. Through my ears, muffled by all the water that had gotten in, I heard a voice.
“Trying to go before this old man? What a rotten little punk.”
When had he gotten here? Jeok Cheongang had closed the distance from the ferry landing in an instant. He looked down at me with a grin.
The moment I saw his face, all the tension left my body.
As I exhaled the breath I had been holding, Jeok Cheongang's grin deepened.
“You’re still breathing, at least.”
“That’s amazing. Am I still alive?”
“Listen to this fool. Yes, you’re alive.”
“Then stop looking at me and pull me up. I think I’m actually about to die.”
“Such an exaggeration. You’re a hundred years too early for that.”
Whoosh. Drip.
He hauled me up by the wrist. River water poured off my swollen body, taking the weeds clinging to it along.
“Do you see them?”
“Who? God?”
“The people waiting for you.”
Exhausted, I blinked. The crowd gathered like clouds at the distant ferry landing was rapidly drawing closer, and I could make out several familiar faces among them.
Cheongpung, waving both arms frantically. Gung Gibang and Hyuk Mujin, their eyes opened wide. Jin Wikyung, who was practically bawling his eyes out.
And... Mungyeong was quietly watching us.
—Welcome to Henan.
With that brief Sound Transmission, Jeok Cheongang landed, holding me in his arms.
At the same time, a clear ringing sounded in my ears.
Ding. Ding. Ding.

System Fake Murim Practitioner, Stage 2 completed successfully! You have achieved the rare achievement Single Reed Crossing the River! You will receive a fitting reward for your remarkable persistence and effort! Your control over internal energy has become freer! The power and efficiency of your martial arts have increased! All attributes have increased slightly! You have acquired 50 bonus points! You have acquired a massive amount of EXP! Level Up!
System notifications rang out one after another, and holographic windows filled the air.
The Level Up message came with a welcome lightness in my body. Then a wave of sleepiness washed over me.
“...Old Master.”
“Hm?”
“Don’t wake me.”
Those were my last words before my eyelids grew heavy and the sleep demon took me.
Where am I?
That was my first thought when I opened my eyes.
I blinked slowly and looked around. Pitch-black darkness surrounded me. As my eyes adjusted, I finally made out where I was.
A swamp.
Yes, this was a swamp.
White bones of uncertain origin—human or beast—were scattered everywhere, and a horrific stench filled the air, strong enough to make me gag.
Worse, my body was moving on its own.
Splosh.
My bare foot, without even a shoe on it, stepped into the sticky mud. I struggled with all my might to stop, but my body had already escaped my control.
One step. Then another.
I was slowly sinking deeper into the swamp when—
Whoooosh.
A wind blew from somewhere, making the skeletal trees that filled the swamp shudder.
Beyond the darkness, an unidentified red light rose.
...What’s that?
It wasn’t a flame. It looked more like someone’s eyes.
The chilling gaze held not a trace of warmth. It stared at me as if to say, Come closer if you can.
If this were an ordinary protagonist from a movie or novel, he would struggle and crawl toward it...
You come here, asshole.
Fuck the cliché.
I’d already sized up the situation. After everything I’d been through lately, I was apparently having a nightmare. I didn’t need to play along.
An ordinary person would have felt the urge to piss himself the moment he saw those red eyes, but I was the kind of person who felt the urge to use Flame Divine Palm.
There was just one tiny problem...
Splosh. Splosh.
Ah, fuck.
My body kept moving forward whether I wanted it to or not.
Slowly, steadily, as though trying to swim with my lower half sunk deep in the swamp.
But I knew I’d never reach those eyes. I would sink out of sight before I met whatever they belonged to.
Fine. Let’s get this over with.
I’d almost resigned myself to it when—
Crack!
Gasp!
Something tightened around my neck.
My eyes flew wide. A huge body covered in smooth scales filled my vision, and a low hiss sounded in my ears.
A snake?
No, it was too big to call a snake. A python was more like it.
Its thick body coiled around my neck, then bound both my arms.
Hngh.
Damn it. Had dreams gotten a graphics patch? Why was this so vivid?
The rotten mud had reached my neck. The stench in my nostrils made me gag.
Unable to move, I sank farther into the swamp—and met that red gaze.
A chill shot up my spine.
A vivid fear, sharp enough to jolt my mind fully awake, swept over me. This couldn't be an ordinary nightmare. It couldn't be.
At the same time, a horrifying sense of incongruity enveloped me.
This feeling... Why do I know it?
When had I felt it? Where? I searched through memories I didn’t want to revisit, and my whole body began to tremble.
Flash!
A blinding light burst forth from somewhere.
The red gaze and the ominous, clammy presence around it broke apart. So did the darkness that had swallowed everything. The chill vanished.
Warmth wrapped around my body. I reached toward the light now right in front of me.
Grab!
...Huh?
Thoughts raced through my head.
Why could I grab the light? Why did it feel so good? I had definitely woken up from the dream, so why could I still feel it?
Rub, rub.
What the hell was this?
After thinking for a moment, I opened my eyes, which I had closed slightly.
The bright light was someone’s smooth, shiny head.
A Buddhist precept seal marked his forehead.
“Krillin?”
The monk, whom I had never seen before—not Krillin—opened his mouth with an awkward expression.
“You have finally awakened, Benefactor Jin.”
“Excuse me, but who...?”
“This humble monk is Jung Ho.”
Who was Jung Ho?
After a moment’s thought, I asked haltingly, my voice thick with sleep.
“Were you perhaps Park Jung Ho from Class 6, Grade 3 at Garam Middle School...?”
“Pardon?”
“When did you become a monk?”
“A good forty years, at least... No, wait. Could you please listen to me, Benefactor?”

“Oh, right, you bastard. Didn’t you say you were going to become a priest? When did you switch? Apostate. Apostate. Did the Full Gospel Church Crusaders beat you up? Look how much your face has aged. Which temple hired you?”
My old classmate answered with a half-resigned expression.
“...I am the Discipline Hall Master at Shaolin.”
“Shaolin?”
“Yes. Shaolin Temple.”
“Wait. If you’re at Shaolin Temple...”
Oh. Fuck. What?
Only then did my mind fully clear. I hurriedly shook my head to dispel the sleep and cautiously opened my mouth.
“Ah, I’m sorry. I wasn’t fully awake.”
“I understand.”
Jung Ho, the middle-aged monk, looked as though he understood nothing of the sort. He continued.
“Could you take your hand off my head now? You’ve been touching it this whole time...”
“Whoops. Sorry.”
“It’s all right.”
His expression said otherwise. He plainly wanted to give me a piece of his mind, but he seemed to be holding back because of the help I’d given him.
Why was Shaolin’s Discipline Hall Master beside me when I woke up, anyway?
Only then did it strike me as strange. I looked around to get my bearings.
The room was big enough to sleep ten people. Sunlight came through a half-open window and gleamed off Jung Ho’s forehead. As for the familiar faces...
They were sprawled all around me.
So it was a dream, but half of it was real.
No wonder it had felt so vivid.
I let out a deep sigh, then first kicked the lump curled up asleep at my feet.
Thump!
“Ah! Meat dumplings for lunch today!”
What kind of wake-up cry was that?
Cheongpung sprang awake from the sudden impact and opened his sleepy eyes.
“Ah, Benefactor. Did you sleep well?”
“I slept. I wouldn’t call it well.”
“Why not? Then sleep some more.”
“...Are you kidding me? Stop talking nonsense and get this thing off me.”
“Oh! Mimi! Come here!”
Cheongpung finally noticed the pet snake coiled around my neck. At his call, its thick body slid down across my chest.
Wait. Thick?
I stared open-mouthed at the Thousand-Year Poison Horned Snake, which looked practically like a python now.
“Cheongpung. Was it always that big?”
“No. It has grown a lot lately. It's right in the middle of its growth period.”
“How old is it?”
“Grandpa Tang says it isn't even a hundred years old yet.”
“...Oh. I see.”
“It might get bigger than me. Ah, I need to hurry up and grow more too.”
“You’re already grown. Waiting won’t make you any taller.”
“No, I’m not. Mimi keeps getting bigger as she gets older. I’ll keep growing too.”
Then shouldn’t Jeok Cheongang and Mungyeong be at least three zhang tall by now?
I gave Cheongpung a troubled look and gave up trying to convince him. Instead, I smacked the mouth beside me that was giving off a horrific stench.
Smack!
“Urgh!”
“I told you to brush your teeth before bed. You damn beggar, your mouth is a swamp. A goddamn swamp.”
“Guh. Guhhh.”
Gung Gibang woke up and glared at me, his eyes watering.
“Why do you always pick on me?”
“I don’t pick on only you. I’m going to deal with this guy the same way.”
People had to be treated equally.
A moment later, Hyuk Mujin, who had been sleeping soundly with one of my legs clutched in his arms, met the same fate.
Whack!
“Argh! Why do you always pick on me?”
“Did you two rehearse that? Or are you brothers separated when you were little?”
“Don’t just hit me. Gung Gibang too—oh, he’s awake.”
“...Hah. You hateful bastards.”
I kicked Hyuk Mujin hard enough to send him tumbling beneath the bed while he muttered under his breath.
Because of these idiots, I'd even had a dream when I hardly ever dreamed at all—and an incredibly unsettling nightmare at that.
That gaze.

“Ah, yes.”

“My Martial Uncle wishes to see you, Benefactor.”

Who is it? The way he put it, we’ve definitely met before.

“Unnamed.”

“Such an exaggeration.

He hauled me up by the wrist.

“Who?
God?”

Cheongpung, waving both arms frantically.
Gung Gibang and Hyuk Mujin, their eyes opened wide.
Jin Wikyung, who was practically bawling his eyes out.

—Welcome to Henan.

Ding.
System Fake Murim Practitioner, Stage 2 completed successfully!
You have achieved the rare achievement Single Reed Crossing the River!
You will receive a fitting reward for your remarkable persistence and effort!
Your control over internal energy has become freer!
The power and efficiency of your martial arts have increased!
All attributes have increased slightly!
You have acquired 50 bonus points!
You have acquired a massive amount of EXP!
Level Up!
System notifications rang out one after another, and holographic windows filled the air.
The Level Up message came with a welcome lightness in my body.

“...Old Master.”
“Hm?”

That was my first thought when I opened my eyes.

Pitch-black darkness surrounded me.

A swamp.
Yes, this was a swamp.
White bones of uncertain origin—human or beast—were scattered everywhere, and a horrific stench filled the air, strong enough to make me gag.

Splosh.
My bare foot, without even a shoe on it, stepped into the sticky mud.
I struggled with all my might to stop, but my body had already escaped my control.
One step.
Then another.
I was slowly sinking deeper into the swamp when—
Whoooosh.
A wind blew from somewhere, making the skeletal trees that filled the swamp shudder.

It wasn’t a flame.

The chilling gaze held not a trace of warmth.
It stared at me as if to say, Come closer if you can.
If this were an ordinary protagonist from a movie or novel, he would struggle and crawl toward it...
You come here, asshole.
Fuck the cliché.
I’d already sized up the situation.
After everything I’d been through lately, I was apparently having a nightmare.
I didn’t need to play along.
An ordinary person would have felt the urge to piss himself the moment he saw those red eyes, but I was the kind of person who felt the urge to use Flame Divine Palm.
There was just one tiny problem...
Splosh.

Ah, fuck.
My body kept moving forward whether I wanted it to or not.

But I knew I’d never reach those eyes.
I would sink out of sight before I met whatever they belonged to.
Fine.
Let’s get this over with.

chapters.title: Chapter 517
paragraphs: “Have you been well, Benefactor?”
I almost didn’t recognize him. Unnamed had changed that much since I’d met him a year ago. His face, his manner of speaking, the air about him—everything felt unfamiliar.
And the reason he’d changed was probably...
It must be because of what happened that day, three months ago.
What was I supposed to say? I had a bitter taste in my mouth. I waited until Jung Ho and Hyuk Mujin had taken the others out of the room before I spoke.
“I haven’t been doing all that well myself. More has happened than I expected.”
Unnamed smiled faintly.
“So it seems. In fact, I only learned what had happened to you two days ago.”

No martial artist could have missed the events of the past three months. If Unnamed, who held an important position at Shaolin, had heard about them only two days ago, I could think of just one reason.
“You were in closed-door training.”
“Amitabha. I was staying in Repentance Cave.”
“Repentance Cave? Does that mean...”
“What you’re thinking is correct. I asked to go there myself, so please don’t worry.”
The first character meant shame; the second, remorse. Repentance Cave was a place where sinners were confined.

What was he ashamed of? What did he feel he had to repent for? Perhaps it was his regret at failing to prevent his Master’s death. Unnamed had spent three months there, calling himself a sinner for failing to protect even the Green Jade Buddha Staff, the divine artifact of Shaolin his Master had entrusted to him before he died.
“In the darkness, where I couldn’t see an inch in front of me, I kept thinking.”
Unnamed ran a callused finger over his cheek. Much of his scar-covered face had turned a dark bluish-black.
It was the mark left by the Yin-Cold Qi of the enemy he had risked his life to stop three months ago. A burden he would never be free of.
“If only I’d been a little stronger, I might have protected my Master. I might have carried out his final request.”

But regret always came too late. A venerable monk respected by all had died unexpectedly. Someone had lost a close friend. And someone else, consumed by guilt at failing to carry out his Master’s final wishes, had gone into Repentance Cave.
Anyone would have felt the same.

I was no different. I didn’t even want to imagine how I would have felt if I’d failed to save Jeok Cheongang and had to let him go. Maybe I would have gone back to being F-rank Hunter Jin Taekyung, trapped in that same cycle of regret and despair.
But pain changes people, for better or worse. In Unnamed’s case, it had changed him for the better. His heart might have been broken, but at least his martial arts had grown stronger.
“This is just my opinion, but I doubt you spent all your time in Repentance Cave thinking.”
“Amitabha. I owe it all to the grace of the Buddha and Shaolin.”

Unnamed pressed his palms together toward the sunlit window, then looked at me with calm eyes. There was a pure power in his gaze. A year ago, his body had been packed with solid muscle. Now he was as lean as an old tree. But the quiet aura flowing from him was on another level from before.
He’s broken through.
He had entered the supreme realm every martial artist dreamed of reaching. There was no doubt about it.
Seeing the awe in my eyes, Unnamed gave a small nod.
“Enlightenment alone wasn’t enough to heal a body in critical condition and reach a higher realm. I needed many other things. The Great Restoration Pill was one of them.”
“Ah.”
Shaolin’s Great Restoration Pill was among the finest elixirs in the world.
Right. With the Great Restoration Pill, it might have been possible.

The pill’s effects were one thing, but Unnamed was the Disciple whom Dharma King Hong Dao, a man capable of reading heavenly patterns, had personally brought in and raised with all his heart. He was a genius born with tremendous martial talent—not quite on Cheongpung’s level, perhaps, but still extraordinary. There was no doubt that he was worthy of the Great Restoration Pill.
He had reached the Supreme Peak realm while still in his thirties. That proved both his Master’s eye for talent and his own ability.
“Congratulations. I’ve heard the Great Restoration Pill is precious even by Shaolin’s standards.”

“That’s why I refused it so firmly. But my Senior Brother, the Abbot, gave it to me and told me not to ask questions. Apparently, my Master had said something to him about it several years ago. Perhaps... he knew this would happen.”
A faint smile touched Unnamed’s lips. He gazed into the distance for a moment, as though remembering his Master, then went on.
“Oh, my Senior Brother Abbot would also like to meet Benefactor Jin.”
“Your Senior Brother Abbot?”

I hadn’t heard who had succeeded Dharma King Hong Dao. Gung Gibang had said it would be one of the Dharma King’s direct Disciples, but one spectacular disaster after another had kept me too busy to think about it.
“I don’t believe you’ve met him. He’s my eldest Senior Brother in our lineage, and he became Abbot less than a month ago. It’s only natural that you wouldn’t know him.”
“Ah, I see.”
“He said he was sorry things had been so chaotic last time that he let you leave without even saying goodbye.”
“He doesn’t need to apologize. I was barely thinking straight myself.”

The Shaolin Bloodshed during the Star-Array Grand Banquet had been unprecedented, but I’d had to leave Henan for Sichuan within a day or two. Jeok Cheongang was in critical condition, and finding the Divine Physician couldn’t wait.

“Amitabha. I was truly glad when I finally heard that Benefactor Jeok had made a full recovery. My Master must be watching over me from somewhere. I’m sure he was relieved to see his friend well again.”
“Ah, speaking of which, you must have met the Old— No, my Master already.”
“We spoke until you woke up. I nearly failed to recognize him at first.”
“Well, he has, uh... changed a little.”
“Yes. About as much as I have.”
What was I supposed to say to that?
While I hesitated over his sudden self-deprecating joke, Unnamed politely pressed his palms together.
“Amitabha. That was a joke.”
“Oh. Ah. Right.”
“You didn’t find it amusing. I’ll refrain from making another.”
Please do rose to the tip of my tongue.
A joke like that was funny coming from someone who hadn’t suffered quite so much. Coming from Unnamed, it made the whole room turn solemn. But I didn’t have the courage to nod.
“...No, it was funny.”
“Amitabha. Then I’ll continue.”
“That was the joke.”
Should I just crack his head open with a wooden fish?
I stared at him, dumbfounded, then let out a quiet laugh. If he could make clumsy jokes like these, he’d come through it better than I’d feared.
I might not be able to comfort him, but I could at least listen to a few temple jokes that pushed the limits.
Anyway...
“Where are we? This doesn’t look like Shaolin Temple.”
Judging by the sun outside, I’d slept for about a full day, but I still had no idea where we were. I looked around again, and Unnamed explained.
“An inn near Mount Song. It’s been rented in the name of the Murim Alliance, so please stay and rest as long as you need.”
“The Murim Alliance.”
The name had always felt distant. Hearing Unnamed say it here in Henan made it suddenly real. I got out of bed and went to the window.
The first thing I saw was a peak of Mount Song rising in the distance as though it might pierce the sky. Buildings crowded the foot of the mountain, and all sorts of people filled the streets.
One martial artist had a narrow-bladed sword at his waist. Another carried a massive saber on his back without a scabbard. Others bore spears and twin axes...
All sorts of people, sure. But something was off.
They’re scary.
Unnamed gave a low laugh as I watched the martial artists everywhere I looked.
“Amitabha. They’ve come from all across the land after hearing the news.”
“Even at a glance, there seem to be more of them than there were at the Star-Array Grand Banquet.”

“The Star-Array Grand Banquet was a festival for young prodigies. The founding of the Murim Alliance concerns everyone. People from both the orthodox and unorthodox factions are here, and quite a few little-known eccentrics have come out of seclusion as well.”

That made sense. The stakes were entirely different, so of course more people had come. If the Star-Array Grand Banquet was the Han River fireworks festival, the founding of the Murim Alliance was Jindotgae One. Unlike at the banquet, there were hardly any commoners in sight.
They can feel it too. They know what’s happening here.

As I thought that to myself, a group of Murim practitioners crossing the main road suddenly caught my eye. Their aura was unusual enough that they could not be mistaken for ordinary martial artists. They clearly belonged to one of the great prestigious factions.
Their clothes are strange, too. Who are they?
I didn’t need to ask Unnamed. Wrapped in furs despite the warm spring day and wearing leather armor unlike the other martial artists, they drew whispers wherever they went.
“Could they be...?”
“That’s right. The Murong Family.”
“My word. It’s well over a thousand li from Liaoning to Henan. They got here quickly.”
“They’re said to have the blood of horse-riding nomads for a reason. What luck. I never thought I’d see members of the Murong Family in my lifetime.”

It was my first time seeing the Murong Family, too. Shanxi Province, where the Jin Family of Taiyuan was located, was also considered a frontier region, but Liaoning lay far to the northeast beyond Hebei. It was not somewhere one could visit as casually as the neighborhood next door.
It was so far away that I’d heard members of the Murong Family rarely came to the Central Plains.
So that’s the Murong Family.

They were among the stronger of the Five Great Families, and I’d heard of their reputation until I was sick of it. Unlike other factions, they even maintained a cavalry unit, or so I’d been told. Maybe that was why every one of them had muscles like a horse.

The orthodox Murim, led by the Nine Sects and One Gang and the Five Great Families. It sounds like the unorthodox Murim has joined in, too. And on top of that, all the martial artists who belong nowhere at all...

People often called the United States a melting pot of races. Right now, Henan looked exactly like that to me. Granted, the people here were of the same or similar races, but every kind of martial artist I’d seldom get to see had gathered in one place.
Three days.
Three days from now, countless martial artists would gather beneath a single banner. United under the name of the Murim Alliance, they would raise their weapons and stand against Dark Heaven.
I was looking out at them and thinking just that when—
Boom!
A tremendous roar sounded from somewhere.

Perhaps it was his regret at failing to prevent his Master’s death.
Unnamed had spent three months there, calling himself a sinner for failing to protect even the Green Jade Buddha Staff, the divine artifact of Shaolin his Master had entrusted to him before he died.
“In the darkness, where I couldn’t see an inch in front of me, I kept thinking.”
Unnamed ran a callused finger over his cheek.
Much of his scar-covered face had turned a dark bluish-black.
It was the mark left by the Yin-Cold Qi of the enemy he had risked his life to stop three months ago.
A burden he would never be free of.
“If only I’d been a little stronger, I might have protected my Master.
I might have carried out his final request.”
But regret always came too late.
A venerable monk respected by all had died unexpectedly.
Someone had lost a close friend.
And someone else, consumed by guilt at failing to carry out his Master’s final wishes, had gone into Repentance Cave.
Anyone would have felt the same.
I was no different.
I didn’t even want to imagine how I would have felt if I’d failed to save Jeok Cheongang and had to let him go.
Maybe I would have gone back to being F-rank Hunter Jin Taekyung, trapped in that same cycle of regret and despair.
But pain changes people, for better or worse.
In Unnamed’s case, it had changed him for the better.
His heart might have been broken, but at least his martial arts had grown stronger.
“This is just my opinion, but I doubt you spent all your time in Repentance Cave thinking.”
“Amitabha.
I owe it all to the grace of the Buddha and Shaolin.”
Unnamed pressed his palms together toward the sunlit window, then looked at me with calm eyes.
There was a pure power in his gaze.
A year ago, his body had been packed with solid muscle.
Now he was as lean as an old tree.
But the quiet aura flowing from him was on another level from before.
He’s broken through.
He had entered the supreme realm every martial artist dreamed of reaching.
There was no doubt about it.
Seeing the awe in my eyes, Unnamed gave a small nod.
“Enlightenment alone wasn’t enough to heal a body in critical condition and reach a higher realm.
I needed many other things.
The Great Restoration Pill was one of them.”
“Ah.”
Shaolin’s Great Restoration Pill was among the finest elixirs in the world.
Right.
With the Great Restoration Pill, it might have been possible.
The pill’s effects were one thing, but Unnamed was the Disciple whom Dharma King Hong Dao, a man capable of reading heavenly patterns, had personally brought in and raised with all his heart.
He was a genius born with tremendous martial talent—not quite on Cheongpung’s level, perhaps, but still extraordinary.
There was no doubt that he was worthy of the Great Restoration Pill.
He had reached the Supreme Peak realm while still in his thirties.
That proved both his Master’s eye for talent and his own ability.
“Congratulations.
I’ve heard the Great Restoration Pill is precious even by Shaolin’s standards.”
“That’s why I refused it so firmly.
But my Senior Brother, the Abbot, gave it to me and told me not to ask questions.
Apparently, my Master had said something to him about it several years ago.
Perhaps... he knew this would happen.”
A faint smile touched Unnamed’s lips.
He gazed into the distance for a moment, as though remembering his Master, then went on.
“Oh, my Senior Brother Abbot would also like to meet Benefactor Jin.”
“Your Senior Brother Abbot?”
I hadn’t heard who had succeeded Dharma King Hong Dao.
Gung Gibang had said it would be one of the Dharma King’s direct Disciples, but one spectacular disaster after another had kept me too busy to think about it.
“I don’t believe you’ve met him.
He’s my eldest Senior Brother in our lineage, and he became Abbot less than a month ago.
It’s only natural that you wouldn’t know him.”
“Ah, I see.”
“He said he was sorry things had been so chaotic last time that he let you leave without even saying goodbye.”
“He doesn’t need to apologize.
I was barely thinking straight myself.”
The Shaolin Bloodshed during the Star-Array Grand Banquet had been unprecedented, but I’d had to leave Henan for Sichuan within a day or two.
Jeok Cheongang was in critical condition, and finding the Divine Physician couldn’t wait.
“Amitabha.
I was truly glad when I finally heard that Benefactor Jeok had made a full recovery.
My Master must be watching over me from somewhere.
I’m sure he was relieved to see his friend well again.”
“Ah, speaking of which, you must have met the Old— No, my Master already.”
“We spoke until you woke up.
I nearly failed to recognize him at first.”
“Well, he has, uh... changed a little.”
“Yes.
About as much as I have.”
What was I supposed to say to that?
While I hesitated over his sudden self-deprecating joke, Unnamed politely pressed his palms together.
“Amitabha.
That was a joke.”
“Oh.
Ah.
Right.”
“You didn’t find it amusing.
I’ll refrain from making another.”
Please do rose to the tip of my tongue.
A joke like that was funny coming from someone who hadn’t suffered quite so much.
Coming from Unnamed, it made the whole room turn solemn.
But I didn’t have the courage to nod.
“...No, it was funny.”
“Amitabha.
Then I’ll continue.”
“That was the joke.”
Should I just crack his head open with a wooden fish?
I stared at him, dumbfounded, then let out a quiet laugh.
If he could make clumsy jokes like these, he’d come through it better than I’d feared.
I might not be able to comfort him, but I could at least listen to a few temple jokes that pushed the limits.
Anyway...
“Where are we?
This doesn’t look like Shaolin Temple.”
Judging by the sun outside, I’d slept for about a full day, but I still had no idea where we were.
I looked around again, and Unnamed explained.
“An inn near Mount Song.
It’s been rented in the name of the Murim Alliance, so please stay and rest as long as you need.”
“The Murim Alliance.”
The name had always felt distant.
Hearing Unnamed say it here in Henan made it suddenly real.
I got out of bed and went to the window.
The first thing I saw was a peak of Mount Song rising in the distance as though it might pierce the sky.
Buildings crowded the foot of the mountain, and all sorts of people filled the streets.
One martial artist had a narrow-bladed sword at his waist.
Another carried a massive saber on his back without a scabbard.
Others bore spears and twin axes...
All sorts of people, sure.
But something was off.
They’re scary.
Unnamed gave a low laugh as I watched the martial artists everywhere I looked.
“Amitabha.
They’ve come from all across the land after hearing the news.”
“Even at a glance, there seem to be more of them than there were at the Star-Array Grand Banquet.”
“The Star-Array Grand Banquet was a festival for young prodigies.
The founding of the Murim Alliance concerns everyone.
People from both the orthodox and unorthodox factions are here, and quite a few little-known eccentrics have come out of seclusion as well.”
That made sense.
The stakes were entirely different, so of course more people had come.
If the Star-Array Grand Banquet was the Han River fireworks festival, the founding of the Murim Alliance was Jindotgae One.
Unlike at the banquet, there were hardly any commoners in sight.
They can feel it too.
They know what’s happening here.
As I thought that to myself, a group of Murim practitioners crossing the main road suddenly caught my eye.
Their aura was unusual enough that they could not be mistaken for ordinary martial artists.
They clearly belonged to one of the great prestigious factions.
Their clothes are strange, too.
Who are they?
I didn’t need to ask Unnamed.
Wrapped in furs despite the warm spring day and wearing leather armor unlike the other martial artists, they drew whispers wherever they went.
“Could they be...?”
“That’s right.
The Murong Family.”
“My word.
It’s well over a thousand li from Liaoning to Henan.
They got here quickly.”
“They’re said to have the blood of horse-riding nomads for a reason.
What luck.
I never thought I’d see members of the Murong Family in my lifetime.”
It was my first time seeing the Murong Family, too.
Shanxi Province, where the Jin Family of Taiyuan was located, was also considered a frontier region, but Liaoning lay far to the northeast beyond Hebei.
It was not somewhere one could visit as casually as the neighborhood next door.
It was so far away that I’d heard members of the Murong Family rarely came to the Central Plains.
So that’s the Murong Family.
They were among the stronger of the Five Great Families, and I’d heard of their reputation until I was sick of it.
Unlike other factions, they even maintained a cavalry unit, or so I’d been told.
Maybe that was why every one of them had muscles like a horse.
The orthodox Murim, led by the Nine Sects and One Gang and the Five Great Families.
It sounds like the unorthodox Murim has joined in, too.
And on top of that, all the martial artists who belong nowhere at all...
People often called the United States a melting pot of races.
Right now, Henan looked exactly like that to me.
Granted, the people here were of the same or similar races, but every kind of martial artist I’d seldom get to see had gathered in one place.
Three days.
Three days from now, countless martial artists would gather beneath a single banner.
United under the name of the Murim Alliance, they would raise their weapons and stand against Dark Heaven.
I was looking out at them and thinking just that when—
Boom!
A tremendous roar sounded from somewhere.

chapters.title: Chapter 518
paragraphs: A middle-aged man, thoroughly drunk, suddenly raised one hand.
“Innkeeper, bring me a bottle of strong liquor!”
“Roast duck, too!”

“Would you look at these petty-minded fools. We’re on the verge of a momentous event—the founding of the Murim Alliance—and you want strong liquor and roast duck? We’ve come to Henan, so we should at least drink Dukang wine!”
“Oh, we’d love that, but aren’t you pushing yourself too far?”
“It’s fine. We’re splitting the bill anyway.”
“...You’ve lost your mind. Make it strong liquor.”
The inn on the main road near Mount Song was packed. Most of the people inside were Murim practitioners, of course.
From wandering martial artists who still looked like greenhorns to old veterans who had roamed the martial world for ten years—or even several decades.
The people gathered there differed in purpose, age, and gender.
Wherever people gathered, conflict was bound to follow. Especially when the people in question were drunk Murim practitioners.
“Wait. You’re...!”
“Oh-ho. Aren’t you the Senior Disciple of the Xiao He Gate? Still missing that finger?”
“You bastard! You came looking for a place to die!”
The world might be vast, but enemies had a way of meeting even on a single-plank bridge.
When people bound by tangled webs of gratitude and grudges happened to meet, blades were sure to come out.
Clang! Slash!
Sharp weapons swung, and blood sprayed through the air. The fierce exchange sent the surrounding Murim practitioners into an uproar.
“Waaah!”
“It’s a fight!”
“One silver nyang on the Senior Disciple of the Xiao He Gate!”
“Then I’ll bet two nyang on the Long Serpent Saber!”
They said nothing was more entertaining than watching someone else’s house burn or watching someone else fight.

The very few people with no connection to Murim backed away with horrified expressions. But the Murim practitioners, who were crazy about fighting regardless of whether it involved the orthodox, unorthodox, or Demonic Path, shouted and applauded without hesitation.
Amid the chaos, almost no one noticed the middle-aged man who had just come through the inn’s old door.
Clang! Bang!
Waaah!
The fight was raging in the middle of the inn, but he did not spare it a glance. He flicked a silver nyang toward the innkeeper.
“Two bottles of strong liquor and one roast duck. Bring them to a seat with a good view outside. Oh, and roast the duck until it’s crisp.”
“Great Hero...”
“Hm?”
The innkeeper bowed to him.
“I’m sorry, but there aren’t any suitable seats available right now.”
“There aren’t?”
“No, Great Hero. As you can see, so many heroes of Murim have come to visit...”
The middle-aged man looked around, then glanced up. Several faces were peering down from above the stairs.
“There seem to be seats up there.”
“Ah, I’m terribly sorry, but there are other guests on that floor—”
“That one looks good.”
“W-wait a moment, Great Hero! Great Hero!”
The middle-aged man ignored the innkeeper’s desperate cries.
He strode up the stairs, ignoring the sharp gazes that poured down on him, and muttered,
“Much better. Quiet, too.”
The inn’s second floor was reserved for people of higher status.

It was only about twenty steps above the first floor, but unlike the noisy chaos below, a serious atmosphere hung over the second floor. Nor were the people seated at its tables anything like Third Rate martial artists.
“G-Great Hero! You can’t go up there!”
At the innkeeper’s cry from behind him, the low conversations stopped.
A graying middle-aged man seated at the table closest to the stairs frowned and spoke.
“What’s all this noise?”
“I-I’m sorry, Great Hero. This gentleman seems to have mistaken where he was going—”
“Send him downstairs. And quiet the first floor while you’re at it.”
“Yes, sir.”
But the middle-aged man was already headed elsewhere.
“That seat by the window looks good.”
“Gasp, Great Hero!”
The one who stepped forward in place of the horrified innkeeper was the graying middle-aged man from before.
“Stop.”
The middle-aged man slowly turned.
“Was that directed at me?”
“Who else would I be speaking to?”
“You?”
“You look a great deal younger than I am, so don’t cause unnecessary trouble. Go back downstairs.”

The graying man added with an air of dignity, “Since you don’t seem to know much about the martial world, I’ll tell you who I am. I’m of the Fang Family. In the martial world, I’m known as Moon Beauty Saber.”
“Oh.”
“Now that you know, stop making a scene and go downstairs quietly.”
The middle-aged man blinked a few times.
“What you just said—was it really true?”
Moon Beauty Saber gave a short laugh.
Who was he? He was a top-tier wandering martial artist who had long since reached the level of injuring others with Sword Energy.
He was on an entirely different level from wandering martial artists like Blood Cudgel, who strutted around despite being merely at the early Peak realm.
“Heh heh. Why would I lie? Then again, I suppose it’s understandable that you don’t believe me. You probably never expected to meet me in a place like this.”
“No, not that. I meant, do I really look that way?”
What was this man talking about?
Moon Beauty Saber stared at him blankly, then frowned.
“What do you mean? I don’t understand you at all.”
“You said I looked young. That was certainly true, wasn’t it?”
“Hm. That’s rather nice to hear. Good. I understand.”
Before Moon Beauty Saber could reply, the middle-aged man laughed heartily and pointed toward the window.
“Don’t mind me. Keep drinking. I happen to know someone.”
“Why, you bastard...”
“Great Hero!”
Moon Beauty Saber and the innkeeper spoke at once. Then the old man drinking alone by the window suddenly cut in.
“I was feeling lonely drinking by myself, so this is perfect. Come, sit.”
The innkeeper and Moon Beauty Saber both fell silent.

The innkeeper could hardly object when the guest himself had invited the man over. Moon Beauty Saber hesitated for a different reason. Something about the old man’s manner had been bothering him since earlier.
He looks like a wealthy old man, but there’s something unusual about him... How does he know that ignorant fool?
Moon Beauty Saber wanted to teach the middle-aged man a lesson right then and there, but he couldn’t shake his unease.
Whether he knew what Moon Beauty Saber was thinking or not, the middle-aged man dropped into the seat across from the old man and immediately tilted back a bottle.
“Ah, that’s good. Is this Yeoahong?”
The old man nodded.
“The innkeeper said it had been aged at least twenty years.”
“Good wine. But strong liquor is still the best there is. The innkeeper will bring some soon. You should try it.”
“I’ll pass. I don’t usually drink much.”
“What a shame. Why are you here alone, then?”
“It’s nothing. I simply thought I would try burying myself among other people after such a long time.”
The old man suddenly turned his head and gazed out the window.
For a while, he watched the people passing through the street and listened to the bustle outside. Then he said, “Now that I’m here, being alone like this isn’t so bad.”
“You don’t seem to have come alone.”
“I have children and grandchildren, of course. Just as you have a Disciple.”
“I do have one fellow, though I’m not sure whether he’s my Disciple or my enemy. How did you know?”
“How could I not? I even saw him myself.”
Clack.
The middle-aged man set down the bottle. Liquor had spilled from the corner of his mouth, dampening his beard. Perhaps because of the soft light, the beard looked unusually red.
“Damn it. I knew it. But that brat kept insisting to the very end that he’d never met you.”
“You certainly raised your Disciple well, Fire King.”
The middle-aged man wiped his beard with his sleeve, then stared at the old man.
“My Disciple caused you trouble last time. So I came to see you myself, Azure Sky Sword King.”
The old man—no, the Grand Family Head of the Namgung Family and one of the Ten Kings, the Azure Sky Sword King—smiled faintly.
“I’m glad to hear it.”
“I knew you, of all people, would recognize this old man.”
“I almost didn’t. Returned to Youth... You were worth waiting for.”
“It’s late, but may I keep the promise I made back then?”
“I’ve waited a very long time to hear you say that.”
Joy filled the Azure Sky Sword King’s eyes.
More than twenty years ago, in exchange for entrusting one person’s life to Jeok Cheongang, he had been promised a duel.
At last, his long wait was over.
“What a shame. The strong liquor will be here soon.”
“Let whoever’s left standing drink it.”
“And your sword? Will you be all right without one?”
“My sword?”
The Azure Sky Sword King picked up the two chopsticks laid neatly on the table.
“These will do.”
Jeok Cheongang gave a short laugh and looked out the window.
“The sky is blue, and you have a sword in your hand.”
“The sun is up as well. Perfect timing.”
Whoooosh.
Wind swept through the room. Invisible waves of qi surged from the two men and spread in every direction.
And before anyone in the inn could notice, the two supreme masters struck at each other.
KABOOM!
Bang! Bang! KABOOM!
“Good Lord.”
What in tarnation is that?
I gaped at the scene in the distance beyond the window.
And it wasn’t just the successive booms or the black smoke rising into the sky.
Unnamed, who realized it a moment after I did, spoke with a hardened expression.
“Did you feel it too, Benefactor?”
I gave a small nod.
Even at this distance, I could feel waves of qi reaching us. This is a clash between at least Supreme Peak masters.
“If something like this has happened, then it must be...”
“Amitabha. Yes. It appears Dark Heaven is attacking.”
“Those Dark Heaven sons of bitches!”
“Though we took every precaution, this has happened again. Given that, this humble monk will have no choice but to break the precept against killing and go all out against them.”
“I’ll join you. Breaking the no-killing precept against Dark Heaven is a hobby of mine.”
And it seemed I wasn’t the only one with that hobby.
Ding. Diiing!
“Dark Heaven! Dark Heaven is attacking!”
“Kill them and uphold justice!”
“Beat those wicked fiends to death!”
Alarm bells rang out, and the Murim practitioners on the main road rushed toward the disturbance like a pack of dogs.
The sight made my blood boil.
Ah, so this is the Murim Crusade.
Our side is fucking strong. And there are a hell of a lot of us.
Until now, I had suffered every kind of hell against Dark Heaven because of our numerical disadvantage—or simply because of the gap in strength.
I could almost cry.
I can’t sit this one out.
“Follow me! Follow me!”
I leaped out the window and stood tall. The people who spotted me widened their eyes.
“The Blazing Flame Divine Dragon!”
“It’s the Blazing Flame Divine Dragon of the Jin Family of Taiyuan!”
“Ooooooh!”
Believe it or not, I was a pretty big name in Murim.
Living proof that even a cramped backwater like Shanxi Province could produce a dragon! A young icon of the orthodox faction!
“Waaah!”
“Let’s go! Let’s sweep Dark Heaven away!”
“The Blazing Flame Divine Dragon is with us!”
Whoosh, whoosh, whoosh, whoosh!
The Murim practitioners charged forward with renewed courage, shouting as they ran.
Unnamed and I were at the very front, of course.
“Fuck! Wreck ’em all!”
I poured my internal energy into the shout, and the roar around me swelled.
With this many Murim practitioners at my side, I was sure we could beat the hell out of anyone.
“It’s a holy war!”
“Great Hero Jin says it’s a holy war!”
“Kill those demons!”
“Amitabhaaa!”
You Dark Heaven bastards! Stay right there! I’m bringing the Murim Crusade to you, and I’m going to bash your heads in. Your heads...
“Ah.”
My brain suddenly stopped working.
A single person was walking out from inside a building burning horribly.
“What the hell are you all doing?”
The fiend was on our side.

“I knew you, of all people, would recognize this old man.”
“I almost didn’t.
Returned to Youth...
You were worth waiting for.”
“It’s late, but may I keep the promise I made back then?”
“I’ve waited a very long time to hear you say that.”
Joy filled the Azure Sky Sword King’s eyes.
More than twenty years ago, in exchange for entrusting one person’s life to Jeok Cheongang, he had been promised a duel.
At last, his long wait was over.
“What a shame.
The strong liquor will be here soon.”
“Let whoever’s left standing drink it.”
“And your sword?
Will you be all right without one?”
“My sword?”
The Azure Sky Sword King picked up the two chopsticks laid neatly on the table.
“These will do.”
Jeok Cheongang gave a short laugh and looked out the window.
“The sky is blue, and you have a sword in your hand.”
“The sun is up as well.
Perfect timing.”
Whoooosh.
Wind swept through the room.
Invisible waves of qi surged from the two men and spread in every direction.
And before anyone in the inn could notice, the two supreme masters struck at each other.
KABOOM!
Bang!
Bang!
KABOOM!
“Good Lord.”
What in tarnation is that?
I gaped at the scene in the distance beyond the window.
And it wasn’t just the successive booms or the black smoke rising into the sky.
Unnamed, who realized it a moment after I did, spoke with a hardened expression.
“Did you feel it too, Benefactor?”
I gave a small nod.
Even at this distance, I could feel waves of qi reaching us.
This is a clash between at least Supreme Peak masters.
“If something like this has happened, then it must be...”
“Amitabha.
Yes.
It appears Dark Heaven is attacking.”
“Those Dark Heaven sons of bitches!”
“Though we took every precaution, this has happened again.
Given that, this humble monk will have no choice but to break the precept against killing and go all out against them.”
“I’ll join you.
Breaking the no-killing precept against Dark Heaven is a hobby of mine.”
And it seemed I wasn’t the only one with that hobby.
Ding.
Diiing!
“Dark Heaven!
Dark Heaven is attacking!”
“Kill them and uphold justice!”
“Beat those wicked fiends to death!”
Alarm bells rang out, and the Murim practitioners on the main road rushed toward the disturbance like a pack of dogs.
The sight made my blood boil.
Ah, so this is the Murim Crusade.
Our side is fucking strong.
And there are a hell of a lot of us.
Until now, I had suffered every kind of hell against Dark Heaven because of our numerical disadvantage—or simply because of the gap in strength.
I could almost cry.
I can’t sit this one out.
“Follow me!
Follow me!”
I leaped out the window and stood tall.
The people who spotted me widened their eyes.
“The Blazing Flame Divine Dragon!”
“It’s the Blazing Flame Divine Dragon of the Jin Family of Taiyuan!”
“Ooooooh!”
Believe it or not, I was a pretty big name in Murim.
Living proof that even a cramped backwater like Shanxi Province could produce a dragon!
A young icon of the orthodox faction!
“Waaah!”
“Let’s go!
Let’s sweep Dark Heaven away!”
“The Blazing Flame Divine Dragon is with us!”
Whoosh, whoosh, whoosh, whoosh!
The Murim practitioners charged forward with renewed courage, shouting as they ran.
Unnamed and I were at the very front, of course.
“Fuck!
Wreck ’em all!”
I poured my internal energy into the shout, and the roar around me swelled.
With this many Murim practitioners at my side, I was sure we could beat the hell out of anyone.
“It’s a holy war!”
“Great Hero Jin says it’s a holy war!”
“Kill those demons!”
“Amitabhaaa!”
You Dark Heaven bastards!
Stay right there!
I’m bringing the Murim Crusade to you, and I’m going to bash your heads in.
Your heads...
“Ah.”
My brain suddenly stopped working.
A single person was walking out from inside a building burning horribly.
“What the hell are you all doing?”
The fiend was on our side.

chapters.title: Chapter 519
paragraphs: KABOOM!
A large inn burned fiercely. Blackened wooden pillars collapsed, sending ash billowing into the air. The face of the fiend who emerged through it all was so familiar it came as a shock.
“What the hell are you all doing?”
That’s what I wanted to ask.
Silence fell. Unnamed stared at me, his gaze shaking as though an earthquake had struck. Sound Transmission slipped through his barely moving lips and reached my ears.
Why—why is Benefactor Jeok coming out of there?
How should I know?
Wasn’t he Dark Heaven?
That’s what I want to ask.
Amitabha. Could you be Dark Heaven?
What kind of crazy question is that?
If we’re Dark Heaven, does that make you a member of the Vatican?
I wasn’t the only one dumbfounded by Unnamed’s words. Jeok Cheongang, who was exceptionally skilled at eavesdropping on Sound Transmission, already had a face twisted like an evil spirit.
“What? This old man is Dark Heaven?”
“N-no, that’s not what I meant. There’s been a small misunderstanding...”
My attempt to clear up that misunderstanding went nowhere. More precisely, our proud Murim Crusade—already burning with fighting spirit ahead of the Murim Alliance’s founding—wouldn’t let it.
“Dark Heaven!”
“The fiend just declared himself Dark Heaven!”
Keyword entered.
“Wait. He seems to know the Blazing Flame Divine Dragon.”
“Of course he knows him! How many times has the Blazing Flame Divine Dragon fought Dark Heaven?”
“I see. He’s a Dark Heaven fiend!”
Miraculous logic.
“You fiend! You look like a demon straight out of hell!”
“And that hair, all bright red! He looks like he’ll dye the world in blood!”
Attacking his appearance.
“Kill him first!”
“Capture him and you’ll become a hero!”
Medieval Crusader-style conclusion.
All of this happened in the blink of an eye. Faced with the collective madness of some thousand Murim Crusaders, Unnamed and I snapped out of our daze and waved our hands frantically.
“No! That’s not it!”
“Amitabha! Everyone, stop! That man is my master, Master Hong Dao’s...”
At Unnamed’s shout, the martial artists nearest us widened their eyes.
“Oh!”
“Is that true?”
Finally. They’re listening.
Unnamed glanced at me as if he thought the same thing, then nodded.
“It is.”
“Good heavens. Not just any fiend, but the villain who harmed Master Hong Dao!”
“What?”
“What an unforgivable fiend! Tear him limb from limb!”
Fuck. I can’t do this.
Would these martial artists suffer qi deviation if they listened to someone finish a sentence? They refused to understand a damn word.
The grand finale of this collective madness came courtesy of a stranger emerging from the wreckage of the collapsed building.
“Stop, you wicked fiend! How dare you commit such a heinous crime in Henan!”
Jeok Cheongang, who had been staring at this insanity with his mouth open, muttered with a pained expression.
“Not one of these people is in his right mind. Listen to this old man first...”
“Enough talk! This Moon Beauty Saber will not forgive you!”
“...Then you can take a beating first.”
Fair enough. For Jeok Cheongang, he’d held back a long time.
Whoosh. Fwoom!
Bye-bye, Moon Beauty Saber. Enjoy the Disco Pang Pang.
Moon Beauty Saber rushed forward like a streak of light, then shot backward like a cannonball and slammed deep into the wreckage.
None of the martial artists gathered there had seen the punch. None of them could have. The sheer force of it froze the air around them.
“M-Moon Beauty Saber, down in a single blow...!”
“Aaah! The fiend’s martial arts have reached the heavens!”
Forget his martial arts. His anger looks like it’s reached the heavens.

Everyone seemed to understand that provoking Jeok Cheongang right now would be a bad idea. They wanted to defeat a fiend and make a name for themselves, sure. They just didn’t want to be the ones getting defeated.
Finally, some quiet.
With everyone silent, I had one chance to clear up the misunderstanding. I cleared my throat and opened my mouth.
Or rather, I was about to.
“There’s been a serious misunderstanding. The man over there isn’t a fiend, he’s—”
“Halt! Make way!”
“Oh, for fuck’s sake!”
I’m going to lose my mind. Who is it this time?
But the man who appeared as the crowd parted like the Red Sea was not someone I could simply call a bastard.
“The Thunderbolt Saber King has arrived!”
“Great Hero Peng has come to punish the fiend himself!”
Thud. Thud.
An enormous old man strode forward as the crowd’s courage surged anew. He had broad shoulders, fierce eyes, and a massive saber slung over one shoulder.
At the sight of the Thunderbolt Saber King, Jeok Cheongang sighed.
“Finally, someone I can talk to.”
Agreed.

The Thunderbolt Saber King and Jeok Cheongang bickered constantly, but they were quite close. Longtime rivals who were, for all practical purposes, friends. He would recognize Jeok without any trouble.
Sure enough, the Thunderbolt Saber King looked him up and down, then opened his eyes wide.
“What are you doing here?”
“It’s a long story. Send these people away first.”
“Answer my question first.”
“Hm?”
“I asked what a bastard fiend who deserves to be torn limb from limb is doing here.”
Jeok Cheongang’s eyelids began to twitch.
Clip-clop. Clip-clop.
Hooves sounded through the silence. The enormous old man gazing out of the carriage window suddenly spoke.
“The truth is, I recognized you the moment I saw you. How could I not?”
With everyone watching, the Thunderbolt Saber King continued in a solemn voice.
“Red hair, red beard. Anyone would know you were the Fire King. The others couldn’t have dreamed you’d Returned to Youth, but I knew.”
“I see.”
I nodded, then asked, “So why did you start swinging your saber?”
“That was...”
“Oh, and while you’re at it, explain why you ordered an all-out attack after one exchange left you shaking in your boots.”
“Shaking in my boots? Ha ha ha.”
A heavy silence settled over the carriage. Faced with everyone’s distrustful stares, the Thunderbolt Saber King stiffened.
“I wanted to give them some real combat experience.”
“Ah. Combat experience.”
“Think of it as preparation for the coming fight against Dark Heaven. Facing the Fire King, Jeok Cheongang, would be valuable experience for all of them.”
I asked seriously,
“By ‘experience,’ do you mean experience of the afterlife?”

That shut him up. If he had a conscience, it had to: twenty people had been carried to the medical clinic. Most were Third Rate martial artists caught in the aftermath of blows exchanged between two of the Ten Kings—the Fire King and the Thunderbolt Saber King.
We’re lucky it stopped there.
If the poet Yun Dong-ju suffered at even the wind stirring a leaf, they suffered like hell in the howling blade wind.
“Still... I heard they’re all safe.”
“They are. They’ll be safe for at least the next fifteen days, since they’ll spend them lying in the medical clinic.”
Their taste of the afterlife had left its mark.
Martial artists might live on the edge of a blade, but PTSD was no joke. I’d visited the victims. Their faces were pale, and they couldn’t even speak.
The worst of all was the wandering martial artist called Moon Beauty Saber. He was trembling so violently that I almost mistook Henan for Antarctica’s King Sejong Station.
“None of this would have happened if you hadn’t ordered that all-out attack, Great Hero Peng.”
The Thunderbolt Saber King’s round eyes widened at my continued criticism.
“And what about you?”
“Me?”
“Yes, you! Weren’t you the one who rounded up every martial artist nearby and brought them here?”
“I admit that part. But given the circumstances, it was unavoidable. Isn’t that right?”
At my question, Unnamed, my accomplice in the corner, ran his fingers over his prayer beads.
“Benefactor Jin is correct. Even if Shakyamuni had been in my position, he would have rushed forward crying out for the destruction of demons.”
“Could you uproot a bodhi tree and crush a fiend’s skull with it?”
“Amitabha. I could.”

The Thunderbolt Saber King had a temper to match Jeok Cheongang’s, but he couldn’t openly pick on Unnamed. The only Disciple left behind by his dear friend, the Dharma King Hong Dao, was a sore spot for him.
“Urgh.”
He glared at me.
“And you’ve been at it this whole time!”
“What? Why?”
“Are you and I friends?”
“No.”
“Then do you think the Hebei Peng Family is a joke?”
“How did you get from one to the other? You’re changing the subject because you’ve run out of things to say.”
“You little brat. The blood on your head hasn’t even dried, and you keep talking back...”
“Oof. Clack, clack. Dentures.”
I didn’t know exactly what dentures had to do with anything, but the feeling behind it clearly got through.
“How dare you!”
The Thunderbolt Saber King’s face flushed red. He was about to leap to his feet when the two men who had been silent all along spoke almost at once.
“Calm yourself, Sir Peng.”
“Quiet. All of you, shut your mouths.”
The voices and moods could hardly have been more different. Perhaps the only thing connecting the two men was the two characters in their title: Ten Kings.
“I was rash,” the Azure Sky Sword King said plainly. “It had been so long since I last felt my blood stir. I let it get the better of me.”
Jeok Cheongang spoke next.
“This old man did nothing wrong. You were the rash ones.”
That’s our Old Master.
An evergreen if ever there was one. The Thunderbolt Saber King stared at Jeok as if wondering whether he was human.
“Jeok, don’t you feel even a little guilty?”
“Why should I? Martial artists can have a little scrap when they meet. There were people fighting in the inn before I even went in.”
“What would have happened if Great Hero Namgung hadn’t stepped in when he did?”
The Thunderbolt Saber King was right about that much. The dove of peace who’d brought the situation under control was the Azure Sky Sword King.

After a brief exchange with Jeok Cheongang, he’d suffered a minor Internal Injury. He appeared only after settling his internal energy, and one of the Namgung Family members among the crowd recognized him.
Whoa, whoa, whoaaa! Grand Family Head!
He’d screamed like he’d seen a ghost.

The other martial artists, who’d lost their heads at the words Dark Heaven, finally came to their senses. One lunatic did ask whether the Namgung Family was part of Dark Heaven too, but fortunately, our proud Murim Crusaders regained their reason.
If Jeok Cheongang hadn’t Returned to Youth, a few of them probably would have recognized him in the first place.
“That was almost a catastrophe!”
“I could have explained everything. And it happened because your eyes are as bad as a dog’s, you Peng bastard.”
“The inn collapsed! People got hurt!”
“Ahem.”
Perhaps he felt a bit guilty himself. Jeok Cheongang cleared his throat, then opened his mouth with a shameless expression.

“Given the location, I held back. At worst, they got bumped by a little falling debris. Put some spit on it and they’ll be fine. I’ll compensate the innkeeper properly. Even I could see the place burned quite badly.”
“...Is that really coming from the man who killed a thousand members of the Demonic Cult for burning Mount Jiuhua? The more I hear, the more my chest swells.”
“Of course they had to die. Those bastards never intended to pay compensation.”
What is this?
It was utter nonsense, yet somehow it had a logic of its own.
Momentarily at a loss for words, the Thunderbolt Saber King muttered,
“Returned to Youth only changed the skin you’re wearing. The contents are still the same. Your personality is still completely fucked.”
“You ought to do something about the skin on your face, Peng. All you’ve done is get old without Returning to Youth.”
“What did you say?”
“Ho. They say a man who failed to Return to Youth gets angry when reminded of it. You’re a perfect example.”
“How dare you, Jeok!”
“Hm? What did you say? I can’t hear you. The words of an insignificant nobody who couldn’t even Return to Youth are hard to make out.”
Would you look at him dishing out area-of-effect damage.
I couldn’t speak for anyone else, but I saw the Azure Sky Sword King’s shoulders twitch in his seat by the window. He quietly avoided my gaze, looked outside, and spoke.
“You two should stop now.”
At first I thought he was only trying to change the subject. Then I followed his gaze.
“Yeah. You definitely should.”
Ahead of us stood a long stretch of city wall and a vast crowd. Above the iron gates, a huge sign bore three characters in bold, soaring strokes.
Murim Alliance.
