chapters.title: Chapter 520
paragraphs: The young man gazed blankly out the window.

It was a beautiful spring day. The sunlight was just right, and the breeze through the half-open window was pleasantly cool. Flowers had come into full bloom, filling the air with their sweet fragrance.
It was a Wuling Peach Blossom Spring in the mortal world.
Everything would have been perfect if a voice had not suddenly spoken behind him.
“It’s a beautiful day.”
The young man was not startled. He had sensed someone approaching long before they spoke.
Nor was it only this visitor he could sense.
In front of him, behind him, to either side. Above and below.
He perceived everything happening around him and took it all in. He did not do it out of necessity or by conscious effort. It came as naturally as breathing.
What a shame. I can’t even enjoy the spring scenery properly anymore.
The young man turned. An old man with the imposing bearing of someone much younger stood smiling at him.
“I stopped by out of an old man’s needless concern, only to find you slacking off.”
His voice carried the weight of his years. His tone was gentle, like a grandfather speaking to a young grandson, but experience had taught the young man what lay beneath it.
The old man before him kept a blade hidden—one whose edge was cold and sharp.
“What are you thinking about so intently?”
“Just that I’m fortunate not to be your enemy.”
The old man chuckled softly.
“Anyone overhearing you might think I was a frightening man.”
The young man knew better than to be taken in by that good-natured laugh. No one could say how many schemes and far-reaching plans lay behind that smiling face.

During the upheaval of the Great Faction War, the chief of the Murim Alliance’s Hidden Shadow Pavilion had read the state of the world as though it lay in the palm of his hand and eliminated countless fiends. No man who had done that could be ordinary.
“I doubt anyone else would agree with you, Thousand-Faced Fox.”
Thousand-Faced Fox Song Ho.
The Hidden Shadow Pavilion’s old fox, said to have a thousand faces, shrugged.
“Some people do fear this old man, of course. But I hardly think the man before me is one of them.”
“Me?”
“Does it not?”
The young man thought about it for a while. Then his eyes widened.
“Oh. You’re right.”
“Aren’t I?”
“Now that I think about it, I’m not particularly afraid of you.”
Had two ordinary Murim practitioners, each willing to stake his life on his pride, exchanged those words, they would have drawn blades by now.
But neither of these men was ordinary. The identity of the man facing Song Ho had much to do with why he took no offense at all.
“Stay alert to everything around you, but fear no one. An Alliance Leader must always do both.”
The young man—Sword Saint Mae Jonghak—looked uncomfortable.
“I’d rather you didn’t call me Alliance Leader.”
“You’ll have to accept it sooner or later.”
“I simply haven’t gotten used to it.”
“But you’ll soon be Alliance Leader.”
“I’m not yet.”
“They say it’s better to take the whipping early.”
“I’ve always wondered why I have to be the one whipped.”
Thousand-Faced Fox’s answer was brief.
“Because the Martial God isn’t here.”
The title Martial God had once meant perfection. No, it still did.
Everyone who had met him even once had praised him in unison, and even after the passage of many long years, that vast and brilliant Fame still illuminated the world.
But...
“We couldn’t find him.”
The Martial God had disappeared. No one knew whether he was alive or dead, or why he had vanished.
Back when the Murim Alliance still existed, Thousand-Faced Fox had cast the Hidden Shadow Pavilion’s entire intelligence network across the world. Not one trace of the Martial God had turned up.
Like a moment of sunlight in the middle of a storm. Like a meteor streaking across the night sky.
He had disappeared that way, leaving behind a title that had become the very heavens and still hung over the world.
“With him gone, Great Hero Mae Jonghak, you are the only one who can serve as Alliance Leader.”
“Hah. There must be plenty of suitable candidates besides me.”
“If you mean the other members of the Three Saints and the Ten Kings, I’ll pretend I didn’t hear that.”
“Why?”
“For one thing, no one knows where the Bow Saint is.”
“Isn’t the Hidden Shadow Pavilion still looking for him?”
“Do you think Dark Heaven will wait? Shall I send a messenger pigeon? ‘We’re looking for the Bow Saint. Please hold off for a while’?”
“Oh. When you put it that way.”
Thousand-Faced Fox held back the urge to bring his fist down on Mae Jonghak’s head and continued.
“And as you know, his personality is somewhat...”
“I liked his fiery spirit.”
“Others won’t be so fond of it if he runs the Murim Alliance into the ground.”
“Hmm. I suppose not.”
“As for the Slaughter Saint... I’d only wear out my mouth explaining.”
“He might be more suitable than you think. His martial arts aside, he had an overwhelming presence. He seemed capable of commanding people.”
“People would follow him, certainly. Anyone who refused would already be dead.”
“Aren’t you treating him too much like the Killing Ghost?”
“His title is Slaughter Saint. What do you expect from me?”
“You have a point.”
Should I actually hit him?
Thousand-Faced Fox looked at Mae Jonghak with exactly that thought in his eyes, then sighed.
“The other members of the Ten Kings are unsuitable for much the same reasons. Some have passed away. The rest cannot take the position for one reason or another.”

Strength in martial arts alone did not make an Alliance Leader. The position demanded someone decisive enough to make important choices, and possessed of the character and breadth of mind to bring others together.
In that sense, Sword Saint Mae Jonghak was the only possible replacement for the Martial God.

“Great Hero, the leaders of the Nine Sects and One Gang and the Five Great Families have given you their approval. You are upright and fair. You show no special favor even to Huashan, your own sect, and you listen to others. You are more than qualified.”

With the rise of the New Murim Alliance, the Hidden Shadow Pavilion had been officially restored, and Thousand-Faced Fox had regained his former standing. But one man’s support could not make an Alliance Leader.
Only someone recognized by all—someone with the qualities of a leader as well as exceptional martial arts—could take that seat.
Not that there were no objections at all.
Thousand-Faced Fox pushed the thought aside and frowned.
“And yet someone like you is leisurely enjoying the spring weather.”
Mae Jonghak glanced wistfully toward the window.
“It was a nice day. I only looked outside for a moment.”
“Do you know how many matters are waiting for you—”
“Oh, right. Take them with you. I put them all together.”
Thousand-Faced Fox stopped in the middle of his scolding.
“What do you mean?”
“The bamboo slips the Hidden Shadow Pavilion brought in earlier. Seventy-eight matters, to be exact. I’ve dealt with all of them.”
All of them? In so little time?
Thousand-Faced Fox stared at the mountain of bamboo slips in the corner of the office. Then his eyes narrowed.
“Did you read the letter from Qinghai?”

“You mean the Kunlun Sect? Of course. It said they were pressed for time because they had to suppress bands of bandits and mounted bandits. It would be good if they arrived on time, but it should not matter much if they are a little late.”
“And the news from Sichuan?”

“Everyone is working together to speed the Tang Clan’s reconstruction. Ah, tell the Inner Hall to prepare an especially potent elixir. I heard the Family Head’s condition is poor. We should send substantial aid, but for now, we can at least do that much.”
“Then the letter from the Nanman Beast Palace...?”
“Was there one? I saw nothing about the Nanman Beast Palace among today’s matters.”
There was a simple reason for that. None of the matters submitted today had mentioned the Nanman Beast Palace.
Only then did a faint smile reach Thousand-Faced Fox’s lips. Until now, he had only half believed Mae Jonghak.
“Hm? Why are you smiling?”
“It’s nothing. I’m simply pleased to see you attending to your duties so—”
“Do not smile so slyly. Someone else might be horrified if they saw you.”
“Anyway, the breeze is lovely. What a fine day.”
Having spoiled Thousand-Faced Fox’s mood, Mae Jonghak went back to gazing out the window. Then he spoke again.
“Would you like to take a walk outside with me? We may not have another day like this after today.”
“I’d rather not.”
Thousand-Faced Fox’s answer was curt.
“I will send up another matter shortly, so do not do anything pointless, Alliance Leader. Get to work.”
“An honored guest is arriving. The least I can do is go out and greet them.”
“Greet them?”
Thousand-Faced Fox paused, then limped toward the window on his prosthetic leg.
“Look over there.”
Something was slowly approaching beyond the city wall.
It was still a considerable distance away and blurred by it, but once he focused his internal energy, he could easily make out a carriage.
What he could not explain was the familiar face on the driver’s bench of that four-horse carriage.
Why is Shadow Killer there?

Shadow Killer was among the Hidden Shadow Pavilion’s finest agents. At the Star-Array Grand Banquet, he had tracked Mae Jonghak while the Sword Saint was hiding his identity. During the Great Faction War, he had taken the heads of countless fiends.
“A familiar face, isn’t it?” Mae Jonghak said.
“Yes. I sent Shadow Killer when I heard there was trouble on the main road, but...”
I sent him to capture them, and now he’s escorting them here.
Thousand-Faced Fox swallowed the rest of his words as Mae Jonghak’s voice reached his ears.
“An urgent report came while you were away,” Mae Jonghak said.
“An urgent report?”
“Yes. Some welcome faces are on their way.”
Mae Jonghak patted Thousand-Faced Fox’s shoulder twice, then leaned out the window and muttered, “Come, let’s go.”
“Welcome.”
The carriage entered the Murim Alliance’s Inner City and came to a stop. The voice that greeted us as soon as we got down was fairly familiar.
Sword Saint Mae Jonghak.
I’d once known him as Always-Victorious Sword Jongni Chu. He spotted me and gave a short laugh.
“How have you been, my friend?”
He’s really sticking with that act.
I dipped my head in greeting. Mae Jonghak smacked his lips as if disappointed, then turned to Jeok Cheongang.
“I’m glad to see you looking well.”
Jeok Cheongang, who had been yawning extravagantly while looking around, furrowed his brow.
“Were you speaking to this old man?”
“It has been a long time. I’m glad to see you again.”
“You must have mistaken me for someone else. This old man has no particular connection to a brat whose blood hasn’t even dried on his head...”
Jeok Cheongang trailed off. He looked Mae Jonghak up and down, and his eyes widened.
“Could it be you?”
“It is. It’s me.”
Mae Jonghak beamed.
“Since we’ve met again, would you consider becoming Alliance Leader?”
Is this the Murim version of picking a group-project captain?

chapters.title: Chapter 521
paragraphs: “Since it’s good to see you again, let me ask you something. Would you consider becoming Alliance Leader?”
If the captain of a group project announced he was quitting, of course the other members would panic.
Mae Jonghak’s question was so far beyond anything I’d expected that the Thunderbolt Saber King’s mouth fell open. The Azure Sky Sword King and Unnamed stared at him in disbelief.
What does being glad to see him have to do with that...?
And this guy is the Alliance Leader?
They didn’t say it aloud, but their faces did.
The last person there, Jeok Cheongang, looked astonishingly calm when he spoke.
“An ordinary person would be unable to continue speaking at a moment like this. But this old man is different. I have met an awful lot of crazy bastards lately.”
The moment our eyes met, I turned around.
By an incredible coincidence, there was nobody behind me. Nobody except a sparrow pecking at something on the ground.
Oh, I see. That must be why he’s looking this way.
“I didn’t know you liked birds. Sparrows are cute, though.”
“I’m looking at you.”
“Me? Why me all of a sudden?”
“Do you really have to ask?”
“Usually people ask because they don’t know. Why ask if they already do?”
“The way you’re flapping that mouth makes me want to bury you.”
That would be a problem.
I thought it over for a moment, then asked, not quite believing it myself, “This is just on the off chance—an extremely remote, one-in-a-million chance—but was I among the lunatics you mentioned?”
“Without question. Absolutely. Beyond the slightest doubt, your name is at the very top of the list.”
I’d come dead last a few times in school, but this was my first time coming first.
I’m so glad I finally managed it—yeah, right. What the hell?
Jeok Cheongang, of all people, calling me a lunatic. And I ranked above Cheongpung.
The psychological damage made my vision swim. I stared at Jeok Cheongang and opened my mouth.
“There’s this guy I know, Tess hyung. He once said, ‘Know thyself.’”
“Was that directed at this old man?”
“Do you really have to ask?”
“You little son of a—”
His half-raised fist stopped. Sensing the stares gathering around us, Jeok Cheongang groaned and turned back to Mae Jonghak.
“In any case, I’ll give you a straight answer. No.”
“Ho. Why?”
“Too much trouble.”
What an answer. You’d think he might at least be tempted, but he’d turned down the Alliance Leader’s seat because he couldn’t be bothered.
“Ah. Can’t argue with that.”
That was even better.
Please don’t agree with him. Can’t you see people slowly gathering around us?
We’re screwed.
A dreadful thought crept up on me: if this conversation spread, the group project—the Murim Alliance—might fall apart.
Unfortunately, the two masterpieces facing each other were both shamelessly manly men who did not care about such things.
“A title like that doesn’t suit me, and I don’t like dealing with people.”
“Ah. Neither do I.”
“Then quit.”
“I can’t do that.”
“Why?”
Mae Jonghak scratched his chin and tossed out a simple answer.
“Because someone has to do it.”
A man who had taken up a sword simply because he loved martial arts, then earned the name Sword Saint.
A true martial artist who, at the end of a brutal war, had turned his back on wealth and glory, chosen the life of a recluse, and returned to the mountains.
But before he was a martial artist, Mae Jonghak was a Great Hero. He hadn’t accepted the title of Alliance Leader out of some shallow desire for fame. He’d accepted it because he was both.
Someone has to do it.
The words were brief, but they carried weight. Jeok Cheongang gazed at Mae Jonghak, then let out a quiet laugh.
“Many years have passed, yet you haven’t changed. It feels as though we met at Mount Jiuhua only yesterday.”
Mae Jonghak’s eyes widened.
“Yesterday? What are you talking about? That happened at least several decades ago.”
Give me back my touching moment, you bastard.
I wasn’t the only one who felt cheated. Under a shower of cold looks, Mae Jonghak tilted his head.
“Am I remembering it wrong?”
All trace of laughter vanished from Jeok Cheongang’s face.
“...You really haven’t changed. I can feel my insides rotting.”
“Are you still unwell? I heard you had recovered fully from the poisoning.”
“Shut that mouth of yours. If you keep talking, I don’t know what this old man might do.”
“Come to think of it, Great Hero Jeok, you were the first person ever to say that to me. This is why I like you.”
“...Are you and that brat Cheongpung really just Master and Disciple? You’re not related by blood?”
That question deserved a place among Murim’s Seven Great Mysteries.
Everyone, myself included, was waiting for Mae Jonghak’s answer with pounding hearts when an elderly voice sounded behind us.
“As far as I know, the Alliance Leader and the Huashan Divine Dragon are not related by blood.”
I recognized the old man limping toward us on a prosthetic leg.
Thousand-Faced Fox Song Ho.
The former Chief of the Murim Alliance’s Hidden Shadow Pavilion, now restored to the same post in the New Murim Alliance, bowed slightly.
“Please come upstairs. Refreshments are ready.”
The Murim Alliance was crowded.
People with the character Alliance embroidered in silver thread on their chests moved about everywhere. They weren’t all armed martial artists, either. Quite a few wore neat scholars’ robes.
Those people...
Song Ho hadn’t won his post as Chief of the Hidden Shadow Pavilion in a game of Go-Stop. Walking beside me, he seemed to read the question in my glance at once.
“They serve directly under the Alliance Leader’s Office.”
“They don’t look like they’re from the Nine Sects and One Gang or the Five Great Families.”

“Good eye. Because they serve directly under the Alliance Leader’s Office, we didn’t select anyone who belongs to another sect or whose identity hasn’t been thoroughly verified. We have to protect confidential information. This way.”

The Murim Alliance grounds were as vast as a plain and as complicated as a maze. Pavilions and other buildings stood packed together wherever I looked, and shouts rang out from a distant training ground.
When I first got off the carriage, I’d thought we were already in the Inner City. But the farther we went, the tighter security became and the fewer people I saw.
No. It’d be more accurate to say I couldn’t see them.

They could hold their breath and use the most advanced concealment techniques they liked. I could still sense them—on the walls, above the ceiling, hidden in the dark. I felt their gazes and their qi as they watched this place.
“I’ve been wondering for a while. Are those people from the Hidden Shadow Pavilion?”
Song Ho’s eyes widened slightly at the sudden question.
“When did you notice them?”
“When we passed the fifth door.”
“Can you still sense them?”
“Yes.”
“Remarkable. Truly remarkable. Those four were trained as assassins even within the Hidden Shadow Pavilion. To detect every one of them...”
I scratched my chin as he marveled.
“Do you really not know, or are you testing me?”
“Hm? What do you mean?”
“If it’s a test, it’s not much fun. There are five, not four.”
Ssss.
A torch hanging on the wall stirred, then went still. It was the only sign that the Hidden Shadow Pavilion agents concealed nearby had been shaken. Their leader’s gaze grew intent.
“I suspected as much. So it wasn’t a coincidence.”
“Actually, I guessed.”
“Kidding. Your people are all skilled. I nearly walked right past without noticing them.”
Something flashed in Song Ho’s eyes. Unlike when he’d been testing me, his admiration and curiosity now seemed genuine.
“Extraordinary. From the information I’d gathered, I thought I had a fairly accurate idea of your martial ability... Have you gained some new insight lately?”
Insight.
I thought of my ten days of training while drifting down the Yangtze and nodded.

The greatest thing I’d gained from the training Mungyeong prescribed was finer control over qi itself, the source of martial arts. Before, it had been like handling a thick rope. Now it was more like handling a spool of thread.
That had improved my understanding of how to use my internal energy, and my Qi Sense had sharpened along with it.
“Maybe a little.”
“Your rate of growth is frightening. Almost unbelievable.”

“Peng Dojin.”

Jeok Cheongang, who’d been swaggering along like a back-alley thug, kindly supplied the details.

sentences.text: “Since it’s good to see you again, let me ask you something.
Would you consider becoming Alliance Leader?”
If the captain of a group project announced he was quitting, of course the other members would panic.
Mae Jonghak’s question was so far beyond anything I’d expected that the Thunderbolt Saber King’s mouth fell open.
The Azure Sky Sword King and Unnamed stared at him in disbelief.
What does being glad to see him have to do with that...?
And this guy is the Alliance Leader?
They didn’t say it aloud, but their faces did.
The last person there, Jeok Cheongang, looked astonishingly calm when he spoke.
“An ordinary person would be unable to continue speaking at a moment like this.
But this old man is different.
I have met an awful lot of crazy bastards lately.”
The moment our eyes met, I turned around.
By an incredible coincidence, there was nobody behind me.
Nobody except a sparrow pecking at something on the ground.
Oh, I see.
That must be why he’s looking this way.
“I didn’t know you liked birds.
Sparrows are cute, though.”
“I’m looking at you.”
“Me?
Why me all of a sudden?”
“Do you really have to ask?”
“Usually people ask because they don’t know.
Why ask if they already do?”
“The way you’re flapping that mouth makes me want to bury you.”
That would be a problem.
I thought it over for a moment, then asked, not quite believing it myself, “This is just on the off chance—an extremely remote, one-in-a-million chance—but was I among the lunatics you mentioned?”
“Without question.
Absolutely.
Beyond the slightest doubt, your name is at the very top of the list.”
I’d come dead last a few times in school, but this was my first time coming first.
I’m so glad I finally managed it—yeah, right.
What the hell?
Jeok Cheongang, of all people, calling me a lunatic.
And I ranked above Cheongpung.
The psychological damage made my vision swim.
I stared at Jeok Cheongang and opened my mouth.
“There’s this guy I know, Tess hyung.
He once said, ‘Know thyself.’”
“Was that directed at this old man?”
“Do you really have to ask?”
“You little son of a—”
His half-raised fist stopped.
Sensing the stares gathering around us, Jeok Cheongang groaned and turned back to Mae Jonghak.
“In any case, I’ll give you a straight answer.
No.”
“Ho.
Why?”
“Too much trouble.”
What an answer.
You’d think he might at least be tempted, but he’d turned down the Alliance Leader’s seat because he couldn’t be bothered.
“Ah.
Can’t argue with that.”
That was even better.
Please don’t agree with him.
Can’t you see people slowly gathering around us?
We’re screwed.
A dreadful thought crept up on me: if this conversation spread, the group project—the Murim Alliance—might fall apart.
Unfortunately, the two masterpieces facing each other were both shamelessly manly men who did not care about such things.
“A title like that doesn’t suit me, and I don’t like dealing with people.”
“Ah.
Neither do I.”
“Then quit.”
“I can’t do that.”
“Why?”
Mae Jonghak scratched his chin and tossed out a simple answer.
“Because someone has to do it.”
A man who had taken up a sword simply because he loved martial arts, then earned the name Sword Saint.
A true martial artist who, at the end of a brutal war, had turned his back on wealth and glory, chosen the life of a recluse, and returned to the mountains.
But before he was a martial artist, Mae Jonghak was a Great Hero.
He hadn’t accepted the title of Alliance Leader out of some shallow desire for fame.
He’d accepted it because he was both.
Someone has to do it.
The words were brief, but they carried weight.
Jeok Cheongang gazed at Mae Jonghak, then let out a quiet laugh.
“Many years have passed, yet you haven’t changed.
It feels as though we met at Mount Jiuhua only yesterday.”
Mae Jonghak’s eyes widened.
“Yesterday?
What are you talking about?
That happened at least several decades ago.”
Give me back my touching moment, you bastard.
I wasn’t the only one who felt cheated.
Under a shower of cold looks, Mae Jonghak tilted his head.
“Am I remembering it wrong?”
All trace of laughter vanished from Jeok Cheongang’s face.
“...You really haven’t changed.
I can feel my insides rotting.”
“Are you still unwell?
I heard you had recovered fully from the poisoning.”
“Shut that mouth of yours.
If you keep talking, I don’t know what this old man might do.”
“Come to think of it, Great Hero Jeok, you were the first person ever to say that to me.
This is why I like you.”
“...Are you and that brat Cheongpung really just Master and Disciple?
You’re not related by blood?”
That question deserved a place among Murim’s Seven Great Mysteries.
Everyone, myself included, was waiting for Mae Jonghak’s answer with pounding hearts when an elderly voice sounded behind us.
“As far as I know, the Alliance Leader and the Huashan Divine Dragon are not related by blood.”
I recognized the old man limping toward us on a prosthetic leg.
Thousand-Faced Fox Song Ho.
The former Chief of the Murim Alliance’s Hidden Shadow Pavilion, now restored to the same post in the New Murim Alliance, bowed slightly.
“Please come upstairs.
Refreshments are ready.”
The Murim Alliance was crowded.
People with the character Alliance embroidered in silver thread on their chests moved about everywhere.
They weren’t all armed martial artists, either.
Quite a few wore neat scholars’ robes.
Those people...
Song Ho hadn’t won his post as Chief of the Hidden Shadow Pavilion in a game of Go-Stop.
Walking beside me, he seemed to read the question in my glance at once.
“They serve directly under the Alliance Leader’s Office.”
“They don’t look like they’re from the Nine Sects and One Gang or the Five Great Families.”
“Good eye.
Because they serve directly under the Alliance Leader’s Office, we didn’t select anyone who belongs to another sect or whose identity hasn’t been thoroughly verified.
We have to protect confidential information.
This way.”
The Murim Alliance grounds were as vast as a plain and as complicated as a maze.
Pavilions and other buildings stood packed together wherever I looked, and shouts rang out from a distant training ground.
When I first got off the carriage, I’d thought we were already in the Inner City.
But the farther we went, the tighter security became and the fewer people I saw.
No.
It’d be more accurate to say I couldn’t see them.
They could hold their breath and use the most advanced concealment techniques they liked.
I could still sense them—on the walls, above the ceiling, hidden in the dark.
I felt their gazes and their qi as they watched this place.
“I’ve been wondering for a while.
Are those people from the Hidden Shadow Pavilion?”
Song Ho’s eyes widened slightly at the sudden question.

“When we passed the fifth door.”
“Can you still sense them?”
“Yes.”
“Remarkable.

Those four were trained as assassins even within the Hidden Shadow Pavilion.

“Do you really not know, or are you testing me?”
“Hm?

“If it’s a test, it’s not much fun.

Ssss.

chapters.title: Chapter 522
paragraphs: Fuck. One problem after another.
I felt like I’d been walloped in the back of the head.
Nothing in this world was absolute, but I had still thought the events in Hubei had been wrapped up properly...
The Water God Dragon wasn’t the only thing affected by magical power.
Had another Gate opened somewhere? Or had magical power the Water God Dragon failed to absorb leaked out and affected something else?
Looking at the drawing left my mouth feeling gritty, as if I’d been chewing sand.
I wasn’t the only one who understood how serious this was.
“What in the world is that?”
“One thing seems certain. Whatever it is, it cannot be called human.”
The Thunderbolt Saber King and the Azure Sky Sword King muttered to themselves. Mae Jonghak spoke up.
“According to Wudang, that bizarre creature is the Killing Ghost that has been terrorizing Hubei of late.”
“The Killing Ghost?”
Jeok Cheongang frowned and looked at me. I understood the question in his eyes and nodded.
“It’s probably the one you’re thinking of.”
“Damn it. Darkest beneath the lamp, indeed.”
He was right. This was exactly what that saying meant.
But in this case, we couldn’t have noticed. The lamp had been so bright we could barely open our eyes.

With hundreds of people dying across Hubei Province, it would have been strange to pay much attention to a Killing Ghost Wudang was already pursuing. Especially when the culprit we’d finally uncovered was an imugi driven mad by magical power.
We didn’t have time to worry about anything else.
It hadn’t occurred to me that another monster might appear. I’d assumed the Killing Ghost was just another lunatic of the kind you found all over Murim.
But what kind of monster is this bastard?
Drawings from this era looked about like the ones in history textbooks. The drawing on the bamboo slip was no different.
Whoever had made it had clearly tried to be accurate, but it fell short in all sorts of ways, including any sense of depth.
There was only one thing I could tell from it: as the Azure Sky Sword King had said, this thing wasn’t human.

A horn jutted from the middle of its forehead. Its arms and legs were absurdly long and thick. Its eyes, the only part drawn in color, were red. This was beyond anything you could explain with the words demonic, heterodox arts.
Definitely a monster. But had magical power mutated it, like the Water God Dragon?
Tap. Tap.
I drummed my fingers anxiously against the wall.
“Are there any other drawings?”
Thousand-Faced Fox, who’d been watching me closely, nodded.
“Unfortunately, no. That was the best Wudang could do.”
“That’s a shame. But I doubt this is all you have.”
“You’re quick. A second letter arrived from Wudang two days ago.”
At a glance from Thousand-Faced Fox, the middle-aged scholar pulled the ring again.
Whoosh! Thunk!
An oval wooden case slid down the round tube. Inside was a letter densely covered in writing.
“Read it yourself. You were at the center of what happened in Hubei. You may spot something the Hidden Shadow Pavilion and I missed.”
“I was planning to do that anyway.”
“This old man will read it too,” Jeok Cheongang said.
We put our heads together and read the letter. Once didn’t seem enough, so we read it a second time, then a third. Only after fifteen minutes did we look up.
“What do you think?” Thousand-Faced Fox asked.
Jeok Cheongang frowned. “Hard to say.”
“I see.”
“...Why aren’t you asking me anything else?”
Because I wasn’t expecting much from you in the first place.
Not that I had much to add myself. From what the letter said, Thousand-Faced Fox and the Hidden Shadow Pavilion had already pieced together some of the circumstances behind the monster’s appearance.
“As you’ve read, this monster was once a fisherman who lived at the mouth of the Yangtze,” Thousand-Faced Fox said.
I pointed to the first line of the letter. “Jang Sam. In his fifties, with a family.”

Wudang hadn’t assumed a monster like this had simply dropped out of the sky. They’d examined its corpse closely, found several distinguishing features, and investigated. That had led them to a fisherman from a village less than a hundred li from Mount Wudang.
“They say he went out alone to fish more than a month ago and vanished without a trace. When he failed to return after several days, his children petitioned the local authorities.”
The authorities probably couldn’t have found him. Fishermen did die now and then, and Hubei Province had been gripped by fear and chaos after one disaster after another.
When even high-ranking people were dropping dead here and there like minions in some canyon, who was going to worry about one fisherman?
Even if they had actively searched for him, they probably couldn’t have found him.
Even Wudang’s masters had taken quite some time to catch Jang Sam. The local authorities would have had no better luck.
How had an aging fisherman, once as ordinary as they came, become a hideous monster known as the Killing Ghost?
“Any idea what caused it?” Thousand-Faced Fox asked.
“The Blood Fish seem the likeliest cause.”
“I’ve already received the report on them. I sent several Hidden Shadow Pavilion agents to Hubei with orders to capture a live one.”
“Good call. Jang Sam, who became a mon—who became a monster, was originally a fisherman, and Dongting Lake is connected to the tributaries of the Yangtze...”
Mae Jonghak, who’d been listening quietly, murmured, “He might have eaten a Blood Fish that came down one of those tributaries.”
“Or been eaten by one.”
“Either way, that seems likeliest for now. It would explain his appearance and how he grew strong enough to evade Wudang for days.”
Thousand-Faced Fox’s expression hardened. “What about the possibility that the same thing happened somewhere else, as it did with the imugi you defeated? What you call a ‘rift.’”
“Tell me. I wanted to hear it from you.”
They called it a rift here. I called it a Gate.
Of course I’d considered the possibility. I just didn’t want to think about it, let alone say it aloud.
I wasn’t superstitious, but there was that saying about speaking things into existence. Honestly, I wanted to rule out even the slightest chance.
Still, I could not avoid answering. I opened my mouth with an uncomfortable expression.
“I can’t be certain, but I think it’s unlikely.”
“Why?”
“If the same thing had happened, it wouldn’t have ended with just this.”
No second Gate had opened. That was my conclusion.
We should have been relieved. Yet the few of us who knew what a Gate meant—including me—looked grim. They’d understood what I was really saying.
Put simply:
It hasn’t happened yet. But if another Gate blows, we’re truly fucked.
“A powder keg,” Thousand-Faced Fox murmured. “A powder keg, indeed.”
A powder keg was safe as long as no fire touched it. But that also meant it became more dangerous than anything else the moment someone set it alight.
You’d wonder what kind of lunatic would do that, except the lunatics of Dark Heaven had already set Hubei Province’s powder keg alight once.
Murim as it stood was like a vast powder keg on the verge of exploding.
And the second and third Gates would be the enormous sparks that set it off.
There is one small mercy.
I didn’t know who the bastard called the Lord of Heaven really was, or how the Southern Heaven Demon Empress had opened a Gate. But I could make one guess.
Opening a Gate isn’t easy for them either.
A Gate wasn’t an inn door. If Dark Heaven could fling them open whenever they pleased, Murim would already be a complete disaster.
Orcs would have founded sects, while Lycanthropes and ogres would be walking arm in arm down the main roads of Henan.
Before the Murim Alliance could even be formed, everyone would be shouting, Uh, fuck, what are those things? Then we would have fallen apart completely.
But Dark Heaven hadn’t done that.
Why? Because it was hard.
Which meant we had to hurry. We had to stop them before another powder keg blew.
And there was a second mercy: this vast group, united under the Murim Alliance’s banner, had the strength to do it.
“...Calamity has come to Murim,” Mae Jonghak murmured with a sigh. “On a far greater scale than I imagined.”
Thousand-Faced Fox turned to him, his face set. “There’s something I must look into at once. Alliance Leader, forgive me, but would you and the others move elsewhere?”
“Of course.”
“Understood. I’ll report to you later. Until next time, everyone.”
That was the last he said to us.

Before we had even left the pavilion, urgent shouts rang out from every direction. The people who had been worn down by exhaustion opened their eyes wide as though they had never been tired and began moving according to their orders.
The Hidden Shadow Pavilion, which had kept itself alive even after the Murim Alliance’s dissolution, was moving again.
They weren’t the only ones about to get busy.
“I should go as well,” Mae Jonghak said. “There will soon be a mountain of work waiting for me.”
The Azure Sky Sword King nodded. “The same goes for me. May I tell my good-for-nothing son what I heard here today?”
“You seem to have forgotten who brought you here.”
If the information were too secret to share with anyone, the Alliance Leader and the Chief of the Hidden Shadow Pavilion wouldn’t have brought us all here themselves.
The Azure Sky Sword King understood and clasped his hands in salute.
“Thank you.”
“Everyone will know in a few days. Until then, take care that nothing gets out.”
“Of course. I’ll keep that in mind.”
The Thunderbolt Saber King seemed to grasp the gravity of the situation too. His face was stiff as he spoke.
“Hey, Sword Saint. I have something to ask as well.”
“The Hebei Peng Family may be told too. There’s no reason—”
“No, not that. What in the world were you all talking about in there?”
Is the Hebei Peng Family’s Grand Family Head really this low on Intelligence? My pecs are swelling with pride...
Everyone, including me, gave him a cold stare. The Thunderbolt Saber King mumbled a defense.
“You could at least talk about something a man can understand. I know a great pleasure has come to Murim, but...”
“Peng.”
“Yeah?”
“Then shut your mouth for a while. This old man thinks that would help.”
“What did you say?!”
Jeok Cheongang heaved a sigh at the Thunderbolt Saber King, then looked at Mae Jonghak.
“I’ll handle this stupid old man. Go on. You must be busy.”
“Thank you. By the way, Great Hero Jeok.”
“Speak.”
Mae Jonghak took Jeok Cheongang’s hand and held it tight.
“Are you sure you won’t be Alliance Leader?”
Be honest. You and Cheongpung are blood relatives, aren’t you?

When even high-ranking people were dropping dead here and there like minions in some canyon, who was going to worry about one fisherman?
Even if they had actively searched for him, they probably couldn’t have found him.
Even Wudang’s masters had taken quite some time to catch Jang Sam.
The local authorities would have had no better luck.
How had an aging fisherman, once as ordinary as they came, become a hideous monster known as the Killing Ghost?
“Any idea what caused it?” Thousand-Faced Fox asked.
“The Blood Fish seem the likeliest cause.”
“I’ve already received the report on them.
I sent several Hidden Shadow Pavilion agents to Hubei with orders to capture a live one.”
“Good call.
Jang Sam, who became a mon—who became a monster, was originally a fisherman, and Dongting Lake is connected to the tributaries of the Yangtze...”
Mae Jonghak, who’d been listening quietly, murmured, “He might have eaten a Blood Fish that came down one of those tributaries.”
“Or been eaten by one.”
“Either way, that seems likeliest for now.
It would explain his appearance and how he grew strong enough to evade Wudang for days.”
Thousand-Faced Fox’s expression hardened.
“What about the possibility that the same thing happened somewhere else, as it did with the imugi you defeated?
What you call a ‘rift.’”
“Tell me.
I wanted to hear it from you.”
They called it a rift here.
I called it a Gate.
Of course I’d considered the possibility.
I just didn’t want to think about it, let alone say it aloud.
I wasn’t superstitious, but there was that saying about speaking things into existence.
Honestly, I wanted to rule out even the slightest chance.
Still, I could not avoid answering.
I opened my mouth with an uncomfortable expression.
“I can’t be certain, but I think it’s unlikely.”
“Why?”
“If the same thing had happened, it wouldn’t have ended with just this.”
No second Gate had opened.
That was my conclusion.
We should have been relieved.
Yet the few of us who knew what a Gate meant—including me—looked grim.
They’d understood what I was really saying.
Put simply:
It hasn’t happened yet.
But if another Gate blows, we’re truly fucked.
“A powder keg,” Thousand-Faced Fox murmured.
“A powder keg, indeed.”
A powder keg was safe as long as no fire touched it.
But that also meant it became more dangerous than anything else the moment someone set it alight.
You’d wonder what kind of lunatic would do that, except the lunatics of Dark Heaven had already set Hubei Province’s powder keg alight once.
Murim as it stood was like a vast powder keg on the verge of exploding.
And the second and third Gates would be the enormous sparks that set it off.
There is one small mercy.
I didn’t know who the bastard called the Lord of Heaven really was, or how the Southern Heaven Demon Empress had opened a Gate.
But I could make one guess.
Opening a Gate isn’t easy for them either.
A Gate wasn’t an inn door.
If Dark Heaven could fling them open whenever they pleased, Murim would already be a complete disaster.
Orcs would have founded sects, while Lycanthropes and ogres would be walking arm in arm down the main roads of Henan.
Before the Murim Alliance could even be formed, everyone would be shouting, Uh, fuck, what are those things?
Then we would have fallen apart completely.
But Dark Heaven hadn’t done that.
Why?
Because it was hard.
Which meant we had to hurry.
We had to stop them before another powder keg blew.
And there was a second mercy: this vast group, united under the Murim Alliance’s banner, had the strength to do it.
“...Calamity has come to Murim,” Mae Jonghak murmured with a sigh.
“On a far greater scale than I imagined.”
Thousand-Faced Fox turned to him, his face set.
“There’s something I must look into at once.
Alliance Leader, forgive me, but would you and the others move elsewhere?”
“Of course.”
“Understood.
I’ll report to you later.
Until next time, everyone.”
That was the last he said to us.
Before we had even left the pavilion, urgent shouts rang out from every direction.
The people who had been worn down by exhaustion opened their eyes wide as though they had never been tired and began moving according to their orders.
The Hidden Shadow Pavilion, which had kept itself alive even after the Murim Alliance’s dissolution, was moving again.
They weren’t the only ones about to get busy.
“I should go as well,” Mae Jonghak said.
“There will soon be a mountain of work waiting for me.”
The Azure Sky Sword King nodded.
“The same goes for me.
May I tell my good-for-nothing son what I heard here today?”
“You seem to have forgotten who brought you here.”
If the information were too secret to share with anyone, the Alliance Leader and the Chief of the Hidden Shadow Pavilion wouldn’t have brought us all here themselves.
The Azure Sky Sword King understood and clasped his hands in salute.
“Thank you.”
“Everyone will know in a few days.
Until then, take care that nothing gets out.”
“Of course.
I’ll keep that in mind.”
The Thunderbolt Saber King seemed to grasp the gravity of the situation too.
His face was stiff as he spoke.
“Hey, Sword Saint.
I have something to ask as well.”
“The Hebei Peng Family may be told too.
There’s no reason—”
“No, not that.
What in the world were you all talking about in there?”
Is the Hebei Peng Family’s Grand Family Head really this low on Intelligence?
My pecs are swelling with pride...
Everyone, including me, gave him a cold stare.
The Thunderbolt Saber King mumbled a defense.
“You could at least talk about something a man can understand.
I know a great pleasure has come to Murim, but...”
“Peng.”
“Yeah?”
“Then shut your mouth for a while.
This old man thinks that would help.”
“What did you say?!”
Jeok Cheongang heaved a sigh at the Thunderbolt Saber King, then looked at Mae Jonghak.
“I’ll handle this stupid old man.
Go on.
You must be busy.”
“Thank you.
By the way, Great Hero Jeok.”
“Speak.”
Mae Jonghak took Jeok Cheongang’s hand and held it tight.
“Are you sure you won’t be Alliance Leader?”
Be honest.
You and Cheongpung are blood relatives, aren’t you?

chapters.title: Chapter 523
paragraphs: Ssssss.
Hot. Scorching Yang Qi surged from my dantian, spreading through my limbs and bones and racing along my acupoints. Everything felt still and vividly clear.
I circulated my internal energy through the Eight Extraordinary Meridians.
Once, twice, three times...
Circulating qi was like rolling a snowball down a high hill. With every pass, the snowball grew. But it could also pick up dirt, stones, and twigs along the way.
Those impurities were turbid qi. They muddied the purity of my internal energy, and each pass burned away more of them, refining it.
More. More. More.
I kept circulating my energy, repeating the words to myself as if entranced.
Three jiazi of internal energy took the shape of a fire dragon and swam unhindered through my body. In the image I held in my mind, the dragon grew larger, its heat burning hotter.
Then I knew.
Now.
Fwoosh.
At my command, Scorching Yang Qi surged in every direction. The heat was overwhelming, as though a small sun had burst inside me.
My closed eyes grew hot. Flames seemed to pour from my nose instead of breath.
No—it wasn’t just a feeling. That had to be what was happening.
Water overflowed when there was too much of it. Now the internal energy filling my body was flowing out.
Heat poured from my eyes, nose, mouth, and the other openings known as the seven apertures, scorching the air around me. The same thing was happening through the countless pores all over my body.
Ssssss.
I could feel an immense flow of qi gathering above my crown. At the same time, I began to draw on the blank canvas of my mind.
I was my own master. Every acupoint in my body was mine, as was every strand of qi that had flowed out of it. None could defy my will.
I couldn’t see the Scorching Yang Qi above my head, but I could feel it taking the shape I wanted.
One, two, three.
Three petals, red as though they were burning.
Three Flowers Gather at the Crown.
This was what enlightenment had brought to my Supreme Peak realm.
It was a realm any martial artist in the world would dream of reaching. For me, though, it was only the first hill.
Hoo.

The short breath I let out carried the last traces of turbid qi I’d filtered away. Once I had expelled even that final handful, leaving my internal energy and mind clear, I stepped toward the next hill.
Five Qi Returning to Origin.
I’d attempted it several times since opening my Middle Dantian, but I’d never succeeded. Another wall stood in my way.
I’ll get past it. Right now.
A sharp tingle ran through my chest as I made up my mind.
I couldn’t lose this edge of tension. Punching blindly at a wall would only hurt my fist. If I wanted to put even a hairline crack in it, I had to stay alert and read the flow precisely.
Let my guard down for even a moment, and my internal energy could reverse its flow.
Following a road someone else had laid was easy. I was carving out a new one of my own. I had to move boulders, cut through undergrowth—and I could always slip while climbing a cliff.
A reversal would cause an Internal Injury. If I kept forcing my way forward while injured, I’d be asking for qi deviation.

According to Jeok Cheongang, plenty of martial artists had died or been left half-crippled that way. I had no intention of ending up in a wheelchair while Dark Heaven was taking a gigantic dump all over Murim.
Slowly. Carefully.
Fortunately, training with Mungyeong had helped a great deal.

The Scorching Yang Qi I’d built through the Fire Gate Divine Technique—the cultivation technique at the heart of the Fire Gate Clan—had power and explosiveness to rival the techniques of other prestigious sects. Its movements, however, were correspondingly rough.
This training had helped me make up for some of that weakness.
I can do this. As long as I keep my head clear, I can do it.
It was warm. The Three Flowers Gather at the Crown trembled above my head.
Don’t worry. Internal energy is faster than hands.
First ring.
I had just begun to move my internal energy with care when someone spoke.
“Rein it in. Trying now is a waste of effort anyway.”
Crack!
The sudden voice shattered my concentration. The internal energy taking shape as Five Qi Returning to Origin scattered.
At the same time, my internal energy reversed its flow. Gastric juices surged up from deep inside my body, and I vomited.
“Oooooogh!”
Splash.
Vomit flecked with blood spilled across the floor.
Fuck. So this is where the Niagara Falls I saw in pictures were hiding.
I poured out what had come up and stood panting. Then I saw the side dishes I’d eaten that morning waving at me from the floor.
“Uweeegh! Bleeegh!”
Ah. Couldn’t hold that back.
Only after emptying my stomach several more times did my mind finally clear. I glared at the owner of the leather shoes who had already moved a considerable distance away.
“What are you doing?”
Mungyeong inspected the shoes on his feet before answering.
“I only bought these three days ago. I’d rather they didn’t get dirty.”
“Not that. Why did you talk to me while I was circulating my qi?”
“I didn’t even shake you, so what’s the problem? You’ve reached that realm, yet your composure is shattered by a few words. That is your deficiency.”
“You startled me!”
“You startled me too. What the hell have you been eating yesterday and today to produce so much...?”
Mungyeong frowned at the vomit spread across the floor.
“The longer I look, the filthier it gets. Though from the shape, it does bear a passing resemblance to Five Qi Returning to Origin.”
“Hey, Mr. Mun!”
“Mr. what?”
I held Mungyeong’s cold stare.
One second. Two seconds. Three.
Hmm. That should do it.
“Slip of the tongue. I must have suffered a serious Internal Injury.”
“Looking at you makes my qi-sea acupoint throb.”
I avoided his flat stare and hurriedly changed the subject.
“What brings you here all of a sudden? No, wait. How did you get in?”
“What do you think the door is for?”
“But Mujin’s guarding the door...”
My voice trailed off.
Slide. Thump!
A figure collapsed with a faint flop through the half-open doorway.
The back of the head was so familiar that my eyes widened before I could stop them.
“Mujin! Hyuk Mujin!”
“Leave him,” Mungyeong said in a grim voice. “He won’t wake up even if you shake him.”
He wouldn’t wake up even if I shook him?
That blood-crazed Killing Ghost had finally done it.
I roared furiously.
“You cold-blooded murderer! You’re just like that bastard the Slaughter Saint!”
“He was asleep blocking the door. I tried to wake him, but he wouldn’t budge... What did you just say?”
“Huh?”
“I asked what you said.”
“What?”
What the fuck?
Right on cue, Hyuk Mujin’s corpse—no, his body—stirred. A vigorous snore followed.
Grrrrrr.
Our gazes met in silence. I gave Mungyeong a charming smile.
“There seems to have been a very slight, insignificant misunderstanding.”
“It didn’t sound like a misunderstanding. Or an insignificant one.”
“Can’t we just agree that good is good?”
“Dead is dead?”
“Oh... How did you get that from what I said?”
“Why couldn’t I? Do you have a problem with it?”
I did have a problem with it, and his cochlea also seemed to have a serious problem, but I lacked the courage to point that out.
“I was wrong.”
“And an apology settles everything?”
“I believe a sincere conversation can untangle any knot.”
“Good. Go have one with Dark Heaven’s Lord of Heaven, then. Now wipe that irritating smile off your face before I tear your mouth apart.”
“Our ancestors said you can’t spit in a smiling face.”
“Ptui.”
Splat.
Hmm. Our ancestors were wrong.
At times like this, I had to regain my composure. I calmly wiped the spit from my cheek.
“That came out incredibly fast. I thought it was a hidden weapon.”
“If I put internal energy behind it, I can burst someone’s eyeballs.”
“Impressive. Are you Zerg, by any chance?”
“I’m the Grim Reaper.”
“...Once again, I’m very sorry.”
Mungyeong looked at me as if calculating how many pieces he’d have to cut me into for people to say he’d killed me properly. Then he clicked his tongue.
“Enough. Every time I talk to you, it drains me.”
He’s one to talk. I’m losing life force by the second.
I’d bet Hyuk Mujin’s left atrium that conversation had shaved at least three days off my life.
I told that bastard Hyuk Mujin to stand guard. He couldn’t even resist falling asleep again.
Mungyeong was something else, but Hyuk Mujin was no less impressive.
“So what brings you here...?”
“That sounded like ‘What shitty thing have you come here to do this time?’”
“Oh.”
“Oh?”
“Oh... no. I was just curious.”
“Your pronunciation seems to have grown rather strange since I last saw you. Must be my imagination.”
“Of course. Just your imagination.”
Mungyeong sighed quietly and tossed me the bundle in his hand.
Thump.
I caught it reflexively and stared at it with wide eyes.
“What’s this?”
“A pill.”
“A pill?”
Is it Santa Claus in spring? What’s with the sudden present?
I opened the bundle, still unsure what to make of it, and found a small, sturdy-looking wooden case inside. A strange fragrance reached deep into my nose.
This is...
They said you could tell how potent some elixirs were before you even saw them. Now I understood what they meant. I knew the pill inside was powerful before I opened the case.
Click.
When I opened the case, a reddish pill came into view. Even at first glance, it was clearly no ordinary pill.
I stared at it for a moment, then looked up at Mungyeong.
“What are you looking at?”
“Why are you giving me something like this all of a sudden?”
“It holds a considerable amount of fire qi. It’ll help you.”
“What?”
“Is there a hidden weapon stuck in your ear? Don’t make me say it twice.”
“No, I wasn’t asking what it does...”
Mungyeong’s face crumpled. For someone who spent most of his time looking bleak, it was a remarkable display of emotion.
“I found it on the way here.”
“Let me correct that. I saw it while passing by and bought it. Satisfied?”
What do you mean, satisfied, old man?
I touched the red pill in its case.
Item check.
Ding.
System Mungyeong’s Specially Crafted Pill for Jin Taekyung Would you like to view more detailed information? Y / N
Yeah. No. That’s enough.
I closed the small System window and gave Mungyeong a lukewarm look.
“‘Saw it while passing by and bought it.’ Right.”
“...What’s that look for?”
“Nothing. Thank you. I’ll take it.”
What I felt toward Mungyeong was half gratitude, half fear.
I appreciate the good pill, but what the hell is the next training session going to be...?
Being treated this well all of a sudden felt like being fed a good meal before an execution.
As if he understood what my trembling gaze meant, Mungyeong opened his mouth.

chapters.title: Chapter 524
paragraphs: Hyuk Mujin woke up fifteen minutes after Mungyeong left.
He poked his head through the gap in the open door. The moment our eyes met, he spoke with a solemn expression.
“Your qi circulation is complete.”
“Yeah. Your life is about to be over, too.”
“Hyuk Mujin, Vice Squad Leader of the Jin Dragon Squad of the great Jin Family of Taiyuan. As the Captain ordered, I was guarding the door so that not even a single ant could get inside.”
“...Are you seriously insane?”
Look at this bastard, acting proud after letting in everything but the ants.
It was ridiculous, but I decided to give him high marks for the sheer nerve it took to lie so brazenly after snoring his head off.
“Close the door and get lost.”
“Yes, sir.”
Perhaps he felt guilty, because he didn’t offer even a word of protest before scampering away.
Just as he was about to shut the door, something occurred to me.
“Wait. What about the others?”
“Who do you mean by ‘the others’...?”
“All of them.”
Hyuk Mujin thought for a moment.
“First, the Lesser Family Head is meeting with the Sect Leaders and Family Heads of the other factions.”
“The Sect Leaders and Family Heads?”
“Yes. It seems he’s been meeting with them more often for the past two days.”
Two days ago. That was when a few of us, including Jeok Cheongang and me, had gone to the Murim Alliance.
It was about time the subject came up.
At the very least, the heads of the Nine Sects and One Gang and the Five Great Families should have received some warning.
With all sorts of information and problems related to Dark Heaven coming to light, it was only natural for them to put their heads together and devise a countermeasure.
“Oh, and we handed the Three Fiend over to the Murim Alliance. I heard they were going to bring in some master to interrogate him...”
“Really?”
The third of the Qilian Three Fiends, who had stained Sichuan with blood under the Western Heaven Demon Lord’s command, was remarkably hard to kill.
Plenty had happened while he was bound and brought all the way to Henan, yet unlike his two brothers, his head was still attached to his neck. That alone proved how lucky the bastard was.
It was just a different part that had fallen off instead.
If he kept saying he didn’t know anything even while they were cutting off his balls, I doubt an interrogation will get much more out of him.
Even for a Supreme Peak master—hell, for anyone—one’s balls were precious.
Gung Gibang and Hyuk Mujin had once held a hundred-minute debate over which mattered most: a man’s life, his dantian, or his balls.
Anyway, I handed the Three Fiend over as ordered. The Murim Alliance can handle the rest.
Well, what happened after that was none of my concern. I could only hope the Murim Alliance managed to obtain more information about Dark Heaven through further interrogation.
“Forget my eldest brother. What about the others? I haven’t seen them anywhere.”
“Gung Gibang moved to a different lodging.”
“He moved? When?”
“About one or two shichen ago. You were busy circulating your qi, so I took the message for you.”
“...You weren’t asleep then?”
“What are you talking about? I told you I stood guard like an iron wall.”
“Ugh. Every time this bastard opens his mouth—”
I raised my fist, and Hyuk Mujin hurried on.
“The Beggars’ Sect! He said he would be staying at the Henan branch of the Beggars’ Sect, so we should come find him anytime something happens.”
I stopped just short of hitting him.
“The Beggars’ Sect? Why would he go there?”
“What?”
Hyuk Mujin looked at me as though I’d said something absurd.
“May I ask which faction you belong to, Captain?”
“What kind of stupid question is that? The Jin Family of Taiyuan or the Fire Gate Clan, obviously.”
“And Gung Gibang?”
“...Oh, shit. Right. He’s the Beggars’ Sect’s Successor Beggar.”
I had forgotten because he clung to me like a burr. Come to think of it, he had a master and a sect of his own. It would be unreasonable for him to stay with us even in Henan.
“Wait. Did Cheongpung leave too?”
“Of course.”
“...Really?”
It’ll be quiet for a while, then.
And yet I felt both relieved and disappointed. I’d keep seeing them both, of course, but without those two making a racket all the time, I could already feel the empty space they’d left behind.
“They could’ve at least said goodbye before leaving.”
At my mutter, Hyuk Mujin looked me up and down as though I were some strange creature.
“Why would they say goodbye?”
“Why are you so heartless? We’ve spent all this time together, and they just leave without saying goodbye?”
“Do they need to say goodbye when they’re only going out for a bit?”
“They went to the marketplace to buy sweetmeats and dumplings.”
Shit. Give me back my sentimentality.
I was momentarily speechless. Hyuk Mujin cast me a meaningful look.
“Captain.”
“Shut up.”
“I haven’t said anything yet.”
“That’s why I’m telling you to shut up.”
“I’ll stay by your side no matter what happens, Captain.”
“...Please get away from me.”
“Come on. You like it, so why are you acting like this?”
I was annoyed, but worse than that, I was embarrassed as hell.
I sighed. Hyuk Mujin, still needling me, suddenly seemed to remember something.
“By the way, you haven’t asked about Mungyeong.”
“I already saw him.”
“You did? He’s seemed pretty busy lately, too. He’s been gathering strange medicinal ingredients, boiling them, pounding them... He looked completely swamped. When did you see him?”
“While you were asleep, you bastard!”
Wham! Wham! Wham!
“Urgh! Oof! Gah!”
“Go! Get out right now!”
After taking a thorough beating, Hyuk Mujin looked at me with tears welling in his eyes.
“Do you hate me that much?”
I immediately shook my head.
“No. I want to kill you.”
“That’s too harsh. Really.”
“I told you to stand guard for a moment, and you went to sleep! You slept long enough to dream the entire Dream of the Nine Clouds. You bastard.”
“Why do you only hate me, Captain?! I hate you too!”
Tap-tap-tap. Slam!
I was speechless as Hyuk Mujin ran off, scattering tears behind him.
What the hell.
The guy was well past his mid-twenties, and that was what he came out with? My fists were growing grander by the second.
I was letting out a heartfelt sigh when the door opened again and Hyuk Mujin poked his head through the gap.
“Welcome back. Our Mujin has come to pick out his burial plot.”
“No. That’s not it. I came because I was worried you might misunderstand.”
“What?”
“I didn’t shut the door that hard on purpose. The wind was strong.”
“Well, I’ll be going now. Good work, sir. Loyalty.”
Should I really kill him?
He was acting exactly like an elementary school kid who’d just been scolded by his mother. I glared at the door as it closed again, this time as gently as a door could close, then shook my head.
I turned back to the empty space I’d been looking at before Hyuk Mujin woke up.
Item Window

System Mungyeong’s Specially Crafted Custom Pill for Jin Taekyung Type: Elixir Grade: Peak Restriction: None (effect increases if taken by Jin Taekyung) Description: A pill focused on stability and recovery rather than increasing internal energy. If taken when internal energy is unstable, it steadies the user’s qi and greatly increases their recovery. Special Note: Made with Jin Taekyung in mind. He will receive an even greater effect if he takes it.
I stroked the reddish pill—otherwise known as the Mungyeong Special Jin Custom Pill—then put it back in its wooden case.
Inventory open. Store.
A System notification appeared, telling me the item had been stored.
But my mind was already on the conversation I’d had with Mungyeong before he left.
“Training ends here.”
“Pardon?”
“Why? Are you disappointed?”
A lot of emotions seemed to pass through me in that moment. After hesitating, I answered,
“...To be honest, I can’t say I’m glad to hear it.”
“Why?”
“I want to get stronger. Much stronger than I am now.”
“Greedy bastard. Aren’t you strong enough already?”
“Isn’t that how people are? No matter how much we have, we always want more.”
Mungyeong stared at me for a long time after I questioned him in return, then let out a quiet laugh.
It was the first time I’d seen him smile since we met.
“You’re finally starting to sound like a Murim practitioner.”
“I am a Murim practitioner.”
“Then let me ask you again. Do you want to become an assassin, or a Murim practitioner?”
“I want to be strong. So strong no one would dare touch me. Strong enough that everyone around me would be safe just because I’m there.”
“The Invincible... That’s an ambitious dream.”
The Invincible. The word sounded distant and grandiose.
Even the Martial God had enemies. The Heavenly Demon, master of the Demonic Cult, and the hundred thousand soldiers of the Demonic Path under his command had been the Martial God’s adversaries.
“You really do dream big.”
“Even if reality is a cesspit, your dreams should be big and lofty.”
“Funny. That’s obviously ridiculous bluster, but coming from you, it sounds almost plausible.”
“Pardon?”
“Nothing. And if that’s your reason, then you must not learn my martial arts.”
“Why?”
“Too much of anything becomes poison. You don’t need two wells right now.”
“...I should dig only one well?”
“Did you just speak informally to me?”
“No, that’s not what I meant.”
“I made this decision after a great deal of thought. Keep that in mind.”
“Is it because I lack talent?”
I’d asked as Mungyeong was about to leave.
His answer was short.
“The opposite.”
“Pardon?”
“If you were weak and untalented, I’d have taught you more. You’d need to learn whatever you could to survive.”
Those words suddenly brought back my days as an F-rank Hunter.
No matter how carefully you chose your position and approached a fight, danger could be lurking anywhere.
Without a tank’s protection or cover from a mage or archer, you were ultimately on your own.
If I dropped my spear by mistake, I cut a goblin’s throat with the dagger I carried. If the dagger broke, I picked up a rock and smashed in its head.
I did whatever it took to survive.
I hadn’t picked a spear because I had any special talent for it. I’d figured that keeping some distance between myself and the monsters might improve my chances of staying alive.
“Judging by your expression, something’s occurred to you.”
“...I think I understand some of what you mean.”

“The martial arts I learned are different in nature from the Fire Gate Clan’s. I was raised as an assassin from the start, and I spent more than half my life as one. We began in different places. Even if I taught you my martial arts, you’d likely be unable to make them your own simply by following the formulas.”
“Is that why you’re ending my training? I thought we’d barely started.”
“Started? You already know everything.”
“Pardon?”
“What matters isn’t martial arts. It’s martial principles. Those principles are everything I have. They’re the foundation on which the name Slaughter Saint was built.”
I could still remember the look in his eyes. I couldn’t begin to tell what lay behind it.
And I could still remember his voice.

“There were three hundred of us at first. We all learned the same martial arts and underwent the same training. Ten years later, only twenty of those three hundred raised as assassins remained. Ten years after that, only one remained.”
I didn’t need to ask who the last person was.
Mungyeong looked back into the distant past with that inscrutable gaze, then turned away. He left me with one final instruction.

“I taught you the martial principles you needed most. Combining martial arts of different kinds is nearly impossible, but principles have no such divide. Work those principles into the martial arts you’ve learned. That’s your final task.”
Thump. Thump.
I came out of my thoughts. A familiar presence outside was knocking on the door.
“Hyuk Mujin?”
“Captain. It’s time. You should come out.”
It’s time?
The question vanished almost as soon as it arose.
I suddenly realized what day it was.
The Murim Alliance.
Today, all of Murim would stand beneath a single banner.
