chapters.title: Chapter 530
paragraphs: Henan truly deserved to be called the Central Plains.

Civilization had begun along the Yellow River, and for thousands of years, Henan had stood at the center of the world. It had been home to the capitals of nine dynasties that rose and fell like wildfire over the ages.
So even now, with the Murim Alliance officially restored and the threat of war hanging in the air, Henan Province had not lost its vitality.
If anything, the opposite was true.
“Is it just me, or are there more people around? The atmosphere seems pretty good, too.”
Hyuk Mujin was right. The broad main street was packed, and there was little sign of serious worry on anyone’s face.
Now and then, someone cast an uneasy glance at a passing martial artist carrying weapons, but that was all.
I pulled my bamboo hat lower. “Yeah, it does.”
“Strange. Until recently, things were pretty grim. Is this the calm before the storm?”
“...You lunatic. Why don’t you pray for something to happen while you’re at it?”
“Considering the situation, I’m not exactly wrong.”
He had a point. But Hyuk Mujin was overlooking something. I considered smacking him upside the head, then shook my head.
“I think those people have realized something.”
“What?”
“That Henan is the safest place in the world.”
To ordinary people, martial artists were like wild beasts no one could control.

But most of the martial artists now in Henan had come together under the banners of chivalry, the greater good, and the Murim Alliance. And there weren’t just dozens or hundreds of them. There were thousands.
News of a war among martial artists must have frightened the commoners at first, but people were quickly settling down.
If this were the modern world, they wouldn’t be so relaxed.
Imagine a war breaking out between the United States and Russia.

The moment the war began, the citizens of Moscow or Washington, DC, would either be running for their lives or staring up at the sky, trying to guess when an intercontinental ballistic missile or a nuclear weapon might come flying toward them.
Not that Henan is guaranteed to be safe.
Could Dark Heaven sweep through half the world and reach Henan?
It wasn’t impossible. The Murim Alliance had formed, and countless martial artists had gathered beneath one flag, but no one could know how the war would end.
The bigger problem was that Dark Heaven had other ways of getting here.
The Moving Formation. Or should I call it a warp magic circle?
It was a disturbing truth, hard to believe and not yet known to everyone.
A truth like that could make people more vigilant. It could also cause tremendous shock and chaos. That was probably why it hadn’t been made public yet.
When that happens, people won’t be smiling like this anymore.
I smacked my lips bitterly and looked around.

Children watched passing martial artists with fascination. Merchants were delighted by the unexpected boom. Martial artists moved along the main street, their faces showing a mix of tension and excitement.
None of them, at least, knew everything about Dark Heaven. Those privy to its deeper secrets were already in a meeting with their new Alliance Leader, one that might go on indefinitely.
“Captain?”
“What are you thinking about so hard? You’re making people stare.”
“...Nothing. Let’s go.”
I must have spaced out. I started walking again.
Standing still in the middle of a crowded main street was bound to draw attention. Sure enough, a few sharp-eyed people were already looking our way.
They’re not ordinary martial artists. They’re masters.
That didn’t make them Dark Heaven’s agents. They wore martial uniforms and carried their weapons openly, and I could sense pure qi from every one of them.
“Captain.”
Hyuk Mujin’s voice came quietly from behind me. I kept walking as though nothing was wrong.
“It’s fine. Just keep going.”
“You knew?”
“Of course.”
“I’m still worried.”
I understood why. Since the Mount Song Resolution, I’d become something of a celebrity.

The Sleeping Dragon of Shanxi and the Blazing Flame Divine Dragon were already epithets firmly imprinted throughout the Murim. But by raising the Murim Alliance’s flag before thousands of martial heroes, I had left an even more definite impression.
I wasn’t on the level of the heads of the Nine Sects and One Gang or the Five Great Families, but more people knew my name and face than those of most Elder-level masters from major factions.
“What’s there to worry about? Pretend you haven’t noticed them and keep walking.”
“No, I’m worried something really bad is going to happen.”
Gung Gibang clicked his tongue.
“What a tiny little heart you have. What serious thing is going to happen just because they recognize his face? It’ll only be annoying. This is exactly why he’s wearing that bamboo hat.”
He glanced at me. “What’s gotten into him?”
“Leave him alone. It’s kind of touching that he noticed them first and started worrying.”
“...I suppose.”
I smiled to myself.

I didn’t usually show it, but I had a soft spot for Hyuk Mujin. Since coming to Murim, I’d spent more time with him than anyone else, and we’d been through all kinds of trouble together. Of course I cared about—
“This is driving me crazy. What are you two talking about?”
“Huh?”
“What?”
Hyuk Mujin looked at Gung Gibang and me, his face pale.
“I’ve been about to shit myself this whole time, and you two keep saying the weirdest things. Seriously.”
Touching, my ass.
When he said something bad was going to happen, he’d meant that.
As Gung Gibang and I stared at him, speechless, Hyuk Mujin broke into a cold sweat and hurried ahead.
“Where are we meeting? Hurry! It’s coming out!”
Look at that determination. I’d never seen him look so desperate, even in a fight. Gung Gibang pointed at a building on reflex.
“O-over there.”
“That one? The three-story inn?”
“Uh? Yeah.”
“Then I’m going ahead. Pooooop!”
Was that last cry sheer determination to hold it in? Or a booster powered by the last of his sphincter’s strength?
Hyuk Mujin staggered as he wove through the crowd at incredible speed. Gung Gibang muttered, “Drunken Eight-Immortals Step...?”
“...Please don’t talk bullshit. He just needs to shit.”
God. Buddha. Why am I surrounded by nothing but idiots?
Lamenting my fate, I looked toward the three-story inn Hyuk Mujin was heading for.
It wasn’t far away. Yet the part of my chest that had settled down during the journey suddenly began to churn.
“...A month? No, has it been two?”
Gung Gibang narrowed his eyes at my unguarded mutter.
“Oh-ho.”
“What, you bastard?”
“Is it what I think it is?”
“You can think?”
“I’m right, aren’t I?”
“Want to get hit?”
“Come to think of it, the atmosphere back then was a little strange.”
“Want me to pick out your grave?”
“That clever dodge tells me I’m right.”
“Want me to hit you so fast you can’t dodge, clever or not?”
“Pfft. That bastard Hyuk should’ve seen this.”
“...No, it’s not— Ah, forget it.”
Normally, Gung Gibang would have changed the subject by now, if only to avoid getting hit. Today was different.
His laughter sounded like air leaking out as he kept glancing at me. My fist clenched, but strangely enough, I didn’t feel like hitting him.
“Pfft, pfft, pfft.”
Bam!
Watching him laugh brought the urge right back.
He couldn’t even scream. I grabbed him by the back of the neck and hauled him up as he clutched his solar plexus.
“So. That’s the place, right? The three-story inn.”
“Urgh. Y-yes.”
“I’m going for the food. Because I’m hungry.”
“I-I know.”

“I heard that Kunlun Cloud Dragon guy or whatever is there, too. I’m going to see him because it’s been a while. And while I’m there, I’ll build a little rapport with that Hwangbo fellow or whatever his name is.”
“...I’ll remember that.”
“See that you do. Unless you want the Ten Dragons and Phoenixes to become the Nine Dragons and Phoenixes.”
That seemed to drive the lesson home. Once I let him go, Gung Gibang rubbed the spot I’d hit.
“Vicious bastard.”
“What was that?”
“N-nothing.”
As if that would fool me. Gung Gibang hastily changed the subject.
“Anyway, I’m looking forward to it. When they hear you’ve come, they’ll welcome you with open arms.”
“I don’t care whether they do or not.”
I wasn’t particularly interested in the Kunlun Cloud Dragon or that Lesser Family Head of the Hwangbo Family.
There was, though, one person I hoped would be genuinely glad to see me.
But Gung Gibang misunderstood my answer and hurriedly continued,
“No! Hwangbo Ak is a bit of a pain, but once he hears you came all this way, he’ll come running out barefoot and—”
He never finished.
Boom!
A thunderous crash swallowed his voice and every sound on the bustling street.
A silence too brief to call an instant fell, then broke.
“Aaah!”
“Eeeeeek!”
“Gowolru! Gowolru is...!”
People screamed and scattered in every direction like a swarm of locusts.
I stood where I was and stared.
Gowolru.
I could see it clearly. A section of the three-story inn where we were supposed to meet had been blown wide open.
Someone came hurtling out through a shower of debris and a cloud of dust.
Whoosh! Crash!
A street stall not far away shattered, and a deep gouge opened in the ground.
A man managed to right himself and get to his feet.
Thud, thud, thud.
Who’s that?
His martial uniform was torn to shreds, and his leather shoes had come off. His handsome face was filled with fury and dismay.
“How dare you... You bastard! I’ll tear you apart...!”
Just then, Gung Gibang gaped at the man, who was speaking through clenched teeth.
“H-Hwangbo Ak!”
“What are you doing out here?”
What? That’s Hwangbo Ak?
Hwangbo Ak faltered at the sound of his name. I looked him up and down.
“He did come running out barefoot.”
Was this a surprise for me? Some impromptu welcome from the Ten Dragons and Phoenixes?
Judging by the way Hwangbo Ak’s face twisted, probably not.
“What did you just say?”
“Oh. Sorry. I didn’t mean it that way.”
“You damned bastard...”
“You look busy. Let’s talk later. Ah, here it comes.”
“What?”
His confusion lasted only a moment. Hwangbo Ak seemed to have forgotten something, but urgency and horror rose across his face.
Whoooosh—boom!
Something enormous shot through the air and slammed into Hwangbo Ak.

I could tell how fast it was moving, and how much force it carried, just from the sound. He would have been hard-pressed to deal with it while fully alert. Distracted as he was, the result was inevitable.
“Guhk!”
Hwangbo Ak went flying, spraying blood. A massive shadow moved to pursue him.
What should I do? I didn’t have to think long.
Never a quiet day around here.

“Me. Don’t want to.”

sentences.text: Henan truly deserved to be called the Central Plains.
Civilization had begun along the Yellow River, and for thousands of years, Henan had stood at the center of the world.
It had been home to the capitals of nine dynasties that rose and fell like wildfire over the ages.
So even now, with the Murim Alliance officially restored and the threat of war hanging in the air, Henan Province had not lost its vitality.
If anything, the opposite was true.
“Is it just me, or are there more people around?
The atmosphere seems pretty good, too.”
Hyuk Mujin was right.
The broad main street was packed, and there was little sign of serious worry on anyone’s face.
Now and then, someone cast an uneasy glance at a passing martial artist carrying weapons, but that was all.
I pulled my bamboo hat lower.
“Yeah, it does.”
“Strange.
Until recently, things were pretty grim.
Is this the calm before the storm?”
“...You lunatic.
Why don’t you pray for something to happen while you’re at it?”
“Considering the situation, I’m not exactly wrong.”
He had a point.
But Hyuk Mujin was overlooking something.
I considered smacking him upside the head, then shook my head.
“I think those people have realized something.”
“What?”
“That Henan is the safest place in the world.”
To ordinary people, martial artists were like wild beasts no one could control.
But most of the martial artists now in Henan had come together under the banners of chivalry, the greater good, and the Murim Alliance.
And there weren’t just dozens or hundreds of them.
There were thousands.
News of a war among martial artists must have frightened the commoners at first, but people were quickly settling down.
If this were the modern world, they wouldn’t be so relaxed.
Imagine a war breaking out between the United States and Russia.

The moment the war began, the citizens of Moscow or Washington, DC, would either be running for their lives or staring up at the sky, trying to guess when an intercontinental ballistic missile or a nuclear weapon might come flying toward them.
Not that Henan is guaranteed to be safe.
Could Dark Heaven sweep through half the world and reach Henan?
It wasn’t impossible.
The Murim Alliance had formed, and countless martial artists had gathered beneath one flag, but no one could know how the war would end.
The bigger problem was that Dark Heaven had other ways of getting here.
The Moving Formation.
Or should I call it a warp magic circle?
It was a disturbing truth, hard to believe and not yet known to everyone.
A truth like that could make people more vigilant.
It could also cause tremendous shock and chaos.
That was probably why it hadn’t been made public yet.
When that happens, people won’t be smiling like this anymore.
I smacked my lips bitterly and looked around.
Children watched passing martial artists with fascination.
Merchants were delighted by the unexpected boom.
Martial artists moved along the main street, their faces showing a mix of tension and excitement.
None of them, at least, knew everything about Dark Heaven.
Those privy to its deeper secrets were already in a meeting with their new Alliance Leader, one that might go on indefinitely.
“Captain?”
“What are you thinking about so hard?
You’re making people stare.”
“...Nothing.
Let’s go.”
I must have spaced out.
I started walking again.
Standing still in the middle of a crowded main street was bound to draw attention.
Sure enough, a few sharp-eyed people were already looking our way.
They’re not ordinary martial artists.
They’re masters.
That didn’t make them Dark Heaven’s agents.
They wore martial uniforms and carried their weapons openly, and I could sense pure qi from every one of them.
“Captain.”
Hyuk Mujin’s voice came quietly from behind me.
I kept walking as though nothing was wrong.
“It’s fine.
Just keep going.”
“You knew?”
“Of course.”
“I’m still worried.”
I understood why.
Since the Mount Song Resolution, I’d become something of a celebrity.
The Sleeping Dragon of Shanxi and the Blazing Flame Divine Dragon were already epithets firmly imprinted throughout the Murim.
But by raising the Murim Alliance’s flag before thousands of martial heroes, I had left an even more definite impression.
I wasn’t on the level of the heads of the Nine Sects and One Gang or the Five Great Families, but more people knew my name and face than those of most Elder-level masters from major factions.
“What’s there to worry about?
Pretend you haven’t noticed them and keep walking.”
“No, I’m worried something really bad is going to happen.”
Gung Gibang clicked his tongue.
“What a tiny little heart you have.
What serious thing is going to happen just because they recognize his face?
It’ll only be annoying.
This is exactly why he’s wearing that bamboo hat.”
He glanced at me.
“What’s gotten into him?”
“Leave him alone.
It’s kind of touching that he noticed them first and started worrying.”
“...I suppose.”
I smiled to myself.
I didn’t usually show it, but I had a soft spot for Hyuk Mujin.
Since coming to Murim, I’d spent more time with him than anyone else, and we’d been through all kinds of trouble together.
Of course I cared about—
“This is driving me crazy.
What are you two talking about?”
“Huh?”
“What?”
Hyuk Mujin looked at Gung Gibang and me, his face pale.
“I’ve been about to shit myself this whole time, and you two keep saying the weirdest things.
Seriously.”
Touching, my ass.
When he said something bad was going to happen, he’d meant that.
As Gung Gibang and I stared at him, speechless, Hyuk Mujin broke into a cold sweat and hurried ahead.
“Where are we meeting?
Hurry!
It’s coming out!”
Look at that determination.
I’d never seen him look so desperate, even in a fight.
Gung Gibang pointed at a building on reflex.
“O-over there.”
“That one?
The three-story inn?”
“Uh?
Yeah.”
“Then I’m going ahead.
Pooooop!”
Was that last cry sheer determination to hold it in?
Or a booster powered by the last of his sphincter’s strength?
Hyuk Mujin staggered as he wove through the crowd at incredible speed.
Gung Gibang muttered, “Drunken Eight-Immortals Step...?”
“...Please don’t talk bullshit.
He just needs to shit.”
God.
Buddha.
Why am I surrounded by nothing but idiots?
Lamenting my fate, I looked toward the three-story inn Hyuk Mujin was heading for.
It wasn’t far away.
Yet the part of my chest that had settled down during the journey suddenly began to churn.
“...A month?
No, has it been two?”
Gung Gibang narrowed his eyes at my unguarded mutter.
“Oh-ho.”
“What, you bastard?”
“Is it what I think it is?”
“You can think?”
“I’m right, aren’t I?”
“Want to get hit?”
“Come to think of it, the atmosphere back then was a little strange.”
“Want me to pick out your grave?”
“That clever dodge tells me I’m right.”
“Want me to hit you so fast you can’t dodge, clever or not?”
“Pfft.
That bastard Hyuk should’ve seen this.”
“...No, it’s not— Ah, forget it.”
Normally, Gung Gibang would have changed the subject by now, if only to avoid getting hit.
Today was different.
His laughter sounded like air leaking out as he kept glancing at me.
My fist clenched, but strangely enough, I didn’t feel like hitting him.
“Pfft, pfft, pfft.”
Bam!
Watching him laugh brought the urge right back.
He couldn’t even scream.
I grabbed him by the back of the neck and hauled him up as he clutched his solar plexus.
“So.
That’s the place, right?
The three-story inn.”
“Urgh.
Y-yes.”
“I’m going for the food.
Because I’m hungry.”
“I-I know.”
“I heard that Kunlun Cloud Dragon guy or whatever is there, too.
I’m going to see him because it’s been a while.
And while I’m there, I’ll build a little rapport with that Hwangbo fellow or whatever his name is.”
“...I’ll remember that.”
“See that you do.
Unless you want the Ten Dragons and Phoenixes to become the Nine Dragons and Phoenixes.”
That seemed to drive the lesson home.
Once I let him go, Gung Gibang rubbed the spot I’d hit.
“Vicious bastard.”
“What was that?”
“N-nothing.”
As if that would fool me.
Gung Gibang hastily changed the subject.
“Anyway, I’m looking forward to it.
When they hear you’ve come, they’ll welcome you with open arms.”
“I don’t care whether they do or not.”
I wasn’t particularly interested in the Kunlun Cloud Dragon or that Lesser Family Head of the Hwangbo Family.
There was, though, one person I hoped would be genuinely glad to see me.
But Gung Gibang misunderstood my answer and hurriedly continued,
“No!
Hwangbo Ak is a bit of a pain, but once he hears you came all this way, he’ll come running out barefoot and—”
He never finished.
Boom!
A thunderous crash swallowed his voice and every sound on the bustling street.
A silence too brief to call an instant fell, then broke.
“Aaah!”
“Eeeeeek!”
“Gowolru!
Gowolru is...!”
People screamed and scattered in every direction like a swarm of locusts.
I stood where I was and stared.
Gowolru.
I could see it clearly.
A section of the three-story inn where we were supposed to meet had been blown wide open.
Someone came hurtling out through a shower of debris and a cloud of dust.
Whoosh!
Crash!
A street stall not far away shattered, and a deep gouge opened in the ground.
A man managed to right himself and get to his feet.
Thud, thud, thud.
Who’s that?
His martial uniform was torn to shreds, and his leather shoes had come off.
His handsome face was filled with fury and dismay.
“How dare you...
You bastard!
I’ll tear you apart...!”
Just then, Gung Gibang gaped at the man, who was speaking through clenched teeth.
“H-Hwangbo Ak!”
“What are you doing out here?”
What?
That’s Hwangbo Ak?
Hwangbo Ak faltered at the sound of his name.
I looked him up and down.
“He did come running out barefoot.”
Was this a surprise for me?
Some impromptu welcome from the Ten Dragons and Phoenixes?
Judging by the way Hwangbo Ak’s face twisted, probably not.
“What did you just say?”
“Oh.
Sorry.
I didn’t mean it that way.”
“You damned bastard...”
“You look busy.
Let’s talk later.
Ah, here it comes.”
“What?”
His confusion lasted only a moment.
Hwangbo Ak seemed to have forgotten something, but urgency and horror rose across his face.
Whoooosh—boom!
Something enormous shot through the air and slammed into Hwangbo Ak.
I could tell how fast it was moving, and how much force it carried, just from the sound.
He would have been hard-pressed to deal with it while fully alert.
Distracted as he was, the result was inevitable.
“Guhk!”

A massive shadow moved to pursue him.

I didn’t have to think long.

I stepped forward with a soft sigh.
An enormous man blocked out the sun, casting a vast shadow over me.
He looked down at me with eyes as big as bowls.
“You.
Move.”
I answered calmly.
“Me.
Don’t want to.”

chapters.title: Chapter 531
paragraphs: “You. Move.”
“No. I don’t want to.”
He clearly hadn’t expected that answer.
The giant’s eyes, each as large as a child’s fist, rolled around as he stammered.
“Y-You don’t want to?”
“Yeah. I don’t want to. I’m not moving.”
“That’s s-strange. Everyone moved until now.”
What kind of character was this?
Did he forget to put any points into intelligence, too?
He was so huge I wondered if he had a Troll among his ancestors, but he talked and acted like a kindergartner.
I scratched my chin as I watched him fidget.
There’s always a new kind of weirdo.
I thought I’d grown used to strange people after meeting so many in Murim, but I’d never met anyone quite like him. Still, settling this commotion came before satisfying my curiosity.
“Come on. Back away slowly.”
“Back away?”
“Yeah.”
I wasn’t trying to play the hero. It wasn’t as though I had some great sense of duty, either.
But we were in the middle of a main street in Henan. If the fight continued, civilians could get caught in it.
“I don’t know what happened, but let’s stop here. All right?”
I kept my voice gentle and glanced at Gung Gibang.
Quick to catch on, Gung Gibang understood what I meant and began evacuating the civilians who had been unable to escape and were still sitting on the ground.
The giant watched them go, his large eyes darting from side to side.
“That guy. Insulted me.”
A finger as thick as a stick pointed toward Hwangbo Ak, who was bent over and coughing weakly.
“He insulted you?”
“Rootless practitioner of demonic, heterodox arts. Pig as stupid as they come. What are you going to do if you glare at me?”
“Ah.”
“My lord said to think three times before fighting. So I thought three times and fought. He drew his sword first, too.”
That gave me a fair idea of what had happened. His words were short and disjointed, but they were enough.

Hwangbo Ak was the Lesser Family Head of the Hwangbo Family, which held sway over Shandong. It wasn’t hard to imagine a Murim golden spoon talented enough to join the Ten Dragons and Phoenixes picking a fight with a martial artist he considered demonic and heterodox. Gung Gibang had called Hwangbo Ak a pain in the ass before, too.
So this guy’s from the unorthodox faction.
No wonder the aura coming off him had felt unusual.
Aside from some Third Rate dark-path figures, I had never met a proper martial artist who practiced demonic, heterodox arts. I had to forcibly suppress the curiosity that suddenly rose inside me.
A thought had just crossed my mind.
“Did you lay a hand on anyone else?”
“Someone else?”
“Yeah. There must have been... other people with him.”
My heart gave a small thump. Ju Hwaran’s three-syllable name hovered on the tip of my tongue, but I couldn’t bring myself to say it.
The giant tilted his head and blinked.
“There were. Two men. One was strong, and one was weak. And...”
“And?”
“A pretty woman. A very pretty woman.”
“Damn. You’ve got a good eye.”
“Huh?”
“Nothing. Did you fight them, too?”
“No. I only hit that guy. The pretty woman. She was as kind as she was beautiful.”
She was safe.
I breathed a silent sigh of relief and patted the giant on the shoulder.
“Yeah, yeah. Good job. What a good little boy.”
“Good job? I’m good?”
“Of course you are. So let’s make up now. Got it?”
“Hmm. Hmmmm.”
I’d almost won him over.
When I heard he was from the unorthodox faction, I’d wondered if I should just knock him down. Apparently, coaxing him like a kindergartner in the Sunshine Class would do.
Just as his eyes began rolling with the effort of thinking it over, an angry shout rang out behind me.
“What do you think you’re doing?”
I turned. Hwangbo Ak had straightened up and was glaring at us, his eyes blazing.
“Blazing Flame Divine Dragon! Are my ears deceiving me? You’re taking the side of a demonic, heterodox practitioner!”
We’d never met, but apparently he knew me. Neither of us had time for introductions anyway, so that was convenient.
I calmly gestured toward Hwangbo Ak.
“You’re up. Come over here and make up with him.”
“M-Make up?”
“From what I’ve heard, he had his reasons. Let’s not cause any more trouble. Be a man, shake hands, and call it done. No hard feelings.”
Hwangbo Ak’s eyes went wide, like someone who’d picked Yasuo and immediately been hit with an insult about his family.
“How can you do this?”
“I can do it just fine. Come over while I’m asking nicely.”
“A fellow orthodox martial artist has been harmed by a practitioner of demonic, heterodox arts. How can you take the side of that vile unorthodox whelp?”
“What does it matter whether he’s unorthodox or orthodox? We’re all one family in the Murim Alliance. Haven’t you heard the song? We are all friends. That’s right, that’s right.”
“What song are you talking about? And one family? Have you forgotten what those demonic, heterodox bastards did during the Great Faction War?”
“Forgot? I wasn’t even there. Were you in the Great Faction War? You look younger than I thought.”
“Enough nonsense. Move! This Young Master will make that bastard kneel and apologize!”
Whoosh.
A warm breeze suddenly blew over my head. It was the breath of the giant, who stood a head—no, two heads—taller than me.
“Kneel? You. Me?”
Hwangbo Ak flinched for a moment, then gritted his teeth.
“Fine. You pushed me back earlier with a despicable surprise attack, but I’ll make you regret provoking this Young Master even after death!”
“This won’t do. You. I kill.”
The giant’s eyes went cold.
Fwoosh—whoosh!
A piercing sound tore into my ears.
Hwangbo Ak shot forward like a ray of light, his body twisting fiercely. His leg whipped out, sheathed in visible internal energy.
A kicking technique?
For generations, the Hwangbo Family had produced masters of punches and kicks. This had to be one of the secret martial arts that had made them the rulers of Shandong.
But...
“You! I kill!”
He’d picked the wrong opponent.
The giant’s martial prowess was certainly no less than Hwangbo Ak’s. He might even have been a move or two ahead.
A massive two-section staff, well suited to his frame, had appeared in his hands.
Whoosh!
Fast and powerful.
The staff swept forward as if crushing the space in its path. I could feel the giant’s tremendous strength and speed behind it.
I watched until the last possible moment, then quietly extended both arms.
Boom!
A deafening crash sent a wave of qi surging outward. Materials, dust, and dirt scattered across the street were driven beyond a three-zhang radius. People gasped.
In the middle of it all, two pairs of eyes trembled.
How?
The question was plain in the giant’s eyes and Hwangbo Ak’s. They stared in shock at the staff and leg caught in my hands.
One movement had stopped both attacks—and the fight.
“Th-This...”
“Strong! You, strong!”
I met their wavering gazes and spoke slowly.
“Now, let’s make up.”
Ah. I’d forgotten to add something.
“Unless you want me to beat you to death.”
Kind words could get you far. Kind words and a fist could get you farther.
The giant stared at me blankly for a moment before stammering, “I-I will make up. I’m good.”
“Yeah, you’re good. Now, who wants to be a bad little boy?”
My gaze turned to Hwangbo Ak. He pressed his lips together.
“Blazing Flame Divine Dragon, are you really planning to—”
“Oh! More information just came in! Every bad little boy I’ve met so far got beaten nearly to death by me and turned good!”
“...Come to think of it, I suppose I was at fault too.”
“Good. Then we’re settled.”
Only then did I release the two-section staff and the ankle I’d been gripping.

The giant kept stealing bewildered glances at me. Hwangbo Ak trembled with humiliation, but he didn’t dare resume the fight. He only glared at me with anger and fear in his eyes, his lips moving soundlessly.
“Blazing Flame Divine Dragon. Can you still call yourself orthodox after this?”
“Wow. That’s exactly what I was about to ask you.”
“I see. You must be acting this way because you don’t know who this Young Master is...”
“Hwangbo Ak. Twenty-nine years old. Lesser Family Head of the Hwangbo Family. Sobriquet: Shandong Fist Dragon.”
“Oh, and you recently had a wet dream.”
“I did not!”
“Then forget I said it.”
Hwangbo Ak’s clenched fist trembled.
“You know who I am, and you still humiliate me like this?”
“A fucking idiot has no gender, age, or orthodox or unorthodox faction. That’s my view, and you’re proving it right.”
If I’d left him to fight, the giant would have beaten the soul out of him. I’d stepped in before things got worse, and now I had to listen to this nonsense.
So why am I not angry?
After a moment, I realized why.
He was an even bigger idiot than I’d expected. And he was too insignificant to get worked up over.
An insect.
That was all Hwangbo Ak was to me. An ant that would die if I flicked it with a finger. A mosquito that a careless wave of my hand would leave half-dead.
I’d spent so long among giants that I’d become one myself. I felt like Gulliver arriving in Lilliput.
Hwangbo Ak was no exception. Even his status as the Hwangbo Family’s Lesser Family Head and one of the Ten Dragons and Phoenixes meant little to me.
Just a Lilliputian who’s a little bigger than the others.
That was how Gulliver—how I—saw him. Maybe some of it showed in my eyes.
Hwangbo Ak’s face darkened with rage.
“Y-You...”
“Want some advice?”
“What?”
“Know where you stand before you pick a fight.”
“You bastard!”
He shouted, but I didn’t blink. He needed to carve my next words into his bones.
“The Roaring Fury Swordsman. The Taeeul Merciless Sword. You’ve heard those names plenty, haven’t you? Though maybe not so much lately. They’re both busy recovering.”
“If you don’t want the Shandong Fist Dragon added to that list, don’t try anything funny. That’s your first and last warning.”
Whoosh.
I focused my aura on him alone. Hwangbo Ak sucked in a breath.
He must have heard what had happened to the Zhongnan Sect Leader’s two Senior Brothers. And now he’d been reminded that Murim ran on two things: a just cause and the law of strength.
Tap.
I patted his trembling shoulder and smiled.
“You look like you’re having a hard time. I’ll explain things to the others, so go home.”
“B-But...”
“Go.”
All Hwangbo Ak could do was grit his teeth and leave.
When his back, looking unusually small, had receded into the distance, a voice reached my ears.
“Sir Jin!”
I hadn’t heard it in a long time, which made it all the more welcome.

I kill.”
The giant’s eyes went cold.
Fwoosh—whoosh!
A piercing sound tore into my ears.
Hwangbo Ak shot forward like a ray of light, his body twisting fiercely.
His leg whipped out, sheathed in visible internal energy.
A kicking technique?
For generations, the Hwangbo Family had produced masters of punches and kicks.
This had to be one of the secret martial arts that had made them the rulers of Shandong.
But...
“You!
I kill!”
He’d picked the wrong opponent.
The giant’s martial prowess was certainly no less than Hwangbo Ak’s.
He might even have been a move or two ahead.
A massive two-section staff, well suited to his frame, had appeared in his hands.
Whoosh!
Fast and powerful.
The staff swept forward as if crushing the space in its path.
I could feel the giant’s tremendous strength and speed behind it.
I watched until the last possible moment, then quietly extended both arms.
Boom!
A deafening crash sent a wave of qi surging outward.
Materials, dust, and dirt scattered across the street were driven beyond a three-zhang radius.
People gasped.
In the middle of it all, two pairs of eyes trembled.
How?
The question was plain in the giant’s eyes and Hwangbo Ak’s.
They stared in shock at the staff and leg caught in my hands.
One movement had stopped both attacks—and the fight.
“Th-This...”
“Strong!
You, strong!”
I met their wavering gazes and spoke slowly.
“Now, let’s make up.”
Ah.
I’d forgotten to add something.
“Unless you want me to beat you to death.”
Kind words could get you far.
Kind words and a fist could get you farther.
The giant stared at me blankly for a moment before stammering, “I-I will make up.
I’m good.”
“Yeah, you’re good.
Now, who wants to be a bad little boy?”
My gaze turned to Hwangbo Ak.
He pressed his lips together.
“Blazing Flame Divine Dragon, are you really planning to—”
“Oh!
More information just came in!
Every bad little boy I’ve met so far got beaten nearly to death by me and turned good!”
“...Come to think of it, I suppose I was at fault too.”
“Good.
Then we’re settled.”
Only then did I release the two-section staff and the ankle I’d been gripping.
The giant kept stealing bewildered glances at me.
Hwangbo Ak trembled with humiliation, but he didn’t dare resume the fight.
He only glared at me with anger and fear in his eyes, his lips moving soundlessly.
“Blazing Flame Divine Dragon.
Can you still call yourself orthodox after this?”
“Wow.
That’s exactly what I was about to ask you.”
“I see.
You must be acting this way because you don’t know who this Young Master is...”
“Hwangbo Ak.
Twenty-nine years old.
Lesser Family Head of the Hwangbo Family.
Sobriquet: Shandong Fist Dragon.”
“Oh, and you recently had a wet dream.”
“I did not!”
“Then forget I said it.”
Hwangbo Ak’s clenched fist trembled.
“You know who I am, and you still humiliate me like this?”
“A fucking idiot has no gender, age, or orthodox or unorthodox faction.
That’s my view, and you’re proving it right.”
If I’d left him to fight, the giant would have beaten the soul out of him.
I’d stepped in before things got worse, and now I had to listen to this nonsense.
So why am I not angry?
After a moment, I realized why.
He was an even bigger idiot than I’d expected.
And he was too insignificant to get worked up over.
An insect.
That was all Hwangbo Ak was to me.
An ant that would die if I flicked it with a finger.
A mosquito that a careless wave of my hand would leave half-dead.
I’d spent so long among giants that I’d become one myself.
I felt like Gulliver arriving in Lilliput.
Hwangbo Ak was no exception.
Even his status as the Hwangbo Family’s Lesser Family Head and one of the Ten Dragons and Phoenixes meant little to me.
Just a Lilliputian who’s a little bigger than the others.
That was how Gulliver—how I—saw him.
Maybe some of it showed in my eyes.
Hwangbo Ak’s face darkened with rage.
“Y-You...”
“Want some advice?”
“What?”
“Know where you stand before you pick a fight.”
“You bastard!”
He shouted, but I didn’t blink.
He needed to carve my next words into his bones.
“The Roaring Fury Swordsman.
The Taeeul Merciless Sword.
You’ve heard those names plenty, haven’t you?
Though maybe not so much lately.
They’re both busy recovering.”
“If you don’t want the Shandong Fist Dragon added to that list, don’t try anything funny.
That’s your first and last warning.”
Whoosh.
I focused my aura on him alone.
Hwangbo Ak sucked in a breath.
He must have heard what had happened to the Zhongnan Sect Leader’s two Senior Brothers.
And now he’d been reminded that Murim ran on two things: a just cause and the law of strength.
Tap.
I patted his trembling shoulder and smiled.
“You look like you’re having a hard time.
I’ll explain things to the others, so go home.”
“B-But...”
“Go.”
All Hwangbo Ak could do was grit his teeth and leave.
When his back, looking unusually small, had receded into the distance, a voice reached my ears.
“Sir Jin!”
I hadn’t heard it in a long time, which made it all the more welcome.

chapters.title: Chapter 532
paragraphs: The young man thought long and hard.
Where did it all go wrong?
Was it when he’d forced down the dumplings someone had bought? Or when he’d ignored the dull ache in his stomach and dozed off while standing guard?
He couldn’t say where or how things had gone wrong. But one thing was certain.
Boom!
The thunderous roar that had suddenly erupted the moment he entered the privy had ended everything for him.
“Ahhh, so warm...”
His Captain had once told him that giving up made things easier.
He had been right. The pleasure was heavenly, and warmth like a mother’s embrace spread through the young man’s lower body.
So why were tears running down his cheeks?
Why else? Fuck.
He’d shit himself. He’d actually shit himself.
In the privy of a large inn on a crowded main street.

It was an expensive inn that only people with money to spare could afford to enter. The partitions between the privies offered a little comfort, but they didn’t change the fact that he could never leave like this.
If anyone finds out what happened, I’m finished.
His spine prickled and his insides twisted at the thought.
Strip a martial artist of his pride and martial arts, and all that remained was skin.
He’d sooner fight a cruel fiend in a life-and-death duel than be discovered like this and have the story spread.
What do I do?
The greatest dilemma of his life.
His pants and underwear had to go. The leather shoes he’d recently splurged on were already beyond saving.
What if he took everything off, pulled his shirt over his face, and ran across the main street as fast as he could?
I’d die.
In Murim, it was practically legal to beat a man to death for sprinting down the main street with everything dangling.
Every passing martial artist would rush out and start swinging their weapons. He might even receive an attack worse than anything a Dark Heaven fiend could unleash.
Then I’ll have to ask someone for help. An inn attendant, maybe.
That was better. If he called an attendant over and slipped him a few silver nyang, the man would bring him a cloth to wipe himself down and some clothes.
If the attendant knew who he was, it might cost extra, but that was still cheaper than a funeral.
What about the others...? No. I can’t let Captain or Gung Gibang see me like this!
Hyuk Mujin made a solemn vow.
Unfortunately, his traveling companions were more persistent than venomous snakes. If they got hold of a weakness like this, they’d tease him for ten years at least. Maybe twenty or thirty.
No, they would probably keep going until the very moment Hyuk Mujin was on his deathbed.
“Mujin...”
“Oh, you Hyuk bastard!”
“Heh heh. You arrived right on time, Captain. And Great Hero Gung.”
“Sob. Of course I had to arrive on time! You were late that day and shit your pants, but I’m not going to be late!”
“Rest easy, Hyuk. You can stink up the place behind the folding screen all you want now.”
“...Please stop.”
A miserable end, even to imagine.
For a moment, he considered asking an attendant to fetch Cheongpung from their lodgings. But that would be digging his own grave.
“Wow! This is the first time I’ve seen someone who shit his pants! At first, I thought you were a snake! You’re a Thousand-Year Dung-Horned Snake that looks just like Mimi!”
“Wait. Cheongpung! Wait!”
“Stay here. I’ll go get the others! Excuse me! Daoist from Wudang! Someone I know shit his pants over here...”
“You fucking bastard!”
He’d be a hundred times better off walking around with a sign around his neck that read I Shit My Pants.
Hyuk Mujin was trembling from the chills brought on by the horrifying images filling his mind when it happened.
Rattle.
The door opened, and he sensed someone’s presence.
Hyuk Mujin’s eyes flew open, and he cleared his throat.
“Ahem. Ahem.”
When no one answered, he coughed louder.
“Ahem! Ahem! Is anyone there? Cough, cough!”
“Hm?”
At last, a response. Hyuk Mujin swallowed and forced his voice into a dignified tone.
“Are you an inn attendant?”
Someone outside answered. The young man’s voice was soft, but he spoke with the easy familiarity of someone addressing an inferior.
“You seem to be looking for an attendant, but unfortunately, I don’t have time to worry about that. You heard it yourself, so you know there’s quite a commotion going on.”
How could Hyuk Mujin not have heard? That damned crash was the reason he was in this mess. The building hadn’t collapsed, but everyone seemed busy dealing with the damage.
At least someone’s still coming to the privy in the middle of all this.
Just as the thought crossed his mind, the man said, “Well, I’ll leave you to it.”
His presence began to recede.
Hyuk Mujin’s heart dropped.
“W-Wait! Just a moment!”
“Hm?”
“Sorry, but could you help me? I really need help.”
“Well, I’m busy myself.”
“A small problem has come up.”
“If it’s small, you can take care of it yourself.”
“Wait! Hyung! Father! Benefactor!”
After a short silence, the voice returned.
“Did you shit yourself?”
Did you shit yourself? Did you shit yourself? Did you shit yourself?
The question echoed in Hyuk Mujin’s ears. He answered through tears.
“Sniff. I did.”
“The big one or the small one?”
“Good grief. Both?”
“Urgh. Sob...”
The man outside muttered, “I suppose taking care of the big one takes care of the small one, too.”
“Please. Please help me.”
“If I see an attendant on my way, I’ll tell him.”
“C-Couldn’t you bring me something now? It might be dry by the time an attendant gets here!”
“...That’s disgusting. I have someone to meet, so I’ll be going.”
“W-Wait!”
Desperate, Hyuk Mujin squeezed his eyes shut.
“I-I’m Hyuk Mujin! You seem to be a martial artist too, Brother. Help me this once and keep quiet about it, and I’ll never forget the favor!”
“Hyuk Mujin? The Blazing Flame Divine Dragon’s little toe?”
“...That’s me. But I’m his right arm, not his little toe.”
Hyuk Mujin’s vision went dark. He’d guessed the man was a martial artist, but he hadn’t expected him to recognize the name so quickly.
At least he’d stopped the man from leaving.
“Coincidence or fate? I’m not sure. Interesting.”
Flap.
Just as Hyuk Mujin was wondering what he meant, a silk outer robe fluttered down over his head, accompanied by a low chuckle whose meaning he could not understand.
Hyuk Mujin caught the robe and stammered his thanks.
“T-Thank you.”
“Clean yourself up and come out. I’ll give you a chance to repay the favor.”
“Um. Do you happen to know our Captain...?”
“We’ve never met. But I doubt the Blazing Flame Divine Dragon will treat me poorly.”
The soft voice continued.
“Not when I’m the benefactor who helped his little toe—or rather, his right arm.”
Hyuk Mujin didn’t know who the man was, but he knew he’d gotten himself into something serious.
It was too late for regrets. His face stiff, he asked, “Is that why you gave me the robe?”
“Why? Have you changed your mind? Then I’ll throw the robe back—”
“If we’re doing this, could you get me some clothes to wear too? Wiping myself down won’t be enough.”
Gowolru.
That was the name of the luxurious three-story inn.
An inn that large must have dealt with trouble often. The moment we stepped inside, the owner came toward us as if he’d been waiting, with a dozen or so hired martial artists in tow.
His face was grim.
“I don’t know who you are, but even young heroes of the martial world must pay for the damage they cause—”
I cut him off.
“First, you have my sympathies. How much will the repairs cost?”
“What?”
“The repairs.”
“...About two hundred silver nyang.”
“Then let’s make it three hundred, including compensation for everything else.”
“What?”
At most, part of the third-floor railing and wall had collapsed.
The owner had gone out on a limb and asked for two hundred nyang, only for me to counter with three hundred. From his perspective, he probably had no idea what kind of person I was.
But I had no qualms about offering an enormous sum.
The reason was simple.
It wasn’t my money.
“Put it on the Hwangbo Family’s tab. If that Lesser Family Head bastard gives you trouble when you go to collect, tell him Jin Taekyung sent you.”
“How am I supposed to say— Wait. Jin Taekyung?”
The owner and the hired blades, who had been studying me suspiciously, opened their eyes wide.
“J-Jin Taekyung? The Jin Taekyung of the Jin Family of Taiyuan?”
“The Blazing Flame Divine Dragon! It’s the Blazing Flame Divine Dragon!”
“I have descended.”
Running an inn this size on a main street in Henan took ability. Gowolru’s owner was certainly quick on the uptake.
“Great Hero Jin Taekyung, it’s the honor of a lifetime to have you here!”
“Call it an honor for your whole family. Anyway, my throat’s been feeling a little dry...”
“I’ll bring out a feast that breaks the table legs! What are you all standing around for?”
Nothing calmed a man down like financial therapy.
The owner’s eyes had brightened as if he’d forgotten all about his anger. He hurried off with the hired blades, and a soft laugh came from beside me.
The sound alone made my ears itch. I turned toward it.
“What?”
Dagger Hidden Flower Ju Hwaran looked at me with eyes like forget-me-nots.
“Nothing. I was just thinking about last time.”
“Last time? Ah.”
“You haven’t forgotten, have you?”
“Of course not.”
The dispute between the Yongbong Escort Bureau and the Zhongnan Sect.

I’d stumbled into it on my way to Sichuan to seek treatment for Jeok Cheongang. After putting a stop to the Taeeul Merciless Sword’s attempt to settle things by force, I’d even taken part in the negotiations.
I uprooted two or three of Zhongnan Sect’s foundation pillars back then.
Hwaran was clearly remembering it too. Her eyes shone softly as she looked at me.
“It hasn’t been that long, but it feels like ages.”
“It does. Strange, isn’t it?”
The strange part was how hard I was finding it to look the person I was talking to in the eye.
“Why do you keep looking away?”
“I’m cross-eyed. I’m looking straight at you.”
“Pfft.”
“W-Why are you laughing?”
Had I said something wrong?
Hwaran smiled at my confusion.
“You really haven’t changed, Great Hero Jin. Not a bit.”
“You haven’t changed either, Young Lady Ju...”
Something else nearly slipped out, but I managed to hold it back.
The several pairs of narrowed eyes watching us from beside me helped.
I pretended to cough and sent a Sound Transmission.
—Gib, what are you staring at? Want a hole punched through your solar plexus?
—Ahem. Ahem.
One down.
Three more to go.
I fixed my gaze on the one who looked least useful.
—Hey.
Hak Woo, the Kunlun Cloud Dragon, was the Kunlun Sect’s finest young prodigy. I’d stepped on the top of his head and sent him tumbling down during the Star-Array Grand Banquet preliminaries.
For some reason, he’d since developed a round bald patch. He flinched when I looked at him and sent a Sound Transmission back.
—W-What is it, Fellow Daoist Jin?
—Nothing much. I thought you might have something to do.
—Hm?
—Be honest. You’re busy right now, aren’t you?
—Infinite Life Buddha. I’m not busy.
—I don’t think so. I think you’ve just remembered something urgent and need to leave right away.
—I have already received permission from my sect regarding today’s appointment. There’s no urgent matter that I need to attend to—
—Hey, Hak.
—Infinite Life Buddha?
—Go. Unless you want me to pluck out every last hair on your head.
To a balding man, every hair was as precious as his life. Hak Woo finally got the message. Looking ready to cry, he turned to Hwaran.
“Um. Young Lady Ju.”
“Yes? What is it?”
“This humble Daoist has remembered an urgent matter and must leave. I’m terribly sorry, Young Lady Ju.”
“It’s all right. Please, go ahead.”
“But it’s still rude of me to—”
“I can’t walk you out very far. Take care.”
“Wait. Could you at least let me finish...”
“I’ll see you next time!”
Now that I thought about it, Hwaran seemed a little impatient.
Kunlun Cloud Dragon Hak Woo looked back and forth between Ju Hwaran and me with eyes on the verge of tears before disappearing, and my gaze naturally shifted to the two people I had yet to deal with.
“I’ll tell you now: I’m not leaving. I’m the Young Bureau Head’s personal escort.”
Song Ilseom, an escort sitting crookedly with a single sword tucked against his chest, spoke flatly.
“I didn’t ask you to. Wasn’t planning to, either.”
“Hm. I’ll take your word for it.”
Song Ilseom was publicly known as Hwaran’s escort, but he had another identity known to only a handful of people.

He was the last descendant of the Guangdong Chen Family, an iron-blooded martial family wiped out by the Demonic Cult during the Great Faction War. He was also an undefeated wandering martial artist once known as the Soul-Chasing Guest.
This guy hasn’t changed, either.
I’d been famous when we first met, but it was nothing compared to now. Song Ilseom was still as calm and prickly as he’d been back then.
Maybe that was why I liked him even more.
But the last one...
“Hungry. Food. Taking too long.”
What was with that shameless attitude?
Why had this giant, whose identity I didn’t know, followed us here? I hadn’t stopped him because I wanted to find out who he was.
Qi Sense could tell me little more than his Level and name. If I wanted to know his sect and who he was connected to, I’d have to talk to him.
“You must be pretty hungry.”
“Yes. I, very hungry.”
The giant continued with a serious expression.
“Today, only ate six meals. Feel like dying.”
Six meals? Seriously?
I didn’t know which sect he belonged to, but I’d bet Hyuk Mujin’s wrist that feeding this guy had already cost them a few foundation pillars.
Wait. Hyuk Mujin?
Come to think of it, he’d gone off to take a shit. Why wasn’t he back yet?
I’d just noticed his absence and was looking around when I heard him.
“C-Captain!”
For some reason, he sounded terribly anxious.
But I wasn’t looking at Hyuk Mujin, who had finally reappeared. I was looking at the unfamiliar man behind him.
He was smiling at me. Our eyes met, and I muttered, “Now who might that be...?”

Anyway, my throat’s been feeling a little dry...”
“I’ll bring out a feast that breaks the table legs!
What are you all standing around for?”
Nothing calmed a man down like financial therapy.
The owner’s eyes had brightened as if he’d forgotten all about his anger.
He hurried off with the hired blades, and a soft laugh came from beside me.
The sound alone made my ears itch.
I turned toward it.
“What?”
Dagger Hidden Flower Ju Hwaran looked at me with eyes like forget-me-nots.
“Nothing.
I was just thinking about last time.”
“Last time?
Ah.”
“You haven’t forgotten, have you?”
“Of course not.”
The dispute between the Yongbong Escort Bureau and the Zhongnan Sect.
I’d stumbled into it on my way to Sichuan to seek treatment for Jeok Cheongang.
After putting a stop to the Taeeul Merciless Sword’s attempt to settle things by force, I’d even taken part in the negotiations.
I uprooted two or three of Zhongnan Sect’s foundation pillars back then.
Hwaran was clearly remembering it too.
Her eyes shone softly as she looked at me.
“It hasn’t been that long, but it feels like ages.”
“It does.
Strange, isn’t it?”
The strange part was how hard I was finding it to look the person I was talking to in the eye.
“Why do you keep looking away?”
“I’m cross-eyed.
I’m looking straight at you.”
“Pfft.”
“W-Why are you laughing?”
Had I said something wrong?
Hwaran smiled at my confusion.
“You really haven’t changed, Great Hero Jin.
Not a bit.”
“You haven’t changed either, Young Lady Ju...”
Something else nearly slipped out, but I managed to hold it back.
The several pairs of narrowed eyes watching us from beside me helped.
I pretended to cough and sent a Sound Transmission.
—Gib, what are you staring at?
Want a hole punched through your solar plexus?
—Ahem.
Ahem.
One down.
Three more to go.
I fixed my gaze on the one who looked least useful.
—Hey.
Hak Woo, the Kunlun Cloud Dragon, was the Kunlun Sect’s finest young prodigy.
I’d stepped on the top of his head and sent him tumbling down during the Star-Array Grand Banquet preliminaries.
For some reason, he’d since developed a round bald patch.
He flinched when I looked at him and sent a Sound Transmission back.
—W-What is it, Fellow Daoist Jin?
—Nothing much.
I thought you might have something to do.
—Hm?
—Be honest.
You’re busy right now, aren’t you?
—Infinite Life Buddha.
I’m not busy.
—I don’t think so.
I think you’ve just remembered something urgent and need to leave right away.
—I have already received permission from my sect regarding today’s appointment.
There’s no urgent matter that I need to attend to—
—Hey, Hak.
—Infinite Life Buddha?
—Go.
Unless you want me to pluck out every last hair on your head.
To a balding man, every hair was as precious as his life.
Hak Woo finally got the message.
Looking ready to cry, he turned to Hwaran.
“Um.
Young Lady Ju.”
“Yes?
What is it?”
“This humble Daoist has remembered an urgent matter and must leave.
I’m terribly sorry, Young Lady Ju.”
“It’s all right.
Please, go ahead.”
“But it’s still rude of me to—”
“I can’t walk you out very far.
Take care.”
“Wait.
Could you at least let me finish...”
“I’ll see you next time!”
Now that I thought about it, Hwaran seemed a little impatient.
Kunlun Cloud Dragon Hak Woo looked back and forth between Ju Hwaran and me with eyes on the verge of tears before disappearing, and my gaze naturally shifted to the two people I had yet to deal with.
“I’ll tell you now: I’m not leaving.
I’m the Young Bureau Head’s personal escort.”
Song Ilseom, an escort sitting crookedly with a single sword tucked against his chest, spoke flatly.
“I didn’t ask you to.
Wasn’t planning to, either.”
“Hm.
I’ll take your word for it.”
Song Ilseom was publicly known as Hwaran’s escort, but he had another identity known to only a handful of people.
He was the last descendant of the Guangdong Chen Family, an iron-blooded martial family wiped out by the Demonic Cult during the Great Faction War.
He was also an undefeated wandering martial artist once known as the Soul-Chasing Guest.
This guy hasn’t changed, either.
I’d been famous when we first met, but it was nothing compared to now.
Song Ilseom was still as calm and prickly as he’d been back then.
Maybe that was why I liked him even more.
But the last one...
“Hungry.
Food.
Taking too long.”
What was with that shameless attitude?
Why had this giant, whose identity I didn’t know, followed us here?
I hadn’t stopped him because I wanted to find out who he was.
Qi Sense could tell me little more than his Level and name.
If I wanted to know his sect and who he was connected to, I’d have to talk to him.
“You must be pretty hungry.”
“Yes.
I, very hungry.”
The giant continued with a serious expression.
“Today, only ate six meals.
Feel like dying.”
Six meals?
Seriously?
I didn’t know which sect he belonged to, but I’d bet Hyuk Mujin’s wrist that feeding this guy had already cost them a few foundation pillars.
Wait.
Hyuk Mujin?
Come to think of it, he’d gone off to take a shit.
Why wasn’t he back yet?
I’d just noticed his absence and was looking around when I heard him.
“C-Captain!”
For some reason, he sounded terribly anxious.
But I wasn’t looking at Hyuk Mujin, who had finally reappeared.
I was looking at the unfamiliar man behind him.
He was smiling at me.
Our eyes met, and I muttered, “Now who might that be...?”

chapters.title: Chapter 533
paragraphs: The third floor, where the commotion had broken out earlier, had long since emptied.
Not many people had the nerve to sit drinking as if nothing had happened after a fight between martial artists had brought down the railings and even parts of the walls.
Besides, martial artists wealthy and important enough to frequent Gowolru were more likely to drink at a winehouse than an ordinary inn.
So it wasn’t hard to guess what the uninvited guest, still smiling amid the wreckage, was.
A martial artist.
That much was obvious.
The man looked thirty at most. He had an open, handsome face, and a dark saber scabbard hung at his waist.
And then there was...
His aura.
I let out a silent whistle. The power and aura I sensed from him surpassed those of every member of the Ten Dragons and Phoenixes I’d met so far.
Even Jin Mukyung before he entered seclusion.
Could it be?
A name I knew but had yet to put a face to flashed through my mind.
Murong Yeonghwi, the One-Ride Heavenly Dragon. Eldest son of the Murong Family, and foremost among the ten dragons and phoenixes hailed as Murim’s greatest young prodigies.
Should I use Qi Sense to check his name?
While I was considering it, Hyuk Mujin approached looking like he desperately needed to shit.
“Um, he’s an acquaintance of mine. He said he really wanted to meet you, Captain...”
I kept my eyes on the man.
“Mujin.”
“Yes?”
“I’m genuinely curious. You didn’t expect me to believe that, did you?”
“Ghk.”
“Tell me the truth. Now.”
“...I shit my pants, and he helped me.”
“I figured it was something like that. We’ll talk later. Step aside.”
As Hyuk Mujin backed away with an expression like he wanted to kill himself, the smile at the corners of the man’s mouth deepened.
“Well, now. You’re quicker on the uptake than I expected.”
“Not really. It’d be stranger if a textile-shop owner’s son had a friend like you.”
“Hm. I didn’t know that. Though, to be honest, I didn’t have particularly high expectations.”
“You’re taking your time introducing yourself. Who are you?”
“A traveler passing through.”
“And you’re talking pretty casually for someone we’ve just met.”
“If it bothers you, speak casually yourself. Make yourself comfortable.”
He was an odd one. He felt different from the others I’d met. I folded my arms loosely.
“Sure. Let’s do that.”
He laughed aloud.
“I’d only heard rumors about the Blazing Flame Divine Dragon. You’re more entertaining than they led me to believe.”
“It’s not exactly a fun situation from where I’m standing. Anyway, are you still planning to introduce yourself as a passing traveler?”
“You don’t know me, then. A few people here seem to.”
His gaze shifted to Ju Hwaran, Gung Gibang, and Song Ilseom.
The faint smile Hwaran had worn only moments ago was gone. Her expression hardened.
“It’s been a while, Young Sect Leader.”
Young Sect Leader?
The question slipped out before I could stop it.
“Young Lady Ju. You know him?”
“We met once. In Gansu.”
“Gansu...”
Along with Qinghai and Sichuan, it was one of the regions hit hardest during the Great Faction War. It was also home to the Kongtong Sect, one of the Nine Sects and One Gang.
I studied the man.
“You don’t look like a Kongtong Daoist to me. Tell me now if I’ve got that wrong.”
“No, you’ve got it right. Quite the opposite, in fact.”
He shrugged.
“If Kongtong found out it had been associated with a demonic, heterodox practitioner like me, it would be displeased. Of course, I feel the same way.”
“A demonic, heterodox practitioner?”
“Ever heard of the Black Dragon Demon Gate?”
Black Dragon Demon Gate. It didn’t take long to place the name.
“I have.”

I’d heard of the unorthodox sect that held sway over Gansu. Kongtong might be among the weakest of the Nine Sects and One Gang, but I’d still been surprised to learn that an unorthodox sect shunned by the public could wield that much power there.
Now I get why this guy isn’t one of the Ten Dragons and Phoenixes.
In that respect, he was much like Song Ilseom.
People could talk all they wanted about all Murim standing together as fellow martial artists. In the end, they still had their own little club.

People—orthodox martial artists, that is—didn’t want wandering martial artists who sold their swords for money or demonic, heterodox practitioners they saw as criminals-in-waiting among the Ten Dragons and Phoenixes.
“So what brings the Young Sect Leader of the Black Dragon Demon Gate here?”
The man’s brow furrowed.
“That’s all?”
“What else do you want?”
“Well...”
“Oh, if you’ve got more to say, give me your sobriquet. I might forget it, but I ought to hear it first.”
“...Black Dragon Saber. Sama Pyo.”
“I didn’t ask for your name. But all right, now I know.”
“Cool name, though. Any relation to Sima Yi?”
“What?”
“What do you mean, what? Sima Yi. The one from Romance of the Three Kingdoms.”
Sama Pyo looked taken aback.
“We share a surname. That’s all.”
“Really? What a shame. If you were sworn enemies of the Zhuge Clan, I was going to introduce you to someone I know.”
“...That doesn’t mean I’m on good terms with the Zhuge Clan.”
“Yeah, fair enough. So why are you here?”
Sama Pyo studied me with a strange gaze before speaking.
“I came for my subordinate.”
“Your subordinate?”
“Yes. That bear of a man sitting over there.”
No one at the table had to ask who he meant. Every gaze, mine included, turned toward the giant.
Despite standing eight cheok tall, he was hunched in on himself, watching Sama Pyo nervously.
“Taishan. Get up.”
He’s with the Black Dragon Demon Gate, too?
Whoever had named him had certainly picked the right name.
At Sama Pyo’s call, the mountain of a man answered in his halting voice.
“Lord. I am not Taishan. You have wrong person.”
He really needs to put some points into Intelligence.
Sama Pyo clicked his tongue.
“You troublemaker. Every time I leave you alone, you cause a scene. Enough. Get up.”
“Cannot. Food not here yet.”
“What a bear of a man. You’ve eaten that much and you’re still not full?”
“Today. Only six meals. Barely ate.”
“What? Six meals?”
Sama Pyo’s face went rigid.
“Only six? Have you suffered an Internal Injury?”
Fuck. I don’t even know what to say.
While the rest of us sat speechless, Sama Pyo gave it some thought and nodded.
“All right. We’ll eat before we go.”
“Food! Good! Taishan eat all food here!”
I spoke from the heart.
“Could you please take that guy—Taishan or the whole beautiful landscape, whatever his name is—and get the hell out?”
Where do these lunatics get off trying to join our table?
Sama Pyo frowned.
“That’s stingy.”
“Yes! Stingy! But Lord, what is stingy?”
“Taishan, it’s short for ‘hey, you fucking bastards.’”
Having kindly explained it to a child from the Sunshine Class, I pointed at the stairs.
“So please leave now, you fucking bastards.”
A heavy tension settled over the room.
Hwaran exhaled and reached for the flexible sword at her waist. Song Ilseom straightened from his relaxed posture.
Their sudden wariness had one target.
Sama Pyo.
But he didn’t move. His eyes widened slightly, and he merely stared at me with an unreadable look.
Then his tightly closed lips parted, and a gentle voice flowed out.
“How refreshing. I’ve never had an experience like this in Gansu—or in my entire life.”
“The first time is the hardest. It gets easier from the second time onward. I’ll give you plenty more of it from now on, so don’t worry.”
“Plenty more in the future, too?”
“I get the feeling we’ll be seeing each other often. Could be wrong.”
“You’re certainly different. Very different. Don’t you agree?”
The question wasn’t for me.
Taishan, whose huge eyes had been darting around, nodded.
“Lord. Yes. That man. Different.”
“Yes, I believe he is.”
A smile I couldn’t read appeared on Sama Pyo’s face, then vanished.
The next moment, Sama Pyo reached up and grabbed Taishan by the nape of his neck, far above his own head, then hauled him upright.
“Hard to linger where we aren’t welcome. Come on, you fool.”
“Taishan disappointed. But Taishan follows Lord. Obeys well.”
“Then we’ll be going. See you again, Blazing Flame Divine Dragon. And you too, Young Lady Ju.”
With that, they went downstairs. A little later, I heard the inn’s door close, and Hwaran’s stiff expression eased.
“Whew.”
She let out a quiet sigh. Song Ilseom leaned back in his chair.
“He’s stronger than before. No—more dangerous might be the better way to put it.”
That only deepened the question I’d been turning over.
From their reactions, they’d clearly met before. More than that, something had happened between them.
What was it?
Perhaps someone noticed my expression, because a foot tapped mine beneath the table.
Tap. Tap.
I didn’t need to look. It was Gung Gibang. He moved his chapped lips.
—Don’t say anything. And don’t ask.
—Why?
—Just don’t, you fucking bastard.
What the hell is his problem? What’s this about?
But that was how people worked. Even if I wasn’t going to ask Hwaran herself, I wanted to hear it from someone who knew.
—What happened?
—Not telling.
—Why?
—You’re better off not knowing.
At that moment, Ju Hwaran, who was sitting right beside Gung Gibang and directly across from me, handed me a plate with a smile.
“Try this, Great Hero Jin.”
“Ah, yes.”
I ought to have smiled back. For some reason, I couldn’t.
I stuffed the food she’d given me into my mouth and kept sending Sound Transmissions.
—Tell me.
—No.
—I said tell me.
—And I said no.
This fucking guy.
He could at least have pretended he knew nothing. Instead, he’d let on that there was a story, then dug in his heels. I was getting pissed off.
I was about to send another Sound Transmission when Hwaran spoke.
“Oh, Great Hero Jin. There’s something I forgot to tell you.”
“Tell me while I’m still asking nicely, okay?”
I nearly made a huge mistake.
I looked up, my mouth full of food, and Hwaran continued.
“That man. The Young Sect Leader of the Black Dragon Demon Gate.”
“Sama Pyo?”
“Mm. Yes.”
“Uh... Did something happen?”
“You could say it did. Or you could say it didn’t.”
Hwaran looked straight at me and said one sentence.
No. It was a bomb.
“He used to be my fiancé.”
“Pffft!”
“Aaaaaah!”
“Uaaaaah!”

chapters.title: Chapter 534
paragraphs: Jingle. Clack.
The inn’s door closed on the final ring of its bell. With it went the stares that had stabbed at the back of Sama Pyo’s head all the way down the stairs.
But Sama Pyo already knew this wasn’t the end. It was another beginning.
“Those two who just came out of Gowolru...”
“That’s them, right?”

“I’m certain. That’s the Black Dragon Saber, Sama Pyo—the Young Sect Leader of the Black Dragon Demon Gate. And the huge fellow beside him is the monster who crushed Blood Cudgel’s skull seven days and nights ago.”
“I heard he got into a fight with the Hwangbo Family’s Lesser Family Head earlier. Making trouble like that at a time like this... Tsk, tsk.”
“Leave them be. What else would you expect from demonic, heterodox practitioners? We need even their help to drive out Dark Heaven.”
“I don’t like it one bit. How do we know they won’t stab us in the back?”
“That’s what I’m saying... Shh. The big fellow is looking this way.”
Countless eyes watched them, and whispers followed. However quietly the onlookers spoke, they were close enough for Sama Pyo to hear every word if he cared to listen.
He kept walking, his expression unchanged.
Nothing unusual about it.

He knew the situation all too well. Even in Gansu, where the Black Dragon Demon Gate held immense influence, people had treated him the same way. The label demonic, heterodox practitioner had followed him since birth, a shackle he could never take off.
“Whoof.”
A rough snort came from beside him. Sama Pyo glanced at Taishan, whose enormous eyes were darting around, and moved his lips.
—Stop.
Taishan’s hand froze on its way to the two-section staff strapped across his back. Sama Pyo put more force into his Sound Transmission.
—Taishan. You little rascal.
—...Understood, Lord. Taishan will hold back.
—That’s right. Good boy.
—Taishan listens well. Taishan likes Lord. Hehehe.
Taishan broke into a broad grin as though nothing had happened, and Sama Pyo let out a quiet laugh.
—Yes. I like you very much, too.
—Taishan got praised a lot today.
—Oh? Who was kind enough to praise you?
—Mm. Blazing Flame Divine Dragon praised me.
Sama Pyo slowed.
—Blazing Flame Divine Dragon Jin Taekyung?
—Yes. Jin Taekyung. Said Taishan was a good boy.
—You seem to like him.
—Like him. Very strong. Good. Taishan praised him.
Sama Pyo gazed at Taishan’s profile as the giant strode along excitedly.

Taishan had been born with outstanding martial talent and divine strength, but an accident long ago had injured his head and left him much like a child. Perhaps because he remembered the accident, he was wary of strangers and slow to trust anyone but Sama Pyo.
It’s rare for him to speak so highly of someone else.
Blazing Flame Divine Dragon Jin Taekyung.
Sama Pyo pictured the young man’s carefree, sly manner—and the unfathomably powerful aura concealed beneath his calm face and voice.
There’s a reason they call him a Divine Dragon.
The world was vast, and masters were plentiful. People admired the Ten Dragons and Phoenixes as Murim’s finest young prodigies, but Sama Pyo had never acknowledged them.
Empty reputations bestowed inside walls they built themselves.
Anyone outside those walls was rejected. He had met plenty of orthodox martial artists who behaved shamelessly while hiding behind tiresome words like righteousness and the orthodox path.
But...
He was different. No question about it.
Blazing Flame Divine Dragon Jin Taekyung.
Although their meeting had been brief, Sama Pyo had realized one thing for certain.
His astonishing martial power, which far surpassed that of any young prodigy, was one reason. But what made him feel even more extraordinary was his attitude—the way he differed from everyone else.
Their conversation from moments ago came back to him.
“I don’t know whether you’ve heard of the Black Dragon Demon Gate.”
“So what brings someone as important as the Young Sect Leader of the Black Dragon Demon Gate here?”
“Is that all?”
“What else do you need?”
The question had caught Sama Pyo so completely off guard that he’d had no answer. No one had ever asked him that in all his years as the Young Sect Leader of the Black Dragon Demon Gate.
What else do I need? What else...
His lips moved soundlessly around the thought. Then he turned to Taishan.
—Let me ask you one thing.
—If you had to fight Blazing Flame Divine Dragon Jin Taekyung, what would you do?
In an instant, the smile vanished from Taishan’s face. His expression hardened, and his Sound Transmission followed without the slightest hesitation.
—Taishan owes Lord a great debt. If Lord commands it, Taishan fights anyone.
—Didn’t you say you liked Jin Taekyung?
—Like Jin Taekyung. But not as much as Lord. Taishan would give his life to obey Lord.
—I see.
Sama Pyo gave a small laugh and shook his head.
—That’s enough. You’re a good fellow.
—Taishan good. And good Taishan hungry.
The enormous child looked at him with a mournful face. Sama Pyo laughed aloud.
“Come on. We’ll go somewhere. Tonight, I’ll feed you until you’re fit to burst.”
“Hehehe. Lord promised. Taishan believes Lord.”
“Yes, yes.”
“But, Lord.”
“Hm?”
“That woman earlier. Pretty. Very pretty. Who?”
Sama Pyo stopped dead. Taishan noticed and tilted his head.
“Lord?”
“No. Was she really that pretty?”
“Yes. Pretty and good.”
“They say you can see ten fathoms into the water, but not one fathom into a person’s heart. How could you know what was hidden inside her after seeing only her face for a moment?”
Taishan shook his head fiercely.
“No! Pretty women are good!”
“Don’t shout. People are staring.”
“Admit it! Taishan is right! Pretty means good!”
“Whew. You damned fool. I’m going on ahead.”
“Lord! Lord!”
Sama Pyo walked away, leaving Taishan’s desperate cries behind him. His face was as dry and expressionless as sand.
Ju Hwaran... I never expected to meet her here.
Whether it was coincidence or fate, Sama Pyo couldn’t say.
But one thing was certain. The woman who had been his fiancée, if only for a short time—Dagger Hidden Flower Ju Hwaran—would consider everything connected to him an ill-fated relationship.
An ill-fated relationship... It wouldn’t be wrong.
His gaze turned cold.
The rest of the meal went smoothly. The innkeeper treated us lavishly, everyone else kept staring, and outside the inn we exchanged farewells.
No. To be precise, it would be more accurate to say that Ju Hwaran said farewell to us.
“I should get going. I have some Escort Bureau matters to take care of.”
Jab.
Gung Gibang poked me discreetly in the side. I’d been standing there in a daze, but my mouth opened on reflex.
“Oh, right. Goodbye.”
“Yes. You too, Great Hero Jin.”
Jab.
Damn it. Apparently that wasn’t the right answer.
“Um, Young Lady Ju.”
“Yes?”
“Would you like me to walk you back to your lodgings?”
“Thank you, but I’ll be fine. I hear you barely have enough time to train as it is.”
“Oh. Who told you? I have been a little busy lately.”
Jab. Jab jab.
Thanks, you bastard.
Gung-vigation was warning me I’d veered off course again. I tightened my grip on the wheel.
“Still, some strange men might approach you. It might be better if I walked you back...”
“Ahaha. I’ll be fine. I’m a martial artist, too.”
“Oh, right. I didn’t mean to underestimate you. It’s just...”
“No, my martial arts really do fall short of yours, Great Hero Jin. Besides, Captain Song is here.”
Song Ilseom spoke bluntly. “If any of them approach, I’ll cut them down in one stroke. Stop worrying about nothing.”
“You heard him, right?”
“...Yes. I heard him.”
Jab jab. Jabjabjabjab!
You’re going to put a hole in my side, you bastard.
But I couldn’t think of anything else to say. Thoughts tangled in my already muddled head, then slipped away. By the time I found any words, the moment had passed.
“I’ll be going, then. See you again.”
Hwaran smiled and turned away. Her fine, silken hair swayed, carrying a faint fragrance through the air.
I stood watching the two of them walk away.
That was when—
“This guy really is a fucking idiot.”
“Wow. You’re something else, Captain.”
I didn’t need to turn to know who’d spoken. I looked at Gung Gibang and Hyuk Mujin with a mournful gaze.
“Where did I go wrong, and when?”
They answered at the same time, as if they’d been waiting.
“Since you spat food in Young Lady Ju’s face.”
“Wasn’t Captain himself the problem from the start?”
Different answers, but they had two things in common: both pissed me off, and both were hard to argue with.
“Damn it.”
I kicked at the ground. Honestly, I felt a little aggrieved. How was I supposed to have stayed calm in that situation?
A fiancé, out of nowhere.
Just thinking about it made my head spin. Forget a grenade—that was a ballistic missile. My only comfort was the word former in front of fiancé.
“I told you not to ask,” Gung Gibang said.
“If I’d known it would be like this, I wouldn’t have asked,” I replied with a sigh. “Besides, Young Lady Ju brought it up first.”
“Because you made it so obvious you wanted to know.”
“Gung Gibang is right. You could have figured there was a reason and left it alone. Why did you have to—”
“The bastard who shit his pants can shut up.”
“...Yes, sir.”
“I didn’t shit my pants,” Gung Gibang said, “so I can keep talking.”
“Not for long. You’ll be shitting blood in a minute.”
“...Calm down. Put your fist down first.”
The truth was, I didn’t have the strength to hit him. At the customer’s request, I lowered my fist and stared into space.
“I want to turn back time.”
“You can’t.”
“You can’t, Captain.”
“Still, I didn’t let it show much afterward, did I? I was pretty calm.”
Gung Gibang and Hyuk Mujin gave me warm smiles.
“Of course. Couldn’t tell at all. Apart from the six times you knocked over your water glass.”
“And the seven times you dropped your chopsticks.”
“The best part was when the server asked us to add anything else we wanted to the order slip and you glared at him.”
“Seriously, how did you connect an order slip to Sama Pyo? It took me ages to work that out.”
“You were practically insane.”
“Dark Heaven, at minimum.”
I get it, so stop it, you fucking bastards.

I wanted to beat the hell out of them, but I didn’t have the energy. Trudging along was about all I could manage. I couldn’t even be bothered to hide my face beneath my crooked bamboo hat, let alone care when people recognized me.
“Th-that man, could he be...?”
“Gasp! It is! It’s Blazing Flame Divine Dragon Jin Taekyung!”
“But why is he walking like that?”
“How would I know?”
“Looks like a woman dumped him.”
“Ha ha. Good one.”
Don’t laugh. It’s not a joke.
I was taking damage from every direction just by breathing. I sighed and adjusted my bamboo hat, my thoughts still hopelessly tangled.
An ex-boyfriend. No, an ex-fiancé.
I knew roughly what had happened. Hwaran had told me about her past plainly and without hiding anything.
“It was a political marriage. I hadn’t even seen his face before that.”
Nothing unusual about that. The Yongbong Escort Bureau had been declining day by day, and the Black Dragon Demon Gate had reached out to Hwaran with an offer she couldn’t refuse.
“I made the decision myself. For my father, after he collapsed.”
Her calm voice and expression were still on my mind when someone called to me.
“My youngest.”
I blinked. We were in front of our lodgings. I hadn’t even noticed us arriving.
Jin Wikyung stood before me, a large man, though not quite as enormous as Taishan.
“Great Hero Mae—no, the Alliance Leader is looking for you.”
