paragraphs: “Great Hero Mae—no, the Alliance Leader is looking for you.”
Jin Wikyung’s sudden announcement stopped me short.
“Me?”
“Yes. And Cheongpung as well.”
Cheongpung too?
I was about to ask why when a familiar face popped out of a pavilion window.
“Grandpa! Are we going to see Grandpa now?”
Cheongpung sounded thrilled. Jin Wikyung smiled faintly and shook his head.
“Not your grandfather. The Alliance Leader is looking for you.”
“Yes. Grandpa!”
“The same man, but it’s different. In any case, Young Hero Cheongpung, get ready and come down as soon as you can.”
“Just a moment! I need to pack some dumplings!”
“All right. Take a variety. And some sweets.”
He’s had some practice, all right. Didn’t even blink.
Jin Wikyung had dealt with Cheongpung enough times by now that it came naturally to him.
Cheongpung vanished amid a clatter, and Jin Wikyung turned to me.
“You aren’t asking why.”
“...I’d say it’s more accurate to say I haven’t had a chance to ask.”
“That’s true.”
“I might as well hear it from him when I get there. Besides, I already have a feeling.”
“What sort of feeling?”
“That he didn’t call us over just to see his grandson.”
He wanted to see Cheongpung and me.
Sword Saint Mae Jonghak—no, the Alliance Leader of the Murim Alliance.
The man was the same, but the title made all the difference. That was probably what Jin Wikyung had meant when he corrected Cheongpung.
The Alliance Leader.
It was a weighty title. The man bearing it carried the countless martial artists crisscrossing the Nine Provinces—and all of Murim—on his shoulders. And he wanted to see me...
No matter how I look at it, that’s ominous.
Had something else happened already?
I was wondering just that when—
Whoosh!
Cheongpung appeared with the sound of rushing wind. A bulging silk bundle hung from one hand, and gleaming silver armor covered his upper body.
Wait. Armor?
Hiss.
“I’m back. What the fuck?”
“It’s Mimi. She’s grown so much I can’t carry her in my arms anymore.”
“...Then how about leaving her here?”
Cheongpung tilted his head.
“Why?”
“Do you seriously not know?”
“Yes!”
“Oh... Not a moment’s hesitation. You’re driving me insane.”
She was a snake. A snake with horns, no less.
She’d grown so bulky that Mimi hardly seemed like the right name anymore.
Bottom line: I didn’t know how many snake lovers there were in the Murim Alliance, but she wasn’t exactly a pet they’d welcome.
“...What the hell have you been feeding her?”
“Hehe. She’s gotten huge, hasn’t she? Guess, Benefactor.”
I answered without hesitation.
“Steroids.”
“Mostly dumplings and sweets. Oh, she definitely seems to have gotten a lot bigger after eating the Blood Fish.”
I was about to ask why he’d fed a snake dumplings and sweets when I caught myself.
“Blood Fish?”
“Yes.”
Blood Fish were fish from Dongting Lake contaminated by magical power.
In other words, she’d eaten something thoroughly tainted...
“No. Mimi stays here.”
“She’s fine.”
“Other people might not be. She could bite someone.”
“No, Mimi wouldn’t bite even if I told her to. Want to see?”
Looking desperate to prove it, Cheongpung reached toward Mimi.
“Mimi, bite!”
Swish. Clack!
It happened in an instant.
Mimi lunged with her jaws wide open, quick as lightning. Cheongpung’s hand vanished even faster.
Her teeth snapped together on empty air. She flicked her tongue as if disappointed.
Hiss.
“See? She didn’t bite.”
Is he insane?
She just missed.
Everyone, myself included, was speechless. Cheongpung’s face fell.
“Sal—no, Mungyeong said she was fine...”
“Mungyeong did?”
“Yes. I see him a lot these days. He checked on Mimi, too.”
Come to think of it, I hadn’t seen much of either Cheongpung or Mungyeong lately. I’d been busy, but from what Cheongpung said, that wasn’t the only reason.
That guy never took an interest in anyone else. What’s gotten into him?
Cheongpung saw my eyes narrow and caught his breath.
“Gasp.”
“Why?”
“It’s nothing.”
That only made him more suspicious.
But I let it go with a shrug. Jin Wikyung was visibly growing anxious.
“My youngest, that...”
“Oh, sorry. Are we in a hurry?”
“Honestly, it wouldn’t be good to arrive late. Others will be waiting too.”
Others?
This was turning out to be a bigger gathering than I’d expected.
I hid my unease and jerked my chin toward Cheongpung.
“Let’s go, Cheongpung.”
“Yes, Benefactor!”
Gung Gibang and Hyuk Mujin nodded, their faces grim.
“Right. Let’s go.”
“I’ll escort you, Captain. And you as well, Lesser Family Head.”
“You two shut up and stay here to clean up the grime and shit.”
The Murim Alliance was like a small city.
At its center stood the Alliance Leader’s Hall. We went inside and stopped before a massive door.
“You’ve arrived.”
The guard had a rigid gaze and expression, along with a carefully contained aura.
He was unmistakably a Peak master who had reached the level of injuring others with Sword Energy. Yet here, this nameless man was only a doorkeeper.
He appeared to know Jin Wikyung. After greeting him quietly, he opened the door.
Rattle. Rattle. Rattle.
The scraping sounds came one after another. Only after five doors had opened in succession did I see what lay beyond.
Good thing I left those idiots behind.
Gung Gibang and Hyuk Mujin ought to thank me. If they’d followed, they’d be standing here stinking of grime and shit, too scared to open their mouths and sweating buckets.
That was how impressive the people seated around the enormous table were—their faces and auras alike.
“Wow.”
A soft exclamation came from beside me. Jin Wikyung poked the wide-eyed Cheongpung in the side and sent a Sound Transmission.

I understood. I nodded and stepped over the threshold.
Step.

The Azure Sky Sword King. The Thunderbolt Saber King. And...

“Yes.

“Grandpa!

Cheongpung sounded thrilled.
Jin Wikyung smiled faintly and shook his head.
“Not your grandfather.

“The same man, but it’s different.

“All right.

And some sweets.”
He’s had some practice, all right.
Didn’t even blink.
Jin Wikyung had dealt with Cheongpung enough times by now that it came naturally to him.
Cheongpung vanished amid a clatter, and Jin Wikyung turned to me.
“You aren’t asking why.”
“...I’d say it’s more accurate to say I haven’t had a chance to ask.”
“That’s true.”
“I might as well hear it from him when I get there.
Besides, I already have a feeling.”
“What sort of feeling?”
“That he didn’t call us over just to see his grandson.”
He wanted to see Cheongpung and me.
Sword Saint Mae Jonghak—no, the Alliance Leader of the Murim Alliance.
The man was the same, but the title made all the difference.
That was probably what Jin Wikyung had meant when he corrected Cheongpung.
The Alliance Leader.
It was a weighty title.
The man bearing it carried the countless martial artists crisscrossing the Nine Provinces—and all of Murim—on his shoulders.
And he wanted to see me...
No matter how I look at it, that’s ominous.
Had something else happened already?
I was wondering just that when—
Whoosh!
Cheongpung appeared with the sound of rushing wind.
A bulging silk bundle hung from one hand, and gleaming silver armor covered his upper body.
Wait.
Armor?
Hiss.
“I’m back.
What the fuck?”
“It’s Mimi.
She’s grown so much I can’t carry her in my arms anymore.”
“...Then how about leaving her here?”
Cheongpung tilted his head.
“Why?”
“Do you seriously not know?”
“Yes!”
Not a moment’s hesitation.
You’re driving me insane.”
She was a snake.
A snake with horns, no less.
She’d grown so bulky that Mimi hardly seemed like the right name anymore.
Bottom line: I didn’t know how many snake lovers there were in the Murim Alliance, but she wasn’t exactly a pet they’d welcome.
“...What the hell have you been feeding her?”
“Hehe.
She’s gotten huge, hasn’t she?
Guess, Benefactor.”
I answered without hesitation.
“Steroids.”
“Mostly dumplings and sweets.
Oh, she definitely seems to have gotten a lot bigger after eating the Blood Fish.”
I was about to ask why he’d fed a snake dumplings and sweets when I caught myself.
“Blood Fish?”
“Yes.”
Blood Fish were fish from Dongting Lake contaminated by magical power.
In other words, she’d eaten something thoroughly tainted...
“No.
Mimi stays here.”
“She’s fine.”
“Other people might not be.
She could bite someone.”
“No, Mimi wouldn’t bite even if I told her to.
Want to see?”
Looking desperate to prove it, Cheongpung reached toward Mimi.
“Mimi, bite!”
Swish.
Clack!
It happened in an instant.
Mimi lunged with her jaws wide open, quick as lightning.
Cheongpung’s hand vanished even faster.
Her teeth snapped together on empty air.
She flicked her tongue as if disappointed.
Hiss.
“See?
She didn’t bite.”
Is he insane?
She just missed.
Everyone, myself included, was speechless.
Cheongpung’s face fell.
“Sal—no, Mungyeong said she was fine...”
“Mungyeong did?”
“Yes.
I see him a lot these days.
He checked on Mimi, too.”
Come to think of it, I hadn’t seen much of either Cheongpung or Mungyeong lately.
I’d been busy, but from what Cheongpung said, that wasn’t the only reason.
That guy never took an interest in anyone else.
What’s gotten into him?
Cheongpung saw my eyes narrow and caught his breath.
“Gasp.”
“Why?”
“It’s nothing.”
That only made him more suspicious.
But I let it go with a shrug.
Jin Wikyung was visibly growing anxious.

“Oh, sorry.
Are we in a hurry?”

Others will be waiting too.”
Others?

chapters.title: Chapter 536
paragraphs: Two Dragons Pavilion.
I’d never heard the name before. Yet I knew what Mae Jonghak meant.
The masters of the Two Dragons Pavilion.
Cheongpung and me.
Then Mae Jonghak spoke, his voice calm and commanding.
“Blazing Flame Divine Dragon Jin Taekyung. Come closer.”
His manner was different. So was the air around him.
There was no trace of the man who called me his friend and liked to tease me.
The person before me was neither Always-Victorious Sword Jongni Chu nor Sword Saint Mae Jonghak.
Step.
I took a deep breath, stepped forward, and respectfully cupped my hands toward the Alliance Leader.
“Jin Taekyung of the Jin Family of Taiyuan greets you, Alliance Leader.”
A light came into Mae Jonghak’s eyes as he looked at me.

“For generations, the Jin Family of Taiyuan has stood as a symbol of righteous spirit. It fed the hungry, cared for the sick, and whenever the Central Plains was in danger, its members fought without regard for their own lives.”
Three hundred years. A full three hundred years.

The Jin Family of Taiyuan had roots deep and strong enough to earn its place among the great families. It might have swayed, but it had never been uprooted. Its steps might have faltered, but it had never strayed from the righteous path.
“Two years ago, in winter, you personally cut down Blade of Flowers Jin Baekyang, your own blood relative and the family’s Head Elder. Chief of the Hidden Shadow Pavilion, why was that?”
The leader of the Hidden Shadow Pavilion, Thousand-Faced Fox Song Ho, who had been standing silently at attention, opened his mouth with a stiff expression.
“Because he was a traitor. He had long been acting on Dark Heaven’s orders. He betrayed not only the Jin Family of Taiyuan, but all of Murim.”
“Are you certain?”
“I stake my life on it.”
He didn’t need to stake his life. Everyone here knew the truth. Anyone who paid the slightest attention to news from Murim knew it.
So why spend precious time on something everyone already knew?
I had a good idea.
To remind them. And to make them accept it.
Mae Jonghak’s words weren’t meant for me alone. His real audience was the twenty-odd giants seated throughout this vast conference hall.
“One year ago, the Star-Array Grand Banquet was held here in Henan, and Dark Heaven’s attack stained Shaolin’s grounds with blood. What did you do?”
I answered without hesitation.
“I fought.”
“Why?”
“That’s...”
I closed my mouth.
Why?
The question caught me off guard. Not because I didn’t know the answer, but because I’d never once thought about it.
Well. Why did I?
I’d long considered myself selfish and materialistic. That didn’t make me a cold-blooded bastard. When people were dying right in front of me, who had time to weigh what was in it for me?
On the day Shaolin was stained with blood, there hadn’t been a question mark in my head. Only exclamation marks. I’d run in and fought.
The answer came easily.
“I’ve never thought about it.”
“Why not?”
“Because it was what anyone would do.”
“What anyone would do...”
Mae Jonghak repeated my answer softly, then turned his smiling eyes toward his Disciple and sworn grandson.
“Pung. What about you?”
“Me?”
“Were you afraid of dying?”
Cheongpung stared at him with wide, clear eyes before answering hesitantly.
“I was. I’d never thought about death before.”
“But you went to Shaolin. Why?”
“...Regret.”
“Hmm?”
“I think I would’ve regretted it for the rest of my life if I’d run away.”
His quiet mumble grew clear.
“I felt like I’d lose something greater than my life.”
That was right. He’d said the same thing when we fought the Blood Lord.
Cut and torn, bleeding heavily and writhing in pain, Cheongpung had refused to retreat. He’d known he was no match for the Blood Lord, but he kept charging at him.
“What the hell? Why are you acting like you’re so desperate to die first?”
And when the Blood Lord had asked him that with confusion and anger, Cheongpung had answered with a clear smile.
“If I retreat... I think I’ll regret it for the rest of my life.”
That regret. I knew what he meant.
Maybe I’d been more afraid of living alone with that regret than I was of dying.
“Regret. Regret...”
Mae Jonghak muttered quietly, then turned his gaze toward me.
“And you?”
“Me, sir?”
My answer hadn’t changed since I first started working as a Hunter.
I gave a short, quiet laugh and answered.
“Death is always scary. I’m afraid of dying.”
Was that too honest?
“Ahem. Hm.”
A few of the people watching in silence cleared their throats uncomfortably. But Mae Jonghak’s smile only deepened.
“Facing the fear of death and helping another in need. That is chivalry.”
The throat-clearing stopped. The room went still.
A man who had been sitting crookedly in his chair spoke up.
“What anyone would do. Thinking it and doing it are worlds apart, though. And you two did it without hesitation.”
There was warmth in his voice. Fire King Jeok Cheongang’s eyes were unmistakably smiling as he looked at me.
“That is humanity.”
Humanity and chivalry. Chivalry and humanity.
Alike in one sense, different in another. Two short words, heavy enough to press down on everyone in the room.
People say a true martial artist does not fear death.
But the world has another name for someone who feels that fear, refuses to yield to it, and acts with humanity and chivalry.
“A knight-errant...”
Someone’s murmur rang strangely loud in the silence.
That was when a graying middle-aged man with a faint smile opened his mouth.
“A knight-errant. Now there’s a word I like.”
His hands were strangely large and thick for a man of his modest build. Only then did I recognize him.
Fist King Yan Hwapyeong.
The last descendant of the Jinzhou Yan Family, which had been utterly ruined long ago by power struggles between orthodox factions.

He had turned his back on the world and lived atop an unnamed mountain. But when news reached him that a hundred thousand demonic soldiers had invaded the Central Plains, he joined the Murim Alliance without hesitation.
“Do you know why the Fist King is such an incredible man?”
“How would I know?”
“I once asked him if he had no pride. The orthodox bastards had ruined his family before he was even born. How many of the men gathered here, I asked him, knew anything about humanity or chivalry?”
“You really have no tact, do you?”
“Shut up and listen. His answer was the best part.”
“What did he say?”
“He said it didn’t matter.”
“What?”
“Just that. None of it mattered. He’d simply come to help. And the moment the Great Faction War ended, he vanished like a phantom. That man was the real thing. Ha ha ha.”
That same Fist King Yan Hwapyeong was smiling at us now. It was a warm smile.
“Doing what ought to be done. Overcoming fear and moving forward. That is a knight-errant. Yes, indeed.”
He wasn’t the only one nodding in approval. Gentle gazes fell on Cheongpung and me from around the room. In the eyes of several familiar faces, I could see unmistakable gratitude.
Myriad-Poison Asura Tang Sadok.
He was pale, as though he hadn’t fully recovered, but his back was straight and the green light in his eyes was clear.
Our eyes met. The corner of his wrinkled mouth lifted slightly, and he spoke.
“As Family Head of the Sichuan Tang Clan, I would like to say a few words.”
The unexpected announcement drew every eye to him. Mae Jonghak gave a small nod, and Tang Sadok continued in his hissing voice.

“Being a pavilion master of the Murim Alliance is a position of tremendous weight and responsibility. I believe it requires not only outstanding martial arts, but also the experience to match. It would be unreasonable to entrust it to young people who are not even thirty, let alone forty.”
A stir ran through the room. Several expressions shifted. Joy crossed some faces, displeasure others.
But...
The rule about hearing someone out before you judge doesn’t just apply to Korean.
Tang Sadok’s next words confirmed my suspicion.

“However, Blazing Flame Divine Dragon Jin Taekyung and Huashan Divine Dragon Cheongpung are exceptions. They fought Dark Heaven in Shanxi, Henan, Sichuan, and Hubei. They showed us what humanity and chivalry mean. This old man and my family owe them a debt we cannot hope to repay.”
Voices of agreement rose around the room.
They belonged to the heads of sects and families who had crossed paths with me personally throughout the Murim, or through Jeok Cheongang or the Jin Family of Taiyuan.
Others nodded as though it were only natural, despite having no connection to me at all.
Encouraged by this response, Myriad-Poison Asura Tang Sadok continued in a clear voice.
“If these two take on important positions within the Murim Alliance, who would dare question their qualifications—or object to the Alliance Leader’s command?”
He put particular force behind those last words. Several people frowned, among them the Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord, Sect Leader of the Zhongnan Sect.
Tang Sadok swept his green-lit gaze across the room, then cupped his hands.
“As you can see, there will be no objections. Alliance Leader, you need only give the order.”
He’d ended the argument before anyone could raise it.

And anyone who did object would be taking on the Family Head of the Sichuan Tang Clan, one of Murim’s most famously uncompromising clans. The Sichuan Blood Tragedy had dealt them a devastating blow, but they were still one of the Five Great Families, with strength no one could afford to dismiss.
Someone let out a low groan.
Then a voice broke the brief silence.
“Blazing Flame Divine Dragon Jin Taekyung. Huashan Divine Dragon Cheongpung.”
Mae Jonghak looked at us warmly.
“I have yet to ask the two of you. Do you wish to join the Two Dragons Pavilion?”
At that moment—
Ding.
System Would you like to join the Murim Alliance?
The notification appeared before my eyes.
Neither Cheongpung nor I took long to decide. Our eyes met, and we answered as one.
“We do.”

“Then I hereby formally decree this. From this moment onward, the two of you shall belong to the Two Dragons Pavilion, directly under the Alliance Leader’s Office and answerable only to the Alliance Leader’s commands. Each of you shall become a pavilion master, with the authority to select the personnel you require...”
I couldn’t make out what came next. No—I couldn’t hear it properly.
Ding. Ding. Ding, ding!
The bells rang without pause, filling my ears.

Only exclamation marks.
I’d run in and fought.
The answer came easily.
“I’ve never thought about it.”
“Why not?”
“Because it was what anyone would do.”
“What anyone would do...”
Mae Jonghak repeated my answer softly, then turned his smiling eyes toward his Disciple and sworn grandson.
“Pung.
What about you?”
“Me?”
“Were you afraid of dying?”
Cheongpung stared at him with wide, clear eyes before answering hesitantly.
“I was.
I’d never thought about death before.”
“But you went to Shaolin.
Why?”
“...Regret.”
“Hmm?”
“I think I would’ve regretted it for the rest of my life if I’d run away.”
His quiet mumble grew clear.
“I felt like I’d lose something greater than my life.”
That was right.
He’d said the same thing when we fought the Blood Lord.
Cut and torn, bleeding heavily and writhing in pain, Cheongpung had refused to retreat.
He’d known he was no match for the Blood Lord, but he kept charging at him.
“What the hell?
Why are you acting like you’re so desperate to die first?”
And when the Blood Lord had asked him that with confusion and anger, Cheongpung had answered with a clear smile.
“If I retreat...
I think I’ll regret it for the rest of my life.”
That regret.
I knew what he meant.
Maybe I’d been more afraid of living alone with that regret than I was of dying.
“Regret.
Regret...”
Mae Jonghak muttered quietly, then turned his gaze toward me.
“And you?”
“Me, sir?”
My answer hadn’t changed since I first started working as a Hunter.
I gave a short, quiet laugh and answered.
“Death is always scary.
I’m afraid of dying.”
Was that too honest?
“Ahem.
Hm.”
A few of the people watching in silence cleared their throats uncomfortably.
But Mae Jonghak’s smile only deepened.
“Facing the fear of death and helping another in need.
That is chivalry.”
The throat-clearing stopped.
The room went still.
A man who had been sitting crookedly in his chair spoke up.
“What anyone would do.
Thinking it and doing it are worlds apart, though.
And you two did it without hesitation.”
There was warmth in his voice.
Fire King Jeok Cheongang’s eyes were unmistakably smiling as he looked at me.
“That is humanity.”
Humanity and chivalry.
Chivalry and humanity.
Alike in one sense, different in another.
Two short words, heavy enough to press down on everyone in the room.
People say a true martial artist does not fear death.
But the world has another name for someone who feels that fear, refuses to yield to it, and acts with humanity and chivalry.
“A knight-errant...”
Someone’s murmur rang strangely loud in the silence.
That was when a graying middle-aged man with a faint smile opened his mouth.
“A knight-errant.
Now there’s a word I like.”
His hands were strangely large and thick for a man of his modest build.
Only then did I recognize him.
Fist King Yan Hwapyeong.
The last descendant of the Jinzhou Yan Family, which had been utterly ruined long ago by power struggles between orthodox factions.
He had turned his back on the world and lived atop an unnamed mountain.
But when news reached him that a hundred thousand demonic soldiers had invaded the Central Plains, he joined the Murim Alliance without hesitation.
“Do you know why the Fist King is such an incredible man?”
“How would I know?”
“I once asked him if he had no pride.
The orthodox bastards had ruined his family before he was even born.
How many of the men gathered here, I asked him, knew anything about humanity or chivalry?”
“You really have no tact, do you?”
“Shut up and listen.
His answer was the best part.”
“What did he say?”
“He said it didn’t matter.”
“What?”
“Just that.
None of it mattered.
He’d simply come to help.
And the moment the Great Faction War ended, he vanished like a phantom.
That man was the real thing.
Ha ha ha.”
That same Fist King Yan Hwapyeong was smiling at us now.
It was a warm smile.
“Doing what ought to be done.
Overcoming fear and moving forward.
That is a knight-errant.
Yes, indeed.”
He wasn’t the only one nodding in approval.
Gentle gazes fell on Cheongpung and me from around the room.
In the eyes of several familiar faces, I could see unmistakable gratitude.
Myriad-Poison Asura Tang Sadok.
He was pale, as though he hadn’t fully recovered, but his back was straight and the green light in his eyes was clear.
Our eyes met.
The corner of his wrinkled mouth lifted slightly, and he spoke.
“As Family Head of the Sichuan Tang Clan, I would like to say a few words.”
The unexpected announcement drew every eye to him.
Mae Jonghak gave a small nod, and Tang Sadok continued in his hissing voice.
“Being a pavilion master of the Murim Alliance is a position of tremendous weight and responsibility.
I believe it requires not only outstanding martial arts, but also the experience to match.
It would be unreasonable to entrust it to young people who are not even thirty, let alone forty.”
A stir ran through the room.
Several expressions shifted.
Joy crossed some faces, displeasure others.
But...
The rule about hearing someone out before you judge doesn’t just apply to Korean.
Tang Sadok’s next words confirmed my suspicion.
“However, Blazing Flame Divine Dragon Jin Taekyung and Huashan Divine Dragon Cheongpung are exceptions.
They fought Dark Heaven in Shanxi, Henan, Sichuan, and Hubei.
They showed us what humanity and chivalry mean.
This old man and my family owe them a debt we cannot hope to repay.”
Voices of agreement rose around the room.
They belonged to the heads of sects and families who had crossed paths with me personally throughout the Murim, or through Jeok Cheongang or the Jin Family of Taiyuan.
Others nodded as though it were only natural, despite having no connection to me at all.
Encouraged by this response, Myriad-Poison Asura Tang Sadok continued in a clear voice.
“If these two take on important positions within the Murim Alliance, who would dare question their qualifications—or object to the Alliance Leader’s command?”
He put particular force behind those last words.
Several people frowned, among them the Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord, Sect Leader of the Zhongnan Sect.
Tang Sadok swept his green-lit gaze across the room, then cupped his hands.
“As you can see, there will be no objections.
Alliance Leader, you need only give the order.”
He’d ended the argument before anyone could raise it.
And anyone who did object would be taking on the Family Head of the Sichuan Tang Clan, one of Murim’s most famously uncompromising clans.
The Sichuan Blood Tragedy had dealt them a devastating blow, but they were still one of the Five Great Families, with strength no one could afford to dismiss.
Someone let out a low groan.
Then a voice broke the brief silence.
“Blazing Flame Divine Dragon Jin Taekyung.
Huashan Divine Dragon Cheongpung.”
Mae Jonghak looked at us warmly.
“I have yet to ask the two of you.
Do you wish to join the Two Dragons Pavilion?”
At that moment—
Ding.
System Would you like to join the Murim Alliance?
The notification appeared before my eyes.
Neither Cheongpung nor I took long to decide.
Our eyes met, and we answered as one.
“We do.”
“Then I hereby formally decree this.
From this moment onward, the two of you shall belong to the Two Dragons Pavilion, directly under the Alliance Leader’s Office and answerable only to the Alliance Leader’s commands.
Each of you shall become a pavilion master, with the authority to select the personnel you require...”
I couldn’t make out what came next.
No—I couldn’t hear it properly.
Ding.
Ding.
Ding, ding!
The bells rang without pause, filling my ears.

paragraphs: “The tea smells wonderful.”

The first to speak was a graying middle-aged man. He looked at least ten years younger than his actual age, which was past sixty. Yet as he faced the man across the teacups, his expression was tight with tension and displeasure.
“Great Hero Mae. No, Alliance Leader.”
Only someone with a mind at ease could enjoy the fragrance of tea. Unable to contain his impatience any longer, the man spoke again. Sword Saint Mae Jonghak smiled at him.
“I’m listening. What is it?”
“You already know, don’t you? The Thousand-Faced Fox...”
“He’s the Chief of the Hidden Shadow Pavilion.”
“Yes. And the Chief of the Hidden Shadow Pavilion must have reported it to you already.”
“Reported what?”
“If you truly haven’t heard, then I’ll tell you myself.”
If Mae Jonghak meant to play ignorant, he would have to show his hand first. The middle-aged man bit his lip and spoke. He was Hwangbo Gun, Family Head of the Hwangbo Family.
“It concerns my son.”
Mae Jonghak’s eyes widened.
“You have a son?”
“Alliance Leader!”
Hwangbo Gun raised his voice before he could stop himself. Realizing his mistake, he lowered his head.

They might once have fought on the same battlefield, but the man before him was now the Alliance Leader of the Murim Alliance. In the past, Sword Saint Mae Jonghak had let almost anything pass with a good-natured smile. An offense against the Alliance Leader, though, could leave the Hwangbo Family in a difficult position.
“I-I apologize. With my son involved, I spoke out of turn.”
Mae Jonghak lifted his teacup with a bright, guileless smile that belied his age.
“Don’t worry about it. These things happen. How many times have we fought together?”
“I’m grateful to hear you say so.”

Hwangbo Gun’s expression brightened a little. Their days on the battlefield were long past, and their positions now stood as far apart as heaven and earth, but Mae Jonghak clearly remembered their bond. Perhaps this would go well after all.
“I’ll get straight to the point. The reason I requested this private audience...”
He quickly recounted what had happened a few shichen earlier. His account was embellished just enough to differ subtly from the truth, though Hwangbo Gun saw it differently.
How dare they do this!

His only son had come along when he was nearly forty. Hwangbo Gun had looked the other way no matter how much trouble the boy caused, and paid no mind to the endless scandals involving women. Now he had been told that his precious son had suffered every kind of humiliation before a crowd of onlookers.
That, Hwangbo Gun could not overlook.

“How can this be allowed? However far the principles of the martial world have fallen, how dare some spawn of demonic, heterodox arts attack the Lesser Family Head of the Hwangbo Family? And furthermore...”
His voice, thick with anger, suddenly dropped.

“An orthodox martial artist who witnessed such injustice and still protected that spawn of the demonic, heterodox arts could no longer be called orthodox, could he? Blazing Flame Divine Dragon Jin Taekyung. I’m speaking of that man.”
“Hmm. So that happened.”
Clink.
Mae Jonghak set down his half-empty teacup and tilted his head.
“But what do you want, exactly?”
“Pardon?”
“I’ve heard your account. I understand what happened. Now tell me what you want.”
Hwangbo Gun stared at Mae Jonghak without speaking, then uttered a single word.
“Punishment. I want appropriate punishment.”
“For example?”
“I had my retainers look into it. The man who attacked my son belongs to the Black Dragon Demon Gate in Gansu.”
“The Black Dragon Demon Gate. I see. Very well.”
Mae Jonghak nodded at once. Hwangbo Gun’s expression brightened. Convinced the Alliance Leader had taken his side, he went on with renewed force.
“And I believe Blazing Flame Divine Dragon Jin Taekyung should be disciplined as well.”
“Disciplined...”
“You’ve heard what happened. He sided with those demonic, heterodox martial artists even after seeing the attack with his own eyes.”
“I suppose so.”
“And such a man is a pavilion master of the Murim Alliance. I’m not the only one who finds that deeply regrettable.”
Regrettable was the mildest word Hwangbo Gun could bring himself to use. This was what infuriated him most.
That young punk is a pavilion master?
A pavilion master was no ordinary post. It placed its holder among the Murim Alliance’s twenty highest-ranking members and carried the authority to command multiple groups and squads.
He’s directly under the Alliance Leader’s Office, so he can’t have subordinate units of his own. But he’s still a pavilion master. How does that make any sense?

Even his son, considered one of Murim’s foremost young prodigies, might or might not receive a Squad Leader’s post. Jin Taekyung had already been raised far above that. And the Jin Family of Taiyuan’s growing influence had lately reached as far as Shandong, where the Hwangbo Family was based. Hwangbo Gun had to put a stop to this, whatever it took.
“The Huashan Divine Dragon’s appointment as pavilion master is a blessing for Murim. I welcome it wholeheartedly. But Jin Taekyung...”
He deliberately trailed off and glanced at Mae Jonghak. The conversation had gone well so far; surely the Alliance Leader understood what he meant.
Mae Jonghak’s answer exceeded even his hopes.
“Now that I think about it, you have a point. I’ll consider not only disciplining him, but taking personnel action as well.”
“Th-Thank you, Alliance Leader!”
Discipline and personnel action? Hwangbo Gun had never expected it to go this well. As he bowed again and again, Mae Jonghak watched him with a smile, then murmured,
“The teacup is empty.”
“Pardon? Oh.”
“Time passes quickly these days.”

Hwangbo Gun froze for a moment. Then he understood and stood. Family Head or not, he could hardly take up more of the Alliance Leader’s time. The time allotted for their private audience—the time it took to drink a cup of tea—had already passed.
“I seem to have stayed too long. Ha ha.”
“Hmm? You’re leaving?”

Even that polite attempt to keep him there warmed Hwangbo Gun’s heart. He had gained more than he’d hoped for, and he appreciated Mae Jonghak’s consideration for his dignity. The bond they had forged during the Great Faction War felt stronger than ever.
“I can’t take up any more of your valuable time. I’ll take my leave, Alliance Leader.”
“Then I suppose it can’t be helped.”
“Yes. I’ll be going.”
“Take care. I’ll see you again.”
Pat, pat.

Someone else might have offended Hwangbo Gun by patting the Family Head of the Hwangbo Family on the shoulder. But this was the Number One Sword Under Heaven, the Alliance Leader of the Murim Alliance. Hwangbo Gun left with a broad smile.
Moments later—
Clack.
The door opened, and a man entered the office. His prosthetic leg made a dull sound as he walked.
“For the Family Head of the Hwangbo Family to request a private audience over something like this... He must have been desperate.”
“That fellow seems to have neglected his martial arts training. His personality has changed a little, too.”
“Pardon?”
“It’s nothing. Sit down.”
Mae Jonghak looked at the hand he had used to pat Hwangbo Gun’s shoulder, then offered his visitor a seat.
The Chief of the Hidden Shadow Pavilion, Thousand-Faced Fox Song Ho, cast a brief glance at the teacup Hwangbo Gun had not even half emptied before speaking.
“Some people are unhappy with the recent appointments.”
“Hmm. Is that so?”
“They met in secret before the Hwangbo Family Head requested his audience.”
“That can happen.”
“Rather than oppose you directly, they seem to have urged him on.”
“Come to think of it, Hwangbo Gun always did tend to put himself forward. He even stood at the vanguard during the battle in Guizhou.”
Mae Jonghak’s eyes widened at Song Ho’s sigh.
“Hmm? What is it?”
“That’s not what I’m talking about.”
“In the end, aren’t we talking about people? Ha ha.”
Song Ho started to answer, then paused.
Mae Jonghak wasn’t wrong. It came down to who did what, and how. Now and then, he would toss off a remark like that, and Song Ho would sense a depth of insight in it.
“In any case, you made the Hwangbo Family Head a promise you can’t keep.”
“A promise?”
“Didn’t you say you would discipline the Black Dragon Demon Gate and the Blazing Flame Divine Dragon, and take appropriate personnel action?”
“Ah, yes. I did. I’m thinking about that now.”
“Alliance Leader, you can’t—”
“Wait. Give me a moment.”
Mae Jonghak scratched his chin. A moment later, he spoke again.
“All right. I’m done. Then let’s pretend the whole thing never happened.”
“Pardon?”
“I’ve considered it, and I don’t think personnel action is necessary. There should be some discipline, but I can decide on that later.”
Song Ho stared at him, his eyes trembling, then let out a disbelieving laugh.
“Of course. You only said you would consider it, Alliance Leader.”
“Even so, he was once a comrade I fought alongside. Shouldn’t I keep my promise?”
“The Hwangbo Family Head is going to clutch the back of his neck.”
“Oh. Don’t you think he’ll understand?”
“Ha ha. I wonder.”
“I was sincere. If he doesn’t understand, there’s nothing I can do.”

Song Ho struggled to hold back his laughter. Mae Jonghak was far better suited to the role of Alliance Leader than he had expected. He was so easygoing by nature that he could let almost anything pass with That can happen. However hard others pressed him, the pressure never seemed to touch him.
His inner resolve is upright and firm.
He was more than Song Ho had hoped for. Song Ho addressed him with genuine feeling.
“Alliance Leader.”
“What is it?”
“I just felt like calling you.”
“Hmm. That can happen.”
“Ha ha ha!”
Mae Jonghak tilted his head at Song Ho’s laughter.
“Oh, right. How are matters with the Nanman Beast Palace and the North Sea Ice Palace?”
Song Ho’s smile faded.
“Neither has replied yet. We sent the letters to both earlier than planned, but they’re a long way off...”
“I see.”
“Yes. But as you know, things are going well with the Green Forest Alliance and the Yangtze River Channel League. Both Alliance Leaders have said they’ll come to Henan in person.”

Neither organization belonged to the orthodox faction, but their leaders were unquestionably giants of the martial world. They commanded forces to rival the great sects and had outstanding masters among their ranks.
“They’ll be a great help if they join us.”
Mae Jonghak gave a small nod, then spoke again.
“Oh. About the discipline.”
“The discipline? Ah, yes.”
“I’ll dictate it. Write a letter and deliver it to the Blazing Flame Divine Dragon—no, to Pavilion Master Jin.”
“As you command.”
Song Ho cupped his hands respectfully. Jin Taekyung’s role from here on would be crucial. Even if the punishment was severe, he had to remain a pavilion master.
I couldn’t believe my eyes or ears.
“Discipline? For me?”
The martial artist from the Alliance Leader’s Office nodded.
“Yes.”
“Why all of a sudden? And this punishment is too harsh.”
“I’ve delivered the message. I’ll be going.”
Whoosh!
What kind of situation is this supposed to be?
I stared blankly after him as he vanished like the wind. Hyuk Mujin came over and asked cautiously,
“Discipline? What did they say?”
I let out a long sigh.
“I have to go hungry.”
“Pardon?”
“I have to skip dinner.”
“Ugh, I was going to have roast duck tonight.”
I grumbled under my breath and kicked Hyuk Mujin in the butt.
“Enough. Let’s go.”
“What kind of punishment is that? And where are we going?”
“To recruit some teammates.”
“Whaaat?”

We sent the letters to both earlier than planned, but they’re a long way off...”
“I see.”
“Yes.
But as you know, things are going well with the Green Forest Alliance and the Yangtze River Channel League.
Both Alliance Leaders have said they’ll come to Henan in person.”
Neither organization belonged to the orthodox faction, but their leaders were unquestionably giants of the martial world.
They commanded forces to rival the great sects and had outstanding masters among their ranks.
“They’ll be a great help if they join us.”
Mae Jonghak gave a small nod, then spoke again.
“Oh.
About the discipline.”
“The discipline?
Ah, yes.”
“I’ll dictate it.
Write a letter and deliver it to the Blazing Flame Divine Dragon—no, to Pavilion Master Jin.”
“As you command.”
Song Ho cupped his hands respectfully.
Jin Taekyung’s role from here on would be crucial.
Even if the punishment was severe, he had to remain a pavilion master.
I couldn’t believe my eyes or ears.
“Discipline?
For me?”
The martial artist from the Alliance Leader’s Office nodded.
“Yes.”
“Why all of a sudden?
And this punishment is too harsh.”
“I’ve delivered the message.
I’ll be going.”
Whoosh!
What kind of situation is this supposed to be?
I stared blankly after him as he vanished like the wind.
Hyuk Mujin came over and asked cautiously,
“Discipline?
What did they say?”
I let out a long sigh.
“I have to go hungry.”
“Pardon?”
“I have to skip dinner.”
“Ugh, I was going to have roast duck tonight.”
I grumbled under my breath and kicked Hyuk Mujin in the butt.
“Enough.
Let’s go.”
“What kind of punishment is that?
And where are we going?”
“To recruit some teammates.”
“Whaaat?”

chapters.title: Chapter 538
paragraphs: I looked at Hyuk Mujin, whose eyes had gone wide.
“What are you so surprised about? Once you become a pavilion master, of course you need to recruit people.”
“No, that’s true, but...”
“But what?”
Hyuk Mujin stared at me in disbelief.
“I’m more concerned about the punishment. What’s with that bizarre order? It’s like a children’s prank.”
“I hear our Alliance Leader personally issued that bizarre, prank-like order.”

“Hmm. On second thought, the punishment must have some profound meaning. Food, clothing, and shelter are the most important things in life. To order you to skip dinner, of all things, must carry some deeper significance...”
Don’t force meaning onto it, you idiot.
They say that once you’re famous, people will applaud even when you take a shit. That fit this situation perfectly.
I gave Hyuk Mujin a long look. He’d changed his tune the instant I mentioned Mae Jonghak.
“You think it’s bullshit too.”
“Then shut up and follow me. And stop worrying about the punishment.”
I shook my head, opened the door, and stepped outside. Hyuk Mujin hurried after me, muttering as he went.
“Wouldn’t it be stranger not to worry? You were appointed pavilion master less than two shichen ago, and you’re already being punished. Did you take a dump in the Alliance Leader’s room?”
Coming from the guy who’d singled me out as the only person who could have taken a dump in a crowded inn. I clicked my tongue.
“Filthy idea. Creative, though. You’re close, but wrong.”
“Close but wrong? Did you pee in there?”
...This bastard.
I held back the urge to punch him and answered.
“Apparently, some people feel shitty about me becoming a pavilion master.”
“Oh.”
“Well, that’s how the world works.”
Pavilion Master of the Two Dragons Pavilion.
That was my official title.
At first, I’d been pleasantly surprised by how cool it sounded. Then I’d learned that a pavilion master of the Murim Alliance held a far more important position than I’d imagined.
I had no idea it was this big a deal.
The title carried that much weight.

A regiment fell directly under a pavilion master, along with the various squads that made up the regiment. Given the Murim Alliance’s current size, the position could mean commanding anywhere from several hundred to more than a thousand martial artists.
Not a position someone my age could even dream of.
Until now, the Murim’s organizational structure hadn’t been my concern.
If I had to put something on my résumé, I’d served as captain of a reconnaissance unit when war broke out between the Jin Family of Taiyuan and the Mount Heng Sword Sect. That was about it.
Afterward...
I wandered all over the damn place.

Maybe I was born under a wandering star. Ever since I’d finished my year of training on Mount Jiuhua and come down from the mountain, I’d done little but travel. Sometimes I couldn’t tell whether I was a martial artist or a traveling peddler.
But my long freelance career had ended today.
The problem was that several company executives weren’t happy about my promotion to full-time employee.
“Who do you think they are?” Mujin asked.
“Who else?”
“Hmm. A few names do come to mind...”
“Then you’ve got your answer. It’s one of them.”
The Hwangbo Family was probably the biggest reason for this punishment, but I didn’t need to spell out every detail for Hyuk Mujin.
I expected something like this, anyway.

Even the kindest, friendliest person in the world couldn’t avoid jealous looks. Someone as round as a balloon would still get knocked this way and that. So what chance did a sharp-edged, sixteen-sided polygon like me have?
No. This is better.
A balloon lost its air when people came at it with words or weapons. Better to be a sixteen-sided polygon that didn’t take so much as a scratch.
That was how Jin Taekyung had lived, and that was how he would keep living.
“If they keep poking at me, I’ll just smash them.”
“What?”
“Nothing. Let’s go.”
I lightly smacked the back of Hyuk Mujin’s head as he stared at me in confusion, then kept walking.
The news of the Murim Alliance’s new young pavilion master must have already spread, because the gazes of the martial artists walking along the main road were burning with interest.
“See him over there? That’s Blazing Flame Divine Dragon Jin Taekyung...”
“Shh. Don’t call him by name so casually. Haven’t you heard? He’s a pavilion master of the great Murim Alliance now.”
“Oh, come on. Does that matter? Don’t pick a fight over nothing. He’s barely twenty—young enough to be my son. He’s just a kid.”
The middle-aged martial artist’s companion clicked his tongue.
“A kid? Has all that martial arts training hardened your brain?”
“What did you say?”

“Just look at yourself, Brother. You’ve joined the Murim Alliance too, haven’t you? Then Great Hero Jin is practically your superior. And you may be old enough to have a son, but you don’t look like you have one.”
“Well, that’s true, but... Why bring that up?”

“Because I don’t want to get dragged down with you. The Enforcement Hall’s martial artists are patrolling Henan with their eyes wide open. I’d rather not be hauled away for insulting a superior just because I was standing next to you.”
The middle-aged martial artist scowled.
“Are you picking a fight with me?”
“I’m not—oh, forget it. No wonder you’re still unmarried at your age. Watch that loose mouth of yours.”
“Fine. I will, you fucker.”
“What was that? You goddamn son of a bitch...”
Are these people insane? How do they even manage to fight like that?
What are they, some kind of battle species?
Maybe the planet Murim was on was actually Planet Vegeta.
Armed with that perfectly reasonable suspicion, I scanned the crowd for yellow hair. More whispers drifted my way.
“What do you think? Should I make an impression on him now?”
“Are you thinking of applying to the Two Dragons Pavilion?”
“Hmm. I’m considering it. Blazing Flame Divine Dragon is much younger than me, but they say his martial arts already rival those of the great sects’ Sect Leaders.”
“Could he really be that strong? And even if the Blazing Flame Divine Dragon’s martial arts are as impressive as the rumors say, you should stay away.”
“Why?”

“Think carefully about everything the Blazing Flame Divine Dragon has done until now. Even if he has the worst luck in the world, how does he manage to choose nothing but deadly situations every time he moves? Accomplishing great deeds is all well and good, but if someone at our level joined the Two Dragons Pavilion, whew.”
“Still, shouldn’t we try to accomplish something?”

“If you want to put up your tombstone first, go ahead. Besides, the Two Dragons Pavilion has two pavilion masters. You might be better off with the Huashan Divine Dragon. Isn’t he the youngest Disciple the Alliance Leader raised like his own grandson? The Alliance is bound to look after him.”
“You might die even faster there.”
“Hm? Why?”
“I heard the snake the Huashan Divine Dragon keeps with him bites people.”
“...Oh dear.”
Word traveled fast.
If this were modern times, the Murim Alliance would have an online petition board by now.

The Huashan Divine Dragon’s snake bit me in the crotch. I demand punishment. Please lend me your support. └ Thousand-Faced Fox\: Agreed. └ Gung Gi\: Agreed. └ Jeok Cheon\: ᄏᄏ, that, snake, bastard, I knew, it would do something like this one day,~~! └ Cheong\: That’s not true. Mimi doesn’t bite people. └ Tang Sa\: Ah, Mimi...
Once the comments piled up and ten thousand people signed in favor of punishment, Mimi’s fate would be sealed. Hmm.
That was when I was spreading my imagination’s wings.
“Was it about half an hour ago? I heard a commoner passing down the main road saw the snake, panicked, and fell while backing away. He was hurt a little.”
“Oh dear. What happened then?”
“I heard that some young medical apprentice who was with the Huashan Divine Dragon took him to a medical clinic. Since it happened because he startled himself, it isn’t that serious—ugh.”
The martial artist cut himself off with a gasp.
I’d come up within a step of him. His eyes shook as he stared at me.
“G-Great Hero Jin?”
“Ah, don’t be startled. It’s nothing serious. I just wanted to ask you something.”
“W-What is it?”
“Where’s that clinic?”
“The clinic? Ah, go straight down that way...”
Still stiff with surprise, he raised a hand to point it out.
I gave him a small nod of thanks and turned in the direction he indicated. Hyuk Mujin looked puzzled.
“Why are we going to a clinic all of a sudden?”
“I told you. I’m looking for a teammate.”
“What? Cheongpung?”
“...How would that work?”
This wasn’t going to be some Cheongpung team without Cheongpung. Cheongpung was a pavilion master in his own right now. I couldn’t put him under my command.
“Think before you speak. Think.”
“Then who else at the clinic could you possibly recruit besides Cheong—”
Hyuk Mujin stopped. His eyes widened.
“No way. You can’t mean...”
“Who knows?”
I left him with that and quietly spoke in my mind.
Open the Quest Window.
Ding.
A cheerful chime sounded, and a translucent holographic window appeared in midair.
It was the first Quest I’d received upon joining the Murim Alliance as Pavilion Master of the Two Dragons Pavilion.

System Quest Become My Companion! At last, you have become a member of the Murim Alliance and been appointed Pavilion Master of the Two Dragons Pavilion. However, one person cannot be an organization. The Murim Alliance has therefore entrusted you with the authority to appoint personnel. Find new members as quickly as possible, form your organization, and give it a name. Only then will you become a pavilion master in the truest sense! Grade: Peak Restriction: Jin Taekyung Mission: Secure at least five companions (Incomplete) Give the organization an appropriate name (Incomplete) Reward: ??? Failure: Acquire the Title “Loner”
Look at that Title. Fuck.
If I failed this Quest, I’d be an outsider officially recognized by the System.
I had to succeed. And with all the trouble ahead, I needed to choose my members carefully.
Leave out anyone who’d follow me without being asked. I need someone I can persuade to come over first—and someone who’ll be a big help.
That was what came to mind the instant I checked the Quest. And I didn’t have to think for long.
The first person I should recruit had practically been decided from the start.
His personality’s pretty damn nasty, but...
He could help in all kinds of ways.
Whatever. Might as well try.
I took a deep breath and headed for the clinic.
“Tony Tony Cho—no, Mungyeong. Become my companion!”
That lunatic’s acting up again.
Mungyeong wasn’t even surprised anymore. Jin Taekyung was always like this.
Jin Taekyung had called Mungyeong out of the blue, saying that the two of them had something to discuss privately, only to start spouting nonsense.
“No.”
“What? Why not?”
Asking why was ridiculous. There were more reasons than Mungyeong could count. But right now, he had a better answer.
“I’ve already agreed to join another group.”
“...What?”
“You got here a step too late. Isn’t that right?”
“Uh, sorry, Benefactor.”
A figure appeared with the sudden voice. Jin Taekyung’s eyes widened as he looked at Cheongpung.

chapters.title: Chapter 539
paragraphs: The Slaughter Saint.
He had entered the world as an assassin, despised by all, and risen at last to become a star that lit the heavens.
He had torn down the fence that admitted only a chosen few, becoming living proof of the four words Might Makes Right.
Yet most people knew neither his age nor his face—not even his name. Assassins worked in the deepest secrecy. They did not reveal themselves.
Decades passed, and the veil over the Slaughter Saint never lifted.

The Slaughter Saint had vanished without a trace immediately after the war ended. He did not show himself even once for a long time, and the words that spilled from the mouths of ordinary people traveled a thousand li, ten thousand li, without needing feet.
The Slaughter Saint is dead!
That was half true and half false.
On the day the Martial God defeated the Heavenly Demon and a hundred thousand demon soldiers fell, an old man in a bamboo hat buried something on an unnamed hill before walking away.
It was not only his beloved weapon, stained with blood. He buried the name Slaughter Saint with it.
The Slaughter Saint died, and Mungyeong emerged into the world. In time, the world began calling him by another name.
The Divine Physician.
The Yangtze has many tributaries, but all their waters join the same river.
Mungyeong was a river like that, bearing two names: the greatest assassin in history and the greatest physician under heaven.
To put it simply...
My number-one recruitment target.
That more than qualified him for a place aboard my Going Murim ship.
Sure, spending time with him meant the occasional attempt on my life. But I’d rather shit blood a few times than die because we ran into a monster like the Western Heaven Demon Lord.
Black cat, white cat. As long as it caught mice, what did the color matter?
It was a shame my first recruitment target wasn’t a cute little deer with horns, but a former assassin who wanted to kill me roughly three times a day. I didn’t have much choice.
Who cares about his personality? He has the strongest damage output and healer abilities, too.
Right. That was enough.
In this harsh Murim, where I couldn’t even get my hands on a cheap potion, I needed Mungyeong. Even if he never saved me, he might save someone traveling with us when their life was in danger.
The problem was that, in my confidence, I’d overlooked one person.
“Hehe.”
“Hello, Benefactor.”
Hello, my ass. What was going on?
No way.
I stared at Cheongpung, my eyes trembling, and finally managed to speak.
“...Why are you coming out of there?”
“Oh, well. I was passing by earlier.”
“No, I know why you came here. I mean—”
This was driving me insane. Seriously.
Mungyeong watched me stammer without a trace of expression and answered for him.
“I told you. You were a step too late.”
Cheongpung smiled brightly.
“Hehe. That’s how it happened, Benefactor.”
It was the one blow that turned my suspicion into certainty. I looked back and forth between them in silence for a moment before managing to part my lips.
“Is this for real?”
Mungyeong nodded.
“It probably isn’t a legend.”
“Then it really happened?”
“Yes. It really happened.”
“Why?”
“I have no reason to tell you.”
“Fair enough. But I think I could give up gracefully if I heard it from you.”
Mungyeong clicked his tongue.
“You’re making an ugly business of it.”
“What if I still want to hear it, even if I have to be filthy?”
“Then I’ll have to find a cleaner way to settle it.”
Shing.
Something silver glinted at the end of his long sleeve. I rubbed my eyes at the sight of the short sword that had popped out like a jack-in-the-box.
“Maybe I’m tired and my eyes are going bad. Why is that coming out now?”
“Because using this would be clean.”
“Maybe, but wouldn’t it make a mess around here?”
“That doesn’t matter. I know a number of methods.”
He must have picked up a few tricks in all his years as an assassin. I had no desire whatsoever to see any of them firsthand.
“Whew. I’ll be going.”
“Go. Forever.”
“See you later, Benefactor!”
I turned away after those two very different farewells.
This is driving me crazy.
Cheongpung had beaten me to it. I hadn’t seen that coming at all.
The Cheongpung I knew should have had a meat dumpling in one hand and a vegetable dumpling in the other, trying to decide which to eat first.
Did he put points into Intelligence instead of me...?
Nothing for it. I’d have to move fast and recruit other people first.
Hyuk Mujin was loitering by the clinic entrance. He hurried over when he spotted me.
“Did it go well—... From your face, I’m guessing not.”
Hyuk Mujin blinked after hurriedly correcting himself upon seeing my face.
“I don’t see Mungyeong. Does that mean...?”
“Can’t you tell?”
“Huh. He turned down the Captain’s offer? He’s better at judging a situation than he looks— I mean, I’m joking. Please, I’m begging you. Put your fist down.”
“Make one more joke and it will become your last will.”
Hyuk Mujin backed away to secure a safe distance before speaking in a solemn voice.
“There is one way.”
“A way?”
“Yes.”
He sounded so sure of himself that I couldn’t help listening. I was grasping at a rotten rope, but I asked anyway.
“What is it?”
“How about I try talking some sense into him? That fellow Mungyeong would do anything I say.”
Hangs on your words, my ass. He’d kill you in the blink of an eye.
If Mungyeong wished, he could turn Hyuk Mujin into a corpse with a single inhale and reduce him to powder with a single exhale.
“Mujin...”
“Don’t worry. We’ve built up a fair amount of affection over the years. If Gung and I go and persuade him, he won’t refuse us coldly.”
“That’s not it, you bastard...”
This bastard was actually trying to commit group suicide now.
I looked at Hyuk Mujin with pity.
“You really hate brothels, huh?”
“What?”
“Never mind. Anyway, don’t try to marry him—no, persuade him. Absolutely not.”
“Why?”
“Just don’t, you bastard.”
Hyuk Mujin did not know Mungyeong’s true identity, so there was no way their conversation could go anywhere.
I sighed at his aggrieved expression.
“Can you write?”
“Write? I’d make Wang Xizhi weep.”
“Answer properly before I beat you until you cry.”
“...I write well enough. Believe it or not, people called me a prodigy when I was little.”
“Then write out a few big notices and put one up.”
“A notice?”
“Yeah. If it’s come to this, we might as well look for some real talent.”
The world was vast, and masters were plentiful.
Henan, right now, was a prince’s residence teeming with dragons and tigers.
What’s so special about holding a public audition?
If you thought about it, even the imperial examinations were the most traditional audition program in existence. With my fame and eye for talent, it was worth trying.
I pictured applicants flooding in.
Let’s do it. Fuck it.
Shik, sssshk!
The movements were fast and fluid, unlike anything the onlookers had seen before. Whenever his hands moved as if dancing, the tip of the large needle flashed, and thread stitched the wound closed.
In mere moments, a swordsman who had been slowly dying from a deep slash across his abdomen had a chance to live.
“How can someone so young possess medical skills of this level...!”
“I’ve never even heard of a medical apprentice like him.”
“Good heavens. That’s nearly divine!”
The gathered physicians, from heavily bearded middle-aged men to white-haired elders, stared in astonishment. A voice snapped them back to their senses.
“Finished.”
Tap.
The treatment was over in a flash. More astonishing than its speed was the fact that it had been done perfectly.
Mouths agape, the physicians turned to the speaker as he rose from his seat.
“H-How can this be?”
“Hey!”
He looked too young to call a young man, yet something about him made boy seem wrong as well.
Mungyeong gathered his belongings and stood.
“Are there any patients left?”
The physicians exchanged glances, then shook their heads all at once.
“N-No, but...”
“Th-That’s right. It’s all thanks to you.”
This was hardly the first time the young medical apprentice had astonished them.
About one shichen earlier, he had arrived with a patient whose injuries were minor. He’d taken one look at the people lying there and remarked:
“This won’t take long.”
Then he’d begun treating them one by one, so quickly and so thoroughly that the physicians who’d come over to scold him and throw him out couldn’t tear themselves away.
Can medicine like this truly exist?
Who is he?
They had waited until now to ask about his identity. But when they finally did, the young medical apprentice’s answer was utterly calm.
“Then that settles it. I’ll be going now.”
“W-Wait! I have a mountain of questions for you!”
“What is your master’s name? Could it be...?”
Questions came at him from every side. Mungyeong inclined his head slightly.
“If I have time, I’ll stop by once more before I leave and check on the patients.”
“You may have been free to enter, but you’re not free to leave!”
“Grab him!”
“Forgive me! We can’t let you go like this!”
Whoosh! Crash!
The physicians threw themselves at him, but their hands closed on empty air. They didn’t so much as brush his collar before tumbling across the floor.
As they stared about in confusion, Mungyeong’s voice rang out.
“I left a prescription for each patient where I was sitting. Read them and carry out the treatments as written.”
“W-What? Prescriptions?”
“Where? Where are they?”
To physicians, a renowned doctor’s prescriptions were like a peerless master’s martial arts manual.
Their eyes all but rolling back, the physicians launched into a fierce struggle over the dozens of prescriptions. Mungyeong slipped outside and walked on, then spoke without warning.
“Come out.”
Swish.
With a faint rustle, a figure emerged from behind a large pillar.
“Oh! How did you know?”
“Just because.”
“You really are amazing. I thought I’d fool you this time. Hehe.”
Mungyeong studied Cheongpung’s cheerful face.
“What martial art was that?”
“A footwork technique.”
“I know that.”
“Oh. I named it Mimi Step.”
“Mimi Step?”
“Yes. After our Mimi. Isn’t it great?”
Cheongpung’s eyes shone. Mungyeong’s reply was cold.
“...What an utterly ridiculous name.”
“Oh. Ah...”
Cheongpung wilted. Mungyeong watched him, his gaze deepening.
What is with this boy?
The name Mimi Step might be ridiculous, but there was nothing ridiculous about the principles behind those movements.
He created a martial art from the way a snake moves.
Most martial artists spent their entire lives trying to understand a single martial art well enough to make it their own. The boy before him had done that as though it were nothing.
Then, having made it his own, he had recreated it entirely.
This boy... has the makings of a Grandmaster.
Jin Taekyung wasn’t the only genius. In some ways, this boy’s genius far surpassed his.
Sword Saint, you’ve raised a monster.
Mungyeong muttered inwardly, then spoke to Cheongpung, who was still looking dejected.
“So why did you offer me your hand?”
“Hmm. Because Benefactor is so amazing.”
“Jin Taekyung?”
“Yes. I used to hope Benefactor would catch up with me soon, but... now I feel like he’s getting farther away, little by little.”
“I see.”
Mungyeong understood at once. A genius who had never had anyone to measure himself against was burning with competitive spirit for the first time.
“Are you hoping to learn martial arts from me?”
“No. You don’t have to teach me.”
“What?”
“I’ll watch and learn from you. That’s enough. Hehe.”
Mungyeong paused, then gave a quiet laugh.
What an absurd boy. He meant to learn just by watching—and the martial arts he intended to watch were Mungyeong’s.
Yet Mungyeong didn’t mind.
“Oh! You smiled.”
“...I did not.”
“You did. You smiled.”
“You impudent little brat.”
“Oh. Now you’re angry.”
“...Brat.”
“Would you like some dumplings?”
Mungyeong hesitated, wondering whether to draw his short sword. Instead, he took the dumpling Cheongpung offered and bit into it.
The taste was not bad.

He had entered the world as an assassin, despised by all, and risen at last to become a star that lit the heavens.

He must have picked up a few tricks in all his years as an assassin.
I had no desire whatsoever to see any of them firsthand.

“Go.

“See you later, Benefactor!”
I turned away after those two very different farewells.

The Cheongpung I knew should have had a meat dumpling in one hand and a vegetable dumpling in the other, trying to decide which to eat first.
