Or perhaps it hadn’t, not entirely.
But right now, at least, I knew what I had to say.
“Yes.
All right.”
A bright smile spread across Ju Hwaran’s face.

chapters.title: Chapter 544
paragraphs: Ju Hwaran had left.
Beyond the window, I watched her walk away, slender yet dignified, with Song Ilseom following like a shadow.
“Young Lady Ju is impressive,” Hyuk Mujin said behind me.
I nodded quietly.
She was like that back then, too.
I remembered the day I first met her: the way she had refused to retreat even when surrounded by hundreds of enemies, and the look in her eyes.
Maybe she’s more of a martial artist than I ever realized.
“I feel sorry for her, too,” Hyuk Mujin said.
“Yeah. She has a lot on her shoulders. Her father still has trouble getting around, and...”
“That’s not what I meant.”
“Hm?”
I turned to find him looking at me with pity.
“If all she wanted was to earn merit, she had plenty of other options. Why come all the way here?”
Why, huh?
I thought it over, then sucked in a breath.
“Wait. Don’t tell me...”
“Yes. Exactly.”
“Because she thought she could earn even more merit?”
“...That’s enough. This is too damn filthy to work with.”
I was debating whether to smack him when a voice came to his rescue.
“Ahh, what a relief.”
Jeok Cheongang emerged from the latrine after half an hour.
Apparently celebrating a smooth delivery, he was grinning from ear to ear as he reached for the liquor bottle first. Then he saw Hyuk Mujin’s expression and paused.
“Why do you look like you’ve been chewing shit?”
“Great Hero Jeok. The thing is...”
Hyuk Mujin launched into an explanation as though he had been waiting for someone to ask. Jeok Cheongang listened in silence, then widened his eyes.
“The Escort King’s granddaughter came here?”
“Yes.”
“Huh. Two people with unusual auras passed by while this old man was straining. She must have been one of them.”
Jeok Cheongang stroked his dark-red beard.
“I heard what happened while I was at death’s door. Now that things have come this far, it seems you share quite a lasting connection.”
“Then why do you think she came to Captain when she had other choices?”
The corner of Jeok Cheongang’s mouth twitched.
“Must this old man really say it aloud?”
“Right? I knew you’d understand, Great Hero Jeok.”
Hyuk Mujin’s face lit up like an LED bulb. Jeok Cheongang smiled knowingly and went on.
“Because she can earn a tremendous amount of merit.”
Oh. The bulb went out.
Hyuk Mujin’s face darkened like night had fallen. His voice dropped with it.
“Are you serious?”
Jeok Cheongang nodded confidently.

“She may have received considerable compensation from the Zhongnan Sect, but she’ll need fame and skill in Murim if she intends to protect and lead the Escort Bureau. The way I see it, the Escort King’s granddaughter understands how the world works.”
“Great Hero Jeok.”
“What?”
“Forgive me for asking, but have you ever had a sweetheart?”
Jeok Cheongang gave it some thought.
“Of course.”
“When?”
“I was about ten. More than a hundred years ago, I suppose.”
“What’s wrong?”
“N-Nothing. It seems I was practicing wall-facing meditation.”
“A real wall. A wall. The Wailing Wall.”
Hyuk Mujin muttered like a monk who had attained enlightenment. Jeok Cheongang looked away from him and turned to me.
“Anyway, what do you intend to do?”
“Hmm.”
“Your face says you’ve already made up your mind. That’s why I’m asking.”
I shrugged.
“You’re psychic. I haven’t even told you yet.”

“From what I’ve heard, it’s not a bad choice. You’re a monster beyond reason, but reaching the Peak realm at her age is an impressive feat. And if she’s been involved in the Escort Bureau since childhood, she’ll have no shortage of experience.”
“I was thinking the same thing. The escort named Song Ilseom would be a major asset on skill alone.”

Jeok Cheongang had been at death’s door when the two of them were here, so he had never met them himself. But he had heard everything that happened after he woke, and had no trouble following the discussion.
“The last of the Guangdong Chen Family’s bloodline. From what I sensed in the latrine, he’s reached a considerable realm.”
“...That’s a little gross, but I agree.”
Jeok Cheongang was a Supreme Peak master who had reached the Returned to Youth realm. If he considered Song Ilseom’s skill considerable, then no one could dispute the man’s martial prowess.
Another genius the world never knew about.
Song Ilseom had lost his family young and been left alone in the world. He had wandered battlefields as a sword boy for wandering martial artists until, at last, he drew a sword of his own.
He wasn’t a flower raised in a greenhouse. He was a weed that had weathered the worst the world could throw at him.
His other name, Soul-Chasing Guest, was the stuff of legend even among wandering martial artists.
He’s no Cheongpung or Mungyeong, but he’d be a valuable addition.
It was a shame, but I had no complaints. The lineup around me had been unusually spectacular until now.
Things were bound to change.
A Supreme Peak master could reverse a losing battle in an instant. With the flames of war spreading in every direction, deploying them where they were needed was only natural.
Mae Jonghak must have separated Cheongpung and me for the same reason.
There were fires burning in several places. We could not keep sending the same fire truck to one location.
If we wanted to win the war against Dark Heaven and prevent even more people from dying, this was the natural course.
And I needed to put together a team to fight those fires with me.
It was time to decide with a cool head.
I guess there’s no helping it.
No matter how I looked at it, this was the best choice. Or if not the best, at least the next best.
I sorted out my thoughts and called a name quietly.
“Hyuk Mujin.”
Hyuk Mujin could seem slow, but he was quick to read the room.
At the very least, he knew something was different whenever I called him by his full name.
“Yes, Captain.”
“Let me ask you straight.”
The choice wasn’t mine alone. Each of us had to make our own, and together those choices would become one decision.
But before I could go on, Hyuk Mujin answered.
“I’ll go with you.”
“What?”
“I said I’ll follow you, Captain. That’s what you were going to ask, isn’t it?”
“...Yeah.”

“Then you didn’t need to ask. The thread follows the needle. Of course, traitors like Gung don’t count. That’s the trouble with outsiders from other sects. They’ve always got some complication or other.”
He gave me a playful smile. I stared at him for a moment, then smiled back.
“You won’t regret it?”
“Regret?”
“Yeah. Regret.”
“Captain. You know what?”
His expression turned serious.
“Ever since I met you, my life has been one long regret.”
“You son of a bitch.”
“But I figured a few more regrets wouldn’t hurt.”
He shrugged and spoke more slowly, gazing into the empty air as though searching through the past.

“A few years ago, people called me the son of the Hyuk Family Textile Shop. Then one day they started calling me the Swift Wind Sword. Some even call me the Blazing Flame Divine Dragon’s right-hand man. I like that.”
“Mujin, you...”
“Hehe. Touched?”
“No, that’s not it. You’re not my right-hand man. You’re my little toe.”
“Wow, Captain. After everything I’ve been through, I’m still just a little toe?”
His indignant face drew a quiet laugh out of me. Maybe it was time for a promotion.
“Fine. Little finger.”
“...On your left hand?”
“Right.”
“Right hand...”
He considered it, then cautiously made a counteroffer.
“I’ll take the right hand. How about the thumb?”
“Try again in your next life.”
“I knew you’d say that. Index finger, then?”
“Not a chance.”
“Damn it. I’ll have to devote my entire life to becoming your right-hand man. Does that make any sense?”
“Yeah, it’ll take your whole life. So stay by my side until then. And don’t die.”
Did I have to say that?
I hadn’t been out of the bath long, but my skin felt strangely itchy. I scratched at my chin for no reason and held out my hand.
“C-Captain.”
His eyes glistening, Hyuk Mujin firmly clasped it.
“Hyuk Mujin, your Captain’s right little finger. I will devote my loyalty to—”
“What are you doing?”
“Huh?”
“Who asked for your hand? Bring me what you received earlier.”
Hyuk Mujin clicked his tongue, looking as if he should have known better, and pulled the two bamboo slips I’d handed him earlier from his robe.
Two names were written in tiny letters on the cords binding them.
Dagger Hidden Flower Ju Hwaran.
Soul-Chasing Guest Song Ilseom.
But these were not the only bamboo slips I needed to receive.
I kept my hand out. Hyuk Mujin seemed to guess what I meant, and his expression soured.
“Captain. Are you serious?”
“Yeah.”
“Whew. I don’t know if this is the right decision.”
With a sigh, he added two more bamboo slips to my hand.
I looked down at the names and epithets on their cords.
Black Dragon Saber Sama Pyo.
Tiger Giant Child Taishan.
I don’t know if this is the right decision.
Hyuk Mujin’s words lingered. The reason was simple: I wasn’t sure this was the best choice, either.
Then Jeok Cheongang spoke, and his words gave me the last bit of certainty I needed.
“What are you hesitating for? Just move forward.”
My tangled thoughts cleared.
After taking a small, deep breath, I whispered toward some place deep within my heart.
Ju Hwaran, Song Ilseom, Sama Pyo, Taishan...
And last, Hyuk Mujin.
I sent all five names through my mind at once, then entered the command.
Approve Two Dragons Pavilion membership.
A voice answered the words no one else could hear.
Ding.

System Membership approval procedure initiated. - Confirmed: Dagger Hidden Flower Ju Hwaran, Soul-Chasing Guest Song Ilseom, Black Dragon Saber Sama Pyo, Tiger Giant Child Taishan, Swift Wind Sword Hyuk Mujin. - Will you accept the five people above as members of the Two Dragons Pavilion?
I already knew my answer.
I gave a small nod of acceptance. With a cheerful chime, the translucent holographic window floating in the air changed as though a page had been turned.
Ding.

System One condition of Quest Become My Companion! has been completed. - Secure at least five companions (Complete) - You have selected the minimum number of members! - One final procedure remains before you become an official Pavilion Master. Choose a new name for the Pavilion assigned to you!
A name, huh?
I hadn’t given any thought to what I’d call the newly formed organization.
But no matter how much I thought about it, nothing could possibly be better than the name that had just flashed through my mind.
Fire Dragon Pavilion.
Ding. Ding. Ding.
Clear bell tones burst out like celebratory fireworks, and resounding System alerts rang in my ears.

chapters.title: Chapter 545
paragraphs: Fire Dragon Pavilion.
The moment I murmured those three words—
Ding. Ding. Ding.
Clear bell tones burst like celebratory fireworks, and a new holographic window flooded my vision.

System Fire Dragon Pavilion has been registered as the new name! - All Quest conditions have been fulfilled! - Quest Become My Companion! has been successfully completed! Fire Dragon Pavilion has been officially established! - You have acquired the unique Title Fire Dragon Pavilion Master! - You have achieved the rare achievement Murim Alliance Civil Servant with a Sword Rice Bowl! - You have acquired a large amount of Fame and EXP!
A completed Quest, an achievement, and even the unique Title Fire Dragon Pavilion Master.
Notifications poured in all at once. But the System had more rewards in store.
Ding. Ding. Ding.

System Even now, your name is echoing throughout Murim. - Your total Fame has surpassed 10,000! - You have achieved the outstanding achievement If You Don’t Know Him, You Must Be Dark Heaven! - As an achievement reward, some Title effects have been strengthened, and Charm and Intimidation have increased significantly! - You have acquired a large amount of Fame and EXP! - Level Up!
Oh, shit.
Was today Christmas or something?
I’d stopped paying much attention to Fame, but the huge amount I’d just gained had pushed my total past 10,000 and earned me an unexpected extra reward.
Some Title effects and stats had been strengthened. And on top of that...
I leveled up.
Even crappy online games made leveling harder the further you progressed, but lately it had become next to impossible. It was almost as if the System had forcibly nerfed me.
With so many battles ahead, every bonus point from a level-up was worth more than any fortune.
Come to think of it, I must have quite a few bonus points saved up. Titles, too.
Was the last time I checked my Status Window right after I defeated the Water God Dragon?
When I first came to Murim, I’d been so anxious that I opened it dozens of times a day. Gradually, I’d checked it less and less. These days, I hardly looked at it at all.
That was because, once my stats had reached a certain level, I had realized that they were little more than luck. What truly determined the outcome of a decisive moment was martial arts.
Still, I should sort everything out soon.

It felt like only yesterday that I had been called the disgrace of my family at Level 10. Now I was a monster who had sailed past Level 100, as well as a nationally famous Supreme Peak master whom no one in Murim failed to recognize.
I was smiling to myself at the thought of how far I’d come when Jeok Cheongang spoke in a disgruntled voice.
“You’re grinning from ear to ear. Does becoming a Pavilion Master make you that happy?”
“Oh, that’s not the only reason.”
“Then what? Are you glad to be rid of this old man?”
“Huh?”
Only then did I understand why he looked so displeased. I stopped short.
“Are you sulking because of that?”
“Sulking? Me? The Fire King Jeok Cheongang?”
His eyes bulged, and he gave a mighty snort.
“Hah! What nonsense!”
“...Easy with the snorting. Your boogers are flying. And with a reaction like that, even a passing mutt could tell.”
“You ill-mannered brat! What do you think you know?”
Well, that settles it.
I took a step back from Jeok Cheongang’s flying spit and tried to calm him down.
“It can’t be helped. It’s not my fault you joined the Five Kings Hall.”
The Five Kings Hall was an organization newly established by the new Murim Alliance, which had carried over the old Murim Alliance’s structure.
It had only five members, but you could call it the strongest fighting force in the Murim Alliance—perhaps in all of Murim.
Just look at the lineup. It was practically Murim’s Avengers.
Thunderbolt Saber King Peng Cheolhu. Azure Sky Sword King Namgung Cheon. Seafaring King Pa Ryun. Fist King Yan Hwapyeong. And...
The man standing right in front of me: Fire King Jeok Cheongang.
With members like that, they hadn’t called it the Five Kings Hall for nothing. Five of the Ten Kings, men who had held their places through the long passage of years, had gathered there.
Living legends. Every one of them.
And Jeok Cheongang sat at their head.

By Murim’s standards of seniority and age, he was old enough to have drunk skull water with Bodhidharma. As for the martial arts that had brought him to Returned to Youth, no one could dispute his mastery.
He was considered the best of the Ten Kings even during the Great Faction War.

When we encountered the Blood Lord during the Shaolin Bloodshed, that bastard had tried to recruit Jeok Cheongang from the outset rather than fight him. He’d even said that if the Great Faction War had lasted a little longer, Jeok Cheongang would have become one of the Four Saints instead of the Three Saints.
But...
“Five Kings Hall, my ass. They’ve stuck me with an office that wasn’t even written in my stars.”
The man himself wouldn’t stop grumbling.
He held the highest seat in a hall of living legends, and he couldn’t have been less pleased.
Hyuk Mujin, who had been watching him closely, raised a tentative hand.
“What?”
“If Great Hero Jeok leaves the Five Kings Hall, could I take his place?”
“With a recommendation, maybe...”
That guy’s a special kind of crazy.
Jeok Cheongang and I fell silent. Then Jeok Cheongang fixed Hyuk Mujin with a long look.
“Go. Unless you want to die.”
“Yes, sir. I’m sorry.”
“If you flap that twitchy mouth of yours one more time, this old man will have something to apologize to your parents for.”
After delivering the threat in a chilling voice, he turned his glare on me.
“And you.”
I quickly waved my hands.
“I don’t need to join the Five Kings Hall.”
“That’s not what I meant.”
“Then what?”
“What do you plan to do from here on?”
He was asking about more than my next move. Pride and worry mingled in his eyes as he looked at me.
“You’ve done well to come this far. I’ll give you that. But from here on...”
“Old Master.”
I cut him off before he could continue and shrugged.
“I’m not as much of a child as you think.”
“And I already know what you’re going to say.”
I wasn’t lying. I could guess well enough what Jeok Cheongang wanted to tell me.
The real war was about to begin. Not a battle—a war. Countless lives would be sacrificed to decide who would rule the world.
The fights I had faced until now had never been easy, but it was obvious that even greater dangers would come crashing down upon us from here on out.
But...
“You said it yourself a moment ago. You asked me what I was hesitating for. You told me to simply move forward.”
That was right. I’d keep moving forward, as I always had. In my own way.
“I’ll hesitate a little, then charge ahead without hesitation.”
Jeok Cheongang watched me smile. Then he gave a quiet laugh.
“If you’re going to move forward, move forward. What’s this about hesitating a little?”
“I can’t help it. Somehow, I’ve ended up with a lot to protect.”

I had blood relatives who were as precious to me as my own life. I had companions and subordinates to whom I could entrust my life. And I had a Master with whom I had formed a bond deep enough for me to throw my life away.
I could not—and should not—ever lose something precious again as I had in the past.
“I’ll protect everything I have as I go.”
“Hah. Greedy bastard.”
Jeok Cheongang let out a short, hollow laugh before continuing.
“But that’s the right answer.”
“Huh?”
“Always be careful. Think. Whatever crisis comes for you, even if you face an opponent you can’t possibly defeat, hold on to that feeling and come back alive.”
“Old Master...”
“And remember.”

sentences.text: Fire Dragon Pavilion.
The moment I murmured those three words—
Ding.
Ding.
Ding.
Clear bell tones burst like celebratory fireworks, and a new holographic window flooded my vision.
System Fire Dragon Pavilion has been registered as the new name! - All Quest conditions have been fulfilled! - Quest Become My Companion! has been successfully completed!

Fire Dragon Pavilion has been officially established! - You have acquired the unique Title Fire Dragon Pavilion Master! - You have achieved the rare achievement Murim Alliance Civil Servant with a Sword Rice Bowl! - You have acquired a large amount of Fame and EXP!
A completed Quest, an achievement, and even the unique Title Fire Dragon Pavilion Master.
Notifications poured in all at once.
But the System had more rewards in store.
Ding.
Ding.
Ding.

System Even now, your name is echoing throughout Murim. - Your total Fame has surpassed 10,000! - You have achieved the outstanding achievement If You Don’t Know Him, You Must Be Dark Heaven! - As an achievement reward, some Title effects have been strengthened, and Charm and Intimidation have increased significantly! - You have acquired a large amount of Fame and EXP! - Level Up!
Oh, shit.
Was today Christmas or something?
I’d stopped paying much attention to Fame, but the huge amount I’d just gained had pushed my total past 10,000 and earned me an unexpected extra reward.
Some Title effects and stats had been strengthened.
And on top of that...
I leveled up.
Even crappy online games made leveling harder the further you progressed, but lately it had become next to impossible.
It was almost as if the System had forcibly nerfed me.
With so many battles ahead, every bonus point from a level-up was worth more than any fortune.
Come to think of it, I must have quite a few bonus points saved up.
Titles, too.
Was the last time I checked my Status Window right after I defeated the Water God Dragon?
When I first came to Murim, I’d been so anxious that I opened it dozens of times a day.
Gradually, I’d checked it less and less.
These days, I hardly looked at it at all.
That was because, once my stats had reached a certain level, I had realized that they were little more than luck.
What truly determined the outcome of a decisive moment was martial arts.
Still, I should sort everything out soon.
It felt like only yesterday that I had been called the disgrace of my family at Level 10.
Now I was a monster who had sailed past Level 100, as well as a nationally famous Supreme Peak master whom no one in Murim failed to recognize.
I was smiling to myself at the thought of how far I’d come when Jeok Cheongang spoke in a disgruntled voice.
“You’re grinning from ear to ear.
Does becoming a Pavilion Master make you that happy?”
“Oh, that’s not the only reason.”
“Then what?
Are you glad to be rid of this old man?”
“Huh?”
Only then did I understand why he looked so displeased.
I stopped short.
“Are you sulking because of that?”
“Sulking?
Me?
The Fire King Jeok Cheongang?”
His eyes bulged, and he gave a mighty snort.
“Hah!
What nonsense!”
“...Easy with the snorting.
Your boogers are flying.
And with a reaction like that, even a passing mutt could tell.”
“You ill-mannered brat!
What do you think you know?”
Well, that settles it.
I took a step back from Jeok Cheongang’s flying spit and tried to calm him down.
“It can’t be helped.
It’s not my fault you joined the Five Kings Hall.”
The Five Kings Hall was an organization newly established by the new Murim Alliance, which had carried over the old Murim Alliance’s structure.
It had only five members, but you could call it the strongest fighting force in the Murim Alliance—perhaps in all of Murim.
Just look at the lineup.
It was practically Murim’s Avengers.
Thunderbolt Saber King Peng Cheolhu.
Azure Sky Sword King Namgung Cheon.
Seafaring King Pa Ryun.
Fist King Yan Hwapyeong.
And...
The man standing right in front of me: Fire King Jeok Cheongang.
With members like that, they hadn’t called it the Five Kings Hall for nothing.
Five of the Ten Kings, men who had held their places through the long passage of years, had gathered there.
Living legends.
Every one of them.
And Jeok Cheongang sat at their head.
By Murim’s standards of seniority and age, he was old enough to have drunk skull water with Bodhidharma.
As for the martial arts that had brought him to Returned to Youth, no one could dispute his mastery.
He was considered the best of the Ten Kings even during the Great Faction War.
When we encountered the Blood Lord during the Shaolin Bloodshed, that bastard had tried to recruit Jeok Cheongang from the outset rather than fight him.
He’d even said that if the Great Faction War had lasted a little longer, Jeok Cheongang would have become one of the Four Saints instead of the Three Saints.
But...
“Five Kings Hall, my ass.
They’ve stuck me with an office that wasn’t even written in my stars.”
The man himself wouldn’t stop grumbling.
He held the highest seat in a hall of living legends, and he couldn’t have been less pleased.
Hyuk Mujin, who had been watching him closely, raised a tentative hand.
“What?”
“If Great Hero Jeok leaves the Five Kings Hall, could I take his place?”
“With a recommendation, maybe...”
That guy’s a special kind of crazy.
Jeok Cheongang and I fell silent.
Then Jeok Cheongang fixed Hyuk Mujin with a long look.
“Go.
Unless you want to die.”
“Yes, sir.
I’m sorry.”
“If you flap that twitchy mouth of yours one more time, this old man will have something to apologize to your parents for.”
After delivering the threat in a chilling voice, he turned his glare on me.
“And you.”
I quickly waved my hands.
“I don’t need to join the Five Kings Hall.”
“That’s not what I meant.”
“Then what?”
“What do you plan to do from here on?”
He was asking about more than my next move.
Pride and worry mingled in his eyes as he looked at me.
“You’ve done well to come this far.
I’ll give you that.
But from here on...”
“Old Master.”
I cut him off before he could continue and shrugged.
“I’m not as much of a child as you think.”
“And I already know what you’re going to say.”
I wasn’t lying.
I could guess well enough what Jeok Cheongang wanted to tell me.
The real war was about to begin.
Not a battle—a war.
Countless lives would be sacrificed to decide who would rule the world.
The fights I had faced until now had never been easy, but it was obvious that even greater dangers would come crashing down upon us from here on out.
But...
“You said it yourself a moment ago.
You asked me what I was hesitating for.
You told me to simply move forward.”
That was right.
I’d keep moving forward, as I always had.
In my own way.
“I’ll hesitate a little, then charge ahead without hesitation.”
Jeok Cheongang watched me smile.
Then he gave a quiet laugh.
“If you’re going to move forward, move forward.
What’s this about hesitating a little?”
“I can’t help it.
Somehow, I’ve ended up with a lot to protect.”
I had blood relatives who were as precious to me as my own life.
I had companions and subordinates to whom I could entrust my life.
And I had a Master with whom I had formed a bond deep enough for me to throw my life away.
I could not—and should not—ever lose something precious again as I had in the past.
“I’ll protect everything I have as I go.”
“Hah.
Greedy bastard.”
Jeok Cheongang let out a short, hollow laugh before continuing.
“But that’s the right answer.”
“Huh?”
“Always be careful.
Think.
Whatever crisis comes for you, even if you face an opponent you can’t possibly defeat, hold on to that feeling and come back alive.”
“Old Master...”
“And remember.”

chapters.title: Chapter 546
paragraphs: “The Alliance Leader is entering.”
At the sound of that deep voice, five doors opened one after another. A figure approached slowly from beyond them, and everyone rose as one, as though they had rehearsed it.
“Chomp, chomp. Smack, smack.”
Everyone except this bastard.
The more I look at him, the crazier he seems.

I wasn’t exactly a model of etiquette myself, but even I could read a room. I leaned toward Cheongpung, who was determined to store every last morsel of food safely in his mouth, and whispered, “What the hell are you doing? Got a problem with society? Don’t like the Murim Alliance?”
Cheongpung swallowed and stood up before answering.
“But there’s still food left, Benefactor.”
“Then stop eating.”
“But the dumplings will get cold.”
You bastard, Cheongpung. You Guan Yu bastard. You know when dumplings are getting cold, but you haven’t noticed everyone’s stares turning cold...
Well, he’s always been like this.
Cheongpung wouldn’t be Cheongpung if he cared what anyone thought. I sighed, poked him in the side, and muttered, “If you’re done eating, pay attention. Our esteemed Azure Dragon Pavilion Master.”
At the words Azure Dragon Pavilion Master, Cheongpung pouted and nodded. His reply came out in a tiny, thoroughly disgruntled voice.
“Yes, Benefactor.”

The name Two Dragons Pavilion remained unchanged, but it had been divided internally into my Fire Dragon Pavilion and Cheongpung’s Azure Dragon Pavilion. On our way to the conference, Cheongpung had told me he’d wanted a different name. Mungyeong had fiercely opposed it.
“I don’t like that name.”
“Why? I think Azure Dragon Pavilion sounds pretty cool. Still, it’s a little unfair. You’re the Pavilion Master. Shouldn’t you at least get to choose the name?”
“I thought so too, but Grandpa Mun hated my idea. He threatened to quit if I used a name like that.”
“It was that bad? What name did you want?”
“Dumpling Pavilion.”
“Or Sweetmeat Pavilion.”
“...Oh. Right.”
“Hoo. I hate Grandpa Mun. What’s so great about Azure Dragon Pavilion, anyway?”
It was ridiculous even now. You should be grateful, you lunatic.
Why not just call it Gim Bugak? The words reached my throat, but I swallowed them. Not because the matter was already settled.
The highest authority in orthodox Murim had finally entered the conference hall.
Step.
Footsteps crossed the silence. Murim Alliance Leader Mae Jonghak reached the seat of honor and smiled at everyone.
“You’re all here.”
Unlike the previous meeting, this one included the heads of the key organizations under the Alliance Leader’s Office. The Murim Alliance’s internal reorganization was finally complete.
That’s quite a crowd when we’re all together.
I swept my gaze around the room. Some faces were unfamiliar—masters whose names and sobriquets I’d heard but whom I’d never met. Among the familiar faces were more than a few I was glad to see.
“You’re awfully late. My backside was about to cramp up.”
Even if you turned the whole world upside down and shook every soul out of it, you could count on one hand the people who could talk to Mae Jonghak like that.

Jeok Cheongang was the foremost among them. Standing with his weight on one leg beside the seat of honor, he spoke in his usual surly tone. Across from him, Jin Wikyung glanced around uneasily before speaking up.
“Great Hero Jeok.”
“What?”
“Well, you know...”
“Good grief. Now that you’ve got a title, are you taking the Alliance Leader’s side?”

Jin Wikyung paused for a moment and gave an awkward smile. In the space of just a year and several months, he had taken the helm of the Jin Family of Taiyuan as Acting Family Head and brought astonishing growth to a family that had been slowly declining. Before anyone knew it, he had become one of their number.
“It’s not that—”
“I know. I know. Now both brothers are making a fuss.”
Mae Jonghak smiled at the grumbling Jeok Cheongang.
“Don’t be like that, Great Hero Jeok. Or should I call you the Five Kings Hall Master now?”
“...Hmph. I get your point, so stop. There are too many people watching.”
“And here I am, wasting busy people’s time with idle chatter.”
It was hard to imagine anyone busier than Mae Jonghak, but he wasn’t wrong. Every person gathered here was a vital cog in the vast Murim Alliance.
The Two Halls, Three Divisions, Five Pavilions, Five Gardens, and Ten Squads.

The only organization standing shoulder to shoulder with the Alliance Leader’s Hall, led by Murim Alliance Leader Mae Jonghak, was the Five Kings Hall, now headed by Jeok Cheongang. Beneath them were the Three Divisions and Five Pavilions belonging to the Inner Hall, followed by the Five Gardens and Ten Squads, which were occupied by people from the Five Great Families and the Nine Sects and One Gang.
And there are more besides.
Remarkably, this wasn’t everyone. Add the unit heads and commanders of the Outer Hall, and even this spacious conference hall wouldn’t hold them all. They’d have to use the training ground.
It showed how enormous the Murim Alliance was. It also meant Cheongpung and I had been recognized as part of its central leadership.
Even if it’s basically an honorary position with no real authority.

A difference between title and standing, perhaps. My title was Pavilion Master, but in the actual pecking order, I was near the bottom of this gathering. Of course, no one else my age held a position like it.
Ah. There was one other person besides Cheongpung.

One-Ride Heavenly Dragon Murong Yeonghwi, a genius who had been called Murim’s greatest young prodigy only two years ago. He was the Lesser Family Head of the Murong Family and had recently been appointed a Squad Leader of the Murim Alliance’s Outer Hall. I had heard that instead of following his father, the Family Head, to Henan, he had remained in Liaoning to oversee the family’s defenses.
I thought I might finally get to see him in person.
Then again, there was no stupider act than leaving one’s base undefended just to attend a meeting in Henan. Everyone else here must have completed their defensive preparations in the same way.
Swish.
Mae Jonghak slowly raised a hand.
“Come, everyone. Sit down. We don’t have time to stand on ceremony.”
But no one sat. More precisely, no one could.
As Mae Jonghak raised his hand, something drifted up from beyond the doors, which still stood open.
“How can he use Seizing an Object Through Empty Space so effortlessly...?”
Someone muttered under their breath.

The object was covered by a cloth, so its identity could not be made out. But it was obviously enormous and seemed to possess considerable weight. Exclamations of admiration rose at Mae Jonghak’s internal energy as he moved it without effort.
Several faces, though, had already gone rigid. Mine probably had too.
His internal energy isn’t the issue. That thing...

Of my five senses, smell was the first to react. The odor was so faint that even a martial artist with sharpened senses might not have identified it right away. But I knew that stench the moment it reached me.
“Benefactor. Is that smell...?”
Cheongpung’s eyes widened. I gave him a small nod.
“That’s right. Corpse stench.”

The reek of a rotting body. I’d smelled it countless times in both the modern world and Murim, and this time I was more certain than anyone. A suspicion about the corpse’s identity flashed through my mind.
If I’m right, that’s...
The next moment, the cloth stained dark red with blood was pulled away, and everyone in the conference hall groaned almost simultaneously.
“Gasp.”
“W-What in the world...?”
“Alliance Leader, what is that thing?”

Voices filled with shock burst out from every corner. Those who already knew about it and those who did not were all forced to feel the same shock at that moment. What the cloth had concealed was that horrifying.
A monster.

There was no other word for it. At a glance, it had a human shape, but unnaturally long, thick joints jutted grotesquely from all over its body. Its wide-open, lifeless eyes were each as large as a child’s fist.
And that wasn’t the end of it.
“Th-There’s a horn.”
“That’s not all. Its arms...”

A black horn rose from the center of its forehead, and four arms protruded from its upper body. The arms varied in length and thickness, perhaps because they’d been severed during the fight. But no one could dispute that they were human arms.
“Hmm.”
“How could this happen?”
As the murmurs of dismay continued, someone spoke up.
“Infinite Life Buddha. It is hard to believe. I felt the same way at first.”
The speaker was an old Daoist with deep-set eyes and a snow-white beard that reached his chest: the Sect Leader of Wudang. The people who turned toward him looked puzzled.
“At first...?”
“Do you mean...?”
The Sect Leader of Wudang nodded.
“That’s right. Some of you may already have heard, but that man—no, that thing—was once a fisherman named Jang Sam.”

The old Daoist was relating what I had heard earlier at the Hidden Shadow Pavilion. A fisherman with an ordinary name, no different from anyone else, had disappeared. One month later, he had reappeared as a monster and a Killing Ghost that had thrown Hubei Province into an uproar.

“When it was first found, its martial arts were only Third Rate. But its strength and movements were said to be inhuman. Each time it reappeared, it looked more grotesque and had grown stronger. As though...”
After a brief hesitation, the Sect Leader of Wudang continued with a sigh.
“As though it harmed people, absorbed their vital essence, and made it its own.”
The shock swept through the hall. Suffocating silence followed, until Jeok Cheongang frowned and spoke.
“Are you saying that goddamn monster learned the Essence-Siphoning Great Technique or something?”
The Sect Leader of Wudang shook his head.
“Infinite Life Buddha. I can’t be certain of that either. But if that thing is what Dark Heaven intended to create, and it truly can use the Essence-Siphoning Great Technique...”
His voice trailed off. His face was rigid, and so were most of the faces around him.
Understandably.
The Essence-Siphoning Great Technique was a vicious demonic martial art said to have been lost even within the Demonic Cult. To orthodox martial artists, it was the work of a fiend.
If Dark Heaven had revived it and taught it to the monsters they’d created...
A catastrophe. Plain and simple.
Fortunately—or perhaps unfortunately—the Sect Leader of Wudang’s guess was wrong. At least, as far as I knew.
Most monsters grow fast.
Didn’t they say an Orc reaches adulthood in a month?
Most monsters grew stronger in one of two ways: they were born with tremendous power, or they absorbed magical power from other monsters.
Eating humans might give them a small amount of strength, but most of the people this thing killed were commoners and Third Rate or Second Rate wandering martial artists.

Humans and monsters were born with fundamentally different kinds of energy. If that sort of exchange between the two were possible, modern monsters would already be sold as aphrodisiacs or health tonics.
I can’t be one hundred percent certain since it’s a mutant.
Still, experience told me that explanation was more likely. No—I hoped it was. If monsters that could directly absorb human energy started pouring into the world, we’d never be able to handle them.
While I was lost in thought, Mae Jonghak’s quiet voice carried through the hall.
“Pavilion Master Jin. What do you think?”
I turned my head toward the voice calling for Pavilion Master Jin—and froze when I felt everyone’s gazes on me.
Wait. Pavilion Master Jin means...
Fuck. Me.
I still wasn’t used to it, so I had forgotten.
“Are you asking me?”
“Yes. I’d like your opinion.”
“Well, this is... Hm.”
“It’s all right. Say whatever comes to mind.”
“I’m not sure how to put it.”
“In your own way. Simply and clearly.”
Simply and clearly. I thought for a moment, then spoke carefully.
“I think things are a little—no, maybe considerably...”
“Considerably?”
I stared into dozens of pairs of burning eyes before answering.
“I think we’re fucked.”

Now that you’ve got a title, are you taking the Alliance Leader’s side?”
Jin Wikyung paused for a moment and gave an awkward smile.
In the space of just a year and several months, he had taken the helm of the Jin Family of Taiyuan as Acting Family Head and brought astonishing growth to a family that had been slowly declining.
Before anyone knew it, he had become one of their number.
“It’s not that—”
“I know.
I know.
Now both brothers are making a fuss.”
Mae Jonghak smiled at the grumbling Jeok Cheongang.
“Don’t be like that, Great Hero Jeok.
Or should I call you the Five Kings Hall Master now?”
“...Hmph.
I get your point, so stop.
There are too many people watching.”
“And here I am, wasting busy people’s time with idle chatter.”
It was hard to imagine anyone busier than Mae Jonghak, but he wasn’t wrong.
Every person gathered here was a vital cog in the vast Murim Alliance.
The Two Halls, Three Divisions, Five Pavilions, Five Gardens, and Ten Squads.
The only organization standing shoulder to shoulder with the Alliance Leader’s Hall, led by Murim Alliance Leader Mae Jonghak, was the Five Kings Hall, now headed by Jeok Cheongang.

Beneath them were the Three Divisions and Five Pavilions belonging to the Inner Hall, followed by the Five Gardens and Ten Squads, which were occupied by people from the Five Great Families and the Nine Sects and One Gang.
And there are more besides.
Remarkably, this wasn’t everyone.
Add the unit heads and commanders of the Outer Hall, and even this spacious conference hall wouldn’t hold them all.
They’d have to use the training ground.
It showed how enormous the Murim Alliance was.
It also meant Cheongpung and I had been recognized as part of its central leadership.
Even if it’s basically an honorary position with no real authority.
A difference between title and standing, perhaps.
My title was Pavilion Master, but in the actual pecking order, I was near the bottom of this gathering.
Of course, no one else my age held a position like it.
Ah.
There was one other person besides Cheongpung.
One-Ride Heavenly Dragon Murong Yeonghwi, a genius who had been called Murim’s greatest young prodigy only two years ago.
He was the Lesser Family Head of the Murong Family and had recently been appointed a Squad Leader of the Murim Alliance’s Outer Hall.
I had heard that instead of following his father, the Family Head, to Henan, he had remained in Liaoning to oversee the family’s defenses.
I thought I might finally get to see him in person.
Then again, there was no stupider act than leaving one’s base undefended just to attend a meeting in Henan.
Everyone else here must have completed their defensive preparations in the same way.
Swish.
Mae Jonghak slowly raised a hand.
“Come, everyone.
Sit down.
We don’t have time to stand on ceremony.”
But no one sat.
More precisely, no one could.
As Mae Jonghak raised his hand, something drifted up from beyond the doors, which still stood open.
“How can he use Seizing an Object Through Empty Space so effortlessly...?”
Someone muttered under their breath.
The object was covered by a cloth, so its identity could not be made out.
But it was obviously enormous and seemed to possess considerable weight.
Exclamations of admiration rose at Mae Jonghak’s internal energy as he moved it without effort.
Several faces, though, had already gone rigid.
Mine probably had too.
His internal energy isn’t the issue.
That thing...
Of my five senses, smell was the first to react.
The odor was so faint that even a martial artist with sharpened senses might not have identified it right away.
But I knew that stench the moment it reached me.
“Benefactor.
Is that smell...?”
Cheongpung’s eyes widened.
I gave him a small nod.
“That’s right.
Corpse stench.”
The reek of a rotting body.
I’d smelled it countless times in both the modern world and Murim, and this time I was more certain than anyone.
A suspicion about the corpse’s identity flashed through my mind.
If I’m right, that’s...
The next moment, the cloth stained dark red with blood was pulled away, and everyone in the conference hall groaned almost simultaneously.
“Gasp.”
“W-What in the world...?”
“Alliance Leader, what is that thing?”
Voices filled with shock burst out from every corner.
Those who already knew about it and those who did not were all forced to feel the same shock at that moment.
What the cloth had concealed was that horrifying.
A monster.
There was no other word for it.
At a glance, it had a human shape, but unnaturally long, thick joints jutted grotesquely from all over its body.
Its wide-open, lifeless eyes were each as large as a child’s fist.
And that wasn’t the end of it.
“Th-There’s a horn.”
“That’s not all.
Its arms...”
A black horn rose from the center of its forehead, and four arms protruded from its upper body.
The arms varied in length and thickness, perhaps because they’d been severed during the fight.
But no one could dispute that they were human arms.
“Hmm.”
“How could this happen?”
As the murmurs of dismay continued, someone spoke up.
“Infinite Life Buddha.
It is hard to believe.
I felt the same way at first.”
The speaker was an old Daoist with deep-set eyes and a snow-white beard that reached his chest: the Sect Leader of Wudang.
The people who turned toward him looked puzzled.
“At first...?”
“Do you mean...?”
The Sect Leader of Wudang nodded.
“That’s right.
Some of you may already have heard, but that man—no, that thing—was once a fisherman named Jang Sam.”
The old Daoist was relating what I had heard earlier at the Hidden Shadow Pavilion.
A fisherman with an ordinary name, no different from anyone else, had disappeared.
One month later, he had reappeared as a monster and a Killing Ghost that had thrown Hubei Province into an uproar.
“When it was first found, its martial arts were only Third Rate.
But its strength and movements were said to be inhuman.
Each time it reappeared, it looked more grotesque and had grown stronger.
As though...”
After a brief hesitation, the Sect Leader of Wudang continued with a sigh.
“As though it harmed people, absorbed their vital essence, and made it its own.”
The shock swept through the hall.
Suffocating silence followed, until Jeok Cheongang frowned and spoke.
“Are you saying that goddamn monster learned the Essence-Siphoning Great Technique or something?”
The Sect Leader of Wudang shook his head.
“Infinite Life Buddha.
I can’t be certain of that either.
But if that thing is what Dark Heaven intended to create, and it truly can use the Essence-Siphoning Great Technique...”
His voice trailed off.
His face was rigid, and so were most of the faces around him.
Understandably.
The Essence-Siphoning Great Technique was a vicious demonic martial art said to have been lost even within the Demonic Cult.
To orthodox martial artists, it was the work of a fiend.
If Dark Heaven had revived it and taught it to the monsters they’d created...
A catastrophe.
Plain and simple.
Fortunately—or perhaps unfortunately—the Sect Leader of Wudang’s guess was wrong.
At least, as far as I knew.
Most monsters grow fast.
Didn’t they say an Orc reaches adulthood in a month?
Most monsters grew stronger in one of two ways: they were born with tremendous power, or they absorbed magical power from other monsters.
Eating humans might give them a small amount of strength, but most of the people this thing killed were commoners and Third Rate or Second Rate wandering martial artists.
Humans and monsters were born with fundamentally different kinds of energy.
If that sort of exchange between the two were possible, modern monsters would already be sold as aphrodisiacs or health tonics.
I can’t be one hundred percent certain since it’s a mutant.
Still, experience told me that explanation was more likely.
No—I hoped it was.
If monsters that could directly absorb human energy started pouring into the world, we’d never be able to handle them.
While I was lost in thought, Mae Jonghak’s quiet voice carried through the hall.
“Pavilion Master Jin.
What do you think?”
I turned my head toward the voice calling for Pavilion Master Jin—and froze when I felt everyone’s gazes on me.
Wait.
Pavilion Master Jin means...
Fuck.
Me.
I still wasn’t used to it, so I had forgotten.
“Are you asking me?”
“Yes.
I’d like your opinion.”
“Well, this is...
Hm.”
“It’s all right.
Say whatever comes to mind.”
“I’m not sure how to put it.”
“In your own way.
Simply and clearly.”
Simply and clearly.
I thought for a moment, then spoke carefully.
“I think things are a little—no, maybe considerably...”
“Considerably?”
I stared into dozens of pairs of burning eyes before answering.
“I think we’re fucked.”

chapters.title: Chapter 547
paragraphs: A chilling silence settled over the great conference hall.
I’d expected that reaction before I opened my mouth. I’d even known which of the dozens gathered here would be the first to take a shot at me.
“Do you call that something to say?”
He never disappoints.
I clicked my tongue inwardly as the half-gray-haired man spoke up, just as if he’d been waiting for his chance.
I already knew his name and position. He’d glared at me so much during our last gathering that I’d wondered what his problem was. It turned out we had an indirect connection.
They say blood never lies.
Father and son did look alike. The sharply raised eyes, the arrogant gaze that looked down on everyone, even the way they spoke.
“It seems you didn’t hear me.”
The man was Hwangbo Gun, Family Head of the Hwangbo Family and father of the Shandong Fist Dragon, Hwangbo Ak. I blinked slowly at his question.
“Of course I heard you. How could I not?”
“Then why didn’t you answer?”
“Because your question is ridiculous. I said it with my own mouth, so of course it was speech. Did I make some kind of animal noise?”
Beside me, Cheongpung pricked up his ears.
“Benefactor, can you make animal noises too?”
“Keep your mouth shut, Cheongpung. Unless you want to puke up those dumplings.”
“Thank you...”
Hwangbo Gun’s face twisted as he watched us.
“Do you not understand what kind of gathering this is?”
“Is there anyone here who didn’t know?”
“And yet you speak so crudely in front of these esteemed Seniors!”
“That’s why I was trying not to say anything. Besides, we should hear what the Seniors think. What do you say?”
At my sudden question, Mae Jonghak nodded.
“Fire Dragon Pavilion Master Jin is right. I have no problem with it. His words may be rough, but we need to face reality.”
“A-Alliance Leader!”
I cut off Hwangbo Gun’s panicked cry.
“Yes, we’ve heard the Murim Alliance Leader’s esteemed opinion. While we’re at it, what does our Five Kings Hall Master think?”
Jeok Cheongang looked at Hwangbo Gun as though he were a bug.
“Why the hell are you asking? We’re fucked. Ignore that bastard’s nonsense and keep going.”
“Thank you for the fiery answer.”
I turned to Hwangbo Gun and shrugged.
“That’s what those esteemed Seniors have to say.”
There were plenty of people here who could be called Seniors, but none of them could compare to Jeok Cheongang and Mae Jonghak.

If the heads of the Nine Sects and One Gang and the Five Great Families were squad-leading corporals with pull or sergeants nearing discharge, Murim Alliance Leader Mae Jonghak was the battalion commander, and Jeok Cheongang was the command sergeant major.
If you don’t have the seniority, keep your mouth shut.
And it wasn’t just seniority. Strip off the insignia and take Jeok Cheongang on as an equal, and one punch from the Fire King would lay you out.
That was why even the Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord, Sect Leader of the Zhongnan Sect and one of the foremost among those who disliked Cheongpung and me, kept his mouth firmly shut.
Which left Hwangbo Gun all alone.
You should’ve looked before stretching out your legs. Why step forward on your own?

I’d heard Hwangbo Gun wielded considerable influence during the Great Faction War. Maybe he’d always lacked political sense. Or maybe a matter involving his only son—the sole heir in three generations—had turned him into a runaway locomotive.
I hummed a mournful tune.
“I’m a firefly. I have no friends.”
“You insolent young punk!”
I couldn’t stop there. I hit him with the combo I’d prepared.
“Waaah. I’m a baby Pavilion Master.”
“You braaaat!”
Crash!
Hwangbo Gun sprang to his feet, veins standing out on his clenched fists. He glared at me, furious and empty-handed, without so much as breaking even.
Then a voice spoke.
“‘Punk,’ you say... Forgive me, Family Head Hwangbo, but may I ask you one question?”
The voice was gentle, with a firmness beneath it. Jin Wikyung’s eyes had gone cold as he looked at Hwangbo Gun.
“What position do you hold within the Murim Alliance, Family Head Hwangbo?”

“Regardless of how young the Fire Dragon Pavilion Master may be, he is the successor to Great Hero Jeok, the Fire King, and a Pavilion Master of the Murim Alliance. Even if we consider seniority within the martial world, he is certainly not beneath you, Family Head Hwangbo.”
That hit the sore spot. Hwangbo Gun’s face stiffened.
He was Family Head of the Hwangbo Family, the hegemon of Shandong, but within the Alliance he was only an Outer Hall Squad Leader charged with defending one region.
In the Murim Alliance’s official hierarchy, that put him below me, an Inner Hall Pavilion Master.
“That...”
Unable to continue, Hwangbo Gun bit his lip and looked around for help.
The response was lukewarm.
“Amitabha. Perhaps it would be best to restrain yourself now, Benefactor Hwangbo.”
“Heavens. Such a disturbance in the sacred Alliance Leader’s Hall.”
“Blazing Flame Divine Dragon—no, Fire Dragon Pavilion Master. I’m not taking your side. Both of you have said enough. Sit down.”
I answered without a hint of shame.
“I’ve been sitting down the whole time.”
“Then there’s only one person left.”
It was obvious whom he meant.
Hwangbo Gun was torn between his rational judgment, which told him he needed to stop, and the last shred of pride possessed by the hegemon of Shandong and Family Head of a great family.
One remark settled his indecision.
“Got a hidden weapon stuck in your ear?”
It came from the Fire King, Jeok Cheongang. The air in the hall heated with those few words.
Hwangbo Gun stood frozen, reflected in Jeok Cheongang’s red-glowing eyes.
“Sit down. Right now.”
Whoooosh!
Jeok Cheongang’s aura surged through the air and crashed over them. Hwangbo Gun’s eyes flew wide.
So did everyone else’s.
“Hmm.”
Fist King Yan Hwapyeong, who had watched in silence, let out a low groan.
“J-Jeok! You bastard...!”
The Thunderbolt Saber King Peng Cheolhu’s gaze wavered.
Jeok Cheongang’s aura was that powerful, that overwhelming—like another sun. Those still in the Peak realm could feel his strength, as could those who had already reached Supreme Peak.
Returned to Youth.
The mountain range called martial arts was vast and treacherous. Sometimes one had to cross a steep ravine or scale a sheer cliff.
Jeok Cheongang was a great martial artist standing proudly atop the peak at the very end.
He had become something beyond his title of Fire King. So had one other person in this room.
“Great Hero Jeok.”
At Sword Saint Mae Jonghak’s quiet call, the hot wind sweeping through the hall vanished.
Jeok Cheongang drew in his aura at once and answered gruffly.
“Did something happen?”
“Hmm.”
“All right, I know. That bastard was making too much noise, so I gave him a little scare.”
No joke—if he scared Hwangbo Gun a second time, the man might wet himself. He was already back in his seat, white as a sheet.
“Finally, some quiet,” Jeok Cheongang muttered.
Mae Jonghak gave him a gently reproachful look, then turned to me.
“Fire Dragon Pavilion Master.”
“Yes.”
“You have stood against Dark Heaven in Shanxi and Henan, and in Sichuan and Hubei.”
Gotten dragged into it would have been more accurate, but I nodded.
This was the great conference hall of the Murim Alliance. Dealing with Hwangbo Gun and discussing matters of such importance were two entirely different things.
“That’s right.”
“I expect few people know Dark Heaven as well as you. I would like to hear your opinion.”

“I was merely present at those incidents. Hidden Shadow Pavilion probably knows the concrete details and what is happening throughout the world better than I do. I already told you everything I knew.”
“I want to hear what you saw and experienced yourself. What the man who went through it all truly thinks.”
There we go.

What I’d said before was only a lead-in. Demurring once or twice was the polite thing to do, and if Mae Jonghak, speaking with the authority of the Murim Alliance Leader, pressed me for my opinion, it would carry that much more weight.
All right.
I took a small breath.
Until now, I’d been sitting in the back seat. From here on, I was in the passenger seat.
I couldn’t tell a driver setting out on an unfamiliar road at dawn, through thick fog and without navigation, everything I knew. But I could point out the speed bumps and warn him what lay ahead.
Including the ominous thought I haven’t been able to shake lately.
I sorted through my thoughts and raised my head. Everyone in the hall was looking at me.
Dozens of pairs of eyes.
They were people who could save—or kill—hundreds, even thousands, of lives in a war that had already begun.
How much heed they would pay to a kid barely past twenty, I couldn’t say.
It doesn’t matter. If we can win this war. If I can reduce the danger and sacrifice even a little.
I had to do what I could. Right now.
Perhaps that was why my voice carried a weight it usually didn’t when I began to speak.
“Dark Heaven...”
Two shichen later, everyone had left the great conference hall except three people.

The chairs that had held dozens of people stood empty, but the silence that had settled over the room remained. Thousand-Faced Fox Song Ho suspected those who had left the Alliance Leader’s Hall were just as quiet.
They had every reason to be.
Jin Taekyung’s words had been that shocking.
Everyone knew Dark Heaven existed and understood that it was dangerous. No one, though, had warned of the coming crisis as forcefully as that young man.
Not even me.

The Hidden Shadow Pavilion gathered intelligence from across the realm and issued countless predictions. Hundreds of messenger pigeons arrived each day with information tied to their slender ankles, then flew off again before long.
As its chief, Song Ho knew how dangerous Dark Heaven was.
But...
The thinking of the Fire Dragon Pavilion’s young master, the Blazing Flame Divine Dragon whose actions had caused one upheaval after another, went far beyond anything Song Ho had expected.
Where others spoke of danger, Jin Taekyung foretold disaster. When someone cited the Great Faction War as grounds for believing the Murim Alliance would win, he answered sharply.
“Are we fighting the Demonic Cult? Our opponent is Dark Heaven. Dark Heaven.”
“What Dark Heaven has shown us isn’t simply demonic martial arts. So what do I call it? Ah, this is driving me crazy. Fine. Let’s call it demonic martial arts for now.”
“I don’t know why Dark Heaven has gone quiet, but we need to use this opening to strike back immediately. If we keep going like this, we’re finished. Everyone dies.”

“Who said I was going too far? You, Family Head. Have you ever fought someone who came back to life even after all four limbs were crushed? Or fought an imugi? When you saw that monster half an hour ago, did you think about nothing but what to eat for dinner?”
“We aren’t fighting ordinary people. Dark Heaven is one enormous monster, and before long, we may have to fight monsters like that one.”
“I went a little too far. But this needs saying: we have to take every measure we can, right now. Especially if you’ve got a divine artifact at home that you guard like an ancestral shrine.”
Song Ho suddenly furrowed his brow.
The place where his prosthetic leg attached had begun to throb when Jin Taekyung started speaking. Now it burned.
It wasn’t like this even a year ago.
The pain had returned at some point and begun tormenting him in his old age, as though warning him this was no time to sit still.
And today, that young man was here too.
It was as though he knew. As though he had experienced something in advance and was predicting some truth that I and the Hidden Shadow Pavilion—no, that everyone else—knew nothing about.
Foresee? No. Song Ho corrected himself.
It was more like a prophecy.
The question was whether it truly was one.
Could he trust the young man who, more than anyone else in the realm, had come into contact with Dark Heaven? How much of what he’d said was truth, and how much was exaggeration?
“Believe him.”
“Hm?”
Song Ho looked up sharply. Jeok Cheongang, still in the hall, continued.
“I said, believe him.”
“Great Hero Jeok.”
“I know what you’re going to say. But...”
His tone softened.
“The kid I know has never once been wrong.”
Song Ho faltered at the absolute trust in those words.
Then Mae Jonghak, the last of the three remaining in the hall, spoke.
“There are certainties in this world that information alone cannot lead us to.”
“Alliance Leader. Do you mean...?”
“That’s right.”
Mae Jonghak rose slowly from his seat.
“Summon him. It’s time to give the Fire Dragon Pavilion its first mission.”

Everyone in the hall was looking at me.
Dozens of pairs of eyes.
They were people who could save—or kill—hundreds, even thousands, of lives in a war that had already begun.
How much heed they would pay to a kid barely past twenty, I couldn’t say.
It doesn’t matter.
If we can win this war.
If I can reduce the danger and sacrifice even a little.
I had to do what I could.
Right now.
Perhaps that was why my voice carried a weight it usually didn’t when I began to speak.
“Dark Heaven...”
Two shichen later, everyone had left the great conference hall except three people.
The chairs that had held dozens of people stood empty, but the silence that had settled over the room remained.
Thousand-Faced Fox Song Ho suspected those who had left the Alliance Leader’s Hall were just as quiet.
They had every reason to be.
Jin Taekyung’s words had been that shocking.
Everyone knew Dark Heaven existed and understood that it was dangerous.
No one, though, had warned of the coming crisis as forcefully as that young man.
Not even me.
The Hidden Shadow Pavilion gathered intelligence from across the realm and issued countless predictions.
Hundreds of messenger pigeons arrived each day with information tied to their slender ankles, then flew off again before long.
As its chief, Song Ho knew how dangerous Dark Heaven was.
But...
The thinking of the Fire Dragon Pavilion’s young master, the Blazing Flame Divine Dragon whose actions had caused one upheaval after another, went far beyond anything Song Ho had expected.
Where others spoke of danger, Jin Taekyung foretold disaster.
When someone cited the Great Faction War as grounds for believing the Murim Alliance would win, he answered sharply.
“Are we fighting the Demonic Cult?
Our opponent is Dark Heaven.
Dark Heaven.”
“What Dark Heaven has shown us isn’t simply demonic martial arts.
So what do I call it?
Ah, this is driving me crazy.
Fine.
Let’s call it demonic martial arts for now.”
“I don’t know why Dark Heaven has gone quiet, but we need to use this opening to strike back immediately.
If we keep going like this, we’re finished.
Everyone dies.”
“Who said I was going too far?
You, Family Head.
Have you ever fought someone who came back to life even after all four limbs were crushed?
Or fought an imugi?
When you saw that monster half an hour ago, did you think about nothing but what to eat for dinner?”
“We aren’t fighting ordinary people.
Dark Heaven is one enormous monster, and before long, we may have to fight monsters like that one.”
“I went a little too far.
But this needs saying: we have to take every measure we can, right now.
Especially if you’ve got a divine artifact at home that you guard like an ancestral shrine.”
Song Ho suddenly furrowed his brow.
The place where his prosthetic leg attached had begun to throb when Jin Taekyung started speaking.
Now it burned.
It wasn’t like this even a year ago.
The pain had returned at some point and begun tormenting him in his old age, as though warning him this was no time to sit still.
And today, that young man was here too.
It was as though he knew.
As though he had experienced something in advance and was predicting some truth that I and the Hidden Shadow Pavilion—no, that everyone else—knew nothing about.
Foresee?
No.
Song Ho corrected himself.
It was more like a prophecy.
The question was whether it truly was one.
Could he trust the young man who, more than anyone else in the realm, had come into contact with Dark Heaven?
How much of what he’d said was truth, and how much was exaggeration?
“Believe him.”
“Hm?”
Song Ho looked up sharply.
Jeok Cheongang, still in the hall, continued.
“I said, believe him.”
“Great Hero Jeok.”
“I know what you’re going to say.
But...”
His tone softened.
“The kid I know has never once been wrong.”
Song Ho faltered at the absolute trust in those words.
Then Mae Jonghak, the last of the three remaining in the hall, spoke.
“There are certainties in this world that information alone cannot lead us to.”
“Alliance Leader.
Do you mean...?”
“That’s right.”
Mae Jonghak rose slowly from his seat.
“Summon him.
It’s time to give the Fire Dragon Pavilion its first mission.”

chapters.title: Chapter 548
paragraphs: “Well done.”
Jin Wikyung said it the moment we left the great conference hall. I answered with a quiet laugh.
“Why are you laughing?”
“I don’t know. Maybe because your expression doesn’t match what you’re saying?”
“Ah.”
Only then did his stiff expression ease. But the smile at the corners of his mouth was so faint it looked ready to disappear.
“To be honest, I don’t know what to make of what you said. Today, you were just so...”
“It’s all right. That reaction is only natural.”
I understood why Jin Wikyung trailed off. I could imagine how he felt.
If I were in his position, I’d react the same way.
In this world, the word death did not carry quite the weight one might expect.
Murders were rare in the modern world, and people learned about them through television and other media. Here, people witnessed death often.
Things were somewhat better in cities with good public order. Outside them, commoners lived under the threat of bandits or mounted bandits, depending on where they were.
Martial artists were another matter entirely.
A life spent walking on the point of a blade.
There was a reason people called it a mountain of sabers and a forest of swords.
They were always prepared to die. They stoked their fighting spirit and trained their martial arts. Jin Wikyung, standing before me, was a martial artist too.
The problem was the environment he and all the others had grown up in.

In Murim, people killed people, and people died by human hands. There were fierce beasts and spiritual creatures, but at least people knew what those were. They were not monsters no one had ever heard of or seen.
And today, I had told them those monsters would cover the world.
I had predicted a fight in which humans and monsters would kill one another.
I don’t know how much of what I said sank in. But they must have felt the danger.
As I spoke, some looked at me with disbelief. Others were confused but fell into deep thought.
They did not all have to believe me right away. Getting them to listen was enough to accomplish what I had set out to do.
It only got through at all because they’re martial artists and I had hard evidence.

If my audience had been a bunch of old Confucian scholars, they would have shouted “Confucius Akbar!” and staged a protest against supernatural powers. The people in the great conference hall were not quite that close-minded.
At least, not with the corpse of a four-armed monster lying in front of them.
There were the Water God Dragon’s remains, too.

Its body had been separated into parts and was still being transported in strict secrecy. But I had quietly slipped some of its byproducts into my Inventory just in case. Those were enough to serve as important physical evidence.
“Come to think of it, Youngest. Where did you get that? I was sure every last piece had been collected.”
“What?”
“You know. The imugi you defeated in Hubei...”
“Ahem. Ahem. Cough-cough-cough!”
I forced out a fit of coughing. Cheongpung, who had been listening beside us, rummaged through his robes.
“Benefactor. Would you like a sweetmeat? Sweetmeats are the best medicine for a cough.”
“...No. They’re the worst.”
“Okay.”
Since when were sweetmeats miracle medicine?
Denied a test subject, mad scientist Cheongpung looked dejected and put a sweetmeat in his own mouth. Jin Wikyung watched him and let out a quiet laugh.
“I understand. I won’t ask again.”
“Good. Thanks.”
I scratched my chin awkwardly. Jin Wikyung watched me for a long moment, then spoke.
“Sometimes I wonder whether you—our youngest—are the same child I knew.”
“I won’t ask you outright. Nor will I harbor any further doubts. But there is one wish I have never told you about.”
His voice remained gentle.
“When all this is over, and the time is right, I’d like to hear the stories you haven’t been able to tell me.”
The stories I haven’t been able to tell.
I repeated the words to myself.
When will that time come?
But if all this really did end, as Jin Wikyung said, and I was ready... maybe I would tell him myself. The secret I had never been able to share with anyone.
Maybe that day would come.
“...I understand.”
I gave him a bitter smile and nodded. At that exact moment, a voice called out.
“There you are, Fire Dragon Pavilion Master.”
Tap.
A dull sound rang out with the elderly voice. I turned my head and saw Song Ho, the Chief of the Hidden Shadow Pavilion of the Murim Alliance—the Thousand-Faced Fox.
“The meeting ended half an hour ago, yet you’re still here. Coincidence?”
I shook my head. Talking to Jin Wikyung was not the only reason I had stayed at the Murim Alliance.
“It must have been inevitable.”
“Inevitability, is it? Yes, I suppose so.”
Something flickered in those old, unreadable eyes. After a brief silence, the Thousand-Faced Fox spoke again.
“Come with me, Fire Dragon Pavilion Master. You know what this is about, don’t you?”
I did. I knew who wanted to see me, and why.
His next words turned my guess into certainty.
“The Alliance Leader is looking for you.”
Thud.
The door closed behind me with an unusually loud sound. Two people were already waiting in an office inside the Alliance Leader’s Hall.
“You’re here?”
After Jeok Cheongang’s flat question, Murim Alliance Leader Mae Jonghak gestured toward a seat.
“Sit down. The rest of you, wait outside for a moment.”
He was not speaking to me or the Thousand-Faced Fox, who had followed me straight into the office. He meant the others who had yet to show themselves.
Swish.
No sooner had Mae Jonghak spoken than several presences vanished like ghosts.
Even the secret guards said to remain at his side at all times had withdrawn. I sat in an empty chair.
“They’re incredibly skilled. I could barely sense them.”
“Most people who enter this room don’t notice them at all. It’s impressive that you did.”
“Even if they don’t know, wouldn’t they at least guess? It would be strange for someone as important as the Murim Alliance Leader to have no guards at all.”
“Ah. You have a point.”
Mae Jonghak scratched his chin like a young man my age, then looked at me. My face was reflected in his clear, deep eyes.
“First, I was impressed by what you said in the great conference hall.”
“I’m glad to hear it. I don’t know what the others thought.”
“They may not believe all of it, but they won’t dismiss it. I promise you.”

Even lightly spoken words carried different weight depending on who said them. And when the speaker was the Alliance Leader of the Murim Alliance, it was only natural for those words to carry tremendous authority.
That gives my argument more weight.
Things were going well. My expression must have relaxed, because Mae Jonghak smiled.
“You were worried.”
“I’d be lying if I said I wasn’t.”
“Since we’re on the subject, how certain are you of your claim?”
“Five out of ten. Fifty-fifty.”
The Thousand-Faced Fox’s face went rigid.
“Did you just say... five out of ten?”
“Yes. Is that lower than you expected?”
“Damn it, the opposite! You’re saying there’s a fifty-percent chance the world will be covered in monsters!”
There was a curse in his outburst, but no one cared about that now. Far from taking offense, I felt relieved.
Their reactions told me that, at the very least, the people gathered here had already accepted my claim as fact.
“What gives you that fifty percent?”
Mae Jonghak was still calm. I answered without hesitation.
“Everything I’ve seen and felt fighting Dark Heaven.”
Jeok Cheongang, who had been sipping strong liquor instead of tea, spoke up.
“You could be wrong.”
“I hope I am. They can curse me for the rest of my life if I am.”
I meant it. I would much rather be completely wrong. Maybe Dark Heaven would turn out to be nothing special, and no mutated monsters would ever appear.
If all it took to get a happy ending was for everyone to curse me, I’d take that deal.
But...
“It sounds insane, but it’s all true.”
“Damn it. This is driving me crazy.”
“Is it that hard to believe?”
“I don’t want to believe it. If it were anyone but you saying it, I wouldn’t.”
Where did that sudden burst of emotion come from? What am I supposed to do with this?
Thud.
But emotional or not, to hell with all that. Jeok Cheongang slammed his liquor bottle down and glared at me.
“Tell me it’s a lie instead. If you confess right now, I’ll let you off with three strikes from the Flame Divine Palm.”
“I swear on my balls, right here and now, that I’m not making this up. Also, three strikes from the Flame Divine Palm would kill me.”
“Whew.”
Jeok Cheongang let out a deep sigh and turned to Mae Jonghak and the Thousand-Faced Fox.
“This old man doesn’t want to believe it either, but it seems the punk is telling the truth. He’s sincere when he puts his balls on the line, at least.”
That was a strange standard for deciding whether something was true. Still, I seemed to have gotten my sincerity across.
As what I feared settled over the office, silence fell. Mae Jonghak broke it.
“I have one more question.”
“You can ask two.”
“No. One is enough.”
Swish.
Mae Jonghak crooked a finger. A large scroll flew out from among the bamboo slips piled behind him and unfurled across our table.
Rustle.
I looked at what was written on it—no, drawn—and muttered, “This is...”
“You are looking at exactly what you think you are. A complete map of the realm.”
It showed the geography and terrain across the realm, with place names marked as well. But it was larger than any map I had seen in Murim, and there was another difference.
“It even shows where the sects are.”
“It was made for the Murim Alliance. Now, tell me...”
Mae Jonghak’s calm voice reached my ears.
“Where do you think Dark Heaven will strike next?”
“I can’t be certain.”
“Who in this world can be certain of the future? A simple guess will do.”
A simple guess...
I remained silent, lost in thought. Then, suddenly, I raised my hand and pointed to one part of the map.
Tap.
“Here.”
The reactions were immediate.
Jeok Cheongang muttered a quiet curse. A sharp light flashed in the Thousand-Faced Fox’s eyes, while Mae Jonghak leaned his upper body toward me.
“Why there?”
“If what happened in Hubei happens again, Dark Heaven would have a hard time finding a better place.”
“You mean that ‘rift.’”
“Yes.”
“You’re certain the rift will open again—or rather, you suspect it will?”
“I think there’s every chance it will. What happened wasn’t a natural disaster. Dark Heaven planned it and made it happen.”
There can only be a first if there’s a second.

I alone had been able to glimpse the Water God Dragon’s memories, however briefly. I had no physical evidence I could offer with confidence, and I could not be certain. But there was a good chance Dark Heaven had its sights on that place.
I continued calmly.
“I don’t know what Dark Heaven is going to do right now. This may not be its next target. But at least one person must have already set out for that place.”
“The Southern Heaven Demon Empress.”
At the sound of the title, the countless bodies I had seen in Hubei flashed before my eyes. My fist clenched.
“That’s right. If it’s the Southern Heaven Demon Empress... she must have that place in mind.”
“Is that another simple guess?”
“A guess. One close to certainty.”
I could not be sure of anything. But a thought that had been haunting me for some time seemed more and more likely.
Mae Jonghak nodded quietly and looked to Song Ho.
“What do you think, Chief of the Hidden Shadow Pavilion?”
“I’ll add my voice to the Fire Dragon Pavilion Master’s.”
Song Ho answered at once, then continued.
“It has been more than seven days and nights since we sent a missive. With no reply yet, there’s a good chance something has already gone wrong.”
“I expected as much, but... that’s fast.”
“Yes. We could send the Outer Hall forces we selected in advance, but we risk arriving too late.”
A missive? Forces selected in advance?
The Thousand-Faced Fox read the question on my face.
“The Hidden Shadow Pavilion has eyes and ears throughout the realm. You weren’t the only one to make this guess.”
“...You had already been considering that place.”

“To be precise, we began considering it immediately after receiving a report on the circumstances surrounding what happened in Hubei Province. However, that strange phenomenon called a rift was something neither I nor anyone else in this Pavilion anticipated.”
I remembered something I had briefly forgotten. The elderly martial artist before me had been the head of the Hidden Shadow Pavilion forty years ago, and he still was.
And there was only one person in this room who could give orders to both of us.
“Fire Dragon Pavilion Master Jin Taekyung.”
Mae Jonghak’s voice rang through the office, heavier than usual.
Mae Jonghak, the great martial artist known as the Number One Sword Under Heaven and the man standing at the pinnacle of Murim today, stared at me with clear blue eyes.
“I’m giving you your first order.”
Whoosh!
A fierce wind rose with every step I took.
Ignoring the eyes of everyone around me, I even used my movement technique to hurry back to my residence. When I arrived, I flung open the door with all my strength.
Bang!
A familiar face came into view.
Hyuk Mujin had been lounging in the annex. He sprang to his feet, looked back and forth between me and the shattered door, and muttered,
“Welcome back... Wow. The owner is going to cry tears of blood. That door was replaced less than half an hour ago.”
I had no time to sympathize with the owner. Instead of greeting Mujin, I gave him an order.
“Summon everyone.”
“What?”
Hyuk Mujin stared at me, dumbfounded.
“What are you talking about all of a sudden? Wait, summon what?”
“The Fire Dragon Pavilion.”
“What?”
“It’s a mission. Right now.”
“Wait. Hold on! Captain, why all of a sudden? Where are we going?”
I answered the wide-eyed Hyuk Mujin in a low voice.
“Nanman.”
