“It has been more than seven days and nights since we sent a missive.
With no reply yet, there’s a good chance something has already gone wrong.”
“I expected as much, but... that’s fast.”
“Yes.
We could send the Outer Hall forces we selected in advance, but we risk arriving too late.”
A missive?
Forces selected in advance?
The Thousand-Faced Fox read the question on my face.
“The Hidden Shadow Pavilion has eyes and ears throughout the realm.
You weren’t the only one to make this guess.”
“...You had already been considering that place.”
“To be precise, we began considering it immediately after receiving a report on the circumstances surrounding what happened in Hubei Province.
However, that strange phenomenon called a rift was something neither I nor anyone else in this Pavilion anticipated.”
I remembered something I had briefly forgotten.
The elderly martial artist before me had been the head of the Hidden Shadow Pavilion forty years ago, and he still was.
And there was only one person in this room who could give orders to both of us.
“Fire Dragon Pavilion Master Jin Taekyung.”
Mae Jonghak’s voice rang through the office, heavier than usual.
Mae Jonghak, the great martial artist known as the Number One Sword Under Heaven and the man standing at the pinnacle of Murim today, stared at me with clear blue eyes.
“I’m giving you your first order.”
Whoosh!
A fierce wind rose with every step I took.
Ignoring the eyes of everyone around me, I even used my movement technique to hurry back to my residence.
When I arrived, I flung open the door with all my strength.
Bang!
A familiar face came into view.
Hyuk Mujin had been lounging in the annex.
He sprang to his feet, looked back and forth between me and the shattered door, and muttered,
“Welcome back...
Wow.
The owner is going to cry tears of blood.
That door was replaced less than half an hour ago.”
I had no time to sympathize with the owner.
Instead of greeting Mujin, I gave him an order.
“Summon everyone.”
“What?”
Hyuk Mujin stared at me, dumbfounded.
“What are you talking about all of a sudden?
Wait, summon what?”
“The Fire Dragon Pavilion.”
“What?”
“It’s a mission.
Right now.”
“Wait.
Hold on!
Captain, why all of a sudden?
Where are we going?”
I answered the wide-eyed Hyuk Mujin in a low voice.
“Nanman.”

chapters.title: Chapter 549
paragraphs: I wasn’t a general leading an army of thousands.
Even counting me, the Fire Dragon Pavilion had only six members. Half an hour was enough to get everyone in one place.
“Everyone, listen up.”

I offered no greeting or honorifics. Sensing something unusual in my abrupt command, all five turned their attention to me. Even Hyuk Mujin, who had gone to summon them, still had no idea what was going on.
I looked from one questioning face to the next, then began.
“To get straight to the point... I’ve been given a mission.”
There was nothing to leave out and nothing to add. I told them exactly what I knew, and the briefing took less than fifteen minutes.
Afterward, everyone fell silent, lost in thought. Then one of them spoke.
“So,” said a familiar, composed voice.
Sama Pyo, Young Sect Leader of the Black Dragon Demon Gate, looked at me.
“We’re heading to Nanman.”
I nodded, with one small correction.
“To the Nanman Beast Palace, to be precise.”
The Nanman Beast Palace was a mysterious sect said to tame countless animals, including spiritual creatures and venomous beasts, and practice martial arts modeled on their movements.
I couldn’t tell whether they were an animal welfare society or a bunch of animal abusers. One thing, though, was certain.
Honglan. No—the Southern Heaven Demon Empress would be salivating over that place.

If a second rift opened, Dark Heaven would be hard-pressed to find a better location than the Nanman Beast Palace. It was an animal kingdom, teeming with more spiritual creatures and venomous beasts than anywhere else under heaven.
Song Ilseom had been listening with his willow-leaf saber held against his chest. He muttered, “We’re in for a rough trip.”
He had good reason to think so.

Nanman, where the Beast Palace stood, was also called Yunnan in the Central Plains. It lay directly south of Sichuan and bordered Guizhou and Guangxi. Put like that, it sounded merely far away. But...
The problem is, Nanman’s terrain and climate are unbelievably fucked.

I’d heard it was sweltering hot, with jungles that went on forever. There wasn’t a decent road to be found. Instead, it had full-grown predators and venomous insects that treated humans like food delivery.
And that’s just what I’ve heard...
I couldn’t imagine what it was like in person. I was beginning to understand why Nanman was considered part of the Outer Lands, despite having a perfectly respectable place on maps of the realm.
Though from a modern perspective, it really is a foreign country.
In the modern world, was Yunnan Vietnam or Myanmar? It had to be somewhere around there, but my memory was hazy because I’d spent world geography class sleeping my ass off.
While I was trying to dredge it up, Hyuk Mujin shot his hand into the air.
“Captain, I have a question.”
“Go ahead.”
“Are we really going?”
“Would we be going fake?”
“It’s just... it sounds too dangerous.”
“So what? It’s always been dangerous.”
“...When you put it like that, I’ve got nothing to say.”
“Then shut up and pack.”
“When are we leaving?”
“Oh. Did I forget to mention that?”
That was important. The others must have been so focused on where we were going and why that it hadn’t occurred to them either.
I looked at each of them in turn and dropped the answer.
“Today. Right now.”
A ripple went through the group, especially Hyuk Mujin and Taishan, the Tiger Giant Child.
“You’re joking, right?”
“Do I look like I’m joking?”
“That’s impossible. What about clothes and supplies? We’d have to pack everything right now.”
“It’s possible. Since when have we worried about having every little necessity? Just bring some fasting pills.”
Huff! Huff!
What the hell? Was that Scorching Yang Qi?
Taishan blew an astonishingly hot breath through his nose and leaped to his feet.
“No! Taishan! Eating meat tonight!”
“Meat? Meat sounds good.”
I turned to Hyuk Mujin. “You heard him. Bring jerky too.”
“Jerky! Tastes bad!”
“...Just shut up and eat whatever the hell you get.”
The guy looked capable of chewing up a pair of chopsticks, and he was picky?
Sama Pyo caught the look I gave him and shrugged.
“Taishan. You little rascal.”
“L-Lord.”
“How long do you intend to carry on like this? If you keep throwing tantrums...”
“Taishan. Won’t do it. Forgive Taishan, Lord.”
The enormous man looked so dejected that I actually felt sorry for him.
I’ll leave Taishan to Sama Pyo from now on.
I turned to Song Ilseom, who was frowning.
“What? You’ve got a problem with it too?”
“Of course. We’re going to Nanman, of all places.”
He clicked his tongue.
“But I’ll act as though I don’t. Unfortunately, I’ve already taken a hefty advance, and I can’t afford to pay a penalty ten times that amount.”
“You’re much more straightforward than I expected. I like it.”
“When I make a contract, I honor it. If I didn’t, I’d never have earned the name Soul-Chasing Guest.”
He said it with quiet conviction and pride, then continued matter-of-factly.
“Of course, the final decision isn’t mine. It’s my employer’s. Isn’t that right?”
Naturally, he wasn’t asking me.
Ju Hwaran, the Dagger Hidden Flower, had been silent and deep in thought the whole time. At last, she spoke.
“I think you already know my answer. Don’t you?”
At the sound of her clear, gentle voice, I let out a quiet laugh. Song Ilseom sighed.
“I knew it. Damn it, Nanman.”
“I trust I don’t need to remind you of the terms of our contract, Great Hero Song.”
Leaving him to groan, Ju Hwaran turned her gaze on me.
My face was reflected in her dark blue eyes. They held a mysterious light. From this close, they looked almost...
“Great Hero Jin?”
“Ah, yes.”
What was that? Did I doze off for a second?
Her voice brought me back to my senses.
No. I can’t do that.
Not now. With what lay ahead, I needed to keep a clear head at all times.
I told myself that a few more times, pulled myself together, and spoke as calmly as I could.
“Good. There’s something I wanted to ask you. Specifically...”
“The fastest route to Nanman and what we’ll need? All right.”
“Pardon?”
“Was I wrong?”
“No. It’s not that.”
Quite the opposite. She’d guessed so precisely that she’d startled me.
What the hell? Can she read minds? Is that some kind of mind-reading technique?
I could only blink at her. Ju Hwaran smiled.
“There’s no need to be surprised. I’ve been thinking about what I can do to help.”
“Oh.”
“I’m officially a member of the Fire Dragon Pavilion now. As I said before, I ought to do my share.”
Tap. Tap-tap.
Her pale, rough fingers drummed steadily on the table, a reminder that she was a swordswoman too.
“First, as you said, Great Hero Jin, we should keep supplies to a minimum. We won’t need extra clothing, and two days’ worth of dry rations should be enough.”
“Dry rations? Please! Anything but that! Taishan will die!”
Ju Hwaran quickly added, “And jerky, of course.”
“What the hell is his guardian doing? Ah, Young Lady Ju, please go on.”
“Of course. Now...”
With the interruption dealt with, Ju Hwaran continued without a pause. She covered everything from the supplies we’d need to the fastest route to Nanman.

Fortunately, she had traveled there on an escort assignment several years ago. She also knew the terrain and hidden roads in various places from the records her grandfather, the Escort King, had left behind.
Even Song Ilseom, who had roamed the realm as a wandering martial artist since he was a snot-nosed kid, was surprised.
“There’s a road like that?”
Ju Hwaran nodded with confidence.
“Of course. According to my grandfather’s records, it’s definitely there.”
“I spent about a year there myself. But as far as I know...”
“According to my grandfather’s records, it’s definitely there.”
“Yes, I know. What I’m saying is—”
“My grandfather’s records.”
“Would you let me finish?”
“The Escort King.”
“...I believe you. I believe you, so please continue.”
And who was the Escort King? The legend among legends who had completed his legendary Ten-Thousand-Li Journey while a hundred thousand Demonic Cultists covered the realm.

Ju P. Hwaran had inherited the will of that very P-King. Like the Going Merry on open water, she sailed ahead without a hitch. Before half an hour had passed, she’d planned every leg of our route to Nanman.
“Whew. That’s everything for now. Any questions?”
Whoosh!
An arm thick enough to make me suspect it belonged to a Troll shot up.
“Yes? Ask away.”
Tiger Giant Child Taishan opened his mouth with a stiff expression.
“Taishan. Understood nothing after jerky.”
Which bastard brought a kid into a no-kids zone?
I glared at Sama Pyo.
“Hey, guardian.”
“My apologies.”
Smack.
“Mmph! Mmph!”
Sama Pyo clamped a hand over Taishan’s mouth at once, then gave Ju Hwaran a small nod.
“My apologies.”
“...It’s all right.”
Her tone was calm, but she could not hide the lowered voice that accompanied it. Given the circumstances, it could not be helped.
No, it was only natural.
Even if it was a political marriage, they were engaged.

Maybe those big-nosed Hollywood bastards, supposedly as cool as ice magic, could shrug off something like that. But the Korea I’d lived in and Murim were both full of Confucian girls and Confucian boys.
It was awkward even for me to watch. How much worse must it have been for Ju Hwaran?
And I don’t even know what happened between them.
The thought left me feeling strange. Suddenly, the fabric against my skin irritated me, as if someone I couldn’t see were pricking me over and over with a tiny, thin needle.
“Captain?”
“Hm?”
Hyuk Mujin’s voice broke through my thoughts. I didn’t need to turn my head to know the others were staring at me.
I pulled myself together and tried to sound casual.
“All right. We’ll follow the plan we’ve discussed. Minimal supplies. As for how long we have...”
Ju Hwaran answered when I looked at her.
“Half a shichen. Even allowing extra time, that should be enough. We need to arrange the horses and carriages without attracting attention.”
“Where should we gather?”
“Hmm. What do you think, Great Hero Jin?”

This wasn’t a public mission. We had to move as quickly as possible, but discreetly too. To slip away from this crowded area unnoticed, we would first have to split up and choose a second meeting point.
“Mount Daebyeol. We’ll meet there.”
“Good idea.”
Ju Hwaran and the others nodded at the answer I had settled on after careful thought.

chapters.title: Chapter 550
paragraphs: After everyone left, Hyuk Mujin hurried off to gather what we needed, leaving me alone. I spoke quietly.
“Quest Window Open.”
Ding.

System Quest Journey to Nanman Murim Alliance Leader Mae Jonghak has given the Fire Dragon Pavilion its first mission. You must now head to Nanman and respond proactively to whatever circumstances may arise. What lies ahead for you and the Fire Dragon Pavilion is unknown. Always remain alert and act with a flexible mindset. Grade: Peak Restriction: Jin Taekyung and Fire Dragon Pavilion members Mission: Enter Nanman (Incomplete) Reward: Linked Quest ??? Failure: Gain the Title Can't Go to Nanman Fame and Trust drop significantly.
The Journey to Nanman Quest had appeared when Mae Jonghak gave me the mission.
Judging by the description and mission field, the System wasn’t offering any useful hints this time.
There’s no time limit, either.
Not because we had plenty of time. Given how little we knew about what lay ahead, I didn’t think it was an overreaction to read it the other way.
I sighed quietly and closed the Quest Window.
If nothing happens, that’ll be a relief in its own way...
But if something did happen, it could spiral out of control. I would have to lead the Fire Dragon Pavilion, bring the situation under control quickly, and get everyone home safely.
I could barely look after myself, and now I was responsible for other people. The words Pavilion Master weighed on me more heavily than ever.
A voice abruptly slipped into my ear.
I turned to find Cheongpung standing before the half-destroyed door, a bundle in his hands, staring at me blankly.
“Benefactor, may I come in?”
“Anyone listening would think you always ask permission before coming in.”
When the door was intact, he’d barged in without so much as a knock. Now he was asking permission in front of the wreckage. I couldn’t believe him.
I let out a quiet laugh and waved him in.
“Just come in. I was going to see you anyway, so this works out.”
“I was going to come in whether you gave permission or not.”
The answer, of course, hadn’t come from Cheongpung.
I looked at Mungyeong, who had appeared like a ghost, and muttered, “I was talking to Cheongpung.”
“And I told you. I don’t need your permission.”
Mungyeong strolled into the annex and glanced at the cups on the table and the chairs left out of place.
“You had visitors. Six people in total, including you and Hyuk. One was a woman.”
“How did you know?”
“I can tell by looking.”
Cheongpung added innocently, “I saw the others leaving. I thought I should come when no one else was here.”
What the fuck?
Mungyeong met my suspicious stare with an expression that said What are you going to do about it?
“By looking,” he repeated.
“So when you said ‘by looking,’ you meant you literally saw them?”
“I could have worked out something this simple without seeing them.”
“Don’t stare off toward the mountains. There are so many buildings around here you can’t see any.”
“I can see your future instead. Say one more word, and I have a feeling this room will smell of blood.”
Damn old man. And he goes around pretending to be a medical apprentice.
I shuddered at the phony medical apprentice’s vicious behavior and turned to Cheongpung.
“So what brings you here?”
“I came to say goodbye.”
“What?”
Cheongpung scratched the back of his head and smiled.
“When you told me to go on ahead outside the Alliance Leader’s Hall, I had a feeling you’d be leaving soon, Benefactor. Hehe.”
I hadn’t told him, but he’d guessed.
After a moment’s hesitation, I nodded. “That’s right. I have a mission.”
“Ah! Where are you going?”
“Nanman.”
“Nan...man?”
Cheongpung’s eyes widened. Mungyeong thought for a moment, then murmured, “Nanman. The Beast Palace?”
“Yes.”
“That strange phenomenon. It must be because of the rift.”
“That’s right. If a second rift opens, Dark Heaven would have a hard time finding a better place for it.”
“It’s certainly possible. Nanman is far from the Central Plains, and the route is difficult. If the Nanman Beast Palace falls, chaos will spread from Yunnan like wildfire.”
I thought so too.
If Dark Heaven really was plotting something in Nanman and succeeded, the flames of war wouldn’t stop at Yunnan Province.
They’d spread to neighboring Guizhou and Guangxi—and to Sichuan, which took considerable damage in the last battle.
Guizhou and Guangxi were particularly vulnerable. Both provinces had fewer sects and martial artists than other regions, and those they had were weaker. The flames would spread faster there.
“Nanman, at a time like this,” Mungyeong said. “It’ll be a difficult journey.”
“If nothing happens, great. If something does... we’ll stop it, whatever it takes.”
“With only six of you?”
“A whole six.”
“I’ve heard one of them is a young, handsome Supreme Peak master taught by the Fire King and the Slaughter Saint. Ever heard of him?”
“No. I’ve certainly never heard anyone call him handsome.”
“Ah. Right.”
He cut me off without a moment’s hesitation.
Having put an end to my nonsense, Mungyeong turned to Cheongpung.
“I have heard another rumor, though. About someone mad for dumplings who’s latched onto a young medical apprentice and is learning martial arts by watching him.”
“Huh?”
What did I just hear?
It must have shown on my face. Mungyeong nodded.
“It’s probably exactly what you’re thinking.”
“Really?”
“It’s true.”

“If he’s threatening you, blink twice.”
“You little bastard...”
“Hehe. It’s all true, Benefactor.”
I studied Cheongpung, then shrugged. “I know. I was joking.”

To become stronger. To change himself to fit this world.
It had been more than a year.
I’d been on my way to an inn when some ragged young man had walked up and asked me for a single sweetmeat. Despite Hyuk Mujin’s protests, I gave him every one I had. That was how I met Cheongpung.
We’ve both changed a lot.

The Third Young Master of the Jin Family of Taiyuan, once called the family’s disgrace, had become a Supreme Peak master who shook Murim. And the young genius who loved martial arts and delighted in everything the world had to offer, large or small, had developed a firm resolve somewhere along the way.
You couldn’t see the change, but you could feel it. Only a handful of people close to Cheongpung, myself included, knew it was there.
Tap.
I reached out and patted his shoulder. His eyes went round.
“Benefactor?”
“Nothing. Just telling you to hang in there.”
He stared at me for a moment, then his eyes curved into crescents.
“I will. You too, Benefactor.”

“Come to think of it, I don’t see that hill.”
“That hill is staying in Henan. The rest of us are going without him.”
“Well, now I’ve seen everything. To think the Fire King would make that decision.”
“It’s embarrassing to say, but let’s call it the greater good. We need as many hands as we can get right now.”

But it’s time for me to stand on my own.
Jeok Cheongang’s arms were wide enough to shelter me, but I’d grown too quickly to stay in them. And with everything changing around us, we could no longer keep traveling together.
Could it be...?
A thought struck me, and I glanced out the window.
The faces passing along the main road were all unfamiliar, blurred together in the distance. The person I was waiting for never appeared.
Come on. That’s a little harsh.
He could at least have come to see my face before I left.

The words lingered on the tip of my tongue, then faded. I’d already said goodbye before leaving his office with my mission, but I couldn’t help feeling disappointed. Before I was a Hunter or a martial artist, I was a person.
“...I’ll see him again soon.”
“What was that?” Mungyeong asked.
“Nothing. Just talking to myself.”
I was about to look away from the window when a small baggage carriage came rattling toward the annex.
That would have been an ordinary sight anywhere, not just in Henan—if the man on the driver’s bench hadn’t been a disguised Peak master.
Song Ilseom.
Finally.
Ju Hwaran must have finished all the preparations within half a shichen, just as she had boasted, and sent a carriage that could leave Henan discreetly.
I could already sense Hyuk Mujin coming up the stairs.
Time to go?
I’d grown used to this annex. But it seemed I was fated to spend this life on the road.
I gave the place one last look, then turned to my visitors.
“I’d better get going before it gets any later. Thank you for coming to see me. You too, Cheongpung.”
Cheongpung hesitated, then thrust out the bundle he’d been holding all this time.
“This is for you, Benefactor.”
“What is it?”
“Dumplings. I bought them from the best shop in Henan. I wanted to eat them, but I thought of you and held back.”
Mungyeong added quietly, “He stuffed down at least five on the way here. That’s how much he held back.”
“Ah! Aah...”
I’d known what was in the bundle from the smell, but I was touched all the same. The missing five didn’t change that.
“Thanks. I’ll enjoy them. I’d better go.”
I laughed quietly, took the bundle, and turned away. Then a line of Sound Transmission reached my ear.
—Do you know? Everyone who has received my teachings up to now has died.
—So don’t die a pointless death. If you die in Nanman, all that I’ve put up with until now will have been for nothing.
What a terrifying way to show concern. But like the dumplings in my hands, his feelings had come through clearly.
I stood there and gave a small nod before immediately setting off.
Step.
It was a powerful stride that echoed unusually loudly.

Judging by the description and mission field, the System wasn’t offering any useful hints this time.
There’s no time limit, either.
Not because we had plenty of time.
Given how little we knew about what lay ahead, I didn’t think it was an overreaction to read it the other way.
I sighed quietly and closed the Quest Window.
If nothing happens, that’ll be a relief in its own way...

I would have to lead the Fire Dragon Pavilion, bring the situation under control quickly, and get everyone home safely.

A voice abruptly slipped into my ear.
I turned to find Cheongpung standing before the half-destroyed door, a bundle in his hands, staring at me blankly.
“Benefactor, may I come in?”
“Anyone listening would think you always ask permission before coming in.”
When the door was intact, he’d barged in without so much as a knock.
Now he was asking permission in front of the wreckage.
I couldn’t believe him.
I let out a quiet laugh and waved him in.
“Just come in.
I was going to see you anyway, so this works out.”
“I was going to come in whether you gave permission or not.”
The answer, of course, hadn’t come from Cheongpung.
I looked at Mungyeong, who had appeared like a ghost, and muttered, “I was talking to Cheongpung.”
“And I told you.
I don’t need your permission.”
Mungyeong strolled into the annex and glanced at the cups on the table and the chairs left out of place.
“You had visitors.
Six people in total, including you and Hyuk.
One was a woman.”
“How did you know?”
“I can tell by looking.”
Cheongpung added innocently, “I saw the others leaving.
I thought I should come when no one else was here.”
What the fuck?
Mungyeong met my suspicious stare with an expression that said What are you going to do about it?
“By looking,” he repeated.
“So when you said ‘by looking,’ you meant you literally saw them?”
“I could have worked out something this simple without seeing them.”
“Don’t stare off toward the mountains.
There are so many buildings around here you can’t see any.”
“I can see your future instead.
Say one more word, and I have a feeling this room will smell of blood.”
Damn old man.
And he goes around pretending to be a medical apprentice.
I shuddered at the phony medical apprentice’s vicious behavior and turned to Cheongpung.
“So what brings you here?”
“I came to say goodbye.”
“What?”
Cheongpung scratched the back of his head and smiled.
“When you told me to go on ahead outside the Alliance Leader’s Hall, I had a feeling you’d be leaving soon, Benefactor.
Hehe.”
I hadn’t told him, but he’d guessed.
After a moment’s hesitation, I nodded.
“That’s right.
I have a mission.”
“Ah!
Where are you going?”
“Nanman.”
“Nan...man?”
Cheongpung’s eyes widened.
Mungyeong thought for a moment, then murmured, “Nanman.
The Beast Palace?”
“Yes.”
“That strange phenomenon.
It must be because of the rift.”
“That’s right.
If a second rift opens, Dark Heaven would have a hard time finding a better place for it.”
“It’s certainly possible.
Nanman is far from the Central Plains, and the route is difficult.
If the Nanman Beast Palace falls, chaos will spread from Yunnan like wildfire.”
I thought so too.
If Dark Heaven really was plotting something in Nanman and succeeded, the flames of war wouldn’t stop at Yunnan Province.
They’d spread to neighboring Guizhou and Guangxi—and to Sichuan, which took considerable damage in the last battle.
Guizhou and Guangxi were particularly vulnerable.
Both provinces had fewer sects and martial artists than other regions, and those they had were weaker.
The flames would spread faster there.
“Nanman, at a time like this,” Mungyeong said.
“It’ll be a difficult journey.”
“If nothing happens, great.
If something does... we’ll stop it, whatever it takes.”
“With only six of you?”
“A whole six.”
“I’ve heard one of them is a young, handsome Supreme Peak master taught by the Fire King and the Slaughter Saint.
Ever heard of him?”
“No.
I’ve certainly never heard anyone call him handsome.”
“Ah.
Right.”
He cut me off without a moment’s hesitation.

About someone mad for dumplings who’s latched onto a young medical apprentice and is learning martial arts by watching him.”
